Harrisburg Jewish federation collapse leaves community rebuilding from the ground up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
00:31:30 UTC
09:31:30 KST

When the Jewish federation in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, laid off its entire support staff earlier this month, the move didn’t come as a surprise. Instead, it felt like an inevitable next step in an inexorable trajectory of decline that has unfolded in public over the course of months, upending the infrastructure that had long organized Jewish communal life in the state capital.
The slow-rolling collapse in Harrisburg, which has roughly 9,000 Jews in the city area, has included the closure of programs, the displacement of Jewish institutions, and the planned sale of the Alexander Grass Campus for Jewish Life, which was purchased by the federation for $4.5 million in 2022 and envisioned as a hub for Jewish life in central Pennsylvania.
The downfall has also featured an unusual intervention by Jewish Federations of North America, the umbrella organization for 141 local federations that usually work highly independently. JFNA dispatched a former federation leader to help the Harrisburg Federation make hard financial decisions as it became clear its situation was not sustainable.
“While well-intentioned, there were clearly mistakes made that have set back Jewish life in Harrisburg and caused distress and division,” JFNA’s president and CEO, Eric Fingerhut, wrote in a letter to the community in April, in which he called the local federation’s business model “not viable.”
At the time, Fingerhut expressed optimism that the situation could turn around, writing, “Despite all that has transpired in recent years, I am confident the members of the Greater Harrisburg community can come together to repair what has been broken and build a bright future.”
Optimism continues to be tested
Four months later, that optimism is being tested as Harrisburg’s Jewish residents have watched core functions of the local federation evaporate.
Gila Ogle, the head of the Silver Academy, a Jewish day school in Harrisburg, said there was a “deep desire to ensure a vibrant future for Jewish life in Harrisburg,” but lamented that there is no longer a local Jewish federation to support it.
“What people are saying is, ‘Well, now what’s our opportunity? How can we come together?’” she said.
The Silver Academy officially learned in June that it could no longer be housed in the Grass Campus, Ogle said. The school will open this fall in the educational wing of Beth El Temple, a Conservative synagogue in Harrisburg. The synagogue is also hosting senior programs previously operated by the JCC.
Ogle said the school had seen a small decline in enrollment over the past year, a trend she attributed to the “unsettlingness of the whole situation” for families.
“Families have a lot of concerns, and I think that’s fair,” Ogle said. “We’ve really done our best to communicate transparently and keep families looped in and part of the process, but it is hard.”
The Silver Academy was not the only institution housed on the Grass Campus that was hurt by the Harrisburg federation’s downfall.
When Rebecca Anzel first heard about the looming closure of her 3-year-old daughter’s preschool in April, she was “shocked and confused.” Her daughter attended the Brenner Family Early Learning Center, which shut down on May 1, just over a week after Anzel and other families were informed of its closing. The preschool has no plans for reopening.
“I was devastated for my daughter, because I was worried about what that would do for her development and progression,” Anzel said at the time.
Now, as the federation’s collapse enters its final stages, the institutions it once supported are beginning to chart a future without it.
“It wasn’t that the Harrisburg Jewish community failed; it was that the business construct, the model, was failing and was faulty,” said Marc Terrill, the former head of the Jewish Federation of Baltimore, whom the national organization dispatched to Harrisburg to help the local federation deal with its finances. “They recognized that this isn’t the end to Jewish life in Harrisburg. They want a reset in putting together a financial and organizational construct that is more similar to what the most thriving Jewish communities in North America have.”
The abrupt closure of the campus comes as Jewish institutions increasingly rethink the necessity of large physical hubs amid rising operational costs and shifting demographics. While closures on the scale of Harrisburg’s are rare, in 2022, the Jewish Federation of New Mexico collapsed following a spate of bitter legal and boardroom battles and a widening financial crisis.
For some in Harrisburg, the federation’s short-lived experiment with the 6.4-acre campus underscored the need to pursue a more flexible model of community building.
Terrill pointed to the purchase of the Grass Campus as the pivotal decision in the federation’s unraveling.
“What’s been called into question is the business model,” said Terrill. “That wrapped around a number of things, but really, the thing that was the large decision that became existential was the purchase of the Grass Campus.”
Rabbi Ariana Capptauber, the former leader of Beth El Temple and ex officio member of the Harrisburg federation’s board, said that she hoped the sale of the campus could serve as a turning point for the local Jewish community to reexamine how it organizes and sustains Jewish communal life.
If these developments serve as “a wake-up call” that lead to a more creative use of the community’s resources, Capptauber said, “then it could be really good.”
The financial strain surrounding the campus had been mounting for years.
While the federation had a net income of $2.9 million in 2023, according to public tax filings, in 2024, the organization operated at a $3.3 million deficit.
Sam Levine, a member of the federation’s transition committee, told The Burg in May that expenses to run the campus were “considerably higher than anticipated,” adding that the organization was also “depending on some donations, which unfortunately did not materialize.”
Since the property was purchased, the mortgage for the Alexander Grass Campus had risen to $9 million, Jeanette Krebs, a member of the federation’s transition committee, told Penn Live.
“We are continuing to work through a debt elimination strategy which includes monetizing real estate. Much remains to be seen regarding how things will turn out,” Krebs told JTA in an emailed statement. “I think there are several things that we can all agree on in Harrisburg. Most importantly, that there is a future, people care deeply, and we are committed to learning from our mistakes.”
Parents and other stakeholders said they learned little about the looming crisis before programs began shutting down. For Anzel, the lack of communication compounded the distress of losing her daughter’s preschool.
“We have not been given any sort of explanation at all other than major donors fell through, and so now we’re sort of left to try to fill in the blanks ourselves,” Anzel said.
Dana Ray, another parent at the Early Learning Center who organized a letter signed by parents calling on the federation to preserve the center, said that the prevailing sentiment among parents at the school had been “anger and sadness.”
Terrill said that there had also been a divide within the community over the initial move to the Grass Campus.
“There were some people that were very anti-campus,” Terrill said. “They thought that there was a different way to go, and ultimately a decision was made to go, and that had certain implications for it.”
Levine, the transition committee member, told local outlets that the federation is not planning to file for bankruptcy in hopes that local donations and the sale of the campus will help buoy the organization as it faces roughly $500,000 worth of debt on top of a large outstanding mortgage.
For Terrill, the “cautionary tale” of the collapse of the Harrisburg Federation was that there’s “no substitute for building community consensus, effective governance, and effective planning.”
The federation’s transition committee, which was announced by Fingerhut in April, has held roughly 200 conversations and listening sessions with community members as it charts what comes next.
“In a nutshell, the business plan, if you could call it that, was very reactionary,” Terrill said. “What they’re looking to put in place in response to lessons learned is an approach that’s quite different. That is linked to transparency, to financial discipline, to right-sizing, to community input.”
But as the Harrisburg federation begins selling off the campus that was intended to secure its future, local rabbis and parents say the federation’s unraveling has meant the loss of a central part of the local Jewish community’s infrastructure.
“It kind of makes me sad that now we’re sort of forced to leave this really, really lovely, vibrant Jewish community where she’s learning and actually retaining information about Judaism,” Anzel said of her daughter, who is now enrolled in a different preschool. “I don’t know where else she’s going to get that, and I’m really sad.”
The situation brings community together
Rabbi Tzvia Jasper, the senior rabbi of Temple Ohev Sholom, said that while many were “understandably upset” by the situation, it had also given way to a new sense of community.
“It’s certainly a really devastating time for our community, but in the same vein, I think there’s a lot of anticipation for what this new moment is going to bring,” Jasper said. “With any big change like this, comes the opportunity for creativity and innovation to sort of rethink and restructure the community and find out what the needs truly are.”

TikTok reaches $400 million settlement with US Justice Department over children’s privacy
TikTok has reached a $400 million settlement with the U.S. Department of Justice, ending a 2024 lawsuit alleging the company violated federal children’s privacy laws.
The DOJ said Friday that TikTok will pay $300 million immediately and another $100 million after an order vacates an earlier consent decree against its predecessor company, Musical.ly.
“This settlement is a major victory for American children and parents,” said U.S. Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward Jr. in a statement. “The Department’s priority is ensuring that children are protected online and that companies entrusted with their personal information meet their legal obligations. This resolution secures a substantial recovery while reinforcing the protections that families expect and deserve.”
Since the DOJ’s lawsuit in 2024, TikTok has undergone major changes, most notably in the ownership structure of its U.S. arm. In January, the social video platform company signed agreements with major investors including Oracle, Silver Lake and the Emirati investment firm MGX to form the new TikTok U.S. joint venture.
Representatives for TikTok did not immediately respond to a message for comment Friday.
The latest lawsuit focused on allegations that TikTok and its China-based parent company ByteDance violated a federal law that requires kid-oriented apps and websites to get parental consent before collecting personal information of children under 13. It also says the companies failed to honor requests from parents who wanted their children’s accounts deleted, and chose not to delete accounts even when the firms knew they belonged to kids under 13.
The settlement comes as social media companies face an avalanche of lawsuits over children’s safety and privacy and a growing number of countries are banning young kids and teens from social media apps. Instagram’s parent company, Meta Platforms, is currently on trial in federal court in Oakland, California, over allegations it violated the 1998 Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA, along with various state statutes.

Federal officials announce water cuts as Colorado River supplies continue to plunge
Federal officials announced sharp water cuts for the next two years on Friday for three Western states that rely on the imperiled Colorado River.
Under the Bureau of Reclamation’s plan, California, Nevada and Arizona will collectively reduce water use by 1.25 million acre-feet (about 1.54 billion cubic meters) annually during that period, with the possibility of larger cuts depending on conditions.
Arizona will see the biggest cuts, while states upstream — Colorado, Utah, Wyoming and New Mexico — do not face any for now.
Meanwhile neighboring Mexico will reduce its intake by 250,000 acre-feet (about 310 million cubic meters) under a U.S.-Mexico treaty.
“We’ve been in this 26-year prolonged drought period,” said Andrea Travnicek, the Interior Department’s assistant secretary for water and science. “We continue to see a prolonged drought in our future. So continuing to work together as a whole within the basin is going to be extremely important.”
The current rules governing the use of the river’s water are set to expire in October, and the seven states have been unable to reach a consensus on sharing it over the long term.
Last winter saw the worst snowpack on record for the Colorado River Basin, adding more stress on farmers, industry, wildlife and hydropower producers, as well as tens of millions of people who rely on the waterway, including in dozens of Native American tribes and in two Mexican states.
Years of overuse combined with drought and rising temperatures due to climate change have depleted the country’s two largest reservoirs, which are both fed by the Colorado. Lake Mead recently plummeted to its lowest level since it began filling nine decades ago, and Lake Powell did the same about a week later. Their combined storage is the lowest it has been in nearly seven decades.
Negotiators in Arizona thanked California and Nevada for their collaboration on sharing the cuts.
“For 2027 and 2028, the reductions that are now memorialized here will provide substantial stability for folks,” said Tom Buschatzke, Arizona Department of Water Resources director. “We’ll continue to negotiate and figure out how we’re going to operate over a longer-term period, which is what we all want.”
JB Hamby, California’s chief Colorado River negotiator, said the plan brings “some badly needed near-term certainty at a moment of extraordinary risk,” though he called it “a bridge, not a permanent solution.”
In Southern Nevada, Kyle Roerink, senior adviser at the conservation group Great Basin Water Network, said efforts to build a new airport and shopping malls and some public land sales have not progressed, reflecting the dire hydrology inked in the federal documents. Further cuts could slow real estate development in metro Las Vegas, he said.
“When the Hoover Dam, a symbol of American fortitude and American power, drops and loses its shine, it can be scary,” Roerink said. “But it can also pose itself as a great opportunity for us to prepare for the next hundred years in a meaningful way.”

Space is becoming the next battlefield, Iranian UN envoy warns of arms race - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
00:11:57 UTC
09:11:57 KST

The United States' efforts to weaponize space threaten to accelerate the proliferation of space weaponization, Ali Bahreini, the Islamic Republic’s ambassador and permanent representative to the UN in Geneva, told the Conference on Disarmament on August 10, Iran International reported Wednesday.
“The development of US military and offensive space capabilities could push other countries to develop counter-capabilities and intensify the arms race in space,” Ali Bahreini said.
The warning comes as Iran continues to expand its own capabilities in space.
A Jerusalem Post report from July detailed Iran’s efforts to expand its space program, including the development of space infrastructure, satellites, and satellite data and imagery services, citing Iranian Space Agency head Hassan Salarieh.
Salarieh said Iran plans to open new space facilities in the coming months, including the Chabahar launch site, while expanding its satellite network and developing its first domestically produced radar satellite.
Iran is also looking to pair satellite imagery with artificial intelligence for civilian uses, while developing communications satellites intended to strengthen the country’s infrastructure.
Israel makes space a top priority
Israel has also made it a priority to become a leading player in the growing competition over military capabilities in space.
In June, the Post’s Yonah Jeremy Bob reported that IDF Technology and Digital Chief Brig.-Gen. Yael Grosman said in an exclusive interview that the military was accelerating its push into space as it prepares for the challenges of future warfare.
“There is a data revolution. We need to bring data and capabilities that the IDF needs everywhere, not just regarding the war that was, but the war that will be," Grosman said. "This means we need to be organized differently.”
Grosman also said Israel understands it cannot compete effectively on future battlefields without developing robust space capabilities to support the IDF’s growing data and intelligence needs.
Referring to IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir’s five-year plan, unveiled in January and highlighting space as a priority, Grosman said, “The IDF chief said we cannot ignore space.
“We are receiving lots of energy and resources to pursue our interests in space since his declaration,” she continued.
Defense Minister Katz announces new space-based laser capabilities
Jeremy Bob also reported in June that Defense Minister Israel Katz said Israel was working to develop space-based lasers capable of carrying out attacks from above Earth.
“One of the central goals that the prime minister and I set is that we are recruiting the best minds,” Katz said in a briefing with military reporters. “As of today, no country has the ability to mount attacks in space. We must be the leading country in the world with this capability.”
“If we achieve this, it will ensure the advantage of deterrence, of the ability to attack, destroy, and all of the other matters, versus our enemies with large resources,” he added.
Israel has already made significant advances in laser technology, including the development of Iron Beam, a ground-based laser air-defense system. The Post has also witnessed and received briefings on an Elbit Systems project aimed at eventually enabling fighter jets to fire lasers.
One of Israel’s primary concerns is that Iran or another adversary could gain an advantage in the military space race and develop the ability to target Israeli satellites. Such capabilities could threaten Israel’s space-based intelligence and surveillance systems and reduce the IDF’s ability to monitor its enemies.
Amit Avitan and Yonah Jeremy Bob contributed to this report.

Pentagon fires editor-in-chief of US military newspaper, reportedly for opposing censorship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
00:11:46 UTC
09:11:46 KST

The editor-in-chief of the Stars and Stripes US military newspaper said Friday that he was being fired for insubordination, and a source familiar with the matter told Reuters the Pentagon had sent notices to the paper's leadership informing them they would be let go.
"According to the notice, I am being fired for stating in a CBS interview that hypothetical censorship of news for service members would constitute a personal red line," Erik Slavin said in a statement.
The source familiar with the matter, who was not authorized to speak publicly, said that Max Lederer, the long-time publisher of the newspaper who was set to retire at the end of September, was also removed.
In his email this week announcing his retirement, Lederer wrote that it was clear that the Pentagon had a new vision for the newspaper that was different from his own.
Lara Korte, who covered the Middle East for the newspaper, said on social media on Friday that she had also been fired. She said it was because she had told CBS News that she works for Stars and Stripes and not the Pentagon.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Stars and Stripes, which has published a newspaper continuously since World War Two and provides news to US troops around the world, receives funding from the Defense Department but has historically been editorially independent.
Military deputy to publisher recently appointed
The Pentagon recently appointed a military deputy to the publisher for the newspaper. In a post on X, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell quoted from an open letter the military deputy had written.
"We may never be able to have the same impact for our service members digitally that our paper had during World War II in a vastly different media environment, but I also believe that we can do better - that we must do better for our most important constituency, the men and women who make up the US Armed Forces," the letter said.
In his first administration, US President Donald Trump reversed the Pentagon's decision to shut down the newspaper altogether.
Press freedom advocates have criticized broader policy changes under the Trump administration that have limited journalists' access to the Pentagon, saying they suppressed freedom of speech.

Police raid two underground gambling establishments in Haifa, arrest 100 - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
00:11:28 UTC
09:11:28 KST

Israel Police arrested 100 gamblers in a raid on two underground gambling establishments in Haifa, N12 News reported Friday.
According to the report, gamblers were arrested around poker tables and slot machines, and approximately 15 computer hard drives, security cameras, cash, and various documents were found at the scene.
The gambling establishments were located on HaMekaleph Street in Haifa.
Administrative proceedings have begun to close the gambling locations, and those involved were detained for questioning at the Zvulon police station.
Back in June, police raided a Tel Aviv apartment that was allegedly being used to operate an illegal gambling establishment organized by Chinese foreign residents.
According to court filings, officers seized approximately NIS 1 million in cash, along with a Glock pistol and ammunition, foreign currency, gambling equipment, two laptops, and other weapons.
Eight Chinese foreign residents between the ages of 40 and 53 were arrested at the scene on suspicion of operating an illegal gambling establishment and other offenses.
Study points to rise in problem gambling after October 7
The raid came amid broader concerns over gambling in Israel. A Hebrew University study published last September found evidence that problematic gambling increased among some Israelis following the October 7 massacre and the war that followed.
Researchers compared gambling behavior recorded before October 7 with data collected in the months after the attack. They found that scores on the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI), which measures the extent of problematic gambling behavior, increased significantly among participants between April 2022 and March 2024.
The increase was particularly pronounced among men who had difficulty managing their emotions. Researchers found that participants who struggled with emotional regulation were more likely to develop gambling problems, suggesting that gambling may have become a coping mechanism for some Israelis dealing with the psychological effects of October 7 and the war.
Jerusalem Post Staff, Esther Davis, and Leo Feierberg Better contributed to this report.

Vladimir Putin visits remains of medieval Russian warrior prince uncovered in Kremlin cathedral
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
00:11:25 UTC
09:11:25 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin inspected on Thursday the open sarcophagus of medieval Russian warrior prince Dmitry Donskoy, whose remains were recently uncovered during restoration work at Moscow's Cathedral of the Archangel.
Lying within the Kremlin fortress, the Orthodox cathedral served as the burial site for more than 40 Russian tsars and princes down the centuries.
The body of Russian Grand Prince Donskoy was known to lie there, but its discovery last month in a crypt by the southern wall surprised historians, who had believed it was located elsewhere in the building.
The lid of Donskoy's sarcophagus was found split into four parts, the Institute of Archaeology of the Russian Academy of Sciences said in a Friday statement. After removing it, archaeologists found Donskoy's remains dusted with white stone chips and bits of mortar that had fallen through the cracks.
Donskoy's remains were clothed in ornate burial attire, according to the statement, with a well-preserved outer layer made of a dense fabric woven in a complex geometric pattern, and a less-well preserved inner layer, including a braided chord, fragments of the sleeve, collar, and a shoe.
"We conducted the research using a specialized method, without a full archaeological protocol," said Nikolai Makarov, Russian Academy of Sciences vice president and Institute of Archaeology director, according to Russian state-owned news outlet RIA Novosti. "Nothing was removed."
"Textile remains and several fragments of remains were collected for subsequent laboratory analysis, but the objective was to avoid damaging anything and preserve the prince's remains as they were found."
Putin lights candle for Donskoy
Putin lit a candle inside the frescoed cathedral and stood beside the white-stone sarcophagus as experts explained how they had identified the remains as those of the 14th-century prince, RIA reported.
The Russian Orthodox Church announced the discovery on Tuesday, saying the well-preserved remains were nearly complete and belonged to a man of just under 180 cm (5 feet 11 inches), who had died of natural causes between the ages of 35 and 45.
"All these characteristics correspond with written sources and historical testimony concerning the life and death of the grand prince," it said.
Overseer of first Kremlin's construction
Donskoy, who died in 1389 aged 39, ruled the principalities of Muscovy and Vladimir, which would later become the core of the Russian state.
A prominent figure in Russian history, Donskoy oversaw the construction of the first stone Kremlin fortress, increased the territory of Muscovy, and routed forces of the Mongol horde in a famous battle near the Don river in 1380.

Tape of Tupac murder suspect played in court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
00:08:38 UTC
09:08:38 KST

Jurors in a Las Vegas court have heard an audio recording of Duane Davis, aka ‘Keffe D’, who is on trial for the murder of US rapper Tupac Shakur, telling detectives that his late nephew Orlando Anderson pulled the trigger.
The hip-hop superstar was shot four times while stopped at a red light in a car with record company executive Suge Knight on the Las Vegas Strip on September 7, 1996. Shakur later succumbed to his wounds.
A tape dated 2008 was presented in Clark County District Court on Thursday and features detectives telling Davis that their discussion is confidential, and that “nothing you say today can be used against you.” The former senior figure in the South Side Compton Crips street gang is heard saying that he was in the car, together with Anderson and two other men, when it pulled up alongside Knight’s vehicle, in which Shakur was riding.
“If we would have been on my side, I would have blasted,” Davis tells the detectives, explaining that the target was, however, on the other side.
According to the tape, Davis passed his gun to Deandre ‘Big Dre’ Smith, who refused to shoot. Then Anderson, who was also in the back seat, allegedly took the weapon and opened fire.
Prosecutors believe it was indeed Anderson who fired the fatal shots to avenge being beaten by Shakur and his entourage a few hours earlier. However, the man was never charged and was fatally shot in an unrelated incident in 1998. The other two alleged accomplices are also dead.
Under Nevada law, Davis can still be prosecuted for murder even if he did not actually pull the trigger.
Prosecutors told the jurors that Davis, who was arrested in 2023, has made multiple public statements since 2008, in which he detailed his alleged role in Shakur’s murder, thus nullifying any agreement he may have had with law enforcement.
These include several interviews, as well as the 2019 memoir ‘Compton Street Legend’ that he co-authored.
Davis has pleaded not guilty to one count of murder with a deadly weapon with intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang. He now insists that he fabricated his previous admissions for money and notoriety.
His defense attorney similarly argued that the suspect was “full of c**p” when he publicly spoke about his supposed role in Shakur’s murder, and that no evidence has been presented to back up the prosecution’s allegations.

Malaysia’s Anwar traded reform for power. Now Umno wants it all
Back-to-back election losses and internal party rifts leave Malaysia’s prime minister clinging to a crumbling coalition
7-MIN READ7-MIN
 Listen
The roar from thousands of People’s Justice Party (PKR) delegates gathered at a grand convention centre in Melaka last weekend exuded all the confidence expected of a party leading Malaysia’s government.
The past three years have been the culmination of more than two decades of struggle for PKR, with it finally achieving its long-held goal of installing leader Anwar Ibrahim as prime minister and wielding the power to push through reforms.
Yet beneath the confident facade lurks a ruling party now scrambling to find its way.
PKR’s victory in the 2022 general election came at the cost of the very reforms it had promised to deliver, as Anwar had little choice but to negotiate compromises with erstwhile rivals, including former ruling party Umno, to steady his administration. Those trade-offs did not go unnoticed.
Anwar’s ruling Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition, of which PKR is a founding and principal member, has suffered a series of bruising defeats across three state elections since November – and whatever platform the prime minister gave a once-deflated Umno has turned the party into the greatest threat to his rule.
Staring down the possibility of being turfed out of Putrajaya after just one term, PKR members are left wondering how to reverse the trend, especially as surging Malay nationalist sentiment carries a resurgent Umno forward.

Wyndham Clark making it look easy at Bellerive and builds 1-shot lead in BMW Championship

Wyndham Clark making it look easy at Bellerive and builds 1-shot lead in BMW Championship
ST. LOUIS (AP) — Wyndham Clark made it through another bogey-free round at Bellerive on Friday, posting a second straight 6-under 64 to build a one-shot lead over Gary Woodland going into the weekend at the BMW Championship.
He might need to brace for another gallery supporting the other guy. Woodland grew up just under four hours away — one of the few times Missouri likes someone from Kansas — and is on the cusp of making it to the Tour Championship all while coping with side effects from his 2023 brain surgery.
Woodland birdied his last two holes, belting a 2-iron into the 608-yard 17th hole and stuffing a wedge to 8 feet on the 18th for a 65.
Clark, who endured a New York gallery pulling for Scottie Scheffler at the U.S. Open, has looked comfortable over 36 holes. His only real stress over a par came on the 10th hole Thursday when he had to make an 18-foot putt. He has no complaints about his game, and the two-time U.S. Open champion is tough when he starts heating up.
Clark was at 12-under 128. J.J. Spaun had a 66 on his 36th birthday and was two shots behind. All three of them are already assured of finishing in the top 30 in the FedEx Cup who advance to the FedEx Cup finale next week at East Lake in Atlanta.
Woodland hasn’t been there in six years, and while he has looked great for two days, there are reminders that keeping his heart rate and energy under control is a constant battle. After ripping his tee shot on the 18th, Woodland sat down.
“I’m tired,” he said after his round with a grin.
His post-round routine includes sitting in a cool, dark room and trying to reset his brain. Adding to the pressure is trying to move from No. 31 into East Lake.
“My focus right now is one day at a time. I don’t have that luxury to look ahead,” Woodland said. “I’ve got to focus on making sure I take care of myself right now. Tomorrow’s a new day, and hopefully I get some rest tonight and I’ll show up tomorrow and see how it comes.
“But I don’t have the luxury to look ahead anymore.”
Those who still have plenty of work ahead of them include Sungjae Im, who had a 64 and was three shots back. Im is at No. 40 as he tries to extend his streak of reaching the Tour Championship every season since he joined the PGA Tour in 2019.
Another shot behind at 8-under 132 were Patrick Cantlay (No. 43) with a 65 and Rocket Classic winner Michael Thorbjornsen (No. 41) with a 66.
Clark has no such concerns at No. 5 in the FedEx Cup, a product of winning the U.S. Open and blowing away the field in The CJ Cup Byron Nelson. Plus, he is helped by getting a harsh reminder to stick to golf.
Clark agreed to throw out the first pitch at a Detroit Tigers game when he was at the Rocket Classic. He warmed up about 20 minutes before his big moment, started feeling good, and decided to throw a little harder. His pitch was right down the middle.
It was the day after that got him.
“I woke up the next day and, oh my gosh, my arm was hurting,” he said. Clark went on to miss the cut at the Rocket Classic.
But he tied for fifth in the PGA Tour playoffs opener last week at the TPC Southwind, and he’s in prime position at the BMW Championship.
He can’t catch Scottie Scheffler at No. 1 — Scheffler already is assured the $23 million bonus for leading the points race going to East Lake — and anyone at the Tour Championship only has to win to capture the FedEx Cup.
Scheffler is still battling an illness. He spoke quietly and quickly, though at least he had something to talk about. He recovered from his 72 with a 65, though he actually lost ground on the lead because of Clark. Scheffler was nine shots behind.
Rory McIlroy managed only two birdies in his round of 69 and was five shots behind.
This is a big opportunity for Woodland, the 36-hole leader at Bellerive in the 2018 PGA Championship until he couldn’t keep up on the weekend. But he’s in control of golf ball, his speed and power is still evident and he’s been through enough to handle what’s in front of him.
“I feel very comfortable. It’s nice being close to home. It’s nice having so much support out here,” Woodland said. “The fans have been amazing. I’m definitely feeding off that energy for sure.”

Myanmar military bombing kills 14 at Buddhist monastery, opposition reports

A military air strike has killed 14 people at a Buddhist monastery in central Myanmar, an opposition group and a local resident have reported.
The attack occurred in Swel Le Oh village in Myaung township, about 75 kilometres (47 miles) west of Mandalay, Myanmar’s second-largest city, Nway Oo, a spokesperson for the Civil Defense and Security Organization of Myaung Township (CDSOM) said Friday.

- list 3 of 3China rejects US claim that Myanmar analyst wrongfully detained
A fighter jet bombed the village monastery’s compound, killing 14, including three women, and injuring 20 more, Nway Oo said.
More than 100 people were staying in and around the monastery for a weeklong retreat for Buddhist Lent, according to a local villager who anonymously told The Associated Press news agency that the plane had dropped two bombs on the village 15 minutes apart.
The villager confirmed CDSOM’s death toll of 14, and said his mother-in-law was killed in the attack.
BBC’s Burmese Service and local media outlets reported the death toll at between 10 and 14.
The military did not immediately comment on the strike, but has previously said it only attacks legitimate targets.
Myanmar has been embroiled in a near countrywide civil war since the army seized power from the elected government in February 2021. After the military government violently suppressed peaceful demonstrations, many opponents of military rule took up arms.
The forces fighting against the government are made up of a diverse array of ethnically or politically divided armed groups, some of which have existed for decades.
Aung San Suu Kyi, the 81-year-old Nobel Peace Prize winner and democracy campaigner who served as Myanmar’s state counsellor (a role equivalent to prime minister), has been detained since the military seized power in 2021. She was moved to house arrest in April.
The war has killed more than 100,000 people and displaced 5.2 million, according to the Washington-based Council on Foreign Relations.
Resistance forces and ethnic armies control an estimated 42 percent of the country, compared with the military government’s 21 percent.
Myaung township is in the Sagaing region, which is a stronghold of armed resistance against the military government.
The United Nations-established Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM) said in August that it observed a notable escalation in aerial attacks preceding the elections held in December and January, and that they have continued unabated afterwards.
Myanmar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs rejected the IIMM report, saying it only targets “terrorists” and that security forces exercise maximum restraint to avoid civilian harm.

Editor of US newspaper Stars and Stripes reportedly fired under Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
23:51:40 UTC
08:51:40 KST

Editor of US newspaper Stars and Stripes reportedly fired under Trump
Editor-in-chief Erik Slavin has suggested his firing was retaliation for speaking out about editorial independence.
The Pentagon has fired the editor-in-chief of the Stars and Stripes, a prominent United States military newspaper, as well as one of its top reporters.
Erik Slavin, the editor-in-chief, told The Associated Press (AP) news agency on Friday that he received a notice of separation, along with the newspaper’s Middle East reporter Lara Korte.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3USS Lincoln crisis: How it compares to past aircraft carrier deployments
- list 2 of 3Publisher of US military newspaper resigns over differences with government
- list 3 of 3Trump’s war on Stars and Stripes: Why has military newspaper chief quit?
Another notice was sent to Max Lederer, the paper’s longtime publisher, who had previously announced he would retire at the end of September.
Slavin credited the termination notices to the group’s decision to speak publicly about efforts to defend the editorial independence of the Stars and Stripes newspaper.
While the Pentagon provides funding for the Stars and Stripes, the newspaper has worked to maintain its ability to report independently on military matters.
“I stand by the principle that Stars and Stripes must remain editorially independent, as required by law and by the department’s own policies,” Slavin told AP.
He believes he was fired for “stating in a CBS interview that hypothetical censorship of news for service members would constitute a red line”.
The Stars and Stripes has had a storied history covering the US military. Founded in the 19th century, the paper gained prominence during World War II, when it became the official news outlet for soldiers deployed abroad.
But the firings on Friday come as the administration of President Donald Trump puts in place policies that civil rights advocates fear will curtail the freedom of the press.
Under Trump’s second term, for instance, the Pentagon has restricted journalists’ ability to access areas including its press office.
Trump has also launched lawsuits against a range of media outlets, including AP, The Wall Street Journal, the BBC and The New York Times, over coverage disagreements.
The Stars and Stripes had generated headlines in recent weeks from its coverage of the USS Abraham Lincoln, an aircraft carrier that has been on a record-long deployment since November.
The newspaper profiled cases where sailors on the ship expressed suicidal ideation or attempted to jump overboard. The Trump administration has dismissed such reports as overblown and “dishonest”.
But the pressure on the Stars and Stripes has been building for months.
In a statement in January, for instance, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced the department would be “returning Stars & Stripes to its original mission: reporting for our warfighters”.
He added that the Pentagon would intervene to “refocus its content away from woke distractions that syphon morale”.
“Stars & Stripes will be custom tailored to our warfighters. It will focus on warfighting, weapons systems, fitness, lethality, survivability, and ALL THINGS MILITARY,” Parnell wrote. “No more repurposed DC gossip columns; no more Associated Press reprints.”
Since then, the publication has seen several changes that have alarmed press freedom groups.
In April, for instance, the newspaper’s ombudsman, Jacqueline Smith, was fired. Her role had been to advocate for the newspaper’s ethics and independence.
A Pentagon spokesperson, Navy Captain William Urban, was also appointed as the publication’s deputy publisher, reportedly without Lederer’s advance knowledge.
In announcing his resignation, Lederer gestured to the changes under way. He wrote in a memo that his “philosophy of leadership” differed in “fundamental ways from the direction the leadership of the Department of Defense has for the organization”.
For his part, Urban published a letter to the Stars and Stripes website on Friday that praised the publication’s efforts during World War II to deliver “credible, editorially independent papers” to US service members.
But he criticised the current management for being “slow to embrace digital storytelling” and pledged “modernization”.
“My commitment is to leave Stripes a better organization than the one I joined two weeks ago,” Urban wrote.
Friday’s staffing shake-up, however, prompted a renewed outpouring of concern about the fate of the newspaper and its ability to report with independence.
Chris Vaccaro, the president of the Society of Professional Journalists, wrote in a statement on Thursday, “Stars and Stripes cannot fulfill its mission if its journalists or newsroom leaders must worry that independent reporting could bring retaliation from the officials they cover.
“Service members and their families deserve journalism that is produced in their interests — not journalism shaped to serve the interests of the Pentagon,” he added.
That same day, three Democratic senators — Richard Blumenthal, Elizabeth Warren and Jeanne Shaheen — sent a joint letter to Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, calling for answers about the “degradation” of the newspaper’s independence.
“For generations, American service members, particularly those stationed overseas and in combat zones, have relied on Stars and Stripes for credible and independent news,” they wrote.
“That trust depends on preserving a clear separation between independent journalism and the Department’s public affairs apparatus. At this critical moment of leadership transition, that independence must not be compromised.”

TikTok to pay $559m in 'one of the largest' child pivacy settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
23:51:07 UTC
08:51:07 KST

In short:
The US Department of Justice has announced a $559 million settlement with the video-sharing platform TikTok over concerns that it had violated children's online privacy.
The government claimed the platform improperly collected and kept minor users' data without parental permission.
The settlement comes as TikTok, alongside other social media platforms, faces increasing scrutiny around the world.
TikTok and parent company ByteDance have agreed to pay US$400 million ($559 million) to settle a lawsuit with the US Department of Justice over claims that the video-sharing platform violated federal children's privacy laws.
"Under the settlement, TikTok will pay $300 million immediately and an additional $100 million upon entry of an order vacating a prior consent decree entered against TikTok's predecessor, Musical.ly," the department said in a statement on Friday.
It is "one of the largest recoveries ever obtained" from a case involving the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), the statement continued.
COPPA bars websites from gathering the personal information of children younger than 13 without parental permission.
The Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission jointly sued TikTok in 2024, alleging that it had placed the safety of millions of children in jeopardy by collecting their personal data without parental permission.
They claimed that TikTok allowed children to use the app in addition to collecting and using personal data from young users without informing their parents.
Even accounts created in a "Kids Mode" intended for users younger than 13 gathered email addresses and other personal information, the suit claimed.
In 2019, the US filed a COPPA lawsuit against an app called Musical.ly, which ByteDance bought in 2017 and then merged into TikTok.
TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
According to America's ABC News report in May, the Trump administration was considering using the funds for ongoing "beautification" projects, which have included resurfacing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, renovating the White House ballroom and building an arch.
It was not immediately clear what the settlement funds will be used for.
Global crackdown
The US settlement comes amid a growing global crackdown on the video app.
Brussels began a probe into TikTok in 2024 under the Digital Services Act (DSA) — a content law and major weapon in the EU's boosted legal armory that it has deployed to rein in big tech in recent years.
In July, the European Union accused TikTok of failing to protect children through account settings that could expose them to risks like cyberbullying and predatory behaviour, putting the company at risk of a large fine.
The EU said minors' accounts should only be visible to those they have given permission to. Children aged 13 and over can use TikTok.
"A high level of protection should not be an opt-in; it should be the default," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement at that time.
Under the DSA, children's account settings have, by default, the strongest safety and security protections.
"TikTok's account settings fail to meet this standard, as they expose minors' accounts and content too widely," the EU said in its preliminary view.
Britain's communications regulator, Ofcom, also launched an investigation into TikTok in July.
The UK probe will look into whether TikTok is doing enough under UK law to protect children from harmful content.
"This investigation will seek to establish whether there are reasonable grounds to believe that TikTok has failed, or is failing, to comply with its legal obligations," Ofcom said in a statement.
It added that it would, in particular, look at TikTok's age-verification model.
In December 2025, Australia took a more radical approach by prohibiting children under 16 from using social media platforms.
The Australian government said this was prompted by increasing concerns about the effects of cyberbullying, sexual exploitation and self-harm content on the mental and physical wellbeing of children.
Under the new law, 10 of the biggest social media platforms could face fines of up to $50 million if they do not take "reasonable steps" to block Australian-based users younger than 16.
Since then, countries including the UK, Canada and Indonesia have announced similar plans.
The EU last month said it would also develop a policy for social media age restrictions in the 27-member bloc.
But the US — home to the companies that run the platforms — remains a hold-out. The legislation governing social media in the US is piecemeal and varies from state to state.
A bill for a national ban on under-13s using social media was introduced to the US Congress last June. It has backers on both sides of politics, but has so far failed to progress and may never go to a vote.
Instead, the House of Representatives last month passed an alternative law that would require platforms to "limit design features that encourage compulsive usage" and give parents some controls over their children's accounts.
But it is not clear if the bill will pass the Senate. Many advocates view it as too weak, and some fear it will stymie tougher state-based action.
The attorneys-general from 44 US states and territories have written to Congress to oppose the bill, saying it would "insulate big tech from appropriate oversight and accountability and imperil the young people it purports to protect".

‘She’s not afraid of anyone’: the prison writings of one of Hong Kong’s last outspoken democracy activists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
23:50:48 UTC
08:50:48 KST

In one essay written from prison, Chow Hang-tung worries about her hairstyle before court appearances because there are no combs or mirrors in her cell.
“In a place like prison, where anything that is personal is stripped away, it’s even more important to hold on to every means by which you can express yourself,” she writes. “Don’t let uniform, depersonalised rules, dress codes, schedules, and behavioural requirements grind down your edges and mould you into a ‘model citizen’”.
The vignette is everyday, almost mundane. It stands in contrast to Chow’s position as one of Hong Kong’s most outspoken dissidents, one who has been detained for nearly five years awaiting trial over her role in organising an annual vigil marking the Tiananmen Square massacre.
Her case represents one of the last high-profile national security trials to be heard in Hong Kong, as the national security law imposed by Beijing in 2020 extinguishes what was once one of the world’s most widely watched pro-democracy struggles.
On Friday, Chow and her co-defendant Lee Cheuk-yan were found guilty of “incitement to subversion” by a Hong Kong court. They face a maximum penalty of 10 years in jail when they are sentenced later in the year.
As the years pass by, the 41-year-old barrister has written screeds from behind bars on everything from the meaning of freedom to the legacy of the 1989 massacre, some of which have been translated by Brian Kern, a writer and human rights activist. Chow’s profile has only grown since she has been detained. She has won several human rights awards, and her social media profiles, which are managed on her behalf, are regularly updated with her writings from prison.
In another essay, she describes being handed a white Mickey Mouse t-shirt to wear in court because she is not allowed to wear clothing that carries the branding of her protest group, the Hong Kong Alliance.
“The Mickey Mouse t-shirt may seem innocent on the surface, but isn’t it still a prison uniform provided by the correctional facility? Even before the Alliance has been convicted, its clothes have already become contraband,” she writes.
While some writings are breezy and irreverent, many are deeply considered essays on defending civil rights in the face of a powerful and oppressive Chinese Communist party. As a highly regarded barrister who has been representing herself in court, she also dives into legal philosophy.
“She’s not afraid of anything or anyone,” said Kevin Yam, a Hong Kong lawyer who now lives in exile. “For a lot of us who are outside Hong Kong now and sometimes feel a bit dispirited by things, her example and her inspiration is a big factor in us not losing hope and keeping our spirits up.”
Wu Yangwei, Chow’s fiance, a Chinese activist better known by his pen name, Ye Du, said it was Chow’s interest in mainland Chinese struggles that first attracted him to her. “From the moment I met her… I felt that she was incredibly innocent, deeply compassionate, and deeply empathetic toward China’s democracy and human rights defense movements,” Wu said. He now lives under close police surveillance in Guangdong province.
‘A society that loses freedom of speech … loses its very soul’
Chow was arrested in September 2021 along with two other organisers of the now disbanded Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Democratic Movements of China.
The Hong Kong Alliance’s annual Tiananmen vigil, which attracted tens of thousands of Hongkongers each year, was banned in 2020 on the grounds of pandemic control.
Chow, along with Lee Cheuk-yan and Albert Ho, were charged with incitement to subversion under Hong Kong’s new sweeping national security law. Chow and Lee pleaded not guilty in their trial, which ended on 19 May, while Ho submitted a guilty plea, which could help him get a sentence reduction. All three have already served shorter sentences for other convictions relating to the vigil.
A Hong Kong government spokesperson said Lee and Chow were prosecuted “because they have overstepped the boundaries of lawful conduct by committing a criminal act of inciting subversion.” The spokesperson said law enforcement actions paid “no regard to their political stance, background or occupation.”
In an essay written this year for the 37th anniversary of the Tiananmen Square massacre, Chow wrote: “A society that loses its freedom of speech never just loses a few articles or events – it loses its very soul”.
“‘Power corrupts’ is a hackneyed phrase, but when the will to power permeates everything … the decline of society becomes inevitable. Conversely, resisting the encroachment of power, or even attempting to put it back in its cage, requires a steadfast return to fundamental human values.”
From studying earthquakes to fighting for human rights
Chow came late to the law. A straight-A student, she had originally gone to Cambridge University to study natural sciences, specialising in seismology. In 2008, a massive earthquake struck Sichuan province, killing 70,000 people. Chow travelled to the region to volunteer as a rescue worker. Friends of Chow said the experience had a profound impact on her. She believed that the failure of the Chinese government to adequately prepare for the natural disaster, and the handling of the aftermath, increased the death toll, said the friends.
Chow dropped out of her PhD programme and returned to Hong Kong to retrain as a barrister. She threw herself into Hong Kong’s then vibrant civil society, volunteering for human rights groups alongside her studies. It was while preparing a bail application for a fellow pro-democracy activist, Gwyneth Ho, that Chow was arrested in September 2021.
“She’s turned her scientific training to the Communist party, dissecting the party’s manoeuvres as clinically as she once looked at tectonic plates and seismic movements,” said Mark Clifford, the president of the Committee for Freedom in Hong Kong Foundation.
Since Chow has been in jail, her fiance Wu has communicated with her by letter, and occasionally through letters published in the newspaper Ming Pao, which is available in prison. In January last year, their correspondence was cut off, Wu said. “It’s even worse than mainland China. In mainland prisons, political prisoners can still communicate with family, but Hong Kong prisons now block even that,” he said.
Hong Kong’s correctional services department said that all prisoners, including Chow, can send and receive letters “subject to the requirements of the prison rules”. The department said Wu’s claim was “totally false and misleading”.
Wu said that Chow’s letters are “full of fighting spirit”. “I am not worried about her,” he said.
As far back as 2021, Chow published an essay about her refusal to plead guilty, writing: “A stubborn freak like me can only march on and fight my case till the end … Having a chance to exhaust oneself is better than living a purposeless life, isn’t it?”

Tesla recalls nearly 3m vehicles in China over door handle safety risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
23:48:16 UTC
08:48:16 KST

Tesla and other carmakers are making a major recall of more than 4m vehicles in China over safety concerns mostly related to their door handles, according to Chinese authorities on Friday.
The US carmaker is recalling about 2.98m China-made and imported EVs including Model 3, Model Y, Model X and Model S over door-handle safety risks, according to China’s state administration for market regulation.
The recall, the largest this year, according to Chinese media, comes a few months after Chinese authorities said in February that starting next year, it would be banning hidden car door handles commonly seen on Tesla electric vehicles and many Chinese EV models.
China has stepped up scrutiny recently on hidden, or flush, car door handles following EV accidents in the country and elsewhere, in which cars’ hidden electronic doors failed and trapped people inside.
In a notice on the Chinese regulator’s website, it cited safety risk. In extreme situations, such as a severe collision that causes an electrical system failure, the car handles could hinder car users from quickly opening the doors to escape, or prevent rescuers outside the car from gaining access, the notice said.
Some experts in the industry said the automakers should value safety over design.
Cui Dongshu, head of the China Passenger Car Association, called the recall “an inevitable step” in the development of the electric vehicle industry and said automakers were “being responsible” by moving toward a more reliable, “safety-first” approach.
“This represents, in part, the growing pains of the industry. At the same time, however, this move signifies a policy-driven safety upgrade,” said Cui.
Tesla will perform software updates on the vehicles to mitigate risks, the notice added.
Tesla did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday.
Xiaomi, the Beijing-based Chinese technology giant, is recalling more than 390,000 vehicles. Hangzhou-based Leapmotor is recalling over 370,000 cars. Other Chinese carmakers, including Geely and XPENG are also recalling some vehicles.
The reasons given in each case were similar, mostly relating to issues with their car door handles.
A report published by the People’s Daily, the official newspaper of China’s ruling Communist party, said the large-scale recall “serves as a unified safety upgrade” for existing vehicle models ahead of the 2027 implementation of the ban on hidden car door handles.
“For the rapidly evolving NEV (new energy vehicle) industry, competition should be defined not only by the pace of technological innovation but also by the high standards set for safety,” the newspaper said.

Russian Communist politician fined over Navalny photo, likely barring him from election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21

08:48:00 KST

Russian Communist politician fined over Navalny photo, likely barring him from election
A Russian court in Saratov fined former regional lawmaker Nikolai Bondarenko 1,000 rubles ($12) on Aug. 21 for allegedly displaying "extremist symbols" over a photograph of late Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny.
Bondarenko, a member of Russia’s Communist Party (KPRF) and a former deputy in the Saratov Oblast legislature, was charged under Article 20.3 of Russia’s Administrative Offenses Code, the legal aid project Slovo Zashchite reported.
The case concerned a 2024 post featuring a photograph of Navalny in the Telegram channel Nikolai Bondarenko Live. Bondarenko said he had no role in administering the channel.
Bondarenko had planned to run for Russia’s State Duma on the Communist Party ticket. A conviction under Article 20.3, however, can make a person ineligible to stand in elections for one year, potentially preventing him from participating in the upcoming parliamentary vote.
Bondarenko reportedly intends to appeal the decision. According to him, during the hearing, the defense pointed out that the content attributed to him had been edited and was not created by the politician himself. The appeal is expected in 10 days.
Russian authorities have used similar charges against other politicians ahead of the election.
Anti-war politician Boris Nadezhdin was fined 1,000 rubles in July under the same administrative article after a video linked from his social media accounts briefly showed a photograph of Navalny. The fine, together with his designation as a "foreign agent," prevented Nadezhdin from running in the parliamentary election.
Nadezhdin gained prominence in 2024 when he sought to challenge Russian President Vladimir Putin on an anti-war platform. He emerged as the only presidential hopeful openly campaigning against Russia’s war in Ukraine before election authorities barred him from the ballot after rejecting thousands of signatures submitted in support of his candidacy.
Russian authorities barred Nadezhdin from leaving the country in July. Nadezhdin later said the restriction disappeared from Russia’s state services portal on July 21, allowing him to go to Kazakhstan. On Aug. 3, he published a video from Paris announcing that he was outside the country.

In temporarily occupied Crimea, explosions rang out in Feodosia and Sevastopol during the night of August 22, while in Yevpatoria, drone debris fell onto a nine-story building. This was reported by the Telegram channel "Crimean Wind," citing local residents, UNN writes.

The debris fell onto a building at 146 Internatsionalna Street, after which a fire broke out on the second floor. Police cordoned off the scene, while a fragment of the drone remained on the road.
The distance from the building to the Moynaki substation is about 350 meters. The 110/35/10 kV substation is an important energy hub for the region. Reports that this substation had been hit had previously emerged during attacks on Crimea.
Explosions rang out in Feodosia and Sevastopol
In Feodosia, according to preliminary information from "Crimean Wind," an explosion occurred near Mount Pasha-Tepe, also known as Bald Mountain. A local resident reported that after the explosion, the red signal lights on the tower located there were no longer visible.
At 02:06 in Sevastopol, according to reports from the channel's subscribers, the gunfire of mobile fire groups and explosions could be heard. No air-raid alert was announced at the time.
At 01:32, "Crimean Wind" reported a powerful explosion in Feodosia. Later, local residents said they had heard a missile flying overhead before the explosion, while at around 01:56, ambulance or fire-engine sirens could be heard in the city.
Information about the causes of the explosions, the extent of the damage, and any possible casualties has not been officially confirmed.

Outrage in India over death of six-year-old ‘slapped’ by his teacher
Andhra Pradesh’s regional minister of education says he is taking legal action with a committee against those responsible.
Authorities in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh have launched an investigation after a six-year-old child collapsed and reportedly died after he was slapped by his teacher in a school classroom.
The incident was captured on a security camera in the school in Visakhapatnam in the southeast Indian state, before being shared widely by local media on Thursday. The incident is already causing an uproar around corporal punishment in the country.

“Our IT and Education Minister, Nara Lokesh Garu, has already formed a committee, and based on the committee’s report, we will definitely take action,” he said.

The Unlikely Place at the Center of China’s AI Boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
23:25:32 UTC
08:25:32 KST

Travel just two hours west of Beijing by train, and you’ll find yourself surrounded by the rolling grasslands and ancient cinder cones of Inner Mongolia. This vast, arid land has long been China’s capital of sheep farming and coal mining, but over the last few years, it has become the hottest place in the country to build an AI data center.
In Ulanqab, a city in Inner Mongolia home to about 1.5 million people, nearly 100 data centers have been opened or begun construction since 2016. Chinese companies have pledged to build projects with a combined estimated capacity of 12.5 gigawatts in the city, and over 70 percent of the total commitments have been announced in just the last year, making it one of the fastest growing compute clusters in Asia, according to a research note published by Goldman Sachs last week. For comparison, OpenAI’s $500 billion Stargate Project is set to reach only 10 gigawatts of total capacity when it’s complete.
Chinese companies are flocking to Ulanqab for a number of reasons. The city sits at high elevation on the Inner Mongolian Plateau and has long, cold winters, which means data centers there don’t need to use as much energy to stay cool. It’s also relatively close to Beijing, so data can be transmitted to China’s populous regions with minimum latency. But the most enticing factor has to do with costs. Electricity is cheaper in Inner Mongolia than almost anywhere else in China, driven by both the strong growth of wind and solar energy and an abundant supply of coal.
What’s also interesting is who is building these data centers. For the first time, Chinese AI companies are making big investments in their own infrastructure, rather than renting compute from cloud companies. DeepSeek is reportedly building a massive AI data center in Ulanqab, as are ByteDance, Alibaba, and Xiaohongshu. For years, Chinese AI companies have spent far less on building physical infrastructure than their American peers, despite developing a number of popular AI models with impressive capabilities. The Ulanqab data center boom signals that now they are finally starting to catch up.
There’s just one problem: finding enough water. Ulanqab is about as dry as Denver, getting only roughly 14 inches of rain each year. The local government is already struggling to provide enough water to meet resident demand—before many of the planned data center projects are even up and running. Last month, the local water company in Ulanqab was forced to turn off several waterworks for seven hours each night to mitigate peak demand. The data centers being built in the city will need less water in the winter—weather data from the local government of Ulanqab shows they only require additional water for cooling during two months out of the year—but all of the new infrastructure could still pose a significant environmental challenge for the region.
The Boonies
Inner Mongolia has been a data center hot spot for at least a decade, long before the current AI boom. Huawei built its first one in Ulanqab in 2016, and Apple followed suit three years later. In 2021, the area was designated as one of the main hubs of a country-wide government project dubbed “Eastern Data, Western Compute,” which aims to build data centers in the Western hinterlands of China.
There was one major drawback, though. Because they are located far from China’s populous eastern coast, these data centers initially faced high latency rates when transferring data to the majority of users. As a result, they were initially largely relegated to backup storage—until AI gave them a new purpose. “With the rise of AI in 2022, there was the realization that actually, those remote data centers could be well-utilized for model training,” says Andrew Stokols, a professor at Singapore Management University who studies China’s compute infrastructure. A training run for an AI model can take months and doesn’t require much real-time tinkering, so latency is less of an issue.
Relatively speaking, Ulanqab is also not really that far away. Inner Mongolia is much closer to Beijing and other major metropolitan areas in China than any Western data center hub is. And it’s now connected by two dedicated fiber optics cables built in 2017 and 2019 that reduced average latency speeds to less than five milliseconds, fast enough to support real-time data exchanges like AI inference.
Compared to other data center hubs in China, Ulanqab’s growth seems to have been driven more by commercial demand than government-led investment, Stokols says. As Chinese AI startups like DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, and Zhiput AI have begun attracting more paying users at home, they have found a viable business case for inference data centers close enough to serve them without excessive latency.
Powered by Renewables
The Chinese government is excited about building data centers in Inner Mongolia for another reason: It could help absorb the country’s excess capacity of renewable energy. Damien Ma, director of Carnegie China, a Singapore-based research center, says there’s a positive correlation between regions in China with the most unused renewable energy and those that have built the most data centers.
In the eyes of the government, this is a win-win strategy. China can catch up to pace of data center construction in the US, while simultaneously increasing demand for renewable energy. So it should come as no surprise that Envision, one of the largest Chinese manufacturers of wind turbines, announced this month that it will build a 2 gigawatt AI data center in Ulanqab connected directly to the company’s own clean power supply.
But experts caution that looking at AI data centers and renewable energy in China as a match made in heaven is too simple of a story. Stokols found in his research that about 37 percent of electricity in Ulanqab still comes from coal. And since data centers need to run around the clock, operators have traditionally favored fossil fuels for their reliability.
“Inner Mongolia has long been the West Virginia of China. It’s a coal country,” says Ma. The region is now racing to replace coal with wind and solar, but it remains unclear how fast that transition will happen or how far it will go. For now, the data centers popping up in China’s remote highlands will have to keep relying on coal to some extent. But “in three years, maybe it will be completely powered by renewables,” Ma says.
This is an edition of Zeyi Yang and Louise Matsakis’ Made in China newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

The PWHL’s Walter Cup championship trophy went missing while in transit to Alberta, league tells AP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
23:23:02 UTC
08:23:02 KST

Victoire’s PWHL championship Walter Cup trophy missing after not arriving in Alberta, AP source says
The Walter Cup is missing — or at least the version of the trophy that belongs to the Professional Women’s Hockey League champion Montreal Victoire, the league told The Associated Press on Friday.
Without going into detail, the PWHL issued a statement saying the trophy “did not arrive as expected at its latest stop,” and added “we are working closely with the shipping company to locate it.”
The trophy was supposed to be shipped to Lethbridge, Alberta, to spend the day with Victoire forward Dara Greig, a person with knowledge of the plans told the AP on the condition of anonymity because those details were not revealed by the league.
A container did arrive, but not the one the PWHL shipped with the trophy inside, a second person with knowledge of the details told the AP. The second person spoke on the condition of anonymity because those details have not been revealed by the league.
As a result, Greig wound up postponing her day with the trophy on Thursday, which included a public event at the city’s VisitLethbridge.com Arena.
It’s unclear where the Walter Cup was last seen. And unlike the NHL and the Stanley Cup, the PWHL does not have a person dedicated to travel with its trophy when it goes on the road to be with players.
The missing Walter Cup in question is not the one presented to teams on the ice upon winning the championship. That one is permanently housed at the Hockey Hall of Fame in Toronto.
The missing version is instead a version issued to championship-winning teams to keep.
The team’s version, like the original trophy, is made of sterling silver and designed by Tiffany & Co. It weighs about 35 pounds (16 kilograms) and measures about 24 inches (61 centimeters) in height and 13 inches (33 centimeters) wide.
The cup rests on two rods, resembling hockey sticks. On the cup are engraved six W’s representing the league’s six original franchises. The base of the cup represents a puck on which the championship teams are etched.
Montreal clinched the cup by defeating Ottawa in Game 4 of a best-of-five series in May to become the PWHL’s first Canadian team to win title. Minnesota won the PWHL’s first two championships.
The trophy is named after PWHL founder and primary financier Los Angeles Dodgers owner Mark Walter and his wife Kimbra.

TikTok agrees to pay $400m to settle US children’s privacy case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
23:13:00 UTC
08:13:00 KST

TikTok to pay $400m to settle US children's privacy case
August 22, 2026
TikTok and its Chinese parent company ByteDance agreed on Friday to pay $400 million (roughly €342 million) to resolve allegations by the US Justice Department that the platform violated children's online privacy laws.
"Under the settlement, TikTok will pay $300 million immediately and an additional $100 million upon entry of an order vacating a prior consent decree entered against TikTok's predecessor, Musical.ly," the department said in a statement.
It's "one of the largest recoveries ever obtained" from a case involving the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), a federal law which safeguards online privacy of minors, the statement added.
What was TikTok accused of?
The Justice Department and the Federal Trade Commission sued TikTok and ByteDance in 2024, alleging that the platform put children's privacy at risk.
The agencies accused TikTok of knowingly allowing children to use the platform and violating federal law that online services directed at children obtain parental consent before collecting their personal data.
The Justice Department said that since the lawsuit was filed, TikTok has "undergone significant changes to its ownership, management, compliance functions and privacy practices" concerning younger users.
TikTok parent company ByteDance sold off a majority stake of its US entity earlier this year in order to avoid a ban by the Trump administration.
TikTok did not immediately comment on the settlement.
TikTok faces growing global scrutiny
The settlement comes as TikTok, alongside other social media platforms, faces increasing pressure around the world.
In 2024, Brussels launched a probe into TikTok under the Digital Services Act (DSA) — a landmark regulation that the European Union has used to curb harmful practices by Big Tech in recent years.
The video-sharing platform risks a large fine after the EU accused TikTok in July of failing to protect children through account settings that can expose them to risks such as "unwanted contact, cyberbullying, or predatory behavior."
The United Kingdom also launched a probe into TikTok in July to investigate whether the app is doing enough under UK law to protect children from harmful content.

Draft officer fatally stabbed in Ukraine (VIDEO)

Draft officer fatally stabbed in Ukraine (VIDEO)
A conscription officer was fatally stabbed in western Ukraine on Friday night, marking the latest violent incident linked to the country’s controversial mobilization campaign during the conflict with Russia.
The altercation took place in the city of Lviv as a group of draft officials were conducting routine document checks, the regional police department said. A 25-year-old local man allegedly “attacked and stabbed” a 55-year-old officer, who succumbed to his injuries in an ambulance, it said.
A police officer accompanying the draft officials fired two shots, wounding the assailant in the leg. The suspect was hospitalized, police said, without providing details about what provoked the attack.
Video from the scene shows an agitated man standing across from an officer, separated by a half-open gate, as three onlookers stand nearby. The man suddenly rushes through the gate at the officer, who steps out of frame. A gunshot is heard, after which the man falls to the ground, apparently clutching his leg. As he sits up and continues to move, the officer shoots him again at close range. The man, however, continues to crawl toward the officer before getting to his feet and struggling with him out of frame.
У Львові чоловік поранив ножем працівника ТЦК, після чого поліцейський вистрілив у нападника. pic.twitter.com/fsFdJHAvf9
— Олег Володарський (@volodarskijo) August 21, 2026
Police released an image of the knife allegedly used by the suspect.
Men aged 25 to 55 are subject to mobilization in Ukraine, while those aged 23 to 60 are generally barred from leaving the country.
The mobilization campaign, dubbed ‘busification’, has involved conscription officers ambushing military-age men on the streets, at workplaces, and outside their homes and shoving them into vans. Officers have often used violence against those attempting to resist or flee. Family members and former recruits have alleged widespread abuse at enlistment offices and training camps, resulting in several deaths. The military maintains that most of the deaths were due to natural causes.
In multiple cases, family members and bystanders have clashed with officers in an effort to prevent recruits from being sent to the front line.

Occupier attacks against Palestinians in West Bank causing ‘serious’ damage to Israel: Report

Said Amori and Mohammad Sio
22 August 2026•Update: 22 August 2026
Israeli security officials have warned that attacks by occupiers against Palestinians in the West Bank are causing “serious” political damage to Israel, public broadcaster KAN reported Friday.
The officials, who were not identified, said soldiers are being forced to deal with incidents on the ground amid “a lack of firm law enforcement by police and other state authorities, in some cases without adequate tools or sufficient support.”
The attacks are “taking place before the eyes of the entire world and causing serious political damage to Israel,” said officials, adding that they are also placing a strain on Israeli forces deployed in the West Bank.
The criticism followed an occupier attack Friday on the West Bank town of Sa’ir, in Hebron province, that killed Karim Shalaldeh, 17, and wounded others.
The Israeli army said a group of occupiers entered the town on a “trip” without prior coordination with the military and claimed they came under stone-throwing by Palestinians, according to the broadcaster.
Earlier Friday, a medical source at the Al-Mizan Hospital in Hebron told Anadolu that Shalaldeh died from gunshot wounds.
His father, Sanad Shalaldeh, told Anadolu that 50 Israeli occupiers attacked the family’s home and that one of them shot his son at close range.
“My son was standing in front of the house and did nothing. When he asked them to move away, one of them shot him in the chest and killed him in cold blood,” he said.
The occupied West Bank has seen a rise in Israeli army incursions and occupiers’ attacks against Palestinians and their property since Israel launched its genocide in the Gaza Strip in October 2023, amid growing warnings about the consequences of continued violence.
