TALLINN – International-level chess will be on display at the Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech) assembly hall on Friday and Saturday, as the Tallinn Chess Festival’s two tournaments at the university are set to host over a hundred players from nearly 20 countries, including 16 international grandmasters.
The TalTech Rapid Tournament / Nomme Open will start on Friday at 4 p.m. in the assembly hall of TalTech's main building, followed by the 4th TalTech Blitz Tournament on Saturday at 11 a.m.
Notable players coming to Tallinn include Estonian chess legend Jaan Ehlvest, multiple-time German champion Daniel Fridman, one of Lithuania's top players Tomas Laurusas, Latvian grandmaster Arturs Neikšāns, and Polish chess legend Michał Krasenkow. Among the women, the most prominent participant is multiple-time US champion Anna Zatonskih. Additionally, three international grandmasters each will be arriving from Sweden and Slovakia.
According to the tournament's chief organizer, Urmas Randma, it is a good sign that many foreign players are returning to the Tallinn tournaments. "It seems they like Tallinn, Estonia, and our tournaments. For an organizer, this is a very good sign," Randma said.
Young players can compete in the same tournament as grandmasters
Alongside the international grandmasters, Estonian chess players and young talents are also invited to compete. Randma stated that one of the festival's goals is to give young players a chance to engage directly with top-level competitors.
"As an organizer, I especially encourage young chess enthusiasts to take an active part, because when else would they get the chance to play in the same tournament as grandmasters and other strong competitors?" Randma said.
In his view, chess is regaining popularity in Estonia. This is evident from the growing interest and participation in tournaments among both youths and adults.
TalTech's Vice-Rector for Entrepreneurship, Erik Puura, also sees a resurgence in chess popularity internationally. He notes that computers have not diminished interest in the game; instead, they enable fans to follow top tournaments in real time and analyze matches. The series "The Queen's Gambit" and popular chess content creators have also helped bring the game to a wider audience.
According to Puura, chess is also excellent training for leadership and decision-making. The game teaches players to formulate a plan, think several moves ahead, react to changing circumstances, and make timely decisions.
TalTech has an active chess club, led by Igor Krupenski and Nikita Rychagov, and the university is hosting international tournaments for the second consecutive year.
Randma considers the collaboration with TalTech crucial for Estonian chess. "In this distinguished university, Estonian chess has found a kindred spirit and a partner," he said. "I believe TalTech could definitely become one of Europe's leading universities for chess."
According to Randma, the most important aspect of the partnership is the shared desire to host high-level chess events. TalTech provides its main building's assembly hall for the tournaments, with both university staff and chess club members contributing to the organization.
Puura believes chess is a great fit for the environment of a technical university. "A new renaissance for chess has begun at TalTech as well," he said. "I am genuinely pleased that, as vice-rector, along with Rector Tiit Land, I have been able to support this endeavor for the second consecutive year."
The Tallinn Chess Festival will run from August 20 to 23 and will feature four international tournaments.
The festival kicks off on August 20 at 3 p.m. with an invitational handicap blitz tournament in the courtyard of the C’est La Vie cafe.
On August 21 at 4 p.m., the TalTech Rapid Tournament / Nomme Open will begin in the assembly hall of Tallinn University of Technology.
On August 22 at 11 a.m., the 4th TalTech Blitz Tournament will be held in the same location.
The festival's grand finale will take place on August 23 in the gaming hall on the third floor of T1 Venue.

Why Dubai may be vital to the Trump administration's economic war on Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:30:12 UTC
00:30:12 KST

Why Dubai may be vital to the Trump administration's economic war on Iran
President Trump threatened this week to wield an "unprecedented" level of economic warfare against Iran, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent vowed to "collapse" the Islamic Republic regime with the "toughest sanctions in history."
But the effectiveness of a bolstered economic campaign against Iran may rest largely on one close U.S. ally in the Persian Gulf, the United Arab Emirates.
The Emirati city of Dubai, the Middle East's leading financial center, has long had a reputation as a hub for opaque economic activity. For Iran in particular, the city has offered ways to skirt international sanctions and gain access to vital funds from its sale of oil to countries like China.
"About 80% of Iran's foreign currency exchange is done in Dubai. So Dubai has served as a major source for Iran's foreign currency," Miad Maleki, a former U.S. Treasury official, told CBS News on Friday.
"Iran's economy today runs based on this kind of scheme of selling oil to China and then either using the funds that are generated from sales of oil to China to pay for imports from China, but also moving some of those funds outside China to jurisdictions like UAE through exchange houses," he said.
Maleki said he believes "the UAE is going to be very instrumental in cutting off the regime's access to procuring foreign currencies, but also getting access to its reserves — so funds that it has generated from oil sales to China and are sitting in different banks."
He told CBS News that if new U.S. sanctions are really going to increase the pain for Iran's economy, the UAE will be a vital actor in helping to crack down on Iran's shadowy banking transactions.
U.S. targets shell companies
The U.S. Treasury has in recent weeks targeted a number of shell companies linked to the UAE. The Trump administration has said these shell companies act as a shadow banking system for the Iranian regime.
The targeted companies include Dubai-based HMS Trading FZE, which the Treasury said in a statement earlier this month, "plays a critical role in helping the Iranian regime retrieve revenue from its oil sales overseas, aiding some of Iran's most prominent exporters of petroleum."
In the Aug. 7 statement shared with CBS News, the Treasury also said Iran's Shahr Bank, which is linked to the country's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, had relied heavily on two Dubai-based currency exchange firms to launder money.
The Treasury said U.S. nationals were barred from doing business with all of the Dubai-based companies named in the Aug. 7 statement and that it was imposing secondary sanctions on foreign banks that knowingly do business with the Dubai-based shell companies.
A Trump administration official told CBS News on Friday that "crushing sanctions" and the U.S. naval blockade on Iran had crippled the country's economy and left it "completely broke."
"There are many levers the president can crank harder in the weeks and months ahead," the official said.
UAE says transactions "halted until further notice"
The UAE has said it is taking action against Iran. Afra Al Hameli, a spokesperson for the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs, announced in a social media post this week that, "all trade, commercial exchanges, and financial transactions with Iran have been halted until further notice."
"The UAE remains firmly committed to safeguarding the integrity of the international financial system," Al Hameli said.
A recent spate of new attacks by Iran may have been a motivating factor behind the Gulf state's announcement.
Emirati officials said not long before the announcement about the severed economic ties that Iran had launched two ballistic missiles at the UAE, triggering the country's air defenses for the first time in weeks, though authorities said the missiles fell into the sea.
UAE officials previously said Iran attacked an Abu Dhabi National Oil Company vessel on Saturday as it transited the Strait of Hormuz, the Reuters news agency reported, citing the state Emirates News Agency.
"I think the UAE and some of these other Gulf countries were getting a lot of hits, or they were feeling the economic effect of Iran's escalation and closure of the Strait of Hormuz. But they were kind of sitting on the side and watching how the U.S. administration might come to some kind of an agreement or deal with the regime to put an end to the hostility," Maleki said.
"I think the Emiratis are now realizing they can't just sit on the side, the economy can't continue to take this current situation … So, I think the Emiratis are becoming more proactive at this point."

VILNIUS - A five-day international air force exercise involving Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, dubbed Baltic Bikini 2026, concluded on Friday.
This year's drills were organised by the Latvian Air Force.
The active phase of the exercise took place in the Baltic Sea, simulating scenarios aircrews might face following an emergency water landing. Crews practised safely evacuating aircraft and deploying life-saving equipment.
The primary objective of the exercise is to improve individual and collective water survival skills, enhancing aircrew endurance after a ditching at sea until rescue arrives. Flight personnel are required to undergo such water survival training every three years.
The international Baltic Bikini exercises were launched in 1999 as part of a search and rescue cooperation agreement between Lithuania and Denmark.
Initial training took place in Denmark, where Baltic military personnel were provided with the knowledge and practical skills necessary to survive and escape after an emergency landing on water.
Since 2004, the Baltic states have organised the drills independently, rotating the host nation between Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia each year.
According to the military, Baltic Bikini strengthens cooperation and interoperability among military units of the Baltic states.

TALLINN - The Estonian Film Institute has joined CODA, a new international initiative for developing animation projects that supports the international co-development of animated films and series from their earliest stages.
The first call for applications is open until September 27.
CODA (Co-Development Animation Awards) is a collaborative project between Estonia, Croatia, Hungary, Kosovo, Poland, Slovakia, and Slovenia. Its aim is to encourage international cooperation in the animation sector from the very start of project development and to help establish strong partnerships.
It is often in the development phase that projects find it most difficult to secure funding, and CODA aims to fill this gap by supporting projects with potential for international distribution, festival circuits, or theatrical release.
Viola Salu, head of the production department at the Estonian Film Institute, said that Estonian animation has already gained significant international recognition, but this new initiative will help increase international cooperation from the development phase. "We invite Estonian producers to participate in the competition and hope that these development awards will lead to fruitful partnerships and noteworthy collaborative projects."
Independent producers from CODA member countries can participate in the first call for applications. A project must be a collaboration between at least two independent production companies operating in two different CODA member countries.
Grants will be awarded in four categories: €5,000 for the co-development of a short animation, €20,000 for a feature-length animated film, €20,000 for an animated series, and €20,000 for a special animated television project.
The total grant fund for 2026 is approximately €65,000. Applications can be submitted until September 27, 2026, and the recipients will be announced in November.
The Co-Development Animation Awards, announced at the 2025 Black Nights Film Festival, grew out of more than a decade of cooperation within the Central and Eastern European animation sector.
The program is organized by CEE Animation and the Slovenian Animated Film Association, with partners including the Estonian Film Institute, the Croatian Audiovisual Centre, the National Film Institute of Hungary, the Kosovo Cinematography Center, the Polish Animation Producers Association, the Slovak Film Institute, and the Slovenian Film Centre.

Specially Trained Police Officers Can Help People in Life-Threatening Conditions  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:30:04 UTC
00:30:04 KST

TALLINN - The Ministry of the Interior is sending a draft amendment to the Law Enforcement Act for a second round of coordination, which would grant police a clearer legal basis and obligation to provide first aid in cases of suspected life-threatening medical conditions.
If the bill becomes law, a police officer with additional medical training arriving at a traffic accident before paramedics will be able to apply first-aid techniques from their training to help stabilize the victim's condition.
According to the Minister of the Interior, the amendment centers on a very practical question: what can a police officer do during the critical minutes while an ambulance is on its way?
"If a police officer is the first to arrive at a traffic accident and finds a person in a life-threatening condition, they must have a clear right and obligation to act within the scope of their training. Sometimes, these first few minutes can determine whether a person's life can be saved," said Minister of the Interior Igor Taro. "This change does not turn police officers into doctors or paramedics. We are giving trained officers a clear legal framework to use the skills they already possess."
Currently, the police lack a clear legal basis to provide first aid in situations where a person's life-threatening health condition is not a result of the use of direct coercion by the police. However, police often arrive at the scene before paramedics. An ambulance typically takes 8-15 minutes to arrive, while in sparsely populated areas, this can extend to 25-30 minutes or more.
In 2025, the Police and Border Guard Board responded to incidents requiring first aid 161 times, and as of the end of July 2026, 92 times.
According to the bill, a police officer will provide aid in a suspected life-threatening medical situation within the limits of their training and capabilities, provided it does not interfere with their primary duties. An officer with additional medical training can use first-aid techniques corresponding to their training. Aid will be provided until an ambulance arrives or the person is handed over to a healthcare provider. The police will not become a healthcare provider under this change, and individuals will retain the right to refuse assistance.
Another significant change involves determining intoxication, which will become faster and more flexible. In the future, in addition to a doctor, other qualified healthcare professionals, such as nurses, can describe a person's condition. Forensic institutions will also be able to consider signs of intoxication documented by the police in their assessment. This will help reduce unnecessary trips and long waits at healthcare facilities, allowing police officers to return to their main duties more quickly.
In 2025, the Police and Border Guard Board used hospital services to determine intoxication 1,769 times, which took up a total of 6,432 police work hours. The amendment does not mean that police will determine intoxication themselves; the final assessment will still be made by a forensic institution, and individuals will retain the right to request a biological fluid test to detect substances.

It is every citizen's duty to affirm that Latvia existed, exists and will continue to exist - Kulbergs  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:30:03 UTC
00:30:03 KST

RIGA - It is every citizen's duty to affirm that Latvia existed, Latvia exists, and Latvia will continue to exist, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List) said during a ceremonial meeting of Saeima marking the 35th anniversary of the restoration of Latvia's de facto independence.
People now have the opportunity to become members of parliament, prime minister, tackle problems, and ensure well-being of the people. "But this is only thanks to the events that took place 35 years ago," said Kulbergs.
Latvia has two birthdays: the first, when the state was founded, and the second, when it regained its independence. Latvia was occupied, but the state did not legally cease to exist, Kulbergs emphasized. "It lived on in people's memories, in the Latvian language, in families, in songs, in the persistent efforts of Latvians in exile, and in international recognition," said Kulbergs.
On August 21, 1991, Latvia regained its de-facto independence, said Kulbergs, adding that he had personal memories of that day. His father was a member of the National Guard battalion tasked with guarding the Cabinet of Ministers. In his speech, Kulbergs recalled how he had wanted to go with his father at the time, but his mother would not let him. However, he did help his father make Molotov cocktails.
"At that time, my father instilled in me this patriotism, this fight for Latvia," said the prime minister.
Kulbergs also said that his father, who was the founder of Riga Motor Museum, had prepared Joseph Stalin's armored ZIS limousine - the best armored car in Latvia at the time - to rescue then-Prime Minister Ivars Godmanis or other top state officials from the OMON if necessary.
35 years ago, the people knew they wanted a free Latvia, but they did not know whether they would live to see the evening in a free country, said Kulbergs. At that time, an attempted coup was underway in Moscow, while in Riga, Soviet military forces had seized the television center, the radio building, the telephone exchange, and the Interior Ministry.
"While the Supreme Council was debating the text of the constitutional law, OMON armored personnel carriers were approaching the building; Latvia's freedom and people's lives were under real threat. Nevertheless, the Supreme Council did convene for a meeting, and 111 deputies voted for a free Latvia," said the prime minister.
On May 4, 1990, when the decision to restore Latvia's independence was made, military, financial, and administrative power still remained in Moscow's hands. "That is why we had to proceed step by step - wisely, with purpose, and without straying from the main goal," said Kulbergs.
On August 21, 1991, a decision was made that Latvia would be an independent and democratic state. At that time, the Supreme Council became a true parliament. "Our Saeima, our parliament, exists when, at a decisive moment, it takes responsibility and acts on behalf of the people," said Kulbergs.
"The people of Latvia regained freedom and independence through courage, perseverance, and the ability to say at a decisive moment: now or never! Today we bow our heads before the leaders of the National Awakening, the Popular Front, members of the Supreme Council, and defenders of the barricades," said Kulbergs.
Kulbergs truly believes that if Latvia were to be threatened today, everyone present at Saeima's ceremonial meeting would be able to make the right decisions at the decisive moment, protecting the country and the people.
Today, more clearly than in 1991, the nation is aware of the significance of Latvia's statehood, freedom, and independence. Russia's brutal war against Ukraine has also served as a harsh reminder of this. Latvia understands Ukraine very well, as the Latvian people have experienced the horrors of war, occupation, and repression brought about by Russian and Soviet rule, said Kulbergs.
"Every day, every moment, the people of Ukraine are proving with their blood what history has already taught us - that freedom is not something to be taken for granted," said Kulbergs.
He emphasized that the Latvian state is the foundation for security, prosperity, national development, language, and culture of the Latvian people. "We, Latvians, have our own country, but the state is not a service that someone guarantees to provide us. Alongside our many daily roles, we are, first and foremost, citizens of Latvia," said the prime minister.
However, people have not only rights but also duties toward Latvia, Kulbergs emphasized. A soldier defends his country through his willingness to sacrifice his life for the sake of the nation's freedom, a teacher - by passing on his knowledge to the next generation, medical professionals - by saving people's lives, businesspeople - by paying their taxes in good faith, contributing to Latvia's economic development, farmers - by cultivating Latvia's land and ensuring food security, and parents - by raising their children to be patriots of Latvia, he said.
As a father of three, Kulbergs is keenly aware that a nation begins with children, with whether they know their history and feel a sense of belonging to Latvia, and whether they see opportunities to study, work, and raise their own children here.
The prime minister emphasized that strong families are the foundation of Latvia's future. "Today, every government decision and every euro spent publicly must serve a single goal: a safe, strong, and prosperous Latvia," Kulbergs stated. He believes that it is the duty of Saeima and the government to strengthen national defense and internal security, as well as to build an economy capable of financing security and giving people confidence in the future.
Democracy is the ability and skill to listen to one another even when the parties disagree, and to debate "without tearing down our shared home." "It is a free press, independent courts, fair public administration, and responsible citizens," said Kulbergs, emphasizing that this was precisely the choice made on August 21, 1991.
"National identity, first and foremost, is the attitude of everyone here toward Latvia and its people. Do we do our work conscientiously and wholeheartedly? Are we able to prioritize the common good over short-term gain, honestly acknowledge our mistakes, and take the next step to ensure these mistakes are not repeated? It is our duty to demonstrate our love for our country through our work every day," the prime minister told the members of parliament.

Forecasts are still subject to change, so residents should stay up to date with the latest information.
A similar storm previously struck Latvia on July 29, 2024, when rescuers received a total of 1,500 calls regarding flood and storm damage. Rain damage is expected to be less severe this time, but the country as a whole may suffer greater losses due to the storm.
On Sunday, a gusty west wind will blow and there will be occasional rain; heavy rain and thunderstorms are expected in some areas. On Monday, the wind will die down, but brief showers will continue in many areas, with thunderstorms expected in some places.

====================================================================================================

A New Japanese Drydock and the Limits of Allied Cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:30:00 UTC
00:30:00 KST

On August 19, Nikkei Asia reported that Namura Shipbuilding was planning to construct a new drydock for large vessel construction by 2035. Japan is already the third-largest shipbuilder in the world, and the expansion carries significant security and economic implications for the region. It follows a renewed commitment by Japan to invest in the shipbuilding sector, amidst growing security concerns around lackluster U.S. capacity and the role allies like Japan can play in filling security gaps.
Yet the announcement highlights a more sobering reality regarding those prospects. Japanese shipyards are expanding because their current capacity is fully maxed out. Consequently, scaling future alliance cooperation may depend far less on reaching formal agreements than on securing available schedule space.
The new drydock would be located in Imari Bay, on the northwestern coast of Kyushu in Saga prefecture, and would be the first new large drydock in Japan since 2017. Upon completion, it will reportedly focus on construction of liquefied natural gas carriers.
The project follows a string of announcements from both the Japanese government and industry aimed at bolstering the sector. In November 2025, Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae designated 17 nationally important sectors – including shipbuilding – as sources of economic growth through public-private investments. The Japanese shipbuilding industry shared this ambition, outlining a roadmap aimed at doubling annual shipbuilding capacity to 18 million gross tons by around 2035. Both Japan’s government and industry are aiming to establish a 1 trillion yen ($6.5 billion) fund aimed at reviving Japanese shipbuilding.
This slew of investments is motivated by multiple factors. For one, the shipbuilding sector was an important driver of Japanese economic growth and industrialization in the post-World War II period. By shoring up the sector, Japan can maintain the industry’s industrial capacity, even though it has gradually lost market share over the past few decades.
Second, the importance of shipbuilding grows in the context of China’s globally dominant shipyards and growing naval presence. This is in marked contrast to the largely inadequate shipbuilding sector of the United States, whose naval shipyards are plagued by delays and maintenance bottlenecks. Meanwhile, supported by protectionist policies, U.S. commercial shipyards remain competitive solely within domestic markets, building ships at roughly quadruple the international price.
U.S. vessels have long conducted maintenance at U.S. bases in Japan. Discussions between Japanese and U.S. officials at the Defense Industrial Cooperation, Acquisition, and Sustainment forum have explored broadening repair operations for U.S. vessels in Japan beyond American bases. Such cooperation offers tangible benefits to both countries.
Utilizing Japanese shipyards for maintenance allows the U.S. to partly sidestep existing naval maintenance backlogs at home. Furthermore, eliminating the need for these vessels to travel to Guam or the U.S. mainland saves up to 17 days in transit.
On the other side, Japanese companies would commercially benefit from attracting the U.S. Navy as a customer. Japan would also enhance the availability of U.S. naval ships and minimize their time away from the operational environment, thereby strengthening regional deterrence in the Pacific.
The difficulty is that Japanese yards do not appear to have the spare capacity this cooperation would need. Namura’s decision to expand followed sustained high utilization at its existing Imari dock, and Tokyo’s own revitalization roadmap identifies capacity shortfall as the principal obstacle to doubling output. The bottleneck in expanding U.S. naval repair work in Japanese yards may be less a matter of interest than of capacity. It will be difficult for the U.S. Navy to schedule space already committed to paying commercial customers.
The new dock won’t relieve that pressure. It is not scheduled for completion until 2035, and its output is already planned: the facility is intended to construct LNG carriers.
Even if space at shipyards were available, major constraints remain. Namura is a commercial builder of bulk carriers and tankers, and conversion from commercial to naval work is not only a matter of scheduling. Yards require cleared workforces, familiarity with U.S. Navy specifications, and qualification processes that take time to establish. A workforce trained on LNG hulls cannot easily redirect to warship repair.
Labor in particular remains a major constraint for Japan. One estimate identified a shortfall of up to 12,000 workers nationwide in shipbuilding-related fields if the industry achieves its goal of doubling orders.
Japan is serious about underwriting shipyard expansion, but that won’t automatically translate into allied cooperation on maintenance. The capacity Japan is now building will not exist for another decade, and even then the dock time has already been claimed by commercial orders.
If both the United States and Japan want Japanese yards to service U.S. ships in a contingency, the arrangement has to be made before spots fill – and not after.

The event will be attended by Speaker of the Seimas Juozas Olekas, relatives of the deceased, signatories of the Act of Independence, the leadership of the Lithuanian Armed Forces and the Ministry of National Defence, and defenders of Lithuanian freedom. Sakalauskas will be remembered with a minute of silence and ceremonial volleys.
A football tournament named after Sakalauskas will be held at the Alytus Dainava Pro-Gymnasium stadium in one week's time.
Sakalauskas joined the National Defence Volunteer Service in January 1991 at the age of 27 and was an active participant in the resistance against Soviet aggression. On August 21, 1991, during the collapse of the coup in Moscow, a clash broke out between Lithuanian volunteers and Soviet special forces units near the Supreme Council-Reconstituent Seimas building. Sakalauskas was killed during the confrontation, while two other volunteers from the Alytus unit were wounded.
Posthumously, Sakalauskas was awarded the Order of the Cross of Vytis, First Class, as well as the January 13th Commemorative Medal and the Medal of the Founding Volunteers of the Lithuanian Army.

RIGA - On Thursday in Kraslava, border guards detected 28 individuals who had illegally crossed the state border through an underground tunnel from Belarus, the State Border Guard informed LETA.
While investigating the circumstances of the border crossing and conducting a thorough survey of the surrounding area, border guards in the territory under the jurisdiction of the Kaplava Border Guard Unit, 20 meters from the border, discovered an underground passage concealed beneath moss.
This is already the second case in which a tunnel has been used to illegally cross the state border into Latvia.
Twenty-eight people were returned to Belarus.

I am pleased that the State Border Guard has managed to discover two tunnels in a short period of time, while also deterring a significant number of illegal immigrants attempting to enter our country. Our goal remains unchanged: to reduce illegal immigration to zero," said Interior Minister Janis Dombrava (National Alliance).
As previously reported, in early August, border guards in the Skrudaliena county of the Augsdaugava municipality discovered 15 people who had illegally crossed the state border through a dug underground tunnel from Belarus.
To ensure the security of Latvia’s eastern border, Operation Vilkatis began on August 11. Its goal is to significantly reduce the number of illegal border crossings in eastern Latvia and prevent such incidents in the future.
Similarly, the State Border Guard, in cooperation with the State Police, has begun scanning soil layers along the Latvian-Belarusian border using a special radar to search for possible underground tunnels.
In Latvia, an enhanced border security regime remains in effect along the border with Belarus until the end of the year, implemented in response to the increased pressure of illegal migration originating from Belarus.

Omniva to install letterboxes in parcel machines  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:29:53 UTC
00:29:53 KST

TALLINN - The Estonian state-owned international technology and logistics group Omniva will begin installing letterboxes for standard letters in its parcel machines this September, aiming to make sending mail more convenient and modern, and to provide customers with a unified service point.
As part of this change, mail collection points will be relocated to the nearest parcel machine. For larger parcel machines, letters can be posted directly into an integrated letterbox. Separate mailboxes will be installed next to older or smaller machines.
"A large portion of people in Estonia regularly use parcel machines located along their daily routes, such as at shopping centers. By bringing mail-posting services to places people already frequent, we are making sending letters simpler and more visible. This gives the traditional postal service a more modern and convenient form," said Martti Kuldma, chairman of the board at Omniva.
Mail collection from the new letterboxes at parcel machines will occur six days a week, up from the current three, as the machines are serviced from Monday to Saturday due to high parcel volumes. This means letters may reach their recipients faster.
Relocating the letterboxes to parcel machines also helps reduce separate vehicle trips, thereby lowering transportation costs and the environmental impact.
Existing letterboxes that are not near a parcel machine will remain in their current locations. Letterboxes with very low usage, consistently receiving fewer than five letters per month, will be gradually removed.
The changes will be implemented gradually throughout this autumn. A sticker with information will be placed on the affected letterboxes at least 30 days before the change. The current locations of Omniva service points can always be found at https://www.omniva.ee/asukohad.
In 2025, people in Estonia sent 780,000 letters by mail. Of these, 515,000 were sent via letterboxes, a 26 percent decrease compared to 2024. Over the past decade, the volume of letters sent in Estonia has declined by approximately 80 percent.

Latvia resumes naming firms trading with Russia or Belarus after nearly three years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:28:52 UTC
00:28:52 KST

Latvia has resumed publishing monthly lists of locally registered companies trading goods with Russia or Belarus after a nearly three-year pause, public broadcaster LSM reported on 20 August 2026.
Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs has pledged to sever its remaining economic ties with Russia and Belarus, but substantial trade remains legal because EU sanctions are not a full embargo. The monthly register makes that commerce visible by identifying the companies involved.
The Central Statistical Bureau, Latvia's national statistics agency, published the names of 171 companies for July. A subsequent analysis by Latvian news agency LETA found that more than two-thirds operated in logistics, food and agriculture, or medicine.
The disclosure is, in effect, a form of naming and shaming. Yet the statistics bureau stopped publishing a similar list in autumn 2023 because names without transaction details could not support objective conclusions. The register is not a sanctions blacklist, and inclusion does not indicate a sanctions violation.
Under an amendment adopted on 18 June 2026, Latvia’s tax authority must send the data to the statistics bureau each month. The change also lifted tax-confidentiality rules that had kept company names private, LSM reported.
The explanatory note accompanying the law said disclosure was intended to support Ukraine. The amendment's authors argued that Latvian companies should not contribute to Russian and Belarusian state revenues while Russia’s invasion continues, according to LSM.
Latvia seeks to cut its remaining trade
The Prime Minister said in June that Latvia must sever its remaining economic ties with Russia and Belarus. However, he indicated that pharmaceutical exporters would likely be exempted on national-security grounds.
Latvia’s exports to Russia and Belarus each fell only about 7% in 2025, while imports from Russia plunged by more than two-thirds, according to official data cited by Euromaidan Press.
EU sanctions do not prohibit all trade
The EU renewed its economic sanctions on Russia through July 2027, preserving restrictions on trade, finance, and energy, as well as on goods and technology with both civilian and military uses, Euromaidan Press reported in June.
The Council of the EU says its trade restrictions exclude health, pharmaceutical, food, and agricultural products to avoid harming Russian civilians. Those exclusions allow EU companies to continue lawful trade with Russia even while other parts of its economy remain under sanctions over the invasion of Ukraine.

Uninhabitable Gaza shelters, Yemen war warnings, and record aid worker deaths: The Cheat Sheet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:26:05 UTC
00:26:05 KST

Share & more
Our editors’ weekly take on humanitarian news, trends, and developments from around the globe.
On our radar
Gaza’s critical shelter crisis
Four out of five households in the Gaza Strip are facing critical or catastrophic living conditions in their current shelters, according to a new report from the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC). Two thirds of households are living in makeshift shelters or tents that are not fit for long-term habitation; 89% reported rodents inside their shelters; 79% reported the presence of mosquitos, ticks, or lice; and 71% said they were affected by flooding during last winter’s rains. Due to Israeli restrictions and funding gaps, only 10% of households received shelter aid in the month before the survey was carried out. The report paints a damning picture of the consequences of Israel’s continued obstruction of aid efforts and stalled progress on reconstruction nearly a year after Israel and Hamas signed a ceasefire last October. Since then, Israel has continued to carry out attacks throughout Gaza, killing more than 1,200 people. Israeli troops are still deployed in nearly 70% of the enclave, where the vast majority of Palestinians are barred from entering. And Israel is still blocking the entry of critical humanitarian supplies, including materials needed for shelter, while reconstruction plans by the US-led Board of Peace have failed to get off the ground.
Yemen heads in a dangerous direction
Fighting is spreading in Yemen on front lines new and old, threatening to rekindle a war that never really ended but has been much quieter since a 2022 truce. This time around, the sides are more or less the same but the violence itself is different, with ground combat largely replaced by drones and long-range missiles. The impetus for the conflict has changed somewhat too, with Saudi Arabia arming its allies on the ground and stepping back into the fray following the Houthi rebels’ decision to support Iran in its war with the US by blockading Saudi shipping. The Houthis, meanwhile, have seized the opportunity to mobilise and extract concessions from the Yemeni government and its Saudi allies. As ever, the stakes are high. Yemen is already an incredibly dangerous place for local aid workers and remains one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world. Attacks on ports and airports are a particularly worrying sign in a country that depends heavily on imports for its food supply.
Syrian air base bombing a sign of rising Israel-Türkiye tensions
Israel bombed an air base in northwest Syria on 18 August, bringing into sharp relief the simmering rivalry between Israel and Türkiye. The attack reportedly came shortly after a Turkish delegation visited the Abu Duhur base in Idlib. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a statement that Israel had attacked the base because Syria was on the verge of breaching the agreed “status quo in security matters” by allowing in Turkish troops. Turkish officials condemned the Israeli bombing and seemed to deny it was planning to deploy at Abu Duhur, which it has reportedly been rebuilding. The two countries are increasingly at odds over each other’s regional presence and power, sometimes out in the open. A campaign billboard for Netanyahu’s Likud party, for example, places Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan alongside the leaders of Iran, Hezbollah, and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (the last of whom is clearly the odd man out, more on that here). “They want Netanyahu to lose,” it says. “Don’t let them win.”
The wider cost of a $50 million JNIM ransom in Mali
A recent UN report highlights how ransom payments can aid JNIM’s war chest in Mali. The al-Qaeda-linked Sahelian group received roughly $50 million from the United Arab Emirates last year for kidnapped nationals, and then spent much of it on financing a massive offensive in April that saw fighters attack Bamako, and assassinate Defence Minister Sadio Camara. Kidnappings in Mali usually target locals, and are often less about money-raising than enforcing JNIM’s rule by punishing dissenters as the group expands territory. Still, high-profile kidnappings of foreign nationals increased significantly last year, boosting JNIM’s revenues, which are otherwise mostly derived from taxing areas it controls and influences. The eye-watering UAE payment has attracted plenty of attention and is reportedly a record ransom, but tens of millions of dollars, mostly from European states with captured nationals, have also flowed to jihadists in Mali since the early 2000s.
Colombia, Venezuela earthquakes threaten access to education
While aid for the displaced continues to arrive in Colombia and Venezuela, it remains unclear how longer-term effects will be addressed, particularly their impact on children’s education. In Colombia, where 319 people were reported dead as of 20 August, nearly 800 schools were affected, leaving 75,000 children without classrooms. More than 200 are in Chocó, a geographically isolated and historically neglected department. President Abelardo de la Espriella announced remote education plans, but poor internet access makes them largely impractical. In Venezuela, the 24 June earthquakes that killed more than 6,400 people have compounded infrastructure and teacher shortages. In La Guaira alone, 115 schools were affected, 14 collapsing completely. Some teachers have started using improvised classrooms, while extra concerns remain for those left disabled by the quakes and over the lack of psychosocial support. For more, read this news feature from Colombia and this in-depth analysis from Venezuela.
Two deadliest years in a row for aid workers
World Humanitarian Day, which recognises aid workers and calls for their protection, typically comes with grim statistics about the dangers they face, and sadly this year’s commemoration on 19 August was no different. The latest Aid Worker Security Report found that violence against humanitarian personnel rose again last year, with Gaza and Sudan the two places most affected. Fatalities did fall slightly from 2024, but the number of kidnappings and serious injuries pushed overall violence higher than before. As ever, national staff make up the overwhelming majority of those affected, yet a recent report from the Humanitarian Advisory Group’s flagship research programme finds that they still have less access to resources and protections than international personnel. One case in point is Yemen, where dozens of local UN staff have been detained by the Houthis for two years and now face death sentences. In a piece we published this week, three authors sharply criticise the UN’s response, and argue that those detained deserve far more than statements of concern. Read the full piece – timed for World Humanitarian Day – by clicking on our weekend read below.
Weekend read
And finally…
Influencing public opinion an age of genocide and AI
How much does it cost to influence the answers AI large language models (LLMs) like Chat GPT spit out when prompted with certain questions? Apparently as little as $100,000. That’s how much the Israel Government Public Advertising Agency has spent on a recent campaign to “educate the US public regarding Israel”. At least some of that money has gone to the creation of a dubious think tank called the Hanover Institute of Public Policy, which is pumping out articles with headlines that appear designed to be used as “training” material for LLMs, Politico recently reported. The articles have headlines like “Is Anti-Zionism a Fig Leaf for Antisemitism?”, “Who Is the Aggressor in the Israel-Palestine Conflict?”, and “Is the IDF the World’s Most Moral Army?” Tests run by Politico showed that Chat GPT and Preplexity, another AI chatbot, both cited the Hanover Institute’s papers in response to neutrally worded questions. Beyond Israel, the implications in terms of the ability of wealthy and powerful countries, corporations, and individuals to influence the responses produced by the LLMs are also concerning – especially as more and more people rely on chatbots as sources of information.

West Nile virus reported in 12 European countries: EU health agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:25:00 UTC
00:25:00 KST

West Nile virus reported in 12 European countries: EU health agency
- Twelve European countries have reported local West Nile virus cases this year, with Italy and Greece having the highest numbers, totaling 99 affected regions.
- The EU health agency urges stronger mosquito control, highlighting the need for cooperation, monitoring, community engagement, and environmentally safe solutions.
- No vaccines or specific treatments exist; care focuses on symptom management, while invasive mosquito species continue to spread, increasing transmission risk across Europe.
AI generated
STOCKHOLM – Twelve countries in Europe have reported locally acquired cases of West Nile virus so far this year, the EU health agency said Aug 21, urging the continent to boost its control efforts.
The mosquito-borne virus can cause symptoms similar to flu but in extreme cases it can result in tremors, fever, comas and a lethal swelling of the brain tissue known as encephalitis. It can also cause meningitis.
The 12 countries are Albania, Austria, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Kosovo, the Netherlands, North Macedonia, Romania, Serbia and Spain, with infections reported in 99 regions, according to the Stockholm-based European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC).
Italy and Greece had the highest number of cases – 311 and 157 respectively – while 21 regions across Europe reported their first ever cases.
By comparison, 67 regions in nine European countries had reported cases during the corresponding period in August 2025.
“The expansion of West Nile virus transmission as well as the spread of invasive mosquito species demonstrate why Europe needs to strengthen its mosquito-control capacity,” Celine Gossner, ECDC’s head of food-, water-, vector-borne and zoonotic diseases said in a statement.
“For effective mosquito control, we need close cooperation in Europe and an integrated approach that brings together mosquito monitoring, community engagement, and targeted mosquito control solutions that take environmental impact into account.”
In Europe, most human infections occur during mosquito season, which generally runs from late spring to autumn, with a peak in transmission between July and September.
There are no approved human vaccines and no specific treatments for the virus, according to the WHO.
Care is limited to managing symptoms and providing supportive hospital treatment for severe cases.
While the mosquitoes that spread West Nile virus (culex mosquitoes) are already widely present in Europe, the Asian tiger mosquito (aedes albopictus), which can transmit the dengue and chikungunya viruses, is now established in 16 European countries, double the number from 12 years ago, the ECDC said. Lebanon's economy to contract by 6.4 pct in 2026 amid renewed conflict: World Bank

00:23:53 KST

BEIRUT, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- Lebanon's economy is projected to contract by 6.4 percent in 2026 as renewed conflict has interrupted a tentative economic recovery, the World Bank said Friday in its latest Lebanon Economic Monitor.
The report said the economy had begun to stabilize in 2025, with real GDP growing an estimated 4.2 percent, marking its strongest performance since 2019. However, the escalation of conflict in March brought the recovery to a halt, with damage to infrastructure, population displacement, and supply-chain disruptions weighing on the economy.
Tourism and domestic consumption, main drivers of the 2025 rebound, were also hit, according to the report, titled "A Conflict-Torn Economy."
"Lebanon's fragile recovery has been sharply set back by the renewed conflict," said Dahlia Khalifa, World Bank division director for the Middle East department, stressing the need for advancing banking and fiscal reforms to restore confidence and mobilize reconstruction financing.
The report noted that Lebanon's fiscal position remained relatively strong during the first half of 2026, building on a surplus of 3.9 percent of GDP in 2025. But public finances are expected to face growing pressure from rising humanitarian and reconstruction costs, wage demands, and slowing revenue growth.
Lebanon's public debt remains unsustainable, with no talks on debt restructuring underway, the report added.
Inflation is forecast to rise to 17.5 percent this year, driven by supply disruptions, higher shipping costs and rising oil prices, further eroding household purchasing power.
The Lebanese pound has remained broadly stable with support from foreign exchange reserves and tighter liquidity, though the World Bank warned of renewed pressure if external inflows weaken or conflict-related shocks persist.
The report estimated that the conflict would reduce GDP growth by 10.4 percentage points compared to a no-conflict scenario.
It warned that prolonged displacement, asset damage, and disruptions to education and health services could weaken medium-term growth. ■

Researchers in Australia develop longer-lasting rechargeable battery
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
23:23:48 CST
00:23:48 KST

CANBERRA, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have developed a rechargeable zinc-iodine battery, offering a potentially safer and more sustainable alternative to popular lithium-ion batteries for large-scale energy storage.
The aqueous zinc-iodine battery, described in the journal Angewandte Chemie, can be charged and discharged over 60,000 cycles, according to a statement released Friday by Australia's Flinders University.
Iodine is an effective rechargeable battery material, with a potential energy storage capacity of about 211 mAh/g (milliampere-hours per gram). However, one of the biggest challenges with this new battery technology is stopping iodine species from moving to places it shouldn't inside the unit, the statement said.
The new battery uses a low-cost organic cyclodextrin-based polymer that helps store and control key chemicals, allowing it to charge quickly while maintaining performance. When fully charged in seven minutes, it can operate at 1.3 to 1.4 volts with a capacity of 200 mAh/g over 8,000 cycles, or charged in just three minutes and last for more than 60,000 cycles at 150 mAh/g, researchers said.
The unique structure of cyclodextrins acts like a cage, locking iodine compounds in place and preventing them from disrupting the battery's operation, they said, adding that zinc is a low-cost and widely available metal, with Australia holding the world's largest known zinc reserves.
The technology could provide a more sustainable option as demand for lithium-ion batteries rises, driven by electric vehicles and portable electronic devices, the study showed.
The team is now working with industry to establish a prototyping platform for the alternative battery system. ■

BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- At more than 1,500 meters above sea level, Tianmen Mountain in central China's Zhangjiajie offers summer temperatures of just 22 to 26 degrees Celsius, drawing a steady stream of visitors.
Among them are growing numbers of European travelers, like Italian Giancarlo Marino. Escaping the relentless summer heat in his hometown, he traveled to China with friends in search of cooler weather.
"Here you can feel the breeze, and while you're resting up on the mountain, you can even buy ice-cold drinks from the many vendors. It's thoughtful and relaxing," he said.
As extremely high temperatures grip many parts of the world this summer, China is emerging as an unexpected destination to avoid the soaring temperatures. With more convenient entry policies and a host of tourism-friendly measures, the country is drawing international visitors in surprising new ways.
NICHE ATTRACTIONS
Jizhou District in north China's Tianjin Municipality is usually known among Beijing residents as a weekend escape. Few would expect to encounter overseas tourists there, let alone visitors from Argentina.
Argentine traveler Michael visited Jizhou during his trip to China to enjoy the mountain scenery around the Huangyaguan section of the Great Wall.
For him, the "coolness" of Jizhou was not just about the pleasant temperature, but also about immersing himself in nature and experiencing rural life.
"The environment here is beautiful, and you can even see the Great Wall from the guesthouse," he said.
Local guesthouse owner Zhang Wei has noticed a growing number of foreign visitors seeking a deeper understanding of local life instead of simply checking off famous attractions.
"We've lately seen a clear increase in overseas guests. Many like to combine countryside experiences with natural scenery, allowing them to experience China in a more in-depth way," Zhang said.
Dutch tourist Noa is another traveler seeking out niche experiences. On a recent independent trip to Nanjing in east China's Jiangsu Province, Noa and friends made a point of visiting local produce markets and public parks, including matchmaking corners where parents gather to find partners for their children, to observe daily life up close.
"Many of the vegetables here are things I've never seen back home. It's really interesting," Noa said.
China's rapid economic and social development is also reshaping inbound tourism. Slovenian tourist Rainer Grega, visiting China for the first time, said he hopes to tour major Chinese technology companies.
"Many Chinese companies and brands are well-known overseas, so I'm really looking forward to visiting the headquarters of some of them. It would be fascinating to tour an electric-vehicle factory or see how those advanced robots are manufactured," he said.
According to a representative of a Suzhou-based international travel agency, foreign visitors are increasingly planning multi-city itineraries, while younger independent travelers, trips to smaller cities and rural areas, and longer stays have all become notable trends.
"Nowadays, many foreign visitors venture into city neighborhoods and rural villages to experience authentic Chinese life. From vibrant urban nightlife to rural revitalization, a vivid, multi-dimensional China is being increasingly shared with the world," said Wu Guoping, president of the Wuxi Tourism Association.
MORE OPEN STANCE
For many overseas visitors, China's increasingly convenient entry policies have provided an important guarantee for more flexible and in-depth travel.
China currently offers unilateral visa-free entry to nationals of 50 countries, including Slovenia and Italy.
"Thanks to the 30-day visa-free policy, you can come whenever you want -- just book a flight and go," Grega said. He added that transfers between airports and high-speed rail stations were seamless, making detailed travel planning largely unnecessary.
Marino echoed the view, saying the visa-free policy was a major reason for choosing China.
"It feels like the policy is becoming more and more foreigner-friendly. You can tell that China is opening its arms and genuinely welcoming more people to visit and learn about the country," he said.
Data from the National Immigration Administration (NIA) showed that China recorded 22.91 million inbound foreign visits in the first half of this year, up 20.4 percent year on year. Of those, 77.7 percent were made under visa-free entry facilitation policies.
China is also expanding the coverage of its 240-hour visa-free transit policy. According to an NIA announcement released on Aug. 20, citizens of Kyrgyzstan and Vietnam became eligible for the 240-hour visa-free transit policy and the 30-day visa-free entry policy for Hainan Province starting Aug. 20. The move increased the number of countries covered by the 240-hour visa-free transit policy to 57.
Vietnamese student Do Thi Huyen My, now in her second year at Hainan University, happily welcomed the new policy.
"I think the policy will definitely attract more Vietnamese tourists to China, especially to Hainan," she said.
"For me personally, it also means my family can visit me in Hainan more conveniently while enjoying a vacation here. By the time I graduate, my parents, relatives and friends will also be able to attend my graduation ceremony without going through complicated visa procedures," My said.
REFINED SERVICES MATTER
As inbound visitors become increasingly diverse and venture beyond traditional destinations, new opportunities have emerged for China's tourism industry, alongside higher expectations for service quality.
The city of Suzhou in Jiangsu Province, for instance, recently introduced a package of incentive measures to boost inbound tourism, offering rewards to travel agencies and online travel platforms that manage to organize overnight stays for foreign tourists and expatriates, or arrange one-day tours, with the annual reward up to 3 million yuan (about 442,000 U.S. dollars). Senior tour guides who manage to cultivate or recruit foreign-language guides are also eligible for incentives.
However, experts warned that feedback from some foreign visitors suggests that information access and language services remain weak links amid the boom of inbound tourism, which underscores the need to improve tourism services for international guests.
Wu Guoping suggested building a more comprehensive support system by developing multilingual digital platforms that seamlessly connect transportation, accommodation, dining, shopping and attractions, making travel planning and consumption more convenient.
To that end, Shanghai has recently launched a type of integrated smart tourism service kiosk that combines abundant online and offline resources.
Resembling a telephone booth, the facility provides access to 14,000 ticketing and shopping links, more than 20,000 dining venues and over 7,500 hotels and guesthouses. Powered by an AI travel assistant, it offers personalized recommendations, real-time interpretation and AI-generated travel journals. Its foreign bank card payment system supports 10 languages and more than 120 currencies.
Zhangjiajie is also improving services to match its surging international guests. From January to July this year, the city received 860,700 inbound visitors from 195 countries and regions, up 19.01 percent year on year. Tourism foreign exchange revenue reached 98.52 million U.S. dollars, an increase of 40.52 percent.
Despite the rapid growth, a previous survey in the Wulingyuan Scenic Area found that fewer than one-third of frontline staff could communicate proficiently in a foreign language.
The scenic area has since partnered with local universities to compile English-, Korean- and other foreign-language learning handbooks, while organizing evening classes for tourism workers.
Chen Heng, a 52-year-old publicity officer and one of the evening school participants, has even purchased language-learning software at his own expense and practices English pronunciation by reading aloud with a chopstick in his mouth.
"Zhangjiajie boasts world-class natural scenery. Our service quality has to keep pace as well," he said. ■

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: China's embodied AI enters critical phase for large-scale application: experts
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
23:23:10 CST
00:23:10 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- China's embodied artificial intelligence (AI) is entering a critical window for large-scale application, with products shifting from small-batch trials toward broader deployment, Xu Xiaolan, president of the Chinese Institute of Electronics, said at the 2026 World Robot Conference.
The annual event in Beijing brought together more than 1,000 Chinese and overseas guests, while over 300 domestic and international companies showcased more than 3,000 innovative products.
A diverse array of embodied AI products made their debut or demonstrated their capabilities at the conference, underscoring the latest technological and manufacturing advances in China's embodied AI sector.
Represented by such innovations, embodied AI has seen rapid development in recent years, unlocking the potential to drive a trillion-yuan-level industry and becoming an important engine for new forms of the intelligent economy, Xu said.
A logistics humanoid robot developed by ROBOTERA, a Beijing-based embodied AI company, is a vivid example of Xu's observation. Capable of accurately picking up and flipping packages of different shapes moving along a conveyor belt, the robot not only drew crowds of onlookers at the conference venue, but also saw scaled application at more than 10 logistics centers across China.
Such scenes point to a shift in the industry from technology demonstrations to real-world applications.
In scenic areas such as West Lake in Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, embodied AI robots provide tourists with route planning and information about attractions.
In residential communities across Suzhou, Jiangsu, these technologies are now used to identify smoke and fires, spot illegally parked vehicles, and detect improperly dumped garbage, expanding their application from preset scenarios to a wide range of everyday services.
Growing demand for such applications is accelerating robot production. Data released by China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) in July showed that more than 400 complete humanoid robot products had been developed in China, accounting for over half of the global total.
According to a report released at the conference, China shipped more than 40,000 humanoid robots in the first half of 2026, accounting for 97 percent of global shipments. The Chinese Institute of Electronics estimates that China's humanoid robot market could reach about 870 billion yuan (about 128.29 billion U.S. dollars) by 2030.
Behind the rapidly expanding figures are increasingly diverse commercial ventures.
At the conference venue, Bumi, a robot that appeared during this year's Spring Festival Gala, performed boxing routines for visitors. Standing just 98 centimeters tall, the humanoid robot has sold thousands of units on JD.com, one of China's major online shopping platforms, since its launch in April. It can chat with children and teach them programming and dance.
"Humanoid robots have actually begun to enter some households," said Yang Shuo, marketing director of Noetix Robotics, developer of Bumi.
The shift toward commercial applications is also being reflected in companies' customer bases and operating models.
Chen Jianyu, founder and CEO of ROBOTERA, said the company's enterprise and institutional customers now span more than 10 cities, where its robots are operating regularly in various logistics and industrial scenarios.
"Starting this year, the embodied AI industry has entered a turning point in commercialization," Chen said.
Wang Xingxing, founder and CEO of Unitree Robotics, noted that over the next decade, the pace of evolution of the entire robotics industry will accelerate significantly. "I think this heralds a completely new phase of our development," he said.
However, the rapid expansion of applications does not mean that large-scale deployment comes without challenges.
Industry experts noted that despite rapid advances in embodied AI technology and industrial development, products still face challenges including complex technological systems, difficulties in adapting to real-world environments, and serious safety and ethical risks.
To address these challenges, coordinated efforts across the industrial chain are needed to tackle key technologies and deepen research into safety and ethical standards for embodied AI, experts said.
In June, the MIIT and the State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission of the State Council jointly issued a notice on a 2026 special initiative for real-world training and application of humanoid robots and embodied AI. The initiative calls for the development of a number of embodied AI foundation models and motion-control algorithms with strong adaptability to application scenarios and leading performance.
The policy push comes as the industry seeks to move beyond limited trials and expand into more complex and diverse real-world environments.
In Wang's view, the industry will reach a genuine tipping point when a robot can accomplish about 80 percent of tasks in virtually any unfamiliar environment. ■

Federal appeals court halts ruling allowing thousands of college players extra year of eligibility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:23:02 UTC
00:23:02 KST

NCAA gets win in court on 5-year eligibility rule, but this is hardly the end of the lawsuits
DENVER (AP) — The NCAA notched an important win in federal court Friday over its much-disputed five-year eligibility rule, though it fell short of shutting down the last-minute shuffling threatening to upend college sports rosters with football season fast approaching.
A 2-1 decision by a panel of the U.S. 10th Circuit Court of Appeals halted, for now, a judge’s order that would have granted thousands of athletes an extra season of eligibility. But it did nothing to resolve dozens of other lawsuits and court orders piling up across the country that allow players in the same situation to join teams for the upcoming season.
Virtually all these lawsuits involve players who graduated from high school in 2022, whose college eligibility ended last season and who were not included in the NCAA’s controversial new rule — less than two months old — that grants most Division I athletes five years of eligibility over five years but doesn’t take effect until next season.
“There’s a reason we saw so many state-court lawsuits filed” after the now-paused federal court ruling that came down July 31, said Sam Ehrlich, a former lawyer who now works at Boise State and operates the College Sports Litigation Tracker. “It was a ‘just in case.’ They did it just in case what we just saw happen actually happened.”
Among the many athletes watching this unfold and wondering where it winds up are defensive linemen Kellan Wyatt and Stephan Daley, both members of the national championship team at Indiana last season who decided to return after the lower-court decision. So are former Ole Miss starters Dae’Quan Wright, Zxavian Harris and Wydett Williams, who won a ruling from a Louisiana state court giving them another season of eligibility even though they had signed with NFL teams this summer.
While some players hope to land back at their schools, whatever the impact on the rosters, how that works isn’t at all clear in many cases. The judge in the case involving the Ole Miss players, for example, gave them a week to enter the transfer portal, which for football players is only open in January.
In appealing the state court cases, the NCAA is expected to invoke parts of Friday’s ruling, which agreed with NCAA arguments that it was likely to win the case when it’s heard in full — probably several months from now — and that the NCAA would suffer more harm than the players if the court didn’t pause the order.
The NCAA can also take heart in an Ohio appeals court that paused a similar injunction involving Xavier basketball Filip Borovicanin and others.
But other than those two cases, Ehrlich said, judges across the country “are unanimous that the NCAA is in the wrong” on the five-year eligibility issue when it comes to the Class of 2022.
Plaintiffs’ attorney Rob Shelquist issued a statement calling the appeals court ruling procedural and “not a decision on the merits of the athletes’ antitrust claims.”
“We are exploring every available option given the split in the panel’s ruling and remain committed to fighting for these college athletes whose opportunities and eligibility have been unfairly restricted,” he said.
The NCAA’s chief legal officer, Scott Bearby, sent a memo to schools telling them they would not be subject to NCAA punishment for allowing any player to compete between the time the July 31 ruling came down and Friday. But he reiterated that those players are no longer eligible.
Bearby also acknowledged that the NCAA would continue to defend lawsuits around the country — a signal that the NCAA knows Friday’s ruling offers no guarantees of an end to the roster chaos.
“If anything, I do wonder if there’s a part of the NCAA that’s, like, ‘Maybe we’d have been better off not getting the stay because, boy, there’s going to be a lot of lawsuits filed over the next couple of weeks,’” Ehrlich said.
Courts that go beyond filing emergency injunctions and take up the cases in their entirety will have to decide who suffers more harm: Is it players who can’t play a fifth year and could lose educational and NIL opportunities? Or incoming freshmen who signed with the idea that they wouldn’t be competing against a class of fifth-year seniors?
When the NCAA decided to have the rule kick in next year, it also grappled with that calculation, knowing it couldn’t be perfectly fair.
“Fairness is in the eye of the beholder,” the NCAA argued in its legal brief in the appeals case. “Countless student-athletes already on campuses, and schools who built their rosters in reliance on the rules the NCAA’s membership wrote and agreed to follow, do not believe it is fair for thousands of formerly ineligible athletes to return to competition at the start of the 2026–27 season.”

Court slashes $50M judgment against Infowars’ Alex Jones over falsely calling school shooting a hoax
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21

Court cuts $50M judgment against Infowars’ Alex Jones over falsely labeling Newtown killings a hoax
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — A Texas court on Friday slashed a $50 million judgment that conspiracy theorist Alex Jones was ordered to pay families of the 2012 Sandy Hook Elementary School massacre over his false claims that one of the deadliest mass shootings in U.S. history was a hoax.
The Infowars founder can only be forced to pay about $6 million, the Texas Third Court of Appeals ruled in a unanimous opinion, citing state laws that limit lawsuit damages.
The ruling does not affect a separate $1.25 billion judgment against Jones in Connecticut, where he was also found liable for defaming and causing emotional distress to relatives of the 20 first-graders and six educators killed in the Newtown shooting.
The punishing financial verdicts against Jones and his company, Free Speech Systems, in recent years have forced him into bankruptcy, led to some of his personal property being put up for auction and led to him leaving his Infowars platform. For decades, he used the platform to push conspiracy theories about the United Nations, the federal government, gun control and more.
Sandy Hook families have yet to collect any money from Jones, who has waged lengthy appeals in state and bankruptcy courts as his company faces liquidation. He remains on air after moving onto new websites and streaming platforms.
Friday’s ruling did not throw out the trial court’s finding of defamation against Jones. Still, he called it “a gigantic victory for the First Amendment,” and said he will continue to appeal the case to the state Supreme Court to get the remaining damages thrown out.
“I got lawyers who are good constitutional lawyers and they are not backing down,” Jones said.
Jones has already tried to appeal the Connecticut judgment to the U.S. Supreme Court but was denied last year.
The decision by the Texas Third Court of Appeals left intact more than $4.1 million in compensatory damages awarded by a jury to Sandy Hook parents Neil Heslin and Scarlett Lewis for defamation and emotional distress. But it slashed more than $45 million in additional punitive damages down to $1.5 million to comply with the state’s $750,000 cap for each plaintiff.
The court found Heslin and Lewis did not show evidence that the harassment following Jones’ hoax claims rose to a level that would allow them to exceed the cap. It also said the trial judge improperly allowed the parents to seek higher damages after trial.
Mark Bankston, an attorney for Heslin and Lewis in the Texas lawsuit, shrugged off the appeals court ruling as “irrelevant” given that Jones still faces massive financial judgments in Connecticut.
“The families care not at all about this irrelevant ruling which affects only two of the 19 claims they all share. Jones still faces over a billion dollars of liability, so this changes absolutely nothing. All it does is highlight the absurdity of Texas law,” Bankston said.
Newtown families harassed as Jones claimed the massacre was a hoax
Heslin and Lewis’s 6-year-old son Jesse Lewis was among those killed in the Sandy Hook attack. Their lawsuit against Jones and the 2022 verdict marked the first time he was held financially liable for peddling lies about the massacre, claiming it was faked by the government to tighten gun laws.
Jones portrayed the lawsuit as an attack on his First Amendment rights, but conceded during the trial that the shootings were “100% real” and that he was wrong to have lied about them.
At the Texas and Connecticut trials, victims’ relatives testified that Jones’ followers -- believing his claims that the shooting didn’t happen -- subjected them to death and rape threats, in-person harassment and abusive comments on social media. Jones argued there was no proof that linked him to those actions.
Heslin and Lewis told jurors that an apology wouldn’t suffice and initially called on them to make Jones pay more than $150 million for the years of suffering he has put them and other Sandy Hook families through.
Almost immediately after the punitive damages in Texas were announced, Jones’ trial attorney predicted the award would be reduced to $1.5 million on appeal.
Christopher Mattei, a lawyer for the Sandy Hook families in the Connecticut lawsuit, said Friday’s ruling has no bearing on the ongoing lower court proceedings in Texas involving the liquidation of Infowars’ parent company.
The Onion steps in to mock Jones and help frustrated families
Jones and his company have filed for bankruptcy, and those legal proceedings continue. The satirical website The Onion also moved to take over Jones’ Infowars platforms and turn his bullhorn of conspiracy theories into parody sites.
Jones took Infowars off the air in April and moved to a new location, switching his shows to new websites and posting them on his personal X account. The Onion, meanwhile, has set up its own Infowars webpage on its website, running videos of shows parodying Jones.
A proposed licensing deal that would give The Onion temporary authority to use Infowars’ trademarks, copyrights and intellectual property has been put on hold because the liquidation proceedings have been stayed during Jones’ appeals.
In November 2024, the Chicago-based satirical outlet was named the winner of a bankruptcy court auction of the assets of Infowars’ parent company, Free Speech Systems, aimed at helping pay some of the defamation judgments. A federal judge overturned the auction results, citing problems with the process and The Onion’s bid.
