US flags do not protect West Bank's Palestinians from Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:00:44 UTC
23:00:44 KST

Breadcrumb
US flags do not protect West Bank's Palestinians from Israeli soldiers and settlers
In one of the most contradictory scenes in the occupied West Bank, Palestinians who hold US citizenship are flying the US flag above their homes, despite knowing that the United States is the Israeli occupation's biggest supporter and arms supplier.
US flags flutter lightly above homes in the towns of Turmusaya and Qusra in the occupied West Bank, but the disappointments on the ground are heavy.
No one is protecting tens of thousands of Palestinians from settler attacks on their homes and land, so each of them has begun thinking about individual ways out, even if that means flying the US flag above their home as a last cry for help.
Businessman Louay Abdel Moneim Abu Rida, 46, from Qusra, south of Nablus in the northern occupied West Bank, arrived at Ben Gurion Airport (Lydda) on Monday evening, 17 August.
Upon his arrival, a team from the US network CNN took him to his home, which is surrounded by Israeli forces in Qusra.
The first thing Abu Rida did was raise the US flag over his home, which overlooks the settlements surrounding his town, as well as numerous outposts seeking to swallow up his home and land as they continue to expand.
In this context, Abu Rida told The New Arab, "I had a CNN team with me, and I came to my home in their car from the Israeli airport. They are a team holding US and French citizenships. Despite being with me, the soldiers stopped me for about half an hour in front of my home before allowing me to enter it."
Abu Rida, like everyone else, understands that US journalists in particular have immunity and that Israeli forces cannot target them as they do Palestinian journalists, as none of them can approach Ras al-Ain Hill.
"I am currently under siege, and I am asking the US Embassy to help lift the siege on my home," Abu Rida described. "The Israeli army is supposed to be stationed in front of my home to remove the settlers, but since 13 Aug. this year, it has been unable to do so. Last Tuesday, a settler attacked the garden of my home, and the soldiers negotiated with him to leave instead of forcibly preventing him from doing so."
Regarding the reason he raised the US flag, Abu Rida said, "This is a political message to the US government. I am a US citizen and have all the rights of a citizen, including having the US Embassy protect me and my home."
"I am a Palestinian American. I left behind a luxurious home, several cars and my family, and came to Qusra because my home in my birthplace is important to me. I asked the US Embassy to visit me at my home, and my request is being considered, according to what they told me," he added. "I want the US Embassy to come here and see the US flag raised over the home of a US citizen. If the settlers succeed in taking over my home, they will remove this flag and replace it with an Israeli flag. Is this permitted under US law?"
US flags had been flying over homes in the town of Turmusaya near Ramallah in the occupied West Bank for months, for the same reasons Abu Rida raised his flag.
Abu Rida is one of 400 Palestinians from Qusra in the occupied West Bank who hold US citizenship and live there, returning to the town during the summer holidays and on special occasions, according to Qusra Mayor Abdel Azim Wadi, who spoke to The New Arab.
Lawyer Yasser Alqam, a member of the Turmusaya municipal council and one of the Palestinian American citizens who have been flying the US flag above their homes for months, told The New Arab, "In short, we are now clinging to a straw to save our homes from the occupation and settlers."
Alqam, 58, who has held US citizenship since birth, explained, "The Palestinian American has seen that there is no one who serves as a point of reference to protect him, whether at the level of the Palestinian Authority or the occupation."
According to Alqam, "Over the long decades we lived in the United States, if we had any problem or someone attacked us, we would call the police to protect us."
"But when we come to the occupied West Bank because we live between America and here, we find that things are very different and that Israel and its army support the settlers and protect them, while no one protects us," he added.
Messages behind raising the flag
"Raising the US flag carries several messages," Alqam said. "First, for deterrence for the settlers; there could be legal consequences for burning or seizing the home of a US citizen. Second, it is an embarrassing message to the US administration and the US Embassy, whose citizens are being attacked. Third, raising the flag means asking the US administration and its embassy to stop supporting the occupation."
"I am a US citizen, and the government transfers my tax money to support Israel, and the latter uses these taxes to kill us and destroy our homes," Alqam noted. "This debate is currently growing in the United States and did not exist before in this form."
Asked whether raising the US flag had achieved its objectives and had come to provide protection, Alqam said, "First, a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step."
"There was a practical experience in Turmusaya about two weeks ago involving the famous New York neurosurgeon Hassan Shukri. After he arrived at his home in Turmusaya, where he spends the summer holiday with his family, the occupation army stormed Turmusaya and turned the house opposite his into a military post," Alqam continued. "They actually spent 72 hours in his neighbour's house and later decided to move to Dr Shukri's home. He holds US citizenship and flies the US flag above his home, and they expelled him and his family from their home."
Alqam noted, "We filmed the soldiers and sent the video to the US Embassy and the US State Department as well. We sent messages saying that the presence of the occupation army in a home flying the US flag constitutes a challenge to the United States. After four hours, the Israeli army withdrew from Dr Shukri's home and apologised to him."
He further said that "the irony is that the occupation army withdrew from Dr Shukri's home, which flies the US flag, after four hours, while it spent three days in his neighbour's home. Both neighbours hold US citizenship, but the doctor raised the flag and his neighbour did not."
"During this period, the US Embassy and State Department have become more responsive to our messages and calls because of the media focus on the presence of Palestinian Americans," Alqam said. We expect a visit early next month by the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, to the town of Turmusaya."
Asked whether raising the US flag insults the Palestinian Authority, Alqam said, "Quite the opposite. There is no intention whatsoever to insult the Palestinian Authority because it is, in fact, an authority under occupation, just like any Palestinian citizen."
"The Palestinian Authority is constantly asking the European Union and the United States to help it against the brutal Israeli practices," he added.
Raising the US flag does not appear to be universally accepted in Turmusaya, where there is a heated debate in the town between those who oppose and those who support raising it.
In this context, Turmusaya municipal council member Awad Abu Samra, who is also a member of Fatah, told The New Arab, "I oppose raising the US flag over the homes of the town because America is occupying Palestine by funding Israel, and it is funding our killing."
He pointed out that months ago, there was a heated debate about a group of citizens' view that the Palestinian flag should be raised over the town's facilities funded by residents of the town.
"Most of them are US citizens and pay taxes in the United States, while the occupation comes at all times to destroy the roads and facilities. But there was opposition to this," Abu Samra remarked.
According to Abu Samra, Turmusaya is one of the Palestinian towns in the occupied West Bank with the highest number of Palestinians holding US citizenship.
"The proportion of Turmusaya residents holding US citizenship is about 90 per cent of the town's residents. The population of Turmusaya is 16,000, of whom 6,000 live in the town permanently. There are thousands of expatriates who live between the United States and the town and hold US citizenship," he said.
Anyone entering Turmusaya in the occupied West Bank may realise that they are entering a wealthy town, with buildings and luxurious villas covered in red tiles and surrounded by orchards, as well as swimming pools.
The town becomes crowded during the summer months when expatriates return for school holidays and the wedding season.
It is normal to enter any supermarket in the town and hear an American accent in everyday conversations among elderly people, children and shopkeepers or among teenagers as they talk in the street.
Notably, nine of the 11 members of the Turmusaya municipal council hold US citizenship.
Thousands of Palestinians hold dual Palestinian and US citizenship, most of them concentrated in the cities of Al-Bireh and Ramallah and their villages in the occupied West Bank, such as Turmusaya, Deir Dibwan, Silwad and Al-Mazra'a al-Sharqiya, among others.
Most of them are from families that migrated to the United States in the last century and maintained their ties with Palestine across generations.
The issue of the US flag is not the only matter of disagreement and debate among Palestinians—there is also the question of how the United States is viewed by people who lived there for decades and loved it as a country, rather than for its foreign policy.
In this context, Mohammad Rabie told The New Arab, "Before my son was killed, I used to hang the US flag on my home. Even months after his death, the flag remained raised. But my relatives and friends gently and kindly blamed me because the United States is responsible for his death just like Israel, so I removed it."
Rabie, who is from Turmusaya, recounts the day his son was killed on 6 April 2025: "Amer was no more than 14 years old, meaning he was a child."
"He was with his friends eating green almonds in one of the village's fields. Nevertheless, the occupation fired 36 bullets at him from several guns, and even after he was killed, they continued shooting at him from point-blank range while he was on the ground, on the pretext that he had thrown stones," he added.
Distinguishing Trump from America
"A senator in the state of New Jersey, where I live in the United States—the state has two senators, Cory Booker and Andy Kim—asked me if I wanted an investigation," Rabie said. "I said yes, so he sent a letter to Congress and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and another letter to President Donald Trump. So far, I have not received any response to these letters."
"No one from the embassy, State Department, or any of these official bodies has formally contacted me to take my statement legally," he said.
Rabie, 50, works as a building contractor in Turmusaya, while his older sons work in the United States and travel between Turmusaya and New Jersey.
Regarding why he placed a picture of his martyred son between the Palestinian and US flags in his living room, Rabie said, "I am a Palestinian American, and my martyred son was also one. The United States should not be reduced to Trump and his group and everyone who supports Israel. There is a wonderful country with good and honest people who genuinely stand in solidarity with Palestine. Palestine is my country and so is America."
He stressed that "there is currently a change taking place among younger generations in the United States in favour of the Palestinian cause, and I believe it will continue in favour of us Palestinians."
Sam Bahour, a businessman and expert in Palestinian-American relations, told The New Arab that he believes "what is currently happening with the raising of US flags is somewhat useful in terms of promoting the Palestinian cause to the world.
"It is a cry that attracts the attention of the press, but it will not attract serious attention from the US administration because the United States is an integral part of the occupation that we Palestinians are suffering from. Any visit by a US Embassy official to Turmusaya, Qusra or Al-Taybeh means absolutely nothing on the ground and will not stop settler attacks," Bahour said.
Asked whether there are statistics on the number of Palestinian Americans, Bahour explained that there are no accurate statistics on the number.
"What foreign agencies have published about between 45,000 and 60,000 Palestinians holding US citizenship are Israeli figures that cannot be trusted and are not from the US Embassy," he opined.
Bahour, 62, said he believes that "the US Embassy will not deal with Palestinian Americans as white American citizens."
"Everything we see in the media in terms of visits or statements is merely symbolic. At the same time, the Palestinian Authority does not properly use the presence of thousands of Palestinians holding US passports on the global stage. It is content to be a spectator. Change is currently happening in the United States, whether flags have been raised in Turmusaya or Qusra or not," he concluded.

What is Woke 2.0 and how is it linked to pro-Palestine views?
Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez recently said in an interview with ABC, “woke 1.0 was crazy,” but what exactly is woke 1.0, what makes woke 2.0 so different, and what role does Palestinian justice play in the newer form of woke?
According to Google Trends data, the term "Woke 1" began gaining popularity in January 2026. It describes social justice activism of the late 2010s and early 2020s. The term usually focuses on anti-racism advocacy, support for transgender people, and the overzealous use of cancel culture -- the concept of trying to 'cancel' people for perceived infractions of social justice norms by encouraging social media users to unfollow them and, at times, attempting to get people fired from their jobs or expelled from their places of education.
Another key feature of Woke 1 is the surrounding corporate culture. Following the murder of African American man George Floyd by white police officer Derek Chauvin in 2020, the Black Lives Matter movement, which was founded in 2013, became mainstream. This included major brands like cosmetics giant L'Oreal and even McDonald's.
The past is a different country https://t.co/D0Jzjzg7Xj
— Sami Gold (@souljagoyteller) June 2, 2025
Despite her recent criticism of the movement, AOC was a key figure in Woke 1. Her decision to wear a dress saying 'Tax the rich' to the 2021 Met Gala, which cost $35,000 a ticket, was highlighted at the time as an example of how members of an elite group of politicians and celebrities criticised the same systems they participated in.
How is Woke 2 different?
Woke 2 was coined to differentiate a newer form of online social justice, with similar progressive goals but newer tactics. It is associated with the second Trump presidency and rising global proto fascism. Some critics of Woke 1 blame the movement's perceived extreme tactics for the backlash against progressive movements and Donald Trump's victory in the 2024 presidential election.
The term, along with the similar 'dark woke ', is often tongue-in-cheek, but reflects a real change in progressive political strategy. A key political figure in Woke 2 is New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani. Mamdani's election campaign focused on the cost of living for New Yorkers of all backgrounds, rather than spotlighting specific identities.
Another key difference between the two eras of woke is the recent attention to Palestinian justice. While Woke 1 highlighted a number of injustices, including racism, homophobia, and ableism, the treatment of Palestinians was rarely on the agenda. However, since October 2023, Israel's increasingly severe tactics against Palestinians, including the genocide in Gaza, settlement expansion in the West Bank, and the adoption of the death penalty for Palestinians, have made the issue a key feature of progressive politics.
However, another key feature of Woke 2 is the adoption of language from alt-right internet culture. The term 'slop,' often used to describe low-quality AI content, comes from an antisemitic conspiracy theory, while the suffix '-maxxing,' as in 'joymaxxing' and other derivatives, comes from 'looksmaxxing,' a term used by the misogynistic incel community. While these terms are both common internet slang, they are particularly popular in progressive spaces.
While Woke 2 is distinct from Woke 1, it is a continuation of internet-focused progressivism, which prioritises online advocacy -- typically on platforms owned by tech giants, like Elon Musk's X and Mark Zuckerberg's Instagram -- over in-person, community-based politics.

How physical stress symptoms shape the emotional content of women’s dreams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:00:16 UTC
23:00:16 KST

Women who experience physical symptoms like headaches or muscle pain without an obvious medical cause often report experiencing more negative and intense dreams. A recent survey of adult women explored how these physical sensations, alongside general bodily awareness, relate to the emotional content of their nighttime experiences. The results, published in Dreaming, reveal a distinct link between daytime physical discomfort and negative dream themes.
The human brain processes emotional and physical stress in varied ways. Sometimes, psychological distress such as anxiety or emotional exhaustion translates into physical symptoms like nausea, back aches, or dizziness. This phenomenon is known as somatization.
Somatization occurs when the body expresses emotional pain through physical language. It is often observed in individuals who find it difficult to identify or verbalize their feelings. The physical symptoms are very real to the person experiencing them, even if they originate from psychological stress rather than a physical injury.
Another aspect of how people experience their physical selves is body awareness. This concept refers to a person’s sensitivity to internal physical sensations and physiological processes. It includes recognizing changes in the body, sensing the sleep cycle, or noticing the early signs of an illness.
People with high body awareness tend to feel more in tune with their physical existence. They often excel at recognizing their own physiological reactions to external events.
Dreams provide another window into how the brain handles emotional regulation. Dreaming happens primarily during the rapid eye movement, or REM, stage of sleep. During this phase, the brain regions responsible for processing emotions become highly active, often generating vivid and emotionally charged narratives.
Caglayan Pinar Ozturk, a researcher at Suleyman Demirel University in Turkiye, wanted to understand how these elements overlap. Past research has questioned the connections between chronic pain and dream activity, but less is known about how general body awareness and non-chronic physical symptoms relate to dream content.
Ozturk designed a study to examine whether a person’s level of body awareness relates to their dream themes. The researcher also wanted to test whether physical symptoms of stress correspond to the types of dreams these individuals experience.
Ozturk recruited 213 adult women between the ages of 18 and 65 to participate in an online survey. The participants were predominantly young to middle-aged and held university degrees. To isolate the effects of everyday physical symptoms and general body awareness, the researcher excluded individuals with diagnosed psychiatric conditions, sleep disorders, and chronic diseases.
The participants completed three separate questionnaires. The first assessed their dream themes over the past six months, asking them to rate how often they experienced specific dream scenarios on a scaled grading system. The second questionnaire measured their body awareness by asking how closely they track their internal bodily sensations.
The third survey evaluated their somatization symptoms, asking participants to report any physical complaints they experienced over the past 15 days. These complaints included everyday ailments such as headaches, chest pain, numbness, and nausea.
When analyzing the responses, Ozturk found that the relationship between a person’s body awareness and their overall level of somatization was not statistically significant. Being highly tuned to internal bodily sensations did not mean a participant was more or less likely to report physical symptoms of stress.
However, the results showed a weak but positive association between body awareness and dream themes. Women who scored above average in body awareness reported more frequent dream themes, particularly negative ones.
This association might occur because people who pay close attention to their bodies also possess better memory recall for their internal experiences, including dreams. Cognitive processes that regulate attention to the body often overlap with the working memory required to encode and recall dream narratives upon waking.
The strongest pattern emerged between physical symptoms and dream content. Ozturk found a moderate, positive association between a participant’s total physical symptoms and their dream themes. As the participants reported more physical symptoms during waking hours, their dream content tended to become increasingly negative.
Headaches emerged as the most common physical complaint, followed by muscle pain and back pain. The researcher analyzed how these specific symptoms paired with particular dream themes. Nearly every physical symptom measured was associated with at least one negative dream theme.
For example, women who reported waking physical pain like headaches, chest pain, and lower back pain frequently reported dreams about being harmed by others. They also experienced dreams centered on feelings of discomfort, hidden emotions, health problems, and anxiety.
Sensations of weakness or heaviness in the body were linked to an especially wide range of emotional dream themes. Participants who felt weak or heavy during the day reported more dreams involving emotional blockages, interpersonal conflict, aggression, and defeat.
Even specific symptoms like a sensation of a lump in the throat correlated with intense nighttime narratives. Women who felt this symptom frequently dreamed about being blocked, experiencing discomfort, and harboring hidden emotions. These patterns suggest that physical discomfort might share a psychological foundation with the emotionally charged narratives the brain constructs during sleep.
The study relied on a cross-sectional design, meaning the data was collected at a single point in time. This approach makes it impossible to determine whether physical symptoms cause negative dreams, or if negative dreams cause subsequent physical symptoms. Both experiences might simply arise from a shared underlying source of psychological stress.
The questionnaires also covered different timeframes, which complicates the interpretation of the results. Participants reported their dream themes over a six-month period, but they only reported their physical symptoms over the past 15 days. Because of this short window, the physical complaints cannot be classified as chronic pain.
The dream assessment tool used in the survey contained mostly negative dream themes. This imbalance likely influenced the finding that higher body awareness corresponds with more negative dreams. A more balanced assessment tool might reveal different patterns for neutral or joyful dream content.
Future research could provide a broader view by assessing positive dream content, dream clarity, and the exact frequency of dream recall. Investigating these variables over a longer timeframe could clarify how daily physical sensations shape nighttime brain activity. Researchers could also explore how these relationships play out in populations with diagnosed chronic pain conditions to see if the emotional themes of their dreams mirror their physical experiences in similar ways.
The study, “An Examination of the Relationship Between Body Awareness, Dream Themes, and Somatization in Adult Women,” was authored by Caglayan Pinar Ozturk.

China’s trade grip tightens in Europe as clock ticks towards October deadline
As Brussels continues its push to rebalance ties, the latest data show China’s trade surplus expanded over all but three EU members in July
China extended its trade surplus over all but three EU members in July compared to a year earlier, calculations based on new Chinese customs figures showed. In some instances, the monthly swing was dramatic.
China’s surplus with Sweden quadrupled, while for Malta it rose by 166.6 per cent. For Romania it expanded 94.4 per cent, and for Finland 93.7 per cent.
For the bloc’s biggest economies, Germany’s deficit shot up 86.5 per cent compared to July 2025, Poland’s was up 31.9 per cent, the Netherlands rose 14.5 per cent, Spain by 12.4 per cent and France by 4.2 per cent.
While the bloc’s officials are not entirely fixated on trade deficits, they have become a symbol of concerns about undeclared Chinese state subsidies and industrial overcapacities that have spilled over from spreadsheets to open geoeconomic rivalry.

40 years after the Lake Nyos disaster in Cameroon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

40 years after the Lake Nyos disaster in Cameroon
August 21, 2026
"The Lake Nyos disaster took everybody by surprise. We had no warning signals before it ever took place," said Isaac Konfor Njilah, a Cameroonian geologist and head of a laboratory in the department of Earth Sciences at the University of Yaounde.
On the night of August 21, 1986, Lake Nyos suddenly released a massive cloud of carbon dioxide that spread through nearby valleys and villages. The gas replaced oxygen, suffocating people and animals as they slept.
Located in Cameroon's Northwest Region, about 315 kilometers (196 miles) northwest of Yaounde, Lake Nyos sits inside an ancient volcanic crater in the Oku volcanic field. At the time of the incident, the area's population exceeded 3,000, with many families relying on farming and cattle ranching.
The disaster claimed the lives of about 1,700 people and some 3,500 head of livestock, making it one of the deadliest natural disasters in Cameroon's history.
How did a lake become deadly?
Following the disaster, scientists from Cameroon and abroad launched extensive investigations to determine what had happened.
They concluded that carbon dioxide from deep underground had been accumulating at the bottom of the lake for years, trapped beneath more than 200 meters (656 feet) of water.
Before the disaster, the upper layers of the lake contained oxygen-rich water, while the deeper layers were saturated with dissolved carbon dioxide. Njilah explains that water has an insatiable appetite for carbon dioxide.
"So when carbon dioxide comes from the [Earth's] mantle, it is being dissolved continuously in the lake," Njilah told DW.
Scientists often compare Lake Nyos to a giant bottle of carbonated water. For decades, carbon dioxide built up in the lake's depths. When that balance was disturbed, the gas escaped in a rapid chain reaction, releasing a deadly cloud that rolled through nearby communities.
Researchers believe a landslide may have triggered the release by disturbing the gas-rich waters at the bottom of the lake.
Carbon dioxide is harmless at normal atmospheric levels. But in high concentrations, it acts as an asphyxiant, displacing oxygen in the air. Because the gas is heavier than air, it flowed downhill into villages, where many residents died in their sleep before realizing anything was wrong.
Tragedy at another lake in Cameroon just two years prior
The Nyos tragedy was not a first in Cameroon. Two years earlier, on August 15, 1984, a similar event occurred at nearby Lake Monoun, about 100 kilometers southeast of Nyos. A sudden release of carbon dioxide killed 37 people.
Scientists were still investigating the Monoun disaster when the far deadlier catastrophe struck at Lake Nyos. Researchers eventually concluded that the deaths were caused by a rare phenomenon known as a limnic eruption, in which gas-rich deep waters suddenly rise to the surface and release dissolved gases.
In the years that followed, engineers installed degassing pipes in Lake Nyos to gradually release carbon dioxide trapped deep below the surface.
Today, Njilah says the lake no longer contains enough dissolved carbon dioxide to trigger a disaster.
"The lake is very safe for the population to return," he told DW.
Survivors still live with the trauma
For survivors, however, the fear remains. Tsang Emelda Njah was just 5 years old when the disaster happened.
"We were at home, and there was a big vibration of the house," she recalled. "We thought it was just the house that was about to collapse. But we were not sure what it was. So we ran out."
Kum Samuel, who was 17 at the time, returned to his village and was confronted with a scene of pure horror.
"I saw my parents lying there dead. Chickens, flies and birds. Dogs together with our elders. I wasn't sure what to do."
For Ndong Frederick Bah, the losses were deeply personal.
"Nine of us went to bed that night, and I was the lone survivor of the family," he told DW, adding that the next day, people who had heard about the disaster came and rescued him.
Entire communities were later relocated to new settlements. Although scientists have reduced the risk of another gas release, many survivors still struggle to overcome the trauma.
"I am a child of Nyos," said Tsang Emelda Njah. "But I am still afraid to go close to the lake. That's because whatever killed people there, I am not sure whether or not it has been stopped from ever happening again. That is why we are still afraid."
Anglophone crisis harms restoration
While scientists consider the lake safe, long-term reconstruction efforts have been slowed by Cameroon's Anglophone crisis.
The conflict erupted in 2016 between government forces and separatist groups in the country's primarily English-speaking Northwest and Southwest regions, where Lake Nyos is located.
According to Njilah, plans to rehabilitate affected communities and encourage people to return to their ancestral lands have been disrupted by insecurity, with the area now difficult to access.
"It is the plight of the survivors to go back home. They want to go back to their ancestral land so that they are able to pour libations on the graves of their forefathers," he said.
The ongoing violence has also hindered scientific work and development projects.
"Nobody can venture [there,] unless you want to have a bullet lodged in your head," Njilah said. "It has affected government and international agencies who are working there."
Blaise Eyong contributed reporting.
Edited by: Keith Walker

Gasoline rationing returns to Moscow and St. Petersburg as Rosneft caps fills nationwide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:57:17 UTC
22:57:17 KST

Russia’s summer fuel crisis is back for a second wave, driven by Ukrainian strikes on its oil refineries. This time, it has forced rationing back into both Moscow and St. Petersburg and pushed its largest oil producer to cap gasoline nationwide.
St. Petersburg drivers ran into limits again on 20 August, when several major oil companies restricted sales across the city, Bumaga first reported. Gazprom Neft reinstated a 60-liter-per-receipt cap it had lifted on 4 August and blocked customers from filling more than one canister.
Tatneft capped AI-95 and AI-92 at 50 liters. Many Gazprom Neft stations carried no AI-95 at all, its own station map showed. “Gazprom and Lukoil are dropping dead,” one driver wrote in a local chat.
The limits followed Moscow’s by a day. There, Gazprom Neft cut sales to 40 liters per car, and AI-95 turned up at a single Neftmagistral station, The Moscow Times reported. Rosneft went furthest, capping gasoline at 30 liters per car at every one of its stations across Russia, with no limit on diesel. In June, the same network was still letting drivers take up to 90 liters a fill.
Russia’s biggest oil company stopped selling gasoline in canisters nationwide after Ukraine’s strikes. It blames “seasonal demand”
By mid-August, gas stations in at least 12 regions were again seeing hours-long lines, Meduza’s regional roundup found, citing a count by the outlet 7×7. Lipetsk Oblast brought back odd-even rationing by license plate on 13 August and held fills to 30 liters, a step Governor Igor Artamonov announced; Sochi’s authorities asked residents and tourists to leave their cars at home.
Ukraine has spent months hitting the plants to choke off both the fuel Russia’s army runs on and the oil revenue that funds its war. At least four refineries went offline in August alone.
Officials say supply is holding. Energy Minister Sergei Tsivilyov said on 18 August that fuel remains available, even as he acknowledged the lines. Gasoline averaged 76.04 rubles a liter ($0.89) on 10 August, off a July peak that ran nearly 20% above where the year began.

Former Ukrainian troops tell RT why they chose to fight for Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:57:13 UTC
22:57:13 KST

Former Ukrainian troops tell RT why they chose to fight for Russia
Former Ukrainian servicemen switch to the Russian side once they get out of the “information bubble” set up by Vladimir Zelensky’s government and see the reality of the conflict for themselves, a high-ranking officer from a unit comprised of ex-Kiev troops has said.
Earlier in August, Russia announced the creation of the Ukrainian Volunteer Brigade out of several smaller formations of Ukrainian nationals who left the ranks of Kiev’s forces and are now fighting for Russia.
In its report on Thursday, RT Russian shared the stories of some members of the newly-formed brigade.
Some decided to join Russian troops because they changed their views after being captured, some because they never wanted to be in the Ukrainian military, but were forcefully mobilized, and others because they supported Moscow from the start.
The Ukrainian Volunteer Brigade will perform different tasks on the front line. It includes reconnaissance units, an FPV-drone strike squad, and teams handling the evacuation of civilians, among other kinds of troops, the report read.
Highly-motivated troops
A fighter with the callsign ‘Zhak’, who serves as deputy commander for political affairs at the separate battalion ‘Maksim Krivonos’, which also joined the brigade, told RT that the soldiers in his unit have high morale.
“If those people simply didn’t want to fight, they could’ve gone to the detention center after being captured, sit there safe and warm, eat three times a day and wait to be exchanged in a prisoner swap,” said the officer, who was born in Ukraine’s Kharkov Region but has been fighting for Donbass since the Western-backed coup in Kiev in 2014.
The people “in Ukraine… live in a very harsh, aggressive information bubble. But when they find themselves here [in Donbass], when they see the Alley of Angels in Donetsk – they see a completely different picture, and a lot changes in their minds,” Zhak explained.
The Alley of Angels is a monument to hundreds of children killed in Ukrainian attacks on Donbass over the past 12 years.
Our own command ‘wanted to destroy us’
Another member of the brigade, called ‘Hunter’, said that he used to be a research fellow at an agricultural academy in Kiev and was never interested in politics. He was recruited into the Ukrainian military in 2023 after his request for a draft deferment to finish his PhD was denied, he said.
According to Hunter, his company was tasked with controlling “a rather pointless” position in a wooded area that was under constant Russian shelling. When the size of the unit fell from more than a hundred to 20 and then 13 troops, he asked his commanders to order a retreat, but was told to stay put and await reinforcements.
But after a week, no additional troops had arrived. Hunter and his fellow servicemen decided to surrender as soon as Russian forces began storming their trenches.
However, when they left their positions with their hands in the air, the Ukrainian military started firing at them, Hunter noted. “Artillery, mortars and kamikaze-drones were deployed. They didn’t even spare cluster munitions, which surprised me greatly. Our own command wanted to destroy us,” he said.
Hunter stressed that only he and three other troops from the company were lucky enough to survive, with one of them now also fighting for Russia together with him.
‘Patriotism ran out’
Another soldier of the Ukrainian Volunteer Brigade, nicknamed ‘Bely’, told RT that he served as a paratrooper in Kiev’s military and used to be a passionate patriot of Ukraine, despite being born in Donbass. When Ukraine sent its armed forces to the east of the country in 2014, he abandoned his home in what is now Russia’s Lugansk People’s Republic, leaving his wife and son behind, and moved to the city of Dnepropetrovsk (Dnepr), he said.
According to Bely, his marriage fell apart because his spouse was pro-Russian and wanted him to join the self-defense forces in Donbass. But instead he signed another contract with the Ukrainian military in 2016, fighting against the units of the Lugansk and Donetsk People’s Republics.
Despite good pay, “my patriotism ran out, at some point, and the realization began to dawn on me that two brotherly nations were fighting,” the soldier recalled. He was especially impacted by an incident in which Ukraine shelled a school in a village near the city of Lugansk, he added.
Bely said he then lost the will to serve, but the Ukrainian Army refused to discharge him after the escalation between Moscow and Kiev in February 2022. When he surrendered to the Russian military in 2023, he was also targeted by fellow Ukrainian troops, suffering shrapnel wounds, the serviceman said.
Russian medics patched him up, and the experienced soldier was invited to join the Maksim Krivonos battalion while in detention. Bely said he initially had concerns about becoming a traitor to his former Ukrainian comrades-in-arms, but eventually came to the conclusion that fighting for Russia was the right thing to do.

Minister: Estonian tax rules prevent disclosure of firms trading with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:55:00 UTC
22:55:00 KST

Minister: Estonian tax rules prevent disclosure of firms trading with Russia
The law currently prevents the state from publishing a list of companies that conduct business with Russia and Belarus, said Minister of Economic Affairs Erkki Keldo (Reform Party). He also could not say whether the law should be amended for that purpose.
"Regarding the publication of such a list, the law as it stands today does not allow the state to publish these companies. To do that, the law would have to be changed," Keldo said.
According to Keldo, the Taxation Act prevents the disclosure of such companies because the information concerns company data.
"We do have annual reports that are public. If someone wishes, they can look up who provides which services, to which countries goods are exported, or with whom cooperation is carried out. But the state cannot publish such information itself — the current law does not allow it," he added.
Keldo could not say whether compiling and publishing such a database by a private individual would be lawful. "Data protection experts would have to answer that," he said.
He added that the government has not discussed whether the law should be amended to allow such lists to be published.
"We need to discuss this. At the moment, it has not been under discussion in the ministry or the government. Since the issue has now surfaced, we will look into it and talk, for example, with the Chamber of Commerce, employers, and entrepreneurs to understand their view — whether and to what extent unequal behavior among Estonian companies can be seen," Keldo said.
"Today I certainly won't say that we will do it, but I also cannot say that we won't. We need to look into what the pros and cons of such a list would be," he said.
"First, we need to understand what exactly we would make public, because there is definitely a data protection issue. If we simply publish company names, I suspect that many of those names will mean nothing to the public. In that case, do we add beneficial owners, ownership structure, shareholders, and so on? Publishing this information is not simple. The question immediately arises: what information and how much do we publish — only companies, or also the physical persons who are owners? All of this needs careful consideration. There are personal data and data protection issues, and we must consider whether this method is effective and what we aim to achieve. All of this needs to be discussed with stakeholders," Keldo said.
Keldo said he would support, as a first step, a complete ban on importing goods from Russia or Belarus at the EU level. "Publishing and public shame or condemnation would certainly put those companies under greater pressure, but I believe most entrepreneurs want equal market conditions and fair competition," he said.
The Latvian Central Statistical Bureau (CSB) will begin publishing a list (link in Estonian) of companies that export goods to Russia and Belarus or import goods from those countries every month, according to amendments to the law on supporting Ukrainian civilians adopted by the Latvian parliament, noted Latvian public broadcaster LSM.lv. The published Excel file lists 170 entities in alphabetical order.
This is not a list of companies violating international sanctions. It includes companies that continue business activities in sectors not covered by sanctions.

"Gold surged again after Thursday's pullback, as long-term Treasury yields rose following Bessent's interview, which failed to dispel investors' concerns about the rapid growth of U.S. government debt and fiscal sustainability," said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank.

Iran set to impose longer prison terms for any contact with foreign media
Unknown

2026-08-21
13:54:27 UTC
22:54:27 KST

Iran set to impose even harsher punishment for any contact with foreign media
Iran's parliament passed a resolution early this week that would increase punishments for Iranians who interact in any way with foreign media outlets, organizations or individuals.
If the legislation is approved by higher authorities as expected, any contact with U.S. media entities, foreign embassies or institutions — whether it takes place inside or outside Iran — could land an Iranian in prison for up to two years unless they first obtain explicit written permission from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, according to state media.
There are already very strict laws in Iran against sending information to exiled, foreign-backed Iranian media outlets, such as Iran International, or the U.S. and U.K. government-funded VOA Farsi and BBC Farsi. But the new legislation would go further, imposing extensive punishment on Iranians for any written or verbal contact with foreigners — especially foreign media.
The legislation would also ban educational and research activities linked to foreign entities, with a possible 10-year prison sentence for any person found to be involved in activities deemed "incompatible with Iranian culture."
Iran's Islamic Republic clerical leaders have, since rising to power in 1979, been extremely concerned about foreign infiltration and influence, especially by the U.S. and Israel.
After the 12-day war launched by Israel in June 2025, which the U.S. joined, the regime became even more paranoid, jailing dozens of people and executing some accused of sending video to outside entities, according to a May report by Amnesty International.
Marjan, a student working toward her political science master's degree at Tehran University, who declined to give her full name, told CBS News in a phone interview that she used to work for some domestic news outlets before the June 2025 war, but that she now refrains from showing her face to any media organizations, and keeps all of her commentary anonymous.
"Iran under the new leadership of Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei is going toward North Koreanization," she said, referring to the authoritarian regime led by Kim Jong Un. "I think Mojtaba is much more hard-line and closed-minded than his father, and the country will become a completely restricted and isolated country."
Many people across Iranian society share her concerns, but few dare to voice them.
"The boundaries set by the new legislation are a serious concern for all Iranians," a former government employee who asked for anonymity told CBS News. "Using basic applications like WhatsApp or other messaging apps could get you into trouble if stopped at mobile checkpoints, where phones are searched."
"To avoid technical and security problems with governmental agencies, many Iranians are now switching to domestic alternatives like Rubika or Kasheef," the man said, also speaking by phone, adding the caveat that such options make "it even easier for the security apparatus to spy on Iranians."
It is a deeply divided country, however, and the regime does have many supporters.
Professor Mohamadyaser Ershadmanesh, a scholar who works as an adviser to senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps officer Yahya Rahimsafavi, told CBS News the legislation was a necessary "response to the country's urgent need for consistency in legal monitoring tools to identify individuals and groups who work" against Iran's interests.
He cited "the previous experience of foreign intelligence organizations' interventions, including Mossad, CIA, MI6 and others," and said the new law would "clearly define a good boundary for security and protection for our people and our institutions."
"Criminalizing cooperation with foreigners will actually be a great help to Iran's internal and national security," he said.
Recently, photographer Yalda Moaiery was sentenced to 15 years in prison after being convicted by Iran's opaque judiciary system of providing photographs of areas targeted by U.S.-Israeli strikes to organizations linked to the U.S. and Israel, as well as giving interviews to media outlets deemed hostile to Iran, according to the Reuters news agency.
Under Iran's constitution, all legislation passed by the parliament requires approval from the Guardian Council and review by the Expediency Discernment Council to become law.
The bill passed Sunday by the parliament is widely expected to gain final approval, however, as the ongoing war has bolstered support for such societal restrictions among Iran's ruling clerics.

Russian businesses are building their own protection against Ukrainian drones - the Kremlin is unable to help
Kyiv • UNN
The Kremlin is shifting responsibility for protecting facilities onto businesses, which are creating mobile groups costing 50–70 million rubles. The lack of standards is causing obstacles.
The Russian leadership's inability to ensure centralized protection of industrial and infrastructure facilities from Ukrainian drones is forcing the Kremlin to shift responsibility for their security onto the enterprises themselves. This is reported by the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, UNN reports.
Details
Large enterprises are forming mobile response groups equipped with drone detection and suppression systems. At the same time, creating one such group costs 50–70 million Russian rubles, equivalent to 600–850 thousand US dollars.
Fuel and energy and industrial enterprises, warehouse and logistics operators, marketplaces, and shipping companies are arming themselves most actively. However, the increase in purchases does not mean that businesses are moving to comprehensive protection: most limit themselves to individual detection or jamming systems, while a multi-level system requires significant investment in personnel, equipment, and infrastructure
However, such measures lack unified data-exchange standards, as well as technical compatibility between detection and jamming systems.
Each enterprise is saving itself as best it can, and this improvisation is turning against the Russians themselves: through false alarms, mutual radio interference between neighboring facilities, and the purchase of expensive equipment that does not correspond to the actual parameters of the threats

Twelve militants were killed in separate operations this week in northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, which borders Afghanistan, the military said in a statement. Another 37 were killed in operations in southwestern Balochistan province.

US Army Corps of Engineers chartered plane crashes near Alaska radar site, killing all 8 aboard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:53:02 UTC

Plane crashed on second attempt to land in heavy fog in Alaska, killing all 8 aboard, officials say
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — A plane that crashed at a remote military site in western Alaska, killing all eight people on board, was making its second runway approach in heavy fog when it lost contact, authorities said Friday.
The Cessna’s two pilots could not see the gravel airstrip and were flying solely by instruments when the plane crashed about midday Thursday, Clint Johnson, the National Transportation Safety Board’s Alaska region chief, told a virtual news conference.
Regulations required that they abort their first landing attempt because of the lack of visibility, he said, and the plane crashed on its second attempt, about one-third of a mile (0.5 kilometers) from the runway. The runway is surrounded by mountainous terrain on three sides, and the Federal Aviation Administration recommends pilots use GPS and other instruments when they land there.
On board were the pilots, two employees of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and four contractors. Two of the contractors were employees of Calista Brice, a collection of companies that perform construction, engineering, logistics and other work in remote areas. Calista Brice is a subsidiary of Calista Corp., an Alaska Native regional corporation.
The military has not said what work they were performing at the Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site, about 450 miles (725 kilometers) west of Anchorage on Alaska’s southwest coast.
NTSB investigators were traveling to the scene Friday.
The radar site was built in the 1950s as part of a network designed to provide early warning of a missile attack by the Soviet Union. Today, it monitors the skies off the coast in the direction of Russia, North Korea and China.
Those on board were “dedicated professionals carrying out a vital mission in a demanding environment,” U.S. Air Force Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, commander of Alaskan Command, the Alaskan North American Aerospace Defense Command Region and Eleventh Air Force, said in a statement Thursday.
“This is a devastating loss for our military family and the communities we serve,” Davis said.
Johnson said search teams found the fragmented wreckage after the twin-engine Cessna 441, also known as a Cessna Conquest, lost contact. Its final flight path was captured by radar at the site, he said.
Weather conditions were changing Thursday as heavy fog rolled through the area. An automated observation system not far from the airport reported a low cloud ceiling, fog and visibility of about 10 miles (16 kilometers) in the minutes before the crash, but the next update about 15 minutes after it showed visibility of less than one-quarter mile (0.40 kilometers), according to Carrie Haisley, the meteorologist in charge of the National Weather Service’s Alaska sector operations center.
Mike O’Donnell, who oversaw airport safety programs and accident investigations for much of his 17 years at FAA, said it sounded as if weather conditions were bad enough that the pilots should have diverted and landed somewhere else.
The airstrip is at a private military site managed by the Pacific Air Forces Regional Support Center. It’s part of a network of remote radar sites that tracks aircraft operating in Alaska’s airspace and along its borders, a statement from Alaskan Command said.
The outpost at Cape Newenham closed in 1983 after a new radar was installed, and now the site is visited only occasionally by civilian contractors who perform maintenance on the system.
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers said the two employees who died were part of a “project delivery team en route to a project site in support of the U.S. Air Force.” The statement did not provide additional details about the work.
Johnson said the flight was operated by Security Aviation based in Anchorage. The charter company did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment.

Myanmar military strike kills 14 people at a Buddhist monastery, opposition group says
BANGKOK (AP) — An airstrike on Friday by Myanmar’s military on a Buddhist monastery in Myanmar ’s central Sagaing region killed 14 people who were taking part in a weeklong meditation retreat, an opposition group and a resident said.
The attack is the latest in a series of frequent and deadly aerial strikes targeting armed pro-democracy forces and ethnic armed groups in the country. The strikes often cause civilian casualties.
The attack occurred in Swel Le Oh village in Myaung township, about 75 kilometers (45 miles) west of Mandalay, the country’s second-largest city, according to Nway Oo, a spokesperson for the Civil Defense and Security Organization of Myaung Township, or CDSOM.
Nway Oo said that 14 people, including three women, were killed and 20 others were wounded when a fighter jet dropped a bomb in the compound of the village’s monastery.
A villager who spoke on condition of anonymity, because he feared for his safety, also confirmed the death toll to The Associated Press. The villager said that the fighter jet dropped two bombs 15 minutes apart, with the second bomb damaging a house near the monastery where more than 100 people were on a weeklong retreat during Buddhist Lent.
The villager, whose mother-in-law was killed in the airstrike, said that people fled to a nearby community after cremating bodies of the victims.
BBC’s Burmese-Language service and Myanmar’s media outlets, including Myanmar Now, reported the death toll at between 10 and 14. They also posted photos and videos showing what they said was the aftermath of the strike, with images of bodies.
The military didn’t immediately comment. In the past, the army has said that it only attacks legitimate targets of war, accusing the resistance forces of being terrorists.
Myanmar has been in turmoil since the army seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in February 2021, triggering a civil war. After peaceful demonstrations were put down with lethal force, many opponents of military rule took up arms, and large parts of the country are embroiled in conflict.
The military has increasingly used airstrikes to counter opposition forces, including the armed People’s Defense Forces in Sagaing region, a stronghold of armed resistance. The resistance has no effective defense against air attacks.
The monastery attack comes a week after the U.N.-established Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar, or IIMM, said that it observed a notable escalation in aerial attacks by the military in the months preceding the elections held in December and January, and that they have continued unabated afterward.
Myanmar’s foreign ministry rejected the IIMM report on Sunday, saying that limited airstrikes and counterterrorism operations solely aim at military targets and were carried out in response to insurgents and terrorist groups in accordance with the rules of engagement, and that the security forces exercise maximum restraint to avoid civilian harm.

Enrollment in SNAP grocery aid is dropping faster than expected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:53:02 UTC
22:53:02 KST

Enrollment in SNAP grocery aid is dropping faster than expected as work requirements kick in
PHOENIX (AP) — Enrollment in the biggest federally funded food aid program in the U.S. dropped by more than 13% in a 12-month span — a decline far steeper than the government estimated as work requirements and other provisions of President Donald Trump’s “big beautiful bill” take hold.
Those losing coverage in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, include people who don’t meet the tightening requirements to participate, and, advocates say, some who qualify for the help but are rejected because they miss deadlines or don’t have the needed documentation handy. It’s too early to tell exactly how many fall into each group.
It’s also unclear how many have lost coverage because some state agencies that run the programs are overwhelmed trying to keep up with changes. That was the case in Arizona, which saw the nation’s largest enrollment drop.
Tia Fields, who analyzes social safety net policies at the advocacy group Invest in Louisiana, said the main reason she’s seeing people lose coverage is not failure to meet work requirements. “A lot of it is administrative paperwork,” she said.
Proponents of welfare reform hope the roll reductions are driven by people earning too much to keep qualifying — a sign that policy changes are behaving as intended for a program they assert is riddled with fraud.
“If there are people that are leaving the welfare rolls because they’re working and they’re moving forward,” said Rachel Sheffield, a research fellow at the conservative Heritage Foundation, which pushed for stricter requirements for SNAP, “that would be a step forward.”
Arizona has had the steepest decline so far, with a 12-month drop of more than 50%, according to data compiled by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which runs SNAP. The decline was more than 20% in Georgia, Louisiana and Nevada — and in Florida, where the Department of Children and Families said in a statement that the decreasing number “is reflective of the state’s strong focus on advancing opportunities for Floridians and their families to achieve economic self-sufficiency.”
Eligibility requirements are tightening
SNAP helps more than 1 in 10 people in the U.S. buy food. Most of the beneficiaries have incomes below the poverty line. The monthly benefit, which is delivered on debit cards that can be used only for groceries, is $344 per household on average.
Newly released federal data found SNAP enrollment fell from 42.2 million in May 2025 to 36.6 million in May, a drop of more than 13% in a year. The May data are preliminary and could be revised.
Since 2010, the average number of monthly beneficiaries has been below 40 million for only two years — 2019 and 2020. The rolls started dropping after a recent peak of 43.3 million in October 2024. They’ve fallen much faster since implementation began last year for Trump’s “one big beautiful bill,” which cut taxes and overhauled social safety net programs.
The expanded SNAP work requirement has now kicked in for most of the country, but it won’t begin in some places until next year.
Many adults 54 and younger without minor children have long been required to work to get SNAP benefits. The new law requires most people who previously had been exempt from requirements to either work, volunteer or go to school to get benefits. It now includes those ages 55 to 64, and those with children ages 14 to 17. Those 65 and older or with children younger than 14 remain exempt, as do those with health limitations. Some other groups that had been exempted from the requirement — including homeless people — no longer are.
In February, the Congressional Budget Office projected that the new requirements and other factors would push SNAP enrollment down over the next decade, falling below 34 million by 2036. But the nonpartisan office did not expect the drop to be as fast as it’s been. By May, the number of people receiving the benefits was about as low as it was forecast to go in 2030.
Experts expect another impact when states are required to pay part of the cost of benefits if their rate of payment errors — when recipients receive more or less than they should — is above 6%. Advocates for recipients say states may deny benefits to some people entirely rather than risk errors.
The cost-sharing is scheduled to start in October 2027, though Congress has considered a delay.
Changes have been hard to implement in Arizona
In Arizona, enrollment plummeted by 55% from April 2025 to April 2026 — the biggest drop in the country, with more than 400,000 fewer people getting benefits now.
The state said the drop was driven largely by the state’s own struggles putting new federal requirements in place.
“Implementing the federally mandated changes triggered unprecedented call volumes and administrative hurdles, including additional verification requirements, creating real barriers for applicants,” said Brett Bezio, a spokesman for the Arizona Department of Economic Security.
Bezio said that hiring more staff members and introducing ways for people to submit their documents online have stemmed the enrollment drop in recent months as the state has reduced the chance for people who qualify to lose benefits.
In Phoenix, LaDiamond Lopez lost her benefits in January, with officials telling her she needed more documentation about her income and household — something that’s needed for officials to determine whether enrollees meet work requirements.
She’s been skipping meals and some bill payments to ensure her children have enough to eat.
In her quest to be reinstated, she had previous employers sign forms confirming she no longer worked for them and added her children — ages 3 and 9 — to her apartment lease. She expected payments to resume in August, but she doesn’t know if they’ll last.
“I was approved at the end of May, but now they’re asking me for more documents,” she said. “It’s a panic.”
Other factors could be driving down enrollment
The Heritage Foundation’s Sheffield says that some of the drop in SNAP use is likely a natural decline after peaks in the coronavirus pandemic era.
Paco Velez, the president and CEO of Feeding South Florida, said the 22% one-year enrollment drop in Florida is driven partly by immigrants who are in the U.S. legally but fear being targeted by Trump’s immigration crackdown if they’re seeking government benefits.
Invest in Louisiana’s Fields said SNAP enrollment declines have broader consequences. For instance, children in households that receive the benefit can be automatically enrolled in free school lunch programs or in the SNAP for Women, Infants and Children program for low-income mothers, young children and expectant parents if they meet the other criteria.
“What happens when that child can’t pay for lunch?” she asked.
Some food banks have ramped up donations to try to meet a demand that they say has risen as SNAP rolls have declined. But that isn’t expected to bridge the gap fully.
“We’re very worried about it because we know that no other organization or program can replicate the scale and success of SNAP,” said Carolyn Vega, a policy analyst at the advocacy group Share Our Strength. “We know that schools can’t fill this gap. We know that food banks can’t fill this gap.”

Ukraine's farmers struggle to sell harvest amid war, drought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:51:00 UTC
22:51:00 KST

Ukraine's farmers struggle to sell harvest amid war, drought
August 21, 2026
Russian attacks on civilian ships have effectively brought the ports in the greater region of Odesa to a standstill. Until recently, they handled about 90% of Ukraine's agricultural exports.
The Ukrainian government has been working on finding alternative routes via rail, road and other waterways. It is also currently in negotiations about an export corridor that would go via Moldova.
But many experts have pointed out that these temporary alternatives cannot replace the ports, and warn that the current blockade of the Black Sea is an even greater threat to the Ukrainian economy than that posed by Russia's full-scale invasion of 2022.
The strained security situation in the Black Sea is already having a palpable effect on Ukraine's domestic market. According to Denys Marchuk, the deputy chairman of the All-Ukrainian Agrarian Council, Ukrainian farmers have already harvested more than 28 million tons of grains and pulses.
But a large part of this harvest cannot be sold, which has led to a shortage of the cash needed to complete the harvest and to plant winter crops. Planting usually begins at the end of August in Ukraine's southern regions.
"Right now, we can barely sell our harvest. Instead, we're storing what we have harvested — that's if we find storage space. At the same time, we are wondering what to do because we need money, especially so we can plant in fall," Marchuk told DW.
He predicted that the situation would continue to worsen in the coming weeks and months when grain and oilseed crops, which are usually harvested later, compounded the crisis.
Farmers plan to leave corn in the fields
The corn harvest alone could reach about 33 million metric tons this year. Yet in the coming months, there could be a shortage of storage capacity totaling up to 10 million tons. Regions on the front, where most silos have been destroyed amid the ongoing war, are particularly affected.
"You often hear that farmers want to leave their corn in the fields to be harvested in spring. It still needs to be dried, which needs a lot of electricity that is very expensive. They don't have the money," said Marchuk. "There aren't enough places where they can sell it, nor are the prices reasonable, so for them it makes more sense to leave it in the fields as that's cheaper."
Domestic prices falling
Maksym Hopka, an analyst at the Ukrainian Agribusiness Club, estimates that Ukraine's agricultural output totaled about 3.7 million metric tons in July, of which about 2.7 million metric tons comprised grain. That was a decline of about a quarter in comparison to the previous month. He expected an additional fall of over 50% in August.
Hopka added that domestic prices were falling, with the price of food-grade wheat declining by 30 to 35%. This meant increasingly difficult economic conditions for production, he explained.
Prices have fallen so sharply because farmers cannot export all of their harvest, and can no longer cover even their production costs.
Some farms are already operating at a loss. According to the Ukrainian Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food, annual losses from unsold agricultural produce could amount to approximately $20.5 billion (approx. €18 billion).
Ukrainian government vows to provide support
The Ukrainian government has insisted it will do everything in its power to find new ways to export Ukrainian agricultural produce by rail or road through neighboring countries or through ports on the Danube.
However, extreme heat and drought have severely reduced the Danube's transport capacity and are also hampering Ukrainian exports. There are also problems with rail and road transport. European railways are already operating at full capacity during harvest season, and transporting large quantities of grain by road is expensive.
For Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky, the top priority remains restoring safe shipping routes to the ports in the Odesa region with the help of Ukraine's military and those of its partners. He told DW that there was no comparable medium-term alternative and that rail connections and dry ports could only serve as temporary measures until the Black Sea ports reopened.
Less help from EU than in 2022
Oleg Nivievskyi from the Kyiv School of Economics said Ukraine today had fewer ways of offsetting losses in maritime trade than it did at the beginning of the full-scale invasion. In 2022, the European Union provided support to Ukraine by establishing "solidarity lanes," and import duties and quotas were temporarily suspended to ease trade.
Nivievskyi pointed out that the conditions were different now. "If we look at trade with the EU, we have gone from a free system to the pre-war trade regime with customs restrictions and quotas," he said.
He added that there were also significant shortcomings in the infrastructure, with the Ukrainian railway currently running 30% fewer trains than before 2022. Russia's constant attacks on rail infrastructure have hampered operations and necessitated regular repairs. Transport via road is also limited due to shortage of truck drivers, not least because many had been mobilized to fight in the war.
Export strategies need rethink
Nivievskyi said the current crisis could help to encourage the government to rethink Ukraine's export policies. He said the country should have developed a long-term strategy right from the beginning of the Russian invasion in order to ensure that its exports could reach global markets.
He explained it wasn't only a question of finding temporary alternatives to the ports of Odesa; the government needed to put in place logistics to ensure that the blockade of one route did not paralyze the entire sector.
Hopka has calculated that Ukraine's exports of agricultural produce will drop by about 9 million metric tons between August and October, and that losses could amount to about $1.9 billion.
In response to pressure from farmers, the government has already extended a loan program to farmers and has also applied for €220 million in aid from the European Commission. The idea is to help small and medium-sized agricultural businesses in particular to cover their payments.

Ukrainian OSINT analysts add new employee data to map of Russian defence industry

Details: As part of the update, the analysts added company groupings. Users can now analyse links between companies based on their participation in conglomerates, holdings, corporations and state-owned corporations.
The analysts also added about 100,000 more employees of Russia's military-industrial complex to the map. The interface was also fully updated and optimised.
Quote: "In the next update, we will add all the companies missing from the groups and update the BDA [Battle Damage Assessment – ed.], as Russian defence businesses have been getting hit hard recently. Many other features are also already in development, but Russians don't need to know about them yet."
Background:
- In July, Varta and Lex Talionis released a version of the interactive map of Russia's military-industrial complex containing information on the aftermath of strikes on Russian companies. The update also added the ability to search for information about company directors, founders and employees.

2026-08-21

The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) stated that North Korea has sent a new military contingent to Russia, including 400 drone operators
Kyiv • UNN
The new wave of North Korean troops in Russia includes 400 drone operators capable of conducting reconnaissance and attacking targets in Ukraine. Pyongyang may be asked to send up to 50,000 more troops.
The new wave of North Korean troops, whose number in Russia has already reached 8,500, includes a drone unit that may attack targets in Ukraine. This was reported by a high-ranking Ukrainian intelligence official, UNN reports, citing CNN.
Details
North Korea, which signed a NATO-style mutual defense pact with Russia two years ago, has been sending troops since late 2024 to assist Moscow’s military operations. According to Major General Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy head of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, it may be asked to provide up to 50,000 more servicemen during President Vladimir Putin’s meeting with his counterpart Kim Jong Un in September.
The outlet notes that such a move would mark a significant expansion of military cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang, taking place amid an acute shortage of air defense systems in Ukraine. This is another sign that Russia’s resources are limited and that it is ready to accept assistance despite public statements about its economic resilience and military-industrial capacity.
Skibitskyi said that the North Korean troops already deployed are spread mostly across Russia’s Kursk region and include 1,000 engineers and sappers. They also include 400 drone operators, many of whom gained experience either during or as a result of previous North Korean deployments, and whose drones will likely be used both for reconnaissance and to attack targets in Ukraine.
The media outlet notes that North Korea’s deepening ties with Russia concern many NATO alliance members, especially after President Donald Trump announced on Sunday that military exercises with South Korea would be scaled back so as not to provoke hostility from Kim Jong Un — the reclusive North Korean leader whom Trump seeks to meet again.
Earlier, Kim’s influential sister, Kim Yo Jong, denied claims that tens of thousands of North Koreans would soon join Russia’s efforts, calling them a "groundless self-invented scenario."
In addition
Ukrainian intelligence believes that the North Korean troops sent to Russia will not fight on Ukrainian territory, Skibitskyi said, but will reinforce Russia’s rear positions, freeing Russian troops for attacks inside Ukraine.
Although Ukraine first warned that North Korean troops were using attack drones on its territory last October, this is the first indication that the new wave of troops will have this capability. In addition to Putin’s likely request for more troops, approximately 25,000 North Koreans have already been deployed or rotated through Russia’s armed forces, Skibitskyi added.
Context
The first North Korean deployment began in the Kursk region in October 2024 to repel Ukraine’s incursion, the first on Russian soil since the Nazis. North Korea remained silent for months about its initial deployment of troops to assist Russia’s war machine and confirmed that its soldiers were fighting against Ukraine only in April 2025. An estimated 10,000 North Koreans were deployed and suffered significant losses, using suicidal tactics to conduct mass assaults on Ukrainian positions.
The media outlet notes that North Korea’s willingness to sustain such losses reflects the scale of Russia’s global alliances and Moscow’s need for additional manpower. The wounded returned to North Korea, where they were able to teach their colleagues how to use drones and about the new reality of technologically dominated front lines.
Underscoring the strength of ties between the two countries, Russian state media over the past year showed photographs of North Korean troops training in Russia, while Kim Jong Un opened a memorial to North Koreans killed in Ukraine in April.

Trump’s ‘economic D-Day’ claims first victim: Not Iran, but US markets
