British spy plane deploys to Norway for Arctic Stone
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:00:45 BST
22:00:45 KST

An RAF Rivet Joint has deployed to Ørland in Norway for a week-long exercise with the Royal Norwegian Air Force, including training intended to improve interoperability with Norwegian F-35A fighters.
An RAF Rivet Joint intelligence-gathering aircraft has deployed to Ørland in Norway for Exercise Arctic Stone, where British personnel are training alongside the Royal Norwegian Air Force and working with Norwegian F-35A fighters, the UK Defence Journal understands.
According to an RAF news update, the activity is intended to strengthen interoperability between Rivet Joint and Norway’s F-35A fleet while contributing to NATO’s situational awareness on its northern flank.
Operated by 51 Squadron, the RAF’s Rivet Joint specialises in gathering intelligence from signals across the electromagnetic spectrum. Sensors aboard the aircraft allow its crew to intercept and analyse signals while airborne, providing strategic and tactical intelligence that can contribute to a wider picture of military activity and the surrounding security environment. Ground-based specialists from No. 54 Signals Unit also process and exploit the information gathered by the aircraft.
The RAF described the aircraft’s role by stating: “The aircraft specialises in monitoring signals across the electromagnetic spectrum, giving it the ability to deliver real-time strategic and tactical intelligence in a way few other assets can match.” It added that the combination of airborne crews and ground specialists provides commanders with improved situational awareness “day and night, whatever the operational conditions.”
Exercise Arctic Stone is using that capability in two connected roles. RAF personnel are training directly with their Norwegian counterparts, including activities designed to improve cooperation between the Rivet Joint and Norway’s F-35A force, while the intelligence gathered during the deployment is intended to give commanders a clearer assessment of the operating environment.
The RAF said the exercise would allow both air forces to improve their ability to work together within NATO operations.
Norway’s location makes it particularly relevant to NATO operations in the High North, where the Alliance maintains air, maritime and surveillance activity across an area extending towards the Norwegian and Barents Seas. The RAF said the deployment reflected what it described as the region’s “growing strategic importance” and its increasing relevance to NATO’s northern defences and wider European security.
The service said: “As the security picture in the region continues to evolve, the presence of RAF assets working alongside key allies and partners in the area is becoming an ever more important part of how NATO maintains stability on its northern flank.”
Rivet Joint’s role differs from that of conventional airborne surveillance aircraft because its principal focus is the detection and analysis of electromagnetic emissions rather than visual reconnaissance alone. The RAF argues that modern intelligence operations increasingly require information from multiple sources to be combined, particularly as military communications, sensors and other systems become more digitally connected.
The deployment also provides an opportunity to test how intelligence collected by the aircraft can support other platforms operating in the same battlespace. Integration with Norwegian F-35As is intended to improve the exchange and use of information between different aircraft types, while giving personnel experience of operating within a multinational NATO environment.

Nigel Farage called us ‘nobodies’ in the Clacton byelection. He seems to treat the town in much the same way | Attieh Fard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:00:34 UTC
22:00:34 KST

In the early hours of last Friday morning, a video was posted. It showed Nigel Farage among his team of volunteers, before the votes had been counted, celebrating his victory and saying that he was not going to humiliate himself by sharing a platform at the count next to “nobodies”.
He was referring to the 33 other candidates who had taken part in what was effectively an unnecessary election, one Farage himself had instigated just a few weeks earlier to send one message: that the people of Clacton were backing him, despite parliamentary investigations into his receipt of an undeclared £5m donation. The election is over, but it’s worth thinking about Clacton and those candidates, of whom I was one.
I migrated to Britain from Iran 27 years ago, and have not been back there for 24 years because my Christian faith and my political activities put me at risk of persecution. Iran’s Islamic regime has massacred thousands of innocent people who want the democracy and freedom we have in Britain and it continues to execute protesters. Perhaps that’s why I felt so passionately about defending our democratic system in Britain from being abused.
Some in the British-Iranian community had high respect for Farage as it was not long ago that he met and embraced protesters outside the Iranian embassy in London after the Islamic regime’s massacres. Many of them were puzzled as to why I was standing against him and why I had left the Conservatives, for whom I had previously stood as a candidate in local elections, to do so. I remember Reform supporters in Surrey asking me: if Farage could not save the country, who could? My decision to stand was not a personal vendetta however. Having closely followed Reform’s campaigns on immigration, borders and security, I had seen the deep divides they created in communities.
Throughout the election, Farage did his best to keep his distance from the other candidates. He refused to engage with us, to attend hustings and ultimately to share a platform on the night of the count.
The campaign itself was revealing, as I met voters who had become disillusioned with Farage. Some were frustrated that he had never visited them or replied to their constituency emails. Others were concerned about his undeclared multimillion pound funds and connections with crypto billionaires. Some felt he had done almost nothing for Clacton, or that he had put Clacton “on the map for the wrong reasons”. Others were angry that he had triggered a byelection, wasting about £250,000 of taxpayers’ money.
Interestingly, some who had previously voted for Reform because they were concerned about immigration changed their minds when they learned more.
As an expert in immigration law, I was able to explain why the small boat crossings were happening. Leaving the EU meant that the UK was no longer part of the Dublin III regulation and could therefore no longer return asylum seekers to the first safe country in which they had arrived. When the UK left the EU, it created a legal void in relation to returning asylum seekers to EU countries.
They also learned how some of our laws do not make sense. An asylum seeker has to be physically present in the UK before making a claim, rather than being able to make a claim from overseas and have their identity and background checked before arrival.
Did they know that Farage had criticised the Rwanda scheme as a “con”? No. Did they know that he said it was “a political impossibility” to deport all illegal migrants? No.
Were they aware that he was planning to take the UK out of the Refugee Convention, which allows those being persecuted by regimes such as those in North Korea and Iran to seek protection in another country? No. Did they agree with protecting genuine asylum seekers? Yes.
Did they know that leaving the European convention on human rights without replacing it with a British bill of rights could affect British citizens and their rights relating to privacy and freedom of expression? No.
Having only two weeks to knock on doors, and a few hours each day on my feet to talk to those who were willing to listen was hard, but 126 residents backed my campaign. I have since received messages of support from some of them, telling me that if I stand again, they would help. I am honoured.
One fact became clear. People want the Clacton MP to tackle crime in his constituency, to address its infrastructure weaknesses, and to create more opportunities for its young people and families. Farage isn’t doing any of these things, so how likely is it that he can renew Britain?
Given all these issues, it was unsurprising that so much of the electorate did not support him. He won, but Nigel Farage MP has some serious work to do in Clacton.
- 
  Attieh Fard is a lawyer who was an independent candidate in the Clacton parliamentary byelection

New study shed light on how estradiol influences memory networks in middle-aged women
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:00:29 UTC
22:00:29 KST

New research published in Brain Imaging and Behavior suggests that estradiol, a primary form of estrogen, influences how different areas of the brain communicate during memory tasks in middle-aged women. The findings provide evidence that higher levels of this hormone tend to allow for more efficient brain connectivity when recalling information. This research offers insights into how hormonal shifts might shape cognitive changes during the transition to menopause.
Midlife in women involves a major hormonal transition known as perimenopause, which leads up to menopause. During this period, the body experiences dropping levels of estradiol, which is the most potent and abundant form of estrogen in the human body before menopause. Because estradiol interacts directly with the nervous system, this decrease often coincides with temporary changes in mood, behavior, and memory functioning.
Scientists aim to understand why some individuals experience persistent memory difficulties as they age, whereas others maintain their cognitive performance. “Menopause is an important neuroendocrine transition and with decades of life left to live after the transition it is important to understand how the brain adapts during this time,” said Abigail Testo, a postdoctoral associate in the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Vermont’s Larner College of Medicine.
Testo co-authored the study with Julie Dumas, a professor and vice chair in the same department. “We hoped with this research to add to the growing body of work being done to better understand how menopause contributes to normal or pathological aging,” Testo said.
A specific area of interest is episodic memory. This type of memory is the brain’s ability to recall specific past events or experiences, such as remembering a person’s name or recalling what happened yesterday.
To explore these individual differences, Testo and Dumas examined how estradiol levels relate to functional connectivity in the brain. Functional connectivity refers to the way distinct brain regions share signals and work together to perform specific tasks. Previous work indicates that estradiol plays a role in regulating these brain networks, but its exact influence during different stages of memory processing remains largely unexplored. The researchers aimed to see how estradiol levels affect the flow of information between brain regions when women encode new memories and when they recall them.
The researchers analyzed data from the Human Connectome Project Aging, a large database designed to track healthy brain aging. They looked specifically at 150 female participants between the ages of 40 and 55. This specific age range allowed the scientists to capture a wide spectrum of estradiol levels, as the group included women who were premenopausal, perimenopausal, and postmenopausal.
To measure hormone levels, medical technicians collected blood samples from the participants after an eight-hour fast. The average estradiol level among the participants was about 83 picograms per milliliter. On the same day, the women underwent functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI. This imaging technique uses powerful magnetic fields to track blood flow in the brain, identifying which specific areas are active during different mental tasks.
During the brain scan, participants completed an episodic memory test called the Face-Name Encoding Task. In the first phase, called encoding, the women viewed faces paired with names and were asked to memorize them. After a brief distractor task, the recall phase began. During this stage, the same faces appeared without names, and the participants had to silently recall the correct names and press a button if they remembered them.
Following the scanning session, researchers tested the participants’ actual memory performance. They asked the women to match the correct names to ten of the faces they had just seen. Overall, the women performed quite well on this cognitive assessment. They correctly identified an average of about 7.5 out of 10 face-name pairs.
To analyze the brain imaging data, Testo and Dumas looked at the functional connections among 132 different regions of the brain. They also controlled for the age of the participants to ensure that chronological aging did not skew the hormonal data. They found five specific brain connections that were associated with estradiol levels during the recall phase of the memory task.
Specifically, higher levels of estradiol were linked to negative functional associations, meaning a decrease in synchronized activity, between certain brain areas. These decreased connections occurred between the left superior frontal gyrus and the brain stem, as well as between the right anterior middle temporal gyrus and the right posterior superior temporal gyrus. The frontal and temporal regions of the brain are well known for supporting human memory functions.
The authors suggest that the lower connectivity seen at higher estradiol levels might represent increased neural efficiency. In other words, with plenty of estradiol available, the brain might not need to work as hard or recruit as many strong connections to successfully recall the required information.
Despite the overall association between estradiol and brain connectivity, the researchers noted an unexpected detail regarding the specific menopausal stages. “We were surprised to find that these brain associations with estradiol levels were not found for women who were perimenopausal,” Testo said. “The reason this was a surprise is because perimenopause is a time with a lot of hormone variability and we thought that variability would lead to greater associations with brain functioning.”
Interestingly, the scientists found no statistically significant relationship between estradiol levels and brain connectivity during the initial encoding phase. This suggests that the hormone’s role differs depending on whether a person is actively learning new information or trying to access a stored memory. The researchers also found no statistically significant correlation between a participant’s estradiol levels and how well they actually scored on the memory test outside the scanner.
It is easy to misinterpret these brain connectivity differences as a direct indicator of everyday memory loss. Because the participants in this sample scored very high on the memory test, the data cannot establish if these specific brain connectivity patterns translate to noticeable memory deficits.
“While estradiol was associated with differences in functional association strengths, it was not similarly associated with differences in memory performance,” Testo explained. “For this reason, we can’t say if the identified functional associations are inherently good or bad for brain functioning.”
Still, the findings point to a lasting biological relationship. “Estradiol likely plays a role in brain functioning throughout the aging process, even after the reproductive period has ended,” Testo noted.
The study relies on a cross-sectional design, meaning it captures a single snapshot in time rather than tracking the same women over several years. This prevents drawing causal conclusions about an individual’s dropping estrogen levels directly causing the observed brain changes. People naturally have individual differences in their brain networks. Observing the exact same participants as they transition through menopause would provide stronger evidence of how hormonal changes alter brain function over time.
The scientists plan to address this gap in the future. “Future HCP-A releases (the dataset utilized in this study) will include longitudinal data,” Testo said. “It would be interesting to revisit this investigation as participants age and estradiol levels continue to fluctuate and decline.”
Future studies may also benefit from observing how other hormones that fluctuate during midlife interact with these brain networks. Hormones like progesterone also drop off after menopause, and observing their interaction with estradiol could offer a better biological picture.
Some participants in the current study used hormonal medications, which could influence brain connectivity differently than naturally produced hormones. Exploring the distinct effects of prescribed hormones versus natural hormones could offer a more detailed picture of cognitive aging in women.
The study, “Estradiol modulated brain connectivity in females during midlife performing an episodic memory task,” was authored by Abigail A. Testo and Julie A. Dumas.

- Saab posted a video showing a Collaborative Combat Aircraft concept marked A3-01, featuring a delta wing and stealth shaping.
- The concept may relate to an October FMV contract for Saab to study future manned and unmanned fighter systems, with demonstrator flights planned through 2027.
Saab has released the first public look at its concept for a Collaborative Combat Aircraft, an unmanned fighter designed to fly alongside crewed jets.
The video shows an aircraft marked A3-01, featuring a delta-wing design, a single jet engine, and two intakes positioned on either side of the fuselage. The airframe shows visible attention to low-observable, or stealth, shaping. Hartpunkt reported that the overall design suggests the aircraft could be capable of supersonic flight, though Saab has not confirmed a speed capability.
Saab did not disclose a name, technical specifications, or a customer for the aircraft in its post.
“The future of air combat is not just about a single aircraft, it’s about a seamless system of systems,” Saab said in the post.
“We are proud to present our concept for a future Unmanned Fighter System. Building on Swedish aviation heritage, this platform is designed to operate in tandem with manned aircraft, ensuring maximum flexibility and safety in the most contested environments. Designed for multi-domain operations and cooperation across the air, land, maritime, space, and cyber domains.”
Hartpunkt reported that the reference to multi-domain operations suggests the aircraft is intended for more than air-to-air missions, since that phrasing typically indicates a capability to operate in at least two domains, such as air and land. The outlet said this could point to an air-to-ground strike role, an electronic warfare role, or both, though Saab’s post does not specify.
A Collaborative Combat Aircraft is an uncrewed aircraft built to operate alongside crewed fighters, typically carrying sensors, weapons, or electronic warfare payloads while taking direction from a manned aircraft or ground controller. The U.S. Air Force, Australia, and other air forces are pursuing similar concepts under their own programs.
The concept may be linked to a contract Sweden’s defense procurement agency, FMV, awarded to Saab in October. That contract covered concept studies for future fighter aircraft systems, addressing both manned and unmanned solutions from a system-of-systems perspective, along with technology development and demonstrator work. Saab said at the time that the concept and technology development phases were scheduled to conclude by the third quarter of 2026, with demonstrator work continuing through 2027, including first flights.
Hartpunkt noted that this timeline lines up with Saab’s release of the concept video this week, though neither Saab nor FMV has confirmed a direct connection between the October contract and the aircraft shown in the video.
Saab has not disclosed a program name, funding level, or development timeline specific to the A3-01 concept. The company also has not said whether the aircraft shown in the video is a design study, a planned demonstrator, or an early depiction of a program still being defined. FMV has not issued a public statement on the video.

Morocco's lower-cadmium fertiliser bound for Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:00:04 UTC
22:00:04 KST

Breadcrumb
With Hormuz disruptions, Morocco's lower-cadmium fertiliser bound for Europe
At a phosphate mine in Morocco, an excavator tears into the earth to extract a mineral that is at the centre of Europe's growing concern over cadmium in the food chain.
Morocco holds vast reserves of phosphate, a key ingredient in fertilisers.
And state-owned OCP, which has a monopoly over the country's phosphate industry, says it has developed technology to reduce the amount of cadmium in its products.
Phosphate often contains naturally occurring cadmium—a heavy metal harmful to living organisms—that can seep into farmland and eventually to food through fertilisers.
According to the French health agency ANSES, phosphate deposits in Morocco naturally contained high levels of cadmium.
In France, lawmakers overwhelmingly backed a bill in June seeking to limit people's exposure to the metal, which can damage the kidneys and has been linked to a high risk of cancer.
Two-thirds of the world's reserve
At a mine in western Morocco's Sidi Chennane, a 3,000-tonne excavator removes layers of earth to reach the phosphate below.
The rock is then washed and exported in raw form or processed into phosphoric acid at an OCP industrial complex south of Casablanca.
The acid is the main ingredient in phosphate fertilisers and is combined with ammonia or other substances, depending on the type of fertiliser being made.
Since early last year, all OCP fertilisers exported to Europe have contained less than 20 milligrammes of cadmium per kilogramme, according to the company.
That's one-third of the European Union's maximum limit of 60 milligrammes per kilogramme.
An EU official told AFP that the bloc was "not in a position to verify" whether Moroccan phosphate and fertiliser exports reduced the cadmium content, due to lack of a monitoring system.
However, the official said OCP "reported" that it had "invested in decadmiation technologies over recent years" to ensure that levels of cadmium in its exports did not exceed 20 milligrammes.
Europe accounted for 17 percent of OCP's exports last year, following Asia with 41 percent and the Americas with 31 percent.
Morocco holds more than two-thirds of the world's known reserves of phosphate with an estimated 50 billion metric tonnes, counting deposits in the disputed territory of Western Sahara, which is claimed by the pro-independence Polisario Front.
The kingdom is the world's second-largest phosphate producer after China.
OCP says it lowers cadmium levels by adding "specific additives during the treatment of phosphoric acid". The metal is captured and separated before the now-purified acid is used to make fertiliser.
The company has made significant investments in the face of "regulatory approaches that vary from one market to another", OCP Nutricrops chief executive Faris Derrij told AFP.
Derrij did not disclose the level of cadmium levels in OCP exports outside of Europe.
Pollution, geopolitics
The industry has not only faced the challenge of limiting cadmium levels.
The process of making fertiliser also generates phosphogypsum, a byproduct containing heavy metals and acidic substances also linked with several health issues.
OCP plans to build a land-based storage facility by 2027 to reduce discharges of phosphogypsum into the sea and has been researching ways to reuse the waste.
Excessive use of phosphate fertiliser on crops can itself harm the environment, said Sylvain Pellerin, a research director at France's INRAE agricultural research institute.
It can lead to water contamination and the emission of nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas, Pellerin explained.
The industry is also facing the challenge of securing raw materials needed to produce fertiliser while global demand is on the rise, Pellerin added.
The US-Israeli war on Iran since late February has tightened fertiliser supplies, much of which in peacetime would have been exported from the Gulf through the disputed Strait of Hormuz.

160 grams, 118-km link, and jam-resistance by frequency-hopping: Ukraine’s answer to drone war’s connectivity problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
12:58:22 UTC
21:58:22 KST

A Ukrainian company has built a drone link designed to keep working when the enemy tries to jam it. Ukraine's defense-tech firm Rise Technologies has developed the Nakande digital communication system, designed for rapid integration into small and large FPV drones, bombers, and fixed-wing platforms, commercial director Viktor Chuikovskyi says, Defender Media reports.
The system attacks the connectivity problem that jamming creates for Ukraine's drones. On a front saturated with electronic warfare, drones that lose their radio link become useless, and Nakande answers that by constantly hopping frequencies to find clear air.
How the frequency-hopping works
Nakande's defining feature is its ability to change frequency. It hops across a tuning range of up to 1,000 MHz, monitoring channels within that band, finding a freer stretch, and automatically switching to it, Chuikovskyi said, which lets operators keep their link to drones amid electronic warfare and a congested radio spectrum.
That is the core countermeasure to jamming. By moving to whatever frequency is clear rather than staying on one the enemy can block, the system stays connected where a fixed-frequency link would be jammed dead.
What the link carries
Nakande's airborne module weighs 160 grams, supports 2×Ethernet and MAVLink, and combines control, telemetry, and video in a single secure link, with a downlink up to 5.2 Mbit/s that the maker says delivers clean video and a compressed 4K stream, protected by AES-256 encryption.
It is built for fast, flexible setup. The ground station deploys in under five minutes. Its standard IP architecture allows the operator, antenna, and control point to be separated over Ethernet, fiber, or VPN, and a single ground station can connect 50 to 100 modules.
It held a link past 100 kilometers
Nakande has been tested in combat, the maker says. It passed bench, field, and combat checks, with a dedicated range class up to 60 kilometers for FPV drones, and in testing its maximum configuration, held a link at 118 kilometers, Chuikovskyi said.
The company did not disclose the module's price but said it is several times lower than foreign equivalents.

Ebola spreading exponentially in Congo as death toll tops 2,500, UN says
More than 2,500 people have now died in the Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ebola outbreak, which is spreading exponentially in an area larger than France, senior United Nations Ebola coordinator Julien Harneis said on Aug 21.
Speaking on a video call from the north-eastern Congolese city of Bunia, Harneis called for more aid, saying an existing pool of funds is set to run out within weeks.
Health workers there were coming under attack by locals angered and terrified by the outbreak, and were themselves falling sick and dying from the disease, he added.
‘Fear translates into angry young men’
Congo’s 17th Ebola epidemic became the biggest in the country’s history in terms of the number of cases in late July, surpassing the previous worst outbreak in 2018 to 2020.
It is caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which has no approved vaccines or treatments.
“The Ebola outbreak is growing exponentially,” Harneis said.
“The epidemic is spreading to an area that is bigger than France, and the outbreak is growing faster and wider than the Ebola response. And all of this is happening in an area that has had three decades of conflict and is generating huge humanitarian needs.”
Some 160 healthcare workers have fallen ill with Ebola, and 43 of them have died, he said.
“And then, when we do respond, apart from the threat from the virus, healthcare workers and front-line workers have been attacked by youth, ambulances have been burned and stoned, and the healthcare facilities have been attacked,” he said.
“Fear translates into angry young men who start throwing stones at their object of fear, the ambulance,” he added.
Other aid workers have said locals have believed conspiracy theories that the outbreak is a hoax, and have reacted angrily when health restrictions prevent them from personally burying loved ones.
There have been more than 260 attacks on health workers in the past six months and eight health workers have been killed, Harneis said, “which is obviously terrifying because people are already risking their lives to deal with Ebola”.
Aid cuts in recent years have reduced the capacity of humanitarian organisations, he said.
Another problem is paying the tens of thousands of people involved in tackling the outbreak, he said. Banking services were hit after the government stopped commercial flights and thereby hobbled the means by which cash is delivered to banks. REUTERS

UK-German strike programme includes hypersonic weapon
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:57:11 BST
21:57:11 KST

The UK and Germany are jointly developing deep-strike options including a stealthy cruise missile and a hypersonic glide vehicle, with both countries working towards outline entry into service during the 2030s.
The UK and Germany are working on both stealthy cruise missile and hypersonic glide vehicle solutions under their joint Deep Precision Strike programme, with outline in-service dates extending into the 2030s, the UK Defence Journal understands.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard provided further detail on the programme in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Stuart Anderson, who asked what the UK’s partnership with Germany on deep precision strike weapons entails.
Pollard confirmed that a Memorandum of Understanding signed by the two countries in March 2026 has allowed British and German teams to begin aligning their military requirements and jointly examining technical solutions with industry.
He said: “The UK and Germany signed a Memorandum of Understanding in March 2026 which has enabled joint activities, including with industry, to align military requirements and invest in technical solutions under the Deep Precision Strike programme.”
The programme is examining two distinct missile approaches. Pollard confirmed: “The programme includes Stealthy Cruise and Hypersonic Glide Vehicle missile solutions.”
A stealthy cruise missile would broadly pursue survivability through reduced detectability and a powered flight profile, while a hypersonic glide vehicle represents a different technical approach, travelling at hypersonic speed following launch and manoeuvring towards its target. The parliamentary answer does not provide performance figures, ranges or details of the propulsion and launch arrangements envisaged for either solution, of course.
Pollard said the two governments had reached what he described as “positive alignment” on some of the principal requirements for the programme. He said: “There is positive alignment between the UK and Germany on key programme parameters, including operational concepts and outline target in service dates into the 2030s.”
The wording indicates that the programme remains at a relatively early technical and requirements stage, with the two countries working towards common operational concepts before later development and procurement decisions. British and German teams are currently overseeing technical work already placed with industry while preparing the next stage of contracting.
Pollard said: “Joint UK and Germany teams are now focused on delivering the currently contracted technical work with industry as well as shaping follow on contracts, underpinned in the UK by the funding outlined under the Defence Investment Plan.”
The Deep Precision Strike effort forms part of growing UK-German defence cooperation and is intended to address future requirements for weapons capable of striking targets at considerable distance. The latest answer is significant in explicitly identifying both stealthy cruise and hypersonic glide vehicle solutions as components of the work, while also placing the anticipated service timeframe in the 2030s.
The current phase is focused on technical work with industry, alignment of military requirements and the preparation of follow-on contracts as Britain and Germany determine how the programme will progress towards development and eventual fielding.

Iran quagmire: Trump’s failed strategy and its heavy cost

Unknown Publisher

Iran quagmire: Trump’s failed strategy and its heavy cost
TEHRAN- Six months into the war with Iran, the Trump administration finds itself trapped in a catastrophic quagmire of its own making. What began as a show of force has devolved into a textbook case of strategic failure, with Americans paying the price at the pump and on the world stage.
The evidence is damning. The administration has been forced into a humiliating retreat from its original war aims. The initial objective—forcing Iranian surrender, regime change, and permanently denying Tehran nuclear weapons—has been quietly shelved. Now, according to Vice President Vance, America’s primary goal is simply ensuring “low-cost oil and gas for Americans”. This is not strategy; it is survival.
The Americans won lost strategically. Tehran holds the stronger hand, leveraging its control over the Strait of Hormuz to force Washington into an impossible position. The administration’s reactive, impulsive decision-making—launching war without congressional approval, proper planning, or even informing allies—has left it with no viable options.
Trump now threatens an “economic D-Day” against any nation aiding Iran, hoping sanctions will force compliance. But this is desperation, not policy. Analysts warn that such measures will backfire, driving up global oil prices and further punishing American consumers. Meanwhile, U.S. military stockpiles are depleted, missile inventories are critically low, and support at home has cratered. With Trump’s approval rating dipping below 35 percent and midterm elections looming, the political calculus has become a death spiral.
The world is not facing an oil shortage, as the New York Times noted; it faces a refining capacity crisis. But Trump’s war has compounded this problem, disrupting global supply chains while offering no coherent exit strategy. “The United States has no usable cards left,” analysts conclude.
Trump inherited challenges. He has instead created a catastrophe—one that weakens America, strengthens Iran, and leaves the region more volatile than before. This is not leadership. It is incompetence on a grand scale.

Days After Putin’s First Visit, Russia Fires Missiles Near Islands Claimed by Japan

Days After Putin’s First Visit, Russia Fires Missiles Near Islands Claimed by Japan
Days after Putin’s first-ever visit to the disputed Kuril Islands, Russia staged rare missile drills nearby—using a nuclear submarine, a missile cruiser, and a Bastion coastal system in a fresh show of force toward Japan.
Russia has carried out rare missile drills involving naval vessels and a ground-based launcher near the disputed southern Kuril Islands, adding to already heightened tensions with Japan, Bloomberg reported on August 21.
Russia’s Pacific Fleet said missiles were launched from a nuclear-powered submarine, a missile cruiser, and a Bastion coastal defense system operating in the area of the southern Kurils. The fleet did not specify when the exercises took place.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Russian military, the missiles were fired at targets located more than 300 kilometers, or about 186 miles, away and successfully struck them.
The Pacific Fleet did not disclose the exact location of the drills. Russia has, however, deployed Bastion coastal defense batteries on Iturup, known in Japan as Etorofu, since 2016.
The exercises drew a sharp reaction from Tokyo.
“Russia’s military buildup on the four Northern Islands runs counter to Japan’s position and is unacceptable,” Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi told reporters.
The southern Kuril Islands have remained under Russian control since Soviet forces seized them from Japan in the final days of World War II. Tokyo continues to claim Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan, and the Habomai islets, collectively referring to them as the Northern Territories.
The missile drills came only days after Russian leader Vladimir Putin made his first visit to the disputed territory, traveling to Iturup last week. Japan formally protested that visit as well.
The long-running territorial dispute has prevented Russia and Japan from signing a formal peace treaty since World War II.
The latest military activity also comes as Japan continues to support Ukraine against Russia’s war of aggression, including through sanctions on Moscow.
Tokyo has also provided Ukraine with non-lethal military assistance, including body armor and vehicles.
During his recent visit to Russia’s Far East, Putin accused Japan of changing its approach toward Moscow without provocation. He criticized Japanese sanctions and pointed to defense documents in which Tokyo identifies Russia as a serious security threat.
The combination of Putin’s first visit to Iturup and the missile drills has added fresh pressure to one of the longest-running territorial disputes in East Asia, with Moscow now visibly demonstrating strike capabilities near islands Japan still considers its own.
Previously, Russia sent four missile-armed warships near Japan, with the vessels passing about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from Hokkaido a day after Putin visited Iturup, one of the disputed Kuril Islands claimed by Japan.

Norway’s King Herald to remain in hospital, cancels engagements

Norway’s King Harald to remain in hospital, cancels engagements
OSLO – Norway’s 89-year-old King Harald, who has been hospitalised since Aug 17 due to complications from a blood condition, has cancelled his royal engagements in early September, the palace said on Aug 21.
Europe’s oldest reigning monarch is being treated for haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells which leads to fatigue, paleness, and shortness of breath.
He was admitted to hospital on Aug 17 due to fluid retention from the cortisone treatment he is receiving, and placed on sick leave for two weeks.
“His Majesty the King will remain at Oslo University Hospital for further treatment,” the palace said on Aug 21.
It said he had cancelled his visit to the central region of Trondelag scheduled for Sept 1 and Sept 2 – after the end of the previously-announced sick leave period.
King Harald, who ascended the Norwegian throne in 1991, has had multiple health problems in recent years but has repeatedly ruled out abdicating.
Several members of his family, including his son Crown Prince Haakon who is serving as regent in Harald’s absence, have visited him in hospital. AFP

The HACC arrested Maksym Mykytas with bail set at UAH 30 million
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:55:59 EEST
21:55:59 KST

The HACC arrested Maksym Mykytas with bail set at UAH 30 million
Kyiv • UNN
The HACC remanded Maksym Mykytas in custody with bail set at UAH 30 million instead of the UAH 200 million requested by the prosecution. He said he was ready to cooperate.
On August 21, the High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC) imposed pre-trial detention on former Member of Parliament and former head of Ukrbud Maksym Mykytas, with the possibility of posting bail in the amount of UAH 30 million. This was reported by UNN.
Details
It should be noted that the prosecution requested bail in the amount of UAH 200 million. However, during the court hearing, Mykytas stated that he was ready to cooperate with the investigation. At the same time, he called the criminal proceedings against him a "political manipulation."
Mykytas's lawyer, in turn, tried to convince the presiding judge that the amount of bail should be "manageable" for his client. After all, according to the lawyer, the former head of Ukrbud does not possess the UAH 200 million insisted upon by the state prosecutor.
The defense lawyer also explained why detention was not the best pre-trial measure for his client. The lawyer told the court that Mykytas did not own financial or business assets in other countries and had no close persons, relatives, or simply good acquaintances abroad. Therefore, he had no motivation to leave Ukraine.
The lawyer placed particular emphasis on the fact that Mykytas himself had agreed to cooperate with the investigation. Consequently, he would not hide from justice. Therefore, it was entirely unnecessary to resort to such a pre-trial measure as arrest.
However, his arguments did not convince the presiding judge.
Context
Mykytas is one of the suspects in the case being investigated by NABU and SAPO as part of the special operation "Forest Gump." According to the investigation, he may have been involved, together with other individuals, in the activities of a criminal organization engaged in corporate raiding and the legalization of funds.
One of the episodes in the proceedings concerns UAH 150 million which, according to the investigation, was to be legalized through controlled companies and used to post bail for one of the suspects in another anti-corruption investigation—the "Midas" operation.
The investigative materials state that in June 2026, participants in the alleged criminal organization received UAH 150 million in cash, which they planned to move through a number of companies in order to make it appear to be funds of legal origin. The money was subsequently supposed to be used as bail. According to anti-corruption organizations, this concerned bail for former Minister of Energy and Justice Herman Halushchenko.
In addition, NABU and SAPO link the group's activities to the alleged corporate raiding of two enterprises in the autumn of 2025. Law enforcement officials estimate the value of their assets at approximately UAH 248 million. The investigation is also examining an attempt to seize other real estate in Kyiv worth more than UAH 200 million.
According to NABU, forged court decisions and documents, interference with the electronic accounts of state registrars, and the registration of corporate rights in the names of nominal owners may have been used in implementing the schemes.
Mykytas's defense denies the criminal nature of the actions attributed to him. The lawyers claimed that the actions concerning certain enterprises were aimed at restoring the businessman's property rights, which, in their version, had previously been violated.
The pre-trial investigation is ongoing.
Reminder
Maksym Mykytas became one of the suspects in the NABU and SAPO special operation called "Forest Gump," which the anti-corruption agencies announced on August 19.

Ebola outbreak in DR Congo growing 'exponentially' as death toll passes 2,500
More than half of the 2,500-plus deaths from DR Congo's Ebola outbreak have occurred within the past 20 days alone, as the virus spreads faster than any recorded outbreak, according to the UN's senior Ebola coordinator. Julien Harneis is urging a rapid scale-up of resources to prevent the epidemic from crossing into neighbouring countries.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The Ebola outbreak raging in DR Congo is growing "exponentially", with more than 2,500 deaths now recorded, with half in the last 20 days, the United Nations' senior Ebola coordinator said Friday.
The Ebola outbreak is already the biggest in the country's history and is spreading faster than any outbreak on record.
According to the latest figures, the virus eruption is "growing exponentially", Julien Harneis told reporters in Geneva, speaking from Bunia, at the epicentre of the outbreak.
He said that in the last three months, "more than 2,500 people" had died, "and half of those in the last 20 days".
'Speading widely'
"The epidemic is spreading widely. It's now covering an area that is bigger than France ... It is growing faster and wider than the Ebola response."
Declared on May 15, DR Congo's 17th Ebola outbreak is thought to have already been spreading for several weeks by that point.
It has hit regions in the north and east where the presence of the state is weak, health infrastructure is largely lacking and myriad armed groups have roamed for decades.

Harneis stressed the need to ramp up the response, insisting that "if we provide more staffing, if we get more resources into remote areas across ... the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo, within months we can slow the transmission and move to stopping it.
"If we do not, ... then this epidemic will become more deadly. It will spread wider and it risks to spread into neighbouring countries."

‘I don’t think beyond tomorrow’: How people in occupied Crimea are surviving one of the hardest summers of the war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
12:55:55 UTC
21:55:55 KST

‘I don’t think beyond tomorrow’: How people in occupied Crimea are surviving one of the hardest summers of the war
This summer in occupied Crimea has been one of the hardest in decades: Crimean cities are regularly shelled by Ukraine, there are few tourists, prices are rising, and there are regular outages of electricity, water, and gasoline. The Bereg cooperative talked to Crimean residents living in different parts of the region, from Dzhankoi to Alupka, about how they’re surviving and why they don’t even consider leaving. Meduza is publishing this piece in full.
The names of the people in this story have been changed for their safety.
‘We live like this: we buy a piece of meat at the store, cook it right away, and eat it’
Iryna
Dzhankoi; about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from mainland Ukraine
I’m from the Kherson region, but I moved to Dzhankoi in 2023. I don’t have any relatives here. We [my husband and I and our two children] moved on our own. We live in a two-story house in Dzhankoi, and when there are strikes, we go down from the second floor and sit in the bathroom.
Strikes happen regularly here. Drones target electrical substations and are shot down right over residential neighborhoods. In May, one hit a house, killing five people, damaging nearby buildings, including stores, and blowing out windows and doors. Since then, drones have also struck the railway station and a substation. Coming from the Kherson region, though, I’ve long since gotten used to all this.
We had no power for two weeks starting July 6. Now it’s back for four hours a day, at just 95 volts — not enough to run a refrigerator or washing machine. The only thing we can manage is charging a phone. We live like this: we buy a piece of meat at the store and cook and eat it right away. It’s not like before, when the refrigerator was always full. And now we wash our clothes by hand.
Authorities promised a [one-time] payment of 15,000 rubles per person to anyone who went without power for more than 48 hours. I applied on July 12, and it’s still under review, even though I’ve seen reports that other people have already been paid.
My older child used to go to daycare, but it closed for two weeks of repairs at the start of summer. It was supposed to reopen on July 1 but never did — all the daycares are now closed because of the power situation. Only emergency programs remain open, for children whose parents work and have no one else to watch them.
We bought an inverter generator for 25,000 rubles, which we turn on in the evening so our son can watch cartoons for a couple of hours. Our daughter, who’s a year old, is afraid of the dark, so turn on a lamp for her before bed to help calm her fears.
Water runs from 6 p.m. to 10 a.m., but the pressure is too weak to wash properly. It’s only strong enough at 3 a.m., so that’s when you wash your hair.
Gas right now [August 10] costs 190 rubles for 95 octane and 150 rubles for 92 octane, though it’s also sold for as much as 300 rubles, with lines stretching for kilometers. My family doesn’t have a car, but I know the going rate because a friend of mine paid that price.
Every product is still available in stores, but prices have risen sharply for staples like bread, sunflower oil, and sugar. A kilogram [2.2 pounds] of sugar used to cost 70 rubles; now it’s 100. Supermarkets bought powerful generators so shoppers could still get butter, sausage, and cheese, and customers can charge phones and power banks inside — the same goes for the city administration building and the local history museum. Walk down the street now and you’ll hear an incredible noise from all the generators.
I’m on maternity leave, and my husband used to work as a freight forwarder, but the company shut down until September. People think everything will get better in the fall, but I wonder what exactly they expect to change come September. Nobody really knows.
In any case, my husband found another job and is now doing an internship. Work is hard to find right now — the Dzhankoi dairy plant and several other companies have closed — and some of our acquaintances are simply staying home.
We’re planning to stay in Dzhankoi — I don’t see the point in fleeing somewhere else, since even a place like Krasnodar gets hit too. What makes me angriest is that the [city] administration isn’t doing anything about the power, while in Krasnoperekopsk, Armiansk, and Krasnohvardiiske, everything has already been fixed and the power is back on. We’re told the electricians are working around the clock, but I don’t believe it. By now, with all the time that’s passed, they could have restored so much of the power supply that I honestly don’t know what to say.
‘Every day, the standard of living falls lower and lower’
Ihor
Sevastopol; about 220 kilometers (137 miles) from mainland Ukraine
I don’t have a car, so the fuel crisis hasn’t hit me the way it has drivers, but it’s still affected me, as supply issues have pushed up prices at supermarkets. At Yeda Voda, for example, shelves were half-empty in early August. There’s also a big problem with Ozon, which has stopped accepting orders from Crimea; [local media] report that its warehouses are overflowing and nothing is being delivered.
Power is cut every day, sometimes for up to eight hours. Usually there’s no electricity from 6 to 8 a.m., then it comes on for four hours before going off again for another four. I work from home, so all of this is genuinely disruptive, and I rely on mobile internet to get by. I haven’t bought a generator since it’s impractical in an apartment, and gas is expensive anyway.
I don’t go to the beach — that’s just how much of a typical local I am. But even on the street, I notice fewer people and cars than last year. Every day, the standard of living falls lower and lower.
Sometimes strikes happen almost every day; other times there’s a lull for about a month. A missile recently hit near my house at 5 a.m., and it was terrifying. At moments like that I hide in the bathroom, though if it hits the house directly, nothing will help, since we have gas. Just as you start getting used to it, another strike comes, and it’s frightening all over again.
I have plenty of reasons not to leave. Just when it seems like it’s time to pack up, something happens [in my personal life] that makes leaving impossible. Plus, I don’t know where I’d go — so for now, I’m staying put.
I just wish Ukraine would come back and life could return to normal. Of course, it will never truly be like before, but at least this whole situation would somehow be resolved.
‘My husband’s workweek was cut from five days to three’
Inga
Ukromnoye, Simferopol district; about 130 kilometers (81 miles) from mainland Ukraine
I live with my husband and our three children. Overall, the power situation is manageable, but on days when it’s out for 5–6 hours, food in the freezer thaws and spoils. Our water comes from a well, so when the power goes, so does the water — we stock up whenever it’s running. We bought a 75,000-ruble generator for the house, essentially a battery that charges up and then supplies electricity.
My husband works in a neighboring village, where the power is often out for entire days, coming and going unpredictably. His company installed a generator too. His workweek was cut from five days to three, and we lost a third of our income. He’s currently our family’s only breadwinner, and I’m afraid he could be out of work entirely by winter if things keep going this way.
Supermarket prices have gone up by 30%. Cheaper chains like “Ambar” have half-empty shelves, though other stores still have a decent selection.
We’ve driven to the mainland three times for gas, buying 200 liters (53 gallons) each trip — it’s cheaper, and the fuel quality is better there.
During shelling we hide with the kids in the bathroom, though it’s been quiet lately. Our oldest, 17, understands everything and is scared just like we are. The middle child, 7, mostly sleeps through it, and so does the youngest, who’s a year old.
We thought about leaving at one point, but for now we’ve decided to stay. With three kids it’s complicated — our oldest is entering his final year of school, and the middle child is just starting. We’ve decided to get through the winter here and see what comes after that.
‘How my animals and I will stay warm this winter is a mystery’
Anna
A village in northwestern Crimea
The district where I was born and still live borders Ukraine by sea. I moved to the district center when I was young, then came back in 2014.
My return coincided with the neighboring state [how Anna refers to Ukraine] declaring a blockade of the peninsula. Many vacation resorts around the village closed as a result, since visitors stopped coming, and the dogs that had guarded those resorts were abandoned. They ran into the village looking for food among the people there.
I felt sorry for them, so I started feeding some and tried to find homes for others through social media, but I wasn’t able to place a single one.
It had the opposite effect: once people saw my posts, they started bringing animals to me from all over the district. Someone once just walked up and tied an adult dog to my fence. Others brought me animals found on the road with broken legs, or rescued from conflict zones. Several small puppies were pulled out literally from under a lawnmower.
In total, I now have 90 cats and 30 dogs. My property has no kennels or other special facilities — they all live with me at home, with some staying with relatives and others at abandoned vacation resorts. I’m a pensioner, and almost nobody helps me. It’s impossible to support that many animals on a single welfare payment, so I rely on people who care to pitch in.
The power problems started sometime in July, though I don’t remember exactly when, since I spend all my time busy with the animals. At first there was no electricity for two days, then it came back briefly before going out again for another two days. Then something serious happened, and we went five days without electricity, water, or gas.
Since I usually feed the animals porridge instead of store-bought pet food, I had to cook for myself and for them over an open fire. Fortunately, the administration brought me and other village residents a free gas canister in early August, but I’m almost afraid to even look at it or breathe on it — I’m trying to conserve it.
We recently bought an electric hot plate and cook on it whenever there’s power. Today [August 10] there was no power at all, so I had to give the animals dry food. The electricity now gets turned on and off at random, with no schedule at all, but we’ve adapted.
I used to buy pet food from Wildberries and Ozon, but now they refuse to deliver here. It’s more expensive at the store, and the nearest one is 25 kilometers (16 miles) away — I don’t have a car, but people help out.
When there are strikes, the animals get anxious. The dogs often start barking even before a drone alert comes in. I head for the bathroom, and the dogs and cats scatter to their hiding spots.
I’ve never even considered leaving the village. My relatives once told me, “If there’s an evacuation, leave them all behind. Health comes first.” But where would I abandon them all? Are they supposed to just die here alone? I’m not going anywhere.
I don’t make big plans — I don’t think beyond tomorrow, and I just deal with things as they come. Winter worries me because we rely on electric heaters. In past winters, only the cats had heating, since they live with me indoors, but heating with convection heaters is expensive, so we saved however we could. Of the eight heaters we needed, only three worked, and five were broken. Building warm enclosures for all the animals is my biggest dream.
How my animals and I will stay warm this winter is a mystery. The other villagers have stoves they can heat with coal and firewood, but no one can imagine how much that will cost.
I try to distance myself from the situation we’re in. I do my own thing, and I’m grateful to the animals for keeping me distracted.
More than anything, I want peace.
‘If the accumulated problems aren’t solved urgently, there will be a revolt’
Oleh
Dzhankoi; about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from mainland Ukraine
I live in Dzhankoi. We had no electricity at all from July 5 to 16. Starting July 17, power was supplied irregularly for 2–4 hours a day, at a catastrophically low voltage of 120–140 volts, or 150 if we were lucky. In some villages, it doesn’t even reach 100 volts.
At that voltage, basic appliances like refrigerators and washing machines would either fail to turn on at all, in the best case, or literally burn out in the worst. I was careful with mine — or maybe just lucky — and nothing burned out. To avoid the risk, I bought a voltage stabilizer, but it doesn’t help much, since most models don’t work at input voltages below 150 volts.
In August, daytime temperatures in Crimea reach nearly 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit), so without a refrigerator, food spoils within hours, and I had to forget about air conditioning entirely. A neighbor with a generator saved me by running power to my refrigerator for four hours a day. Stable power was restored in Dzhankoi on August 12, though in the surrounding villages, the situation still leaves much to be desired.
I live on the first floor and have been lucky with water — it’s almost always available. It’s much harder for village residents and for Dzhankoi residents on higher floors, since the water supply depends on electricity. For them it often comes out as a thin trickle for 2–3 hours, and sometimes there’s no water at all for a whole day.
Food prices have risen noticeably. Perishable goods like vegetables, fruit, and sausages have disappeared from stores, though everything else is still available.
Overall, people are desperate — they’ve been pushed to the limit. If the accumulated problems aren’t solved urgently, there will be a revolt.
I’ve thought about moving, but for now, that’s all it is — a thought.
‘I’m getting by however I can, and I’m not planning to leave’
Anton
Alupka; about 980 kilometers (609 miles) from mainland Ukraine
Starting around July 21, the city went four days straight without power. Now it’s supplied from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. Conditions are worse in other cities, but we may get more [electricity] because we have no gas.
I recently passed through Yalta and saw people crowding outside supermarkets to charge their phones, since the stores had put out extension cords. We’ve had something similar here too, but only during total power outages.
I have a car and a scooter, but I haven’t been to a gas station in a while. I only heard that [Kremlin-appointed Crimea head Sergey] Aksyonov [as of August 4] set the price of 92-octane gasoline at 100 rubles. In early July, I drove to the mainland and brought back 100 liters (26 gallons) of gasoline, waiting in line eight times at four different stations over the course of a day. People around me were tense and angry.
The last time I filled up was in early August, at 190 rubles, with no lines at all. I just drove up and that was it. The most I’ve ever paid was 275 rubles, and resellers have charged as much as 350, even 500 rubles. But what choice do you have?
I ride a motorcycle to work now to save fuel. Since the start of August, I’ve been working as an assistant at a private villa. Before that I worked at a factory, but construction was frozen due to logistics problems along the “Novorossiya” highway.
I used to give tours for tourists every summer, and my pay depended on how much work I did. This year there are no tourists at all, so I didn’t even bother trying.
These days I hardly go anywhere except work — only on weekends do I treat myself to the beach. Everyone there is local; I can tell from the license plates.
In Crimea they banned riding motorcycles from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m., saying they sound like drones — they can tow your scooter to an impound lot and fine you 30,000 rubles. I once got lost near Sudak and had to sleep on a mountain pass; luckily, I had a sleeping bag and a hammock with me, and something was being bombed in the distance all night. Now I always race home by 9:30 to make it in time.
Drones almost never fly over Alupka. There was only one time, [July 22], when I heard explosions at night, after which the power went out. But near Sevastopol, where I vacationed last year, there was constant cannon fire. It was scary.
Because of the power outages, various products disappeared from supermarkets for a while — dairy, for example — but now there are almost no empty shelves anywhere. The one thing I’ve noticed missing is cigarettes. At Yeda Voda, 70% of the products are gone. Only vodka is left. Other stores bought generators and reorganized how they operate.
At the store near my house, while there was no power, employees would unscrew the cap off a bottle of water I wanted to buy, keep it, and screw on a different one. That way, once the power came back, they could scan the item into the Chestny Znak system. Sellers also copied barcodes into a notebook by hand.
Prices have gone up by about 30%. I used to buy the “Adrenaline” energy drink for 110 rubles; now it costs 160. Camping gas canisters have gotten a lot more expensive too — they used to cost 100 rubles, peaked at 250, and now sell for 170. These canisters are the main lifesaver for people when the power goes out.
I’m getting by however I can, and I’m not planning to leave. My mother is here, and I don’t want to abandon her. The mood, of course, isn’t great, but we’re living one day at a time. Back in late May there was still confidence that the tourist season would take off and we’d be able to earn good money. This summer, there’s no hope of that.
Winter is coming soon, and I hope I’ll be able to earn at least a little money to buy alternative energy sources — a big gas canister, say — so I’ll have something to cook and heat the apartment with.
I really want all of this to end.

MOSCOW, August 21. /TASS/. The Russian Foreign Ministry is concerned about instances in which law enforcement officials from unfriendly states directly send investigative requests to Russian legal entities, bypassing competent authorities, Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
Journalists asked Zakharova to comment on reports that law enforcement officials from unfriendly countries had sent such requests directly to Russian legal entities to obtain information about people they suspected of committing criminal offenses.
"We note such cases with concern. I would remind you that in 2022, almost all Western countries unilaterally halted cooperation with Russia in providing mutual legal assistance in criminal matters. Now they are trying to bypass competent Russian authorities, violating established procedures and bilateral and multilateral obligations. In other words, they are behaving as though they were at home," she said.
Zakharova reminded former partners that such unauthorized activity on Russian territory is subject to criminal penalties. She noted that the Russian Criminal Code was supplemented in 2025 with Article 294.1, "Illegal conduct of investigative and other procedural actions and operational-search activities on the territory of the Russian Federation," specifically to counter attempts to unlawfully obtain information. The article provides for fines of 500,000 to 2 million rubles (roughly $6,000 to $24,000) or imprisonment for up to five years.
According to the diplomat, the amendments were also needed to prevent unfriendly countries from interfering in Russia's internal affairs and to disrupt schemes whereby Western intelligence services had, in effect, lured Russian nationals abroad in order to detain them.
"We recommend that accredited diplomatic missions of unfriendly states carefully review the relevant explanatory material and bring this information to the attention of their national law enforcement agencies," the spokeswoman said.

Hendrik Johannes Terras: Where will agriculture's €546 million go?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
12:55:00 UTC
21:55:00 KST

Hendrik Johannes Terras: Where will agriculture's €546 million go?
Estonia's lower level of agricultural support was taken into account when calculating funding for the next EU budget period. This increased Estonia's allocation by roughly €546 million. The European Commission left it to Estonia to decide how to use this opportunity, writes Hendrik Johannes Terras.
At the Ministry of Finance, a working group of 17 specialists assessed ministries' requests and drafted the first allocation proposal. According to the sector, only €295 million of this would actually go toward developing agriculture and food production: €245 million for food security and €50 million for the food industry.
Finance Minister Jürgen Ligi has said he fought to keep the money within the agricultural field. Looking at the budget lines, that is true. But within those lines, the money is intended for very different purposes.
The Ministry of Climate is slated to receive €117 million from agricultural funding. This would go toward biodiversity in private forests in Natura 2000 areas, maintaining heritage meadows, protecting water and soil, and forestry investments. To find this money, agricultural measures had to be reduced.
These expenses serve environmental goals. Agriculture needs fertile soil and clean water, and heritage meadows can combine nature conservation with livestock grazing. But biodiversity support in Natura 2000 private forests does not build pig farms or increase egg production, and forestry investments do not improve Estonia's food self‑sufficiency.
If agricultural money is used for forest‑related environmental obligations, a choice has been made in favor of environmental goals at the expense of agriculture and food production. This cannot later be counted as investment in production capacity.
Of the €245 million planned for food security, €85 million would go toward increasing self‑sufficiency and critical production capacity — pig farming, poultry meat and eggs, horticulture, potatoes, greenhouses, irrigation, storage, and breeding.
€110 million is intended for productivity and competitiveness: technology, resource efficiency, biogas, renewable energy, and value‑adding.
€50 million goes toward crisis resilience. This includes biosecurity and land improvement, but also reserves, logistics, food safety, and the capabilities of the Agriculture and Food Board (PTA) and the state's laboratory and risk assessment center (LABRIS). Not all of this money goes to agricultural enterprise investments.
The food industry would receive €50 million over seven years — down from €78.1 million in the current budget period.
This is how the sector arrives at €295 million. Even that figure includes activities that do not result in new farms, greenhouses, production lines, or processing capacity.
Farmers view the funding plan differently than budget planners. A pig farmer wants to know whether he can build or modernize a farm. A horticulture producer needs greenhouses, irrigation, and storage. A dairy producer needs processing capacity. The food industry needs new lines and technology. More value must be created from grain in Estonia.
Our starting point is not good. In 2024, the value of buildings, machinery, and equipment in Estonian agricultural enterprises was €1,567 per hectare, compared with the EU average of €2,456. Output value was €1,350 per hectare in Estonia and €3,025 in the EU.
Last year, Estonia imported €539 million more in agricultural and food products than it exported. These numbers will not improve through environmental obligations, crisis reserves, or agency capabilities — only through increased production and processing capacity in Estonia.
Since February, I have said that the €546 million opportunity must be used to develop agriculture and food production. Prime Minister Kristen Michal has said the €546 million must go to agriculture and food production.
That promise must be visible in the funding plan. Environmental money must be called environmental money, crisis reserves must be called crisis reserves, and production investment must be called investment.
Seventeen specialists made the first allocation proposal based on the entire country's financial needs. The sector looks at the same proposal through the lens of whether Estonia will have more capacity to produce food domestically in 2034. The government must now decide which need carries more weight when allocating the €546 million.

Why are Hong Kong’s Tiananmen vigil organisers facing prison?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
12:54:44 UTC
21:54:44 KST

Why are Hong Kong’s Tiananmen vigil organisers facing prison?
Amnesty International said they ‘must be released immediately and unconditionally’.
Two prominent Hong Kong activists who helped organise annual vigils commemorating China’s deadly 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown have been convicted of inciting subversion under the city’s national security law.
On Friday, Hong Kong’s High Court found former legislator Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and lawyer Chow Hang-tung, 41, guilty of what is one of the most serious offences under the sweeping security law imposed by Beijing in 2020.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Pakistan’s Imran Khan back to prison after evaluation at hospital
- list 2 of 4Philippines floods fuel anger over alleged corruption
- list 3 of 4Nord Stream bombing suspect to Hollywood fixer: Who is Volodymyr Zhuravlev?
- list 4 of 4Northern Italy seeks to keep the pressure on the south as Serie A returns
The pair, who pleaded not guilty to inciting subversion, have been held in detention since they were charged in September 2021. They face up to 10 years in prison, with sentencing to take place at a later date. A third defendant, veteran activist Albert Ho, 74, pleaded guilty before the trial began.
The case is among Hong Kong’s highest-profile prosecutions under the national security law and has renewed scrutiny of the erosion of political freedoms in the territory as Beijing expands its influence there. Here is what we know.
Who are Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung?
Lee and Chow were leading members of the now-disbanded, pro-democracy action group Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, which for decades organised Hong Kong’s annual candlelight vigil commemorating those killed in the Tiananmen crackdown.
The alliance was established in May 1989 as protests calling for political reform in China gathered momentum in Beijing and other cities. Over the following three decades, it campaigned for accountability over the brutal crackdown on protests, the release of political dissidents and democratic reform in China.
Lee, a former Hong Kong politician and veteran labour activist, served as the alliance’s chairman, while Chow, a barrister, was its vice chairwoman.
Prosecutors accused the alliance and its leaders of inciting others to subvert state power. Central to the case was the organisation’s longstanding slogan calling to “end one-party” system in China.
The court ruled that the slogan sought to instigate hostility towards the Chinese Communist Party and undermine the political system established under China’s constitution. Lee and Chow maintained that their political advocacy was peaceful and protected by Hong Kong’s guarantees of freedom of expression.
Both were convicted on Friday. Ho, another former alliance leader, had already pleaded guilty to the same charge.
What happened to Hong Kong’s Tiananmen vigils?
Hong Kong was previously one of the few places under Chinese sovereignty where large public commemorations of the Tiananmen crackdown were permitted.
On June 4, 1989, Chinese troops opened fire on demonstrators after weeks of largely peaceful protests centred around Beijing’s Tiananmen Square, calling for political reform. Hundreds – possibly thousands – of people were killed, while thousands more were arrested.
Public discussion and commemoration of the crackdown have long been heavily censored in mainland China.
Hong Kong was different. Under the “one country, two systems” arrangement established when Britain handed the territory back to China in 1997, Hong Kong retained some of the freedoms unavailable on the mainland.
Every June 4, crowds gathered in the city’s Victoria Park for a candlelight vigil commemorating those killed and demanding accountability from Beijing. At their height, the commemorations drew crowds numbering in the tens of thousands.
The last major vigil organised by the alliance was held in 2019, the 30th anniversary of the crackdown. The authorities banned the gatherings in 2020 and 2021, initially citing COVID-19 restrictions. They have not resumed.
What is Hong Kong’s national security law?
The vigils ceased just as Hong Kong was undergoing a much broader political transformation following months of mass antigovernment and pro-democracy protests in 2019.
In June 2020, Beijing imposed a new national security law in Hong Kong, criminalising secession, subversion, terrorism and collusion with foreign forces.
Chinese and Hong Kong authorities said the legislation was necessary to restore stability following the 2019 unrest and to ensure rights and freedoms remained protected.
Human rights groups say, however, its broad provisions have been used to dismantle much of Hong Kong’s organised political opposition and restrict some individual freedoms that once distinguished the territory from mainland China.
Since the law was introduced, leading opposition figures have been prosecuted, political organisations and civil society groups have disbanded, and independent media outlets have closed.
Why is this case so controversial?
Rights groups say the prosecution of Lee and Chow in effect criminalises peaceful political advocacy and the commemoration of one of the most difficult episodes in modern Chinese history.
Responding to Friday’s verdict, Amnesty International Hong Kong Overseas spokesperson Fernando Cheung said it showed how the national security law was being used to “punish people for peacefully remembering” the Tiananmen crackdown.
“For decades, Hong Kong was the only place on Chinese soil where large-scale public remembrance of the Tiananmen crackdown could take place,” Cheung said, describing the convictions as another step in what Amnesty says is a campaign to erase its legacy and silence demands for accountability.
Amnesty International Deputy Regional Director Sarah Brooks called Lee and Chow “prisoners of conscience” and said they “should never have been prosecuted in the first place”, calling for their immediate and unconditional release.
