Ceuta: Spanish police arrest 5 alleged migrant traffickers
August 21, 2026
Spanish police have arrested five people suspected of charging migrants thousands of euros to bring them from Ceuta, Spain's North African exclave, to mainland Spain.
The arrests come less than a month after the Spanish territory, which borders Morocco, saw a deadly border rush in which over 70,000 migrants entered Ceuta irregularly, with many swimming or crossing on foot.
Dozens of people died in the chaotic scenes. Ceuta's leader Juan Jesus Vivas told EU lawmakers that some 100 people had died, while Spanish NGO Caminando Fronteras said the death toll was 141 people.
The incident renewed debate in Europe on the sensitive issue of migration. Italy temporarily suspended Schengen border-free travel with Spain in response, with Madrid retaliating by imposing border controls on travelers from Italy.
What did Spanish police say about the arrests?
Five people were arrested after two investigations in Ceuta and in La Linea de la Concepcion in Andalusia, which borders British overseas territory Gibraltar.
The suspected traffickers allegedly charged migrants up to €9,000 ($10,500), Spain's Interior Ministry said in a statement, adding that the suspects used small boats "to smuggle migrants from Ceuta to the mainland."
Four of the people arrested are alleged members of a trafficking network that picked up undocumented migrants, sheltered them in houses or garages in Ceuta before smuggling them across the Strait of Gibraltar to Spain.
"Boat drivers were selected for their experience navigating fast and their ability to make evasive manoeuvres and avoid police checks," the statement said.
In one of the crossings, seven people were crammed into an overcrowded dinghy that was barely five meters (16 feet) long and two meters wide for five hours, without life jackets or other adequate safety equipment, police said. The boat ran out of fuel and was left adrift in the Strait of Gibraltar.
Strong currents, changing tides, high winds and heavy maritime traffic combine to make the Strait of Gibraltar extremely dangerous for people attempting to cross it in small boats.
What is the current situation in Ceuta?
Most of the estimated 72,000 migrants who entered Ceuta in late July have returned to Morocco, Spanish officials say. But thousands remain in the enclave, sleeping in makeshift camps, on the street or on the beach.
More than 1,000 migrants were cleared from Trampolin Beach on Friday, after more than 1,200 people were evacuated from the site the day before and moved to shelters.
The Spanish government in Madrid has said it will open temporary centers to ease the burden on Ceuta's overcrowded migrant shelters.

19:54:33 CST
20:54:33 KST

WASHINGTON, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- U.S. housing starts fell sharply in July, dropping 12.4 percent from the previous month, data released Tuesday by the U.S. Census Bureau and the Department of Housing and Urban Development showed.
Privately owned housing starts fell to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.239 million units, down 13.5 percent from a year earlier. The reading was also weaker than economists had expected.
"The drop in starts was striking," Dean Baker, a macroeconomist and co-founder of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, told Xinhua.
"It's clearly a response to higher interest rates," Baker said.
The average contract rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage stood at 6.77 percent in the latest Mortgage Bankers Association survey, close to its highest level in more than a year.
Single-family starts fell 9.9 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 808,000 units, the lowest level since November 2022. Multifamily starts dropped 16.8 percent after surging in June.
Regionally, housing starts fell 27.6 percent in the Midwest, 13.8 percent in the West and 12.6 percent in the South. The Northeast was the only region to post an increase, with starts rising 17.1 percent.
Baker said whether housing starts remain low or begin to recover depends on several factors, including interest rates and the Iran war.
"We may also get a recession if the war continues and oil prices go even higher," he said.
The weak housing data could also carry political implications ahead of November's midterm elections.
Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, said the drop in housing starts indicates businesses are not confident in the overall economy.
"They don't want to invest money in a situation where they are not sure about the rate of return," West told Xinhua.
"This is just one more sign of an economy that is not going well and that likely will harm Republican prospects in November," he said. ■

BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- China has unveiled a plan to build a modern climate service system by 2030, with a strong focus on innovation and digital intelligence to bring key areas to world-class levels.
The plan, issued by the China Meteorological Administration, calls for major progress during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) in technological independence, digitized operations, scenario-based services, and integrated platforms to enhance climate services.
The country will establish a national-provincial data-sharing network and a coordinated working framework, so that any update made at one level is instantly available across the entire system, according to the plan.
National-level institutions will take the lead in technology research and development, platform construction, and standard setting. They will also develop Earth system models and AI-based climate prediction tools, according to the plan.
Provincial weather services will zero in on detailed local monitoring, impact evaluation, and customized forecasting and risk assessment. They will also protect climate resources, carry out feasibility studies, and tailor their products to fit the specific needs of different regions.
City- and county-level offices will apply national and provincial products locally, establish their own procedures and norms, and provide climate monitoring and prediction services suited to their administrative areas, according to the plan.
Over the next five years, the plan outlines 19 priority tasks aimed at strengthening five areas, including Earth system monitoring, independent climate prediction and disaster risk assessment, sector-focused services, basic support infrastructure, and institutional reforms for high-quality development.
China has already deployed advanced technologies such as drone swarms for typhoon observation and AI-driven early warning models. These tools have benefited not only China but also communities worldwide by improving early warning and disaster preparedness. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: From Homer to Hollywood, how the ancient city of Troy won't stay buried
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
19:54:20 CST
20:54:20 KST

CANAKKALE, TÜRKIYE, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- More than 3,000 years after the legendary Trojan War, the ancient city of Troy is once again in the global spotlight.
With Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey now in theaters worldwide, audiences are revisiting the story of Odysseus, the hero in Greek mythology who embarks on a long journey home after the Trojan War. Many episodes in the film are closely linked to Troy.
But Troy is more than a setting for mythology. Located in northwestern Türkiye near the Dardanelles, the ancient city remains an active archaeological site, while the nearby Troy Museum houses artifacts spanning its long history. Tourism and cultural events are prevalent.
"Hollywood has already made quite a few films about Troy," said Reyhan Korpe, deputy head of the archaeological excavation team.
The 2004 film Troy generated considerable interest, he said, and The Odyssey is likely to bring renewed attention to the ancient city.
A giant wooden horse prop from the 2004 film now stands on the waterfront in Canakkale, a city roughly 30 km north of Troy, where it has become a local landmark.
The real Troy, however, dates back much further than either Homer or Hollywood.
According to Korpe, the earliest settlement at the site dates to around 3000 B.C. Situated near the Dardanelles and the Aegean Sea, Troy occupied a strategically important location and grew into a significant regional center during the Late Bronze Age.
Archaeological excavations, which began in the late 19th century, gradually revealed layers of settlements built and rebuilt over thousands of years. Archaeologists have now identified nine major layers and 54 building phases, according to Sinem Duzgoren, director of the Troy Museum.
One of these layers, Troy VIIb, contains sling stones, arrowheads, knives, spearheads and traces of burning, suggesting that a major conflict took place there in the 12th century B.C.
Inside the museum, archaeology also intersects with mythology and local memory.
The Polyxena Sarcophagus, dating from the late sixth to early fifth century B.C., depicts the tragic story of Polyxena, a Trojan princess who, according to Greek mythology, was sacrificed after the fall of Troy.
Duzgoren said the person who commissioned the sarcophagus appears to have drawn on Polyxena's story to commemorate a daughter who had died young. The sarcophagus was discovered at a place called Kızöldün, roughly meaning "the place where the girl died." Centuries later, local people may no longer know who Polyxena was, but the memory of a girl's death survives.
Troy's enduring popularity, however, also presents a modern challenge: how to protect an ancient site while allowing visitors to experience it.
Korpe said the excavation team has introduced designated walking routes to limit visitors' direct contact with the ruins and is using technologies such as ground-penetrating radar, drones and digital mapping.
"Our goal is to protect Troy and make sure it continues to exist for thousands of years to come," he said.
The surrounding community is part of that effort -- and also benefits from the site's popularity. Local governments and villages support the management of the archaeological site, while tourism provides additional income for residents through excavation work, souvenir sales, guesthouses and restaurants.
Cultural events further connect the ancient city with modern life. Canakkale recently hosted the 63rd International Troy Festival, featuring music, exhibitions, discussions and sports.
From Homer's epics to modern cinema, Troy has survived through repeated retellings and reinterpretations. Today, the challenge is to ensure that as its story reaches new audiences, the ancient city itself survives for generations to come. ■

Feature: Chinese film "Dear You" bridges communities in Myanmar with shared memories
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
19:54:11 CST
20:54:11 KST

People attend the Yangon premiere of the Chinese film "Dear You" in Yangon, Myanmar, Aug. 20, 2026. (Photo by Haymhan Aung/Xinhua)
YANGON, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- When "Dear You", the Chinese word-of-mouth blockbuster, reached Myanmar audiences, it generated an even greater stir. Audiences see reflections of their own lived experiences in its narrative, where the virtues of solidarity, benevolence and resilience shine through.
At the film's Yangon premiere held on Thursday, the cinema drew a full house. Zeng Yuanxiang, honorary board chair of the Eastern Language and Business Center in Myanmar, said the film's plot brought back vivid memories of her parents' generation. She recalled that whenever her father managed to save money, he would ask her to write letters and send remittances back to their ancestral homeland.
Rooted in the historical "qiaopi" culture, the film was shot predominantly in the Teochew dialect with a largely non-professional cast. It officially premiered on the Chinese mainland in April and has since rolled out across Southeast Asian markets, including Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam and Myanmar.
"This film is like watching my father's life unfold," Zeng said.
"My father took odd jobs, and my mother carried water to sell. They denied themselves proper food and clothing, sending every penny they could back home. It was not that the ancestral homeland was in desperate need of the money, but because their parents and siblings were there."
She singled out the scene that struck her most deeply: elderly Xie Lanzhi losing her memories of the past. "She should have remembered," Zeng said. "If only she could recall, she and Grandma could sit down and talk through the stories of those years."
Also in attendance were faculty and Chinese-language students from the Yangon University of Foreign Languages (YUFL). Htay Htay Myint, associate professor with YUFL's Chinese Department, noted that the film offers a window into the value of solidarity and mutual support within Chinese communities.
Aung Nyein Tun, a second-year Chinese-language student at YUFL, said the film impressed upon him the power and significance of love. "I learned how precious love is. We ought to cherish our loved ones while we still have them, before it is too late," he said.
Li Li Myint, president of the Myanmar-China Women's Association, said the film can foster closer ties between Myanmar and Chinese-origin communities by advancing mutual understanding and cultural exchanges.
Echoing those remarks, actress and director Swe Zin Htike observed that families sustain mutual support and care even when separated by national borders -- a universal sentiment that resonated with theater-goers and underscores the film's strong international relevance.
"I appreciate this kind of warm, heartfelt film," she said. ■

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
19:54:04 CST

BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- Impressed by their performance and efficiency, a hotel in Panama has placed a new order for Chinese smart service robots to serve as its new "staff members."
The round-the-clock fleet, capable of handling services ranging from food delivery to laundry pick-up, was developed by Beijing Yunji Technology Co., Ltd. They are one of the latest high-tech additions to the Central American country's hospitality sector.
Founded in 2014, the Beijing-based company has deployed products in more than 40,000 hotels and 200 hospitals across the Americas, the Middle East, and other regions worldwide.
"Looking ahead, we aim to deliver essential services to tens of millions of people on a daily basis, while staying committed to building a bridge that connects the digital and physical worlds," said Li Quanyin, CEO of the company.
Yunji Technology is part of a broader wave. In recent years, Chinese high-tech manufacturers have made inroads into the Latin American market, injecting fresh momentum into sectors ranging from transportation to healthcare.
"I was captivated by this BYD bus from the very first drive," said Alexandra, a driver from the Brazilian state of Sao Paulo.
An experienced operator of vans and conventional diesel buses, she expressed a clear preference for the high-tech electric vehicles, which feature an air suspension system tailored to local complex road conditions and an air disinfection system integrated into the air conditioning units.
Chinese electric bus manufacturers, notably BYD and Yutong Bus Co., Ltd., have steadily won over local consumers, playing an active role in advancing the region's low-carbon transition.
A number of Latin American nations are advancing their green transition agendas, primarily aimed at reindustrialization via energy transformation, the development of new economic frameworks, and a gradual reduction of reliance on low-value-added exports, said Marcos Cordeiro Pires, a political economist from Brazil.
Beyond the transportation sector, Chinese innovation is helping upgrade regional infrastructure. In Chile, Chinese companies including Huawei are actively engaged in the country's digital infrastructure development, with multiple data centers under construction to deliver artificial intelligence (AI) and big data services, while also contributing to the creation of a regional data hub that extends coverage to neighboring countries.
In Brazil, Chinese tech teams have developed an AI-powered transmission line inspection platform that uses image recognition and big data to navigate the complex rainforest terrain, sharply reducing the safety risks of manual fieldwork.
Inside a 270-square-meter facility in Sao Paulo, Brazil, a range of laboratory instruments from China's MGI Tech has been providing genetic technology support to local researchers and clinical medical professionals, offering advanced technology at more competitive prices.
Since its opening in 2024, the facility has created new possibilities for Latin American researchers to circumvent the high-cost constraints traditionally associated with genomics research in the region.
Latin America has one of the world's most diverse populations, presenting considerable challenges to genomic research, said Zhang Yongwei, general manager of MGI Tech's Latin American branch.
"Biotechnology has evolved in tandem with information technology to become a fundamental enabling technology that sustains economic and social progress while transcending conventional sectoral divides. It is therefore essential that the fruits of science and technology benefit developing nations and their populations," Zhang added.
In the first seven months of 2026, China's exports of mechanical and electrical products saw a year-on-year increase of 21.2 percent. Meanwhile, the country's trade with Latin America grew 15.4 percent year on year, official data showed.
China's remarkable progress in emerging fields such as AI and 5G is providing new opportunities for developing countries to share in technological dividends, said Luciana Acioly da Silva, a senior researcher at the institute for applied economic research of Brazil. ■

Feature: China-proposed space weather program draws international interest, support
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
19:53:55 CST
20:53:55 KST

KRAKOW, Poland, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- On Thursday morning, Chinese scientist Zhang Qinghe stood before an international audience in Krakow, presenting a plan to connect observation facilities, data and researchers around the world for space weather studies.
Zhang was speaking at a forum during the 36th General Assembly and Scientific Symposium of the International Union of Radio Science (URSI GASS 2026), held in Krakow from Aug. 15 to Aug. 22, where he introduced the International Meridian Circle Program (IMCP), a flagship initiative spearheaded by China's scientific community to advance worldwide space-weather monitoring capabilities.
The setting carried a personal echo for Zhang.
At the 2014 URSI General Assembly in Beijing, he was among the recipients of the union's Young Scientist Award. Now, 12 years later, he returned to the same international scientific community in a different role -- representing a major science program proposed by Chinese scientists and inviting researchers worldwide to help build it.
One response came almost immediately. As Zhang finished his presentation, Jonah Colman, scientist from the U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory, raised his hand.
What interested Colman was also central to making such international cooperation work: how observation data from different parts of the world can be shared and used together.
For Zhang, the scientific reason for building such a network is straightforward.
"The Earth keeps rotating. When one part of the world can no longer make certain observations, another can take over," he told Xinhua.
"Only through this kind of relay can we better serve space weather," Zhang said.
The program plans to incorporate existing facilities where observation capabilities are already strong, while adding new ground-based instruments in less-covered regions, including parts of Africa and South America.
Zhang said China can provide equipment and technical support, while local partners provide sites, personnel and operational support. The resulting data will be shared.
"Data sharing is the link," Zhang said, explaining that data are at the core of scientific research and can help bring researchers from different countries together.
The cooperation will go further. The program also plans to provide funding for international teams to conduct research and attract scientists from around the world for full- or part-time research and exchanges.
"Scientists have a shared language and a shared understanding of the physical world," Colman said. "I'm excited to see where it goes," Colman said.
According to Zhang, more than 50 institutions from about 20 countries have signed memorandums of understanding or letters of support for the program.
The next IMCP workshop is expected to be held in Beijing in March 2027. Colman, who has not yet participated in the project, said he is considering going.
By then, Zhang will once again be welcoming international colleagues through a scientific community he first entered as a young researcher. ■

China

2026-08-21
19:53:53 CST
20:53:53 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- China recorded an increase in newly established foreign-invested enterprises and robust growth in foreign direct investment (FDI) in high-tech industries in the first seven months of 2026, despite a decline in overall inflows, official data showed Friday.
During the period, 37,711 new foreign-invested enterprises were set up, up 4.4 percent year on year, while FDI in actual use came in at 438.33 billion yuan (about 64.63 billion U.S. dollars), down 6.2 percent from a year earlier, the Ministry of Commerce said.
By sector, manufacturing attracted 109.43 billion yuan in FDI, while the service sector drew 319.95 billion yuan.
Despite the overall drop, FDI in high-tech industries surged 32.7 percent to 182.31 billion yuan, accounting for 41.6 percent of the national total, a rise of 12.2 percentage points from a year ago.
Specifically, FDI in R&D and design services, services for the commercialization of sci-tech achievements, and electronic and telecommunications equipment manufacturing jumped 72.1 percent, 62.2 percent and 39.9 percent, respectively.
During the same period, actual investment from Saudi Arabia, France and the Republic of Korea grew by 343.7 percent, 36.1 percent and 15.8 percent, respectively, with investment via free ports included in the calculations.
In June, China unveiled a 15-measure action plan to stabilize and optimize foreign investment utilization, focusing on expanding market access, streamlining investment procedures, boosting investment promotion, strengthening services and safeguards for foreign investors, and improving foreign capital management.
A new version of the Catalogue of Encouraged Industries for Foreign Investment, which took effect on Feb. 1 this year, aims to steer more foreign capital into advanced manufacturing, modern services, high-tech industries, energy conservation and environmental protection, as well as into the central, western and northeastern regions of the country. ■

One photo shows the human and environmental dimensions of artisanal mining in Congo

Unknown Publisher

One photo shows the human and environmental dimensions of artisanal mining in Congo
IGA-BARRIÈRE, Congo (AP) — Dieudonne Dirole is based in eastern Congo, where he started working for The Associated Press this year as the region recorded an Ebola outbreak that is spreading at unprecedented speed with no sign of slowing. He made this photo while on assignment with colleagues reporting on mobile gold miners whose movements and remote locations complicate efforts to track and slow the virus.
Here’s what he had to say about this extraordinary photo.
Why this photo?
In this photo of the mine, I wanted to show the true scale of artisanal mining and the impressive number of people who depend on this activity. I didn’t just want to photograph an individual scene, but instead I wanted to give the viewer a broader view of what is really happening on the ground. The presence of child miners, women, and men in the mud, the polluted water used for washing, and the transformed hillside all demonstrate the human, economic, and environmental dimensions of mining.
How I made this photo
To take this photo, we had to do a lot of negotiating with the local mine service managers on site. They absolutely refused to accept because they know they are exploiting children and women in the mine, even though it is prohibited by the law protecting children. Ultimately, he said he’s going to have one of his agents accompany us everywhere I want to film, but under his supervision.
Why this photo works
I think this photo is successful because it tells a story without needing a long explanation. At first glance, you immediately understand that it is an extremely active mining site; then your gaze discovers the different individual stories: the people who dig, those who transport, those who wash the ore, the women and men who work in the water and mud. And what makes this image powerful is the contrast between the very intense human activity in the foreground and the natural landscape in the background. The photo simultaneously shows the people, the work, and the impact of this activity on the environment.

Ukraine’s failure to anticipate and prepare for Russian threats is a bigger problem than the shortage of air defenses, says Oleksandr Kovalenko of the Information Resistance group. Russia, meanwhile, has demonstrated its ability to develop and execute medium-term plans for terror operations that can take years to prepare, according to Obozrevatel.
Russian forces adapt almost every month to new challenges and opportunities, scaling up their attacks. The use of jet-powered Banderol drone missiles is one example.
Russia is now employing a “tactical adaptive distribution” approach, flexibly redirecting missiles and strike drones toward different regions and rear cities depending on Ukrainian air-defense capabilities.
The main difference
The key change in Russia’s 2026 campaign against Ukraine’s rear areas has been the growing use of jet-powered drones based on the Iranian Shahed-238 and Karrar, which Russia has localized as Geran-3/4/5.
Russia first used a jet-powered kamikaze drone against Ukraine in January 2024. These weapons have been continuously upgraded over the past two years.
Ukraine, however, failed to adequately anticipate the threat and now lacks an effective, low-cost way to intercept Geran-3/4/5 drones, Kovalenko says. Russian forces used more than 1,400 jet-powered drones in the first half of 2026 alone, compared with 180 throughout all of 2025.
“It is possible that the facility in Alabuga, Tatarstan, could eventually be fully converted to producing jet-powered kamikaze drones as part of this strategy,” the analyst said.
What comes next: strikes on Kyiv to exert psychological pressure
A significant share of Russia’s new hard-to-intercept weapon variants appears to be concentrated for strikes on Kyiv.
Russian forces are seeking to exploit Ukraine’s acute shortage of Patriot and SAMP/T interceptors, using the opportunity to intensify their campaign of terror. Russia has previously used similar tactics to exert psychological pressure on civilians and disrupt economic activity in regions including Kharkiv and Odesa.
The same approach could increasingly be directed at the capital, particularly ahead of and during Ukraine’s Independence Day.

Porn-content creator picked to promote Warsaw Uprising memory
An adult-content creator was presented as a potential ambassador for the memory of Poland’s 1944 Warsaw Uprising before public outrage forced a reversal, according to local media reports. The campaign commemorating the revolt’s 82nd anniversary has the honorary patronage of the Polish Culture Ministry.
Monika Laskowska, known in Poland as an OnlyFans creator, appeared in a photo published by the Warszawa44 Association wearing a T-shirt commemorating the uprising and was presented as an ‘Ambassador of Remembrance’, multiple media outlets reported on Thursday. OnlyFans is a subscription platform widely associated with adult content.
The Warsaw Uprising was launched by the Polish resistance against Nazi German forces on August 1, 1944, in an attempt to liberate the capital as Soviet troops approached. The revolt was crushed after 63 days of fighting, leaving much of the Polish capital destroyed and an estimated 150,000-200,000 civilians dead.
Warszawa44, the association behind the commemoration, said it had selected Laskowska because of her public profile, social-media reach and “declared willingness to promote the memory of the Warsaw Uprising.”
Laskowska has also interviewed celebrities associated with Poland’s so-called “freak fights” – combat events that typically pit influencers and other internet personalities against each other – and has herself participated in such bouts.
The choice quickly drew backlash on social media, with users questioning whether an adult-content influencer was an appropriate figure to promote the memory of one of the most significant events in modern Polish history.
Polish media personality Karolina Korwin-Piotrowska, whose father fought in the uprising, also blasted the campaign for chasing social-media reach with controversial figures. She sarcastically suggested that organizers recruit even more provocative personalities.
“I propose, therefore, to co-opt Mrs. Polański, who Onet interviewed and who poses nicely with or without a shirt, some whores, drug addicts, maybe a few rapists,” she wrote.
Sebastian Meitz, an expert at Poland’s Sobieski Institute, publicly questioned Culture Minister Marta Cienkowska over the campaign and asked whether Laskowska had received the title under “culture” or “national heritage.”
The Culture Ministry rushed to distance itself from the decision, saying on Thursday that the list of ambassadors “was not consulted with the Ministry.” While the project had received its honorary patronage, the ministry stressed that it provided neither funding nor organizational support.
Warszawa44 president Dariusz Michalak confirmed that Laskowska was their own choice. The association, however, reversed course after the controversy erupted, suspending her ambassador role and removing her photo from Instagram.

The UK and France signed a new deal in April to strengthen efforts to combat irregular migration in northern France and prevent crossings to Britain, backed by a significant increase in dedicated personnel, technology and intelligence resources.
As of Aug. 10, more than 14,800 people had reached the UK by small boat this year, according to provisional Home Office data cited by the BBC, representing a 43% year-on-year drop and a 16% decline compared with the same period in 2024.

Israel admits killing Hind Rajab after 933 days. Why now?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
11:49:35 UTC
20:49:35 KST

Israeli forces killed five-year-old Hind Rajab alongside her family on January 29, 2024, in what has become one of the most shocking acts of violence against Palestinian civilians in Gaza in nearly three years.
Hind lived through the initial gunfire only to be left trapped among her family's dead bodies in the wreckage of the car, as she waited for a rescue that could never reach her.
Her final phone call pleading for someone to come, was heard by millions of people around the world, and it turned her into a symbol Israel has spent over two years trying, and failing, to bury along with her.
For most of that time, Israel denied its soldiers had even fired on the car, before shifting to acknowledging troops had been in the area, and only this week admitting, for the first time, that its own forces shot at the vehicle.
The military says a criminal investigation is now open into Hind's killing, citing "alleged failures in the coordination of the movement of the Palestine Red Crescent ambulance," alongside a separate probe into the killing of 15 medics and rescue workers in Rafah last year.
Announced two and a half years after Hind’s death, the investigation follows a pattern that the existing evidence has made all too familiar, according to Nasir Qadri, international law practitioner and critical legal scholar at Koc University.
“Every significant Israeli military investigation into the killing of journalists, civilians, and aid workers has followed an identical institutional sequence: initial denial, factual assessment by operational military personnel rather than criminal investigators, and referral to the Military Advocate General,” Qadri tells TRT World.
“This is followed by an extended review and eventual closure without prosecution, usually on grounds of insufficient evidence or legitimate combat decision-making,” he adds.
Why now?
The announcement by the genocidal army comes as Israel faces renewed legal scrutiny over its genocide in Gaza, its strikes in Lebanon and elsewhere.
Under the Rome Statute's complementarity regime, the International Criminal Court is only meant to step in when a state is "unwilling or unable" to genuinely investigate its own nationals, which means a state facing prosecution has a direct incentive to manufacture the appearance of domestic proceedings before the admissibility question is decided against it.
Qadri argues that it is precisely what is happening now, with Israel producing its first public accounting of wartime conduct at the exact moment its legal position before the Court has become hardest to defend.
“Israel is currently subject to active ICC proceedings, faces genocide referrals before the ICJ, and is operating under the July 2024 Advisory Opinion finding its occupation violates peremptory norms,” Qadri says.
“Under Article 17 of the Rome Statute, a state may challenge admissibility before the ICC by demonstrating that genuine domestic investigations are underway.”
The timing of the announcement lines up with Israel losing ground on its case before the ICC, not with any new evidence coming to light, he adds.
The Hind Rajab Foundation, a Brussels-based legal advocacy group that pursues international accountability for Israeli military conduct against Palestinians, has no faith in Israel’s investigation, calling the announcement "little more than a masquerade meant to deflect accountability and preserve its impunity."
That framing captures what two years of watching Israel investigate itself has taught rights groups and the family alike: an internal probe has never once translated into meaningful accountability for Palestinian deaths, and there is little in the record to suggest this case will be the exception.
According to an independent review the foundation cites, of 52 publicly known Israeli military investigations into violations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, 88 percent were closed without any finding of wrongdoing or left open indefinitely with no outcome ever published, and only one produced a prison sentence.
“We see this new probe as a pattern, not a genuine pursuit of justice, but a charade meant to whitewash crimes against Palestinians,” a spokesperson of the Hind Rajab Foundation tells TRT World.
“The timing is obviously strategic. These announcements come when international pressure is high, and they serve to create the illusion of accountability.”
“Given Israel’s history of such probes ending without meaningful consequences, this appears designed to deflect criticism, not to deliver justice,” the spokesperson adds.
An illusion of accountability
Israel says it referred over 1,000 wartime incidents to its own internal review mechanism and opened 74 criminal cases as a result, but no comprehensive public accounting exists of where most of those cases actually stand.
Israel's own military conceded in 2022 there was a "high possibility" its soldiers killed Al Jazeera correspondent Shireen Abu Akleh, and it still declined to open a criminal investigation, closing the case without a single charge.
Also, the same week Israel opened a criminal probe into Hind's killing, it closed another case on the April 2024 strike that killed World Central Kitchen worker Zomi Frankcom and six colleagues, ruling out any criminal investigation despite the military's own earlier admission that it had killed them "unintentionally."
According to Qadri, Israeli investigations are structurally designed to produce the appearance of accountability while delivering impunity as their default output.
“Out of hundreds of cases raising criminal suspicion that Israeli soldiers killed Palestinian civilians, only three led to indictments, a prosecution rate of 0.87 percent,” Qadri says.
“Israel's own internal documents confirm that investigations do not need to produce convictions, they simply need to exist, exploiting Article 17 of the Rome Statute's complementarity principle to sustain domestic proceedings as a jurisdictional bar against the ICC,” he explains.
The Hind Rajab Foundation has already submitted to the ICC the names of Colonel Beni Aharon of the 401st Armored Brigade, Lieutenant Colonel Daniel Ella of the 52nd Battalion, Major Sean Glass of the “Vampire Empire” Company and 22 other soldiers whose names it is withholding for now.
“We know who killed Hind,” foundation director Dyab Abou Jahjah said, arguing that any real path to justice runs through the ICC and courts abroad rather than Israel’s own military justice system.
335 bullets tore through Hind’s car
Hind was fleeing Tel al-Hawa with her uncle, aunt and four cousins when Israeli forces opened fire.
Her 15-year-old cousin Layan Hamada stayed on the phone with the Palestinian Red Crescent, telling them a tank was closing in and that everyone in the car except her and Hind had been killed.
Seconds later, gunfire erupted again and Layan's screaming stopped.
A Forensic Architecture investigation later found that the Israeli tank was positioned just 13 to 23 metres from the car, close enough for a clear view of the two children inside. It also found that 335 bullets were fired at the vehicle, 64 of them in six seconds while Layan was still on the line.
Paramedics Yusuf al-Zeino and Ahmed al-Madhoun drove out to reach Hind and were never heard from again.
Israeli forces held the area for two weeks before anyone could reach the wreckage. When rescue teams finally got in, they found the bodies of Hind and her family beside the burnt-out ambulance, the two paramedics still inside.
For international lawyers, prosecuting those directly involved would not be enough for justice.
“Individualised criminal prosecution, even where it succeeds, cannot deliver what Palestinians and other peoples living under military occupation actually need: self-determination,” Qadri says.
“Real accountability requires prosecuting the decision-makers who designed the rules of engagement, not only the soldiers who carried them out, and dismantling the arms transfers, trade relations, and diplomatic cover.”
Hind's grandmother has already rejected the Israeli investigation. She told Anadolu that the family has no confidence in Israel's judiciary, that the car was deliberately targeted, and that only an independent international investigation can meet the moment.
"We are not demanding justice only in Hind's name as a child from Gaza," she said, "but in the name of all our child martyrs in Gaza."
Kaouther Ben Hania, the Tunisian director of The Voice of Hind Rajab, also rejected the investigation, calling it “a smokescreen.”
"Look at the cases the Israeli military is choosing to speak about today: they are precisely the ones that international public opinion has made impossible to ignore. And what about all the others? Those whose names we will never know because their deaths never broke through the wall of international indifference?" Ben Hania said.
“Real accountability would require independent, neutral bodies, not the same military that committed the crime. Genuine justice means investigation by the ICC and national courts abroad,” a Foundation spokesperson tells TRT World.
“We have already identified the Israeli unit and commanders responsible and submitted their names and evidence to the ICC, and will continue pursuing complaints in other countries until justice is served.”

Russian strikes on Odesa ports push Ukrainian farms toward bankruptcy, Bloomberg reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
11:47:57 UTC
20:47:57 KST

Ravil Dzhamally fled when Russian forces occupied his farm in Kherson Oblast, then returned after liberation to clear mines and plant again. Now, tons of his grain lie unsold in plastic sleeves across his fields because Russian attacks have nearly halted exports through Odesa, Bloomberg reported on 20 August.
Odesa’s Black Sea ports handle almost all of Ukraine’s grain exports, Bloomberg reported. Weekly grain and oilseed exports have fallen by more than 90% since early July, data from commodity-data firm Kpler show. That threatens fall planting and the sector that generates more than half of Ukraine’s export revenue. The disruption is also raising food costs in countries that rely on imported grain, Reuters reported.
Farmers must either store harvests they cannot export or sell locally at about one-third of global prices, Bloomberg reported. They say this year’s crisis is worse than the 2022 blockade because the financial reserves that carried them through six months of disruption then have since been depleted.
Russian attacks drive ships from Ukraine’s grain corridor
Ukraine’s Black Sea grain corridor—the wartime shipping route from Odesa—was never formally closed, Euromaidan Press reported. Four or five ships entered Ukraine’s ports on 21 July. Still, none arrived the next day because shipowners had paused calls, not because Ukraine had restricted navigation, Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi told Ukrainian agricultural outlet Latifundist.
Ukraine’s state railway, Ukrzaliznytsia, subsequently restricted selected wheat and barley shipments to Odesa ports. Its register did not state a reason, and the railway did not publicly link the orders to the shipping disruption.
Oleksandr Havryliuk, who farms near the front in Kharkiv Oblast, told Bloomberg that losing his harvest would probably bankrupt him and force him to sell the farm. The National Bank of Ukraine estimates that Ukraine could lose about $2.5 billion in export revenue during the second half of 2026, Reuters reported. Bloomberg said the disruption could trigger widespread farm bankruptcies.
Ukraine seeks EU aid and export routes as losses mount
Financing was already constrained before the port crisis: available financing and insurance were “enough to keep the sector surviving, not enough to keep it growing,” Vysotskyi told Euromaidan Press in May.
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion, agriculture accounted for more than 10% of Ukraine’s economic output, according to World Bank data cited by Bloomberg.
The sector has since grown more important as Russian attacks have destroyed much of the country’s heavy industry, Evghenia Sleptsova, a senior economist at the economic forecasting firm Oxford Economics, told Bloomberg.
Her firm estimates that the disruption could cost the equivalent of 1.8% of GDP this year and 2.1% in 2027. Under a prolonged severe disruption, the 2027 loss could instead reach 5.3%, Oxford Economics said.
Ukraine could exhaust its grain-storage capacity by early November if exports do not recover, the Agriculture Ministry said, according to Bloomberg. Even using every available route, the country may export only about 30 million tons this season, leaving roughly the same volume stored or rotting, Vysotskyi said.
Ukraine’s Agriculture Ministry requested a €220 million EU grant to subsidize interest and unlock up to €4 billion in loans, the ministry said.
Ukraine and Moldova are also discussing a rail route through Moldova to Romania’s port of Constanța, Reuters reported, citing unnamed sources in both countries. Kyiv estimates the route could carry about 10% of its grain exports.
Western rail corridors have limited capacity, while low water levels restrict traffic through Danube ports. Both alternatives cost more than shipping through the Black Sea, Bloomberg reported.

“They treated him with water for two days”: relatives of a man who died in a Bila Tserkva hospital are convinced of medical negligence
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:46:20 EEST
20:46:20 KST

“They treated him with water for two days”: relatives of a man who died in a Bila Tserkva hospital are convinced of medical negligence
Kyiv • UNN
48-year-old Ihor Yatelo died in hospital after misdiagnoses; according to his family, he died from undiagnosed leptospirosis. The police are investigating possible negligence.
On August 4, a patient died at Bila Tserkva City Hospital No. 2. According to his relatives, the man was given an incorrect diagnosis and did not receive proper medical care. The family is convinced that 48-year-old Ihor Yatelo died from leptospirosis, which doctors failed to identify in time. UNN spoke with the deceased man's daughter, Diana.
A story that began with a slight fever and ended in death
"Dad was given the wrong diagnosis and treated with water for two days," Diana says.
She is convinced that her father could have been saved if the necessary treatment had been started in time.
It all began with a low-grade fever that developed on the second day after he had spent time by a river.
"On July 26, he was relaxing by the river with my mother and sister. He did not swim; he was launching a little boat (feeding the fish — ed.), went in up to his knees, and that was all," Diana recounts.
A day after spending time by the river, Ihor Yatelo developed a fever, but everything seemed like an ordinary cold.
"At first, his temperature was around 37°C, but then his calves began to hurt. We contacted the family doctor, who issued him a sick leave certificate and sent him for tests," his daughter says.
But by that evening, the man's condition had worsened.
"In the evening he felt ill, and his blood pressure dropped. We called an ambulance and waited 40 minutes. An emergency medical team arrived. As it turned out later, these are different things, and according to the doctor, an ambulance comes only for those who are already dying. The emergency doctor offered a choice of two injections… At that moment, the test results arrived, and my mother showed them to him — he replied that he did not understand the tests and that there were no grounds to take Dad to the hospital," Diana describes the situation.
By that time, Ihor Yatelo's test results indicated a critically high level of C-reactive protein and uric acid in the blood. The family decided to take the man to Bila Tserkva City Hospital No. 2.
There, according to his relatives, they encountered the absence of a doctor on duty and an indifferent attitude. Eventually, the man was admitted.
"We showed them the test results and described all the symptoms. They did not understand what was wrong with him and spent two hours making a diagnosis. They performed an X-ray, even though he had a fluorography scan from a couple of days earlier. At around one in the morning — it was already August 1 — they admitted him to the neurology department with a diagnosis of Guillain–Barré syndrome (a rare autoimmune disease in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the peripheral nerves — ed.) and started intravenous drips," Diana recounts.
The daughter shows photographs of the medications administered to her father. They show that Yatelo was given intravenous drips containing sodium chloride solution, paracetamol, and "Soda Buffer," apparently to reduce blood acidity. No other medications were administered at that time, and the treatment appears to have been purely symptomatic.
The relatives begged the doctors to conduct further examinations of the man, whose condition was rapidly deteriorating.
"Now Hruzynskyi says that we brought our father in a completely critical, terminal condition. Let them look at the surveillance cameras in the admissions department — he was still smiling, but his legs hurt badly, so I seated him in a wheelchair. But once he was in the hospital, he got worse, and they wasted time there," Diana recounts.
Eventually, additional examinations were carried out and a new diagnosis was made — kidney stones. By that time, the patient had developed jaundice and his abdomen had become enlarged. According to his relatives, they asked for an additional consultation with a specialist in the relevant field, but were told that this was not possible at the moment because it was the weekend. In general, the deceased man's family describes his entire stay in the hospital as a constant search for someone who could take responsibility for treating Ihor Yatelo: first the doctor on duty, then the head of the intensive care unit, a specialist in the relevant field, and the chief doctor. They insisted that the man might have had leptospirosis.
After the diagnosis was changed, Ihor Yatelo's condition continued to deteriorate; according to his relatives, he needed to be transferred to intensive care. But this happened only when the doctor on duty changed.
"On Sunday (August 2 — ed.) in the morning, a doctor comes in and says: ‘Why is he still here? He should be in intensive care. Why has no one sent him anywhere?’” Diana recounts.
She says that the doctor immediately suspected leptospirosis.
The next day, the family was informed of the man's death. Yatelo spent a total of a day and a half in the hospital, and judging by his relatives' account, they spent most of that time persuading the staff to conduct an appropriate examination and prescribe appropriate treatment.
From Promises of Recovery to Death: Three Odrex Patients’ Stories12.08.26, 14:00 • 53604 views
The hospital's position, the autopsy, and the criminal proceedings
The hospital denies that its staff acted negligently. General Director Oleksandr Hruzynskyi claims that Ihor Yatelo was brought to the hospital with critical vital signs that were practically incompatible with life, but at the same time insists that the man was not taken to intensive care because there were no indications for it. Hruzynskyi acknowledges that diagnostic errors do occur.
"There are errors in diagnosis. I am not saying that they should have diagnosed him correctly 100% of the time," Hruzynskyi says in a comment to Espresso.
He also rejects the family's claims that there was no doctor on duty. At the same time, the deceased man's daughter released a recording in which Hruzynskyi allegedly says that there is no doctor on duty on weekends.
  Посмотреть в Threads
The relatives also reject the claims that the man had been treated at home for two weeks, since only eight days passed between his rest by the river and his death.
Based on the relatives' statement, criminal proceedings were initiated under Part 1 of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — improper performance of professional duties by a medical or pharmaceutical worker, if this occurred through negligence and resulted in serious consequences for the patient. Notably, as part of these proceedings, a forensic medical examination was ordered, the conduct of which the hospital allegedly attempted to halt by interfering with the documentation.
The relatives are convinced that Ihor Yatelo became a victim of doctors' negligence and lack of professionalism. They are now awaiting the results of the forensic medical examination and are convinced that they are in the right.
In lieu of conclusions
Unfortunately, Ukrainians are increasingly encountering medical negligence, which often causes tragic consequences. And this happens not only in state-run or municipal hospitals, but also in private institutions. In each specific case, the final word should belong to the court. But the families of deceased patients deserve justice and answers.

El Nino, not quake, to hit Colombian coffee harvest, sector leader says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
11:45:00 UTC
20:45:00 KST

El Nino, not quake, to hit Colombian coffee harvest, sector leader says
BOGOTA - Colombia’s coffee harvest has dodged the impact of a powerful earthquake that hit farming regions throughout the western part of the country, the head of the National Coffee Growers Federation told Reuters in an interview on Aug 20.
Despite widespread damage wreaked by the 7.4-magnitude quake, coffee growers view the severe weather of an El Nino year as the bigger threat, said the federation’s head, German Bahamon.
“Production itself is not affected by the earthquake. Production will very likely be affected by the El Nino phenomenon,” Bahamon said in an interview.
El Nino is a periodic warming of sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific caused by weakening trade winds. Global forecasters say an El Nino weather pattern is strengthening and could develop into a very strong event later this year into early 2027 that boosts temperatures, disrupts rainfall and poses risks to crops the world over.
The federation expects production in 2026 to drop 8 per cent to 12.5 million 60kg bags, down from 13.7 million bags in 2025, due to heavy rains earlier in 2026 and the onset of El Nino.
The quake in Colombia on August 10 killed 319 people and damaged infrastructure throughout provinces responsible for about a third of the nation’s crop.
Initial surveys identified 10,500 coffee-growing families in the disaster zone, with 8,000 reporting partial or total destruction of homes and processing facilities. The federation plans to spearhead a reconstruction programme alongside government aid, including a programme to purchase harvested coffee cherries.
Exports from Buenaventura – Colombia’s main coffee port, which handles 60 per cent of shipments – have returned to normal following temporary safety inspections and road closures.
“There have been no issues with exports... They are proceeding perfectly,” Bahamon said.
Colombia is the world’s third-largest coffee producer and the top supplier of washed Arabica. Approximately 540,000 families depend on the industry, which covers 840,000ha.
Beyond climate concerns, Bahamon warned that the strength of the Colombian peso – at its highest level since October 2018 – is eroding farmer margins. He estimated growers are losing 700,000 pesos (S$290) per 125kg load due to the rising value against the dollar. REUTERS

Study reveals mismatch between Greek livestock numbers and EU subsidy records
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
11:44:19 UTC
20:44:19 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
Greek farmers claimed EU livestock subsidies for tens of thousands more animals than were recorded in the country’s official statistics, POLITICO reported Thursday, deepening a wider scandal over agricultural funds.
The discrepancy concerns cattle, sheep and goats and has prompted complaints to the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO), according to the analysis.
POLITICO said the gap was particularly evident between Greece’s declining cattle herd, according to ELSTAT, the country’s statistics agency, and the number of animals covered by subsidies recorded by the Agriculture Ministry.
Ministry data showed Greek authorities paid EU subsidies for about 260,000 lactating cows in 2024, while around 70,000 cattle were slaughtered for meat that year, according to figures cited by POLITICO and confirmed by the ministry.
The analysis noted that lactating cows generally produce about one calf a year, meaning the number of calves added to the national herd should have been broadly comparable with the number of lactating cows.
Three Greek cattle breeders told POLITICO that cattle removals due to age, declining productivity or disease accounted for about 20% of the herd annually.
Given that Greece had about 600,000 cattle in 2024, according to ELSTAT, such removals would amount to around 120,000 animals.
Combined with the subsidy data, the figures would suggest the national herd should have increased by about 70,000 animals in 2024.
Instead, ELSTAT data based on annual surveys showed the cattle population continued to decline, falling from about 640,000 in 2023 to 600,000 in 2024 and 520,000 in 2025, according to figures published in June.
Nikos Dimopoulos, chairman of the Kavala Livestock Farmers’ Association, said the discrepancy could be even greater because some cattle slaughtered in Greece may have been imported rather than removed from the domestic herd.
“There’s no oversight and we cannot have an exact figure because there is no accurate data,” Dimopoulos said.
Similar discrepancies were found in Greece’s sheep and goat records. ELSTAT reported about 8.8 million animals in 2025, while around 15.7 million were registered in the government’s Integrated Veterinary Information System, according to the analysis.
“Unless we carry out a nationwide census of livestock to see what we actually have, we will not have a clear picture,” Dimopoulos said.
Complaints over the discrepancy between livestock subsidy records and the official cattle population have been submitted to the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO), according to POLITICO.
EPPO, which did not confirm whether it was investigating the discrepancy, is already handling dozens of cases related to alleged irregularities in the use of EU agricultural funds, POLITICO reported.
The cases include allegations that subsidies were obtained for pastureland that applicants did not own or lease, as well as for agricultural activities that were allegedly not conducted.
An EPPO document submitted to the Greek parliament also alleged that veterinarians and officials from OPEKEPE, the former agency responsible for distributing EU agricultural funds, were involved in manipulating livestock records.

As the ministry emphasized, Russia continues to deliberately attack civilian vessels and Ukraine’s port infrastructure, threatening not only the lives of seafarers but also freedom of navigation and global food security.
Ukraine’s Minister of Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport Mykola Kalashnyk appealed to Arsenio Antonio Domingues Velasco, Secretary-General of the International Maritime Organization (IMO), in connection with the sharp deterioration of the security situation in the Black Sea.
At Ukraine’s request, the IMO Secretariat circulated the appeal among all member states of the Organization, as well as international and non-governmental organizations holding consultative status with the IMO
"During July and the first half of August 2026 alone, Russia attacked 52 civilian vessels. These included vessels carrying food and other cargo to or from Ukrainian ports, as well as vessels located directly in ports," the statement said.
The Infrastructure Ministry noted that the most high-profile incidents included:
-  On July 13, the AIDA was attacked while unloading fertilizer at the port of Pivdennyi. Three crew members were killed and five others were injured; 
-  On July 14, the ATLAS BEY was attacked at the port of Odesa. The vessel’s captain was killed and three crew members were injured; 
-  On July 19, the GOLDEN LEO, which was carrying more than 6,000 tonnes of corn, was attacked while leaving the port of Chornomorsk. Nine crew members and a pilot were killed. The vessel sank on July 26; 
-  On August 5, the EMIL, which was carrying iron ore through the Ukrainian maritime corridor, came under repeated drone attacks. A fire broke out on board, and the vessel became unseaworthy; 
-  That same day, the MERA QUEEN, which was carrying wheat from the port of Odesa, was attacked. A Ukrainian crew member was killed as a result of damage to the hull. 
"Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, Russia has damaged or partially destroyed 1,090 port infrastructure facilities and 262 merchant vessels. As a result of the attacks, the number of people killed and injured has reached 329," the ministry reported.
"Russia’s escalation of the security situation in the Black Sea threatens the continued operation of the Ukrainian maritime corridor and the ability of vessels to safely enter and leave Ukrainian ports," the Infrastructure Ministry emphasized.
The ministry, in cooperation with the Foreign Ministry and the Embassy of Ukraine in the United Kingdom, as noted, "is systematically working with the International Maritime Organization to increase pressure on Russia and convey information to participating countries about violations of international conventions and regulations at sea."
"Ukraine will continue to take all possible measures to guarantee freedom and safety of navigation in the Black and Azov seas in accordance with its international obligations," the statement said.

NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Friday hit back at the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom after it urged Washington to impose sanctions on members of Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, calling the body "biased" and lacking credibility.In a bi-weekly press briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said such organisations have no credibility and operate to peddle their own agenda."The organisation you are talking about is known to everyone as a biased organisation, and for many years, it has been making misleading and provocative statements about India," Jaiswal said."I would say that we should stay away from such organisations because they peddle their own agenda and, at the same time, have no credibility," he added.This comes days after USCIRF urged the US government to impose sanctions on RSS members, rather than honouring them with "high-level meetings."In a post on X, the commission shared remarks from Asif Mahmood, a Pakistani-American physician who serves as its chair, and Commissioner Gene Mills.

It’s Harry and Meghan in Finding Freedom 2: Back in Blighty | Marina Hyde
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
11:42:32 UTC
20:42:32 KST

Wednesday night brought an absolute cloudburst of psychic rain for our parched land, as it emerged that Prince Harry and Meghan were reversing their self-styled “freedom flight” to California and returning to live in the UK. Nature is healing! Is that … is that how the expression goes? Either way, all humans in Britain have taken the announcement brilliantly, while fatted calf prices climbed steeply at the news that the reverse Megxit is imminent, with only an adequate headline soubriquet yet to be found. Megain? Megraine?
Inevitably, thoughts turned swiftly to what it all meant. One of the funniest aspects of Meghan and Harry coverage is how their decisions are always analysed as though we were parsing the 4D chess moves of 19th-century master strategists. We are forever imagining we are dealing with a couple of Bismarcks or Clausewitzes, as opposed to a resting actor and the “chief impact officer” of a firm designed to offer tech-based solutions to men crying in their cars or something.
And so it is that motive is being obsessively pored over. There’s definitely some eye-catching speculation out there. Some feel that Meghan being willing to step so much as a toe on to our toxic shores can only be a way of telegraphing the unfortunate suggestion that the king’s days are numbered. Or maybe Harry just wants to spend more time with his £9.5m legal bill. Others have spicier takes. I saw a few horrified Sussex Squad Americans on social media suggesting that the only conceivable explanation is that Prince Harry is simply a world-beating god of sex. Allow me to expand. I’m sure the squad diehards won’t mind me projecting their own psychological projections on to Meghan, but the logic seemed comparable to someone saying: “Sorry, so the suggestion is that I move back to live on top of a live volcano, in a plague-ridden failed state, run by psychopathically violent warlords. Who’s asking?” 1990s-era Keanu Reeves. “BRB just calling the removal firm.”
Multiple other takes are of course available. In Hong Kong, they used to have an acronym for bankers who were too stupid to get the good jobs in London but were able to move out there and do very nicely: Filth (Failed in London, try Hong Kong). It’s not as good, acronym-wise, but I guess we could be looking at a Fimuk situation – Failed in Montecito, try UK. No doubt we’ve all forgotten the full ins and outs, but I believe Ellen DeGeneres has been on a similar journey. It’s possible that the Sussexes have just failed to keep pace with the elite fruit-spread makers of California, and that Meghan believes the waters of home counties jam-making will be much less competitive. I look forward to her conveying this judgment to the local Women’s Institute at her earliest convenience.
Or, look, possibly the real reason for this move is something in between all these things – but which of us wants to be wasting time on nuance right now?
What we do know is that it’s definitely on, and the couple’s children are enrolled in a school for September. Early thoughts? Mainly that someone’s class WhatsApp group just got an incredible new member. Speaking as a veteran of these digital abysses of passive aggression, may I state that the absolute last thing you need on one is someone whose stated life philosophy is to “create wonder in every moment”.
Seriously. You simply cannot run the risk of the following message materialising at Christmas/in high summer when you are limping towards the holidays. “Thinking about end-of-term presents, I thought it would be really magical to create a mirror where the frame is our children’s handprints. I can organise?” Really? Because I’ve been hurt before. But go on. “Literally all I would need from you ladies is a clay cast of your daughter’s hand with a pressed daisy picked by moonlight embedded in it. If anyone hasn’t pressed flowers before I would be very happy to offer a (fun!) tutorial at my place on Tuesday after drop-off.” Aaaaaaaaaaaagh. Please, I HAVE A JOB. I CAN’T DO ANY OF THIS. You know what everyone loves? John Lewis vouchers. Please. PLEASE. As for other events during the school year, might as well call the Vatican right now because I can assure you we have a nailed-on bake sale martyr on our hands right here.
Still, this is all very sad news for the country of the United States of America, and its now decimated entertainment industry, as Harry and Meghan leave behind them failed deals with Spotify and Netflix, among others. Then again, have they? Recent years have seen the Sussexes hamstrung by having exhaustively told the only story of theirs that anyone is remotely interested in. I can hardly believe I’m typing this, but it turned out no one wants to watch documentaries about global justice activism or polo. But this week’s news could easily reignite the only kind of content Netflix’s degraded first-look deal with Meghan would be extremely interested in having a first look at: the one where their life is made miserable by a toxic family in a toxic country with a toxic press. And then you make TV all about it.
It’s a bit like when there’s been a hugely successful movie with a crazy, high-concept situation, and the producers of the sequel just have to work out a way to get the characters back into the same crazy, high-concept situation, or at least a similar one, so they can go back to the money well for a second time. Having been on board a bus that can’t slow down, Speed 2 finds Sandra Bullock on a runaway cruise ship. Home Alone 2 sees Kevin once again left behind, this time in New York as opposed to Chicago, where the same burglars have somehow rematerialised. In Finding Freedom 2, it’ll probably work best for the Sussexes to embrace the absurdity with a cheeky one-liner. When Harry and Meghan are battling remorseless tabloid attention, poisonous family dynamics, and deranged public antipathy, let’s hope he turns to the Netflix cameras and quotes Bruce Willis in Die Hard 2: “How can the same shit happen to the same guy twice?” I don’t know, mate – but I assume you’re getting first-dollar gross on the box office.
In the meantime, the shock news continues to spark an hourly carousel of #onlyinBritain questions. What’s going to happen on Remembrance Sunday? Will this mean “rival courts”? Hand on heart, it’s hard to escape the conclusion that there are, amazingly, a whole lot of people who are even more ridiculous and even more emotional than Harry and Meghan. And – also amazingly – they are not the population of the state of California.
- 
  Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnist

Iran’s president says war with US should end while Tehran is in position of ‘power, dignity’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
11:41:38 UTC
20:41:38 KST

Sahin Demir
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Friday that the war with the US should be brought to an end while Iran is in a position of “power and dignity,” as he defended Tehran’s recent agreement with Washington.
Speaking at an event, Pezeshkian said the outcome of the negotiations was a “major achievement” approved by Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, according to a statement from the Iranian presidency.
“What was achieved during the negotiations was a major accomplishment,” he said, adding that members of the council who were directly involved had firmly defended it.
Pezeshkian described the recent agreement as “honorable and valuable,” rejecting criticism that Tehran had made concessions.
“They cannot find even a single clause in this agreement that indicates surrender; all the commitments are related to the other side,” he said.
The Iranian president stressed, however, that the agreement did not mean Tehran would submit in the event of another attack.
“We will under no circumstances bow to bullying,” he said. “We will stand against them until our last breath and give them a crushing response.”
Pezeshkian said the war should come to an end at some point, arguing that the current circumstances offered an appropriate opportunity.
“It is better to end the war today, when we are in a position of power and dignity,” he said, arguing that the US had violated international rules by attacking Iranian schools, hospitals and infrastructure.
He said Iran’s military commanders and armed forces remain fully prepared to defend the country, while stressing the importance of maintaining domestic unity.
Iran and the US signed a 14-point memorandum of understanding in Islamabad on June 18 under Pakistani and Qatari mediation, providing for an end to the war and a 60-day period of negotiations toward a final agreement.
Tehran later accused Washington of violating the memorandum, while Pakistan and Qatar have continued mediation between the two sides.

Driver mechanics of Yars missile systems undergo training on new simulators

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
11:39:51 UTC
20:39:51 KST

MOSCOW, August 21. /TASS/. Driver mechanics of the Yars land-based mobile missile systems are being trained using new simulator systems at the Strategic Missile Forces Technicians’ School, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"At the Strategic Missile Forces Technicians’ School, driver mechanics of the Yars land-based mobile missile systems are being trained on new simulator systems. The training facilities and equipment are constantly being upgraded, and new simulator systems are being introduced," the ministry noted.
Cadets training as multi-axle wheeled chassis driver mechanics hone their driving skills on specialized simulators capable of simulating driving in various weather and climatic conditions. The visualization system simulates various road situations in real time. The training complex is equipped with duplicate screens for the instructor who monitors the trainee’s actions in real time.
Simulator systems are created for each weapon system supplied to the Strategic Missile Forces, ensuring training according to a single concept. To train driver mechanics, the Strategic Missile Forces’ school is equipped with special classrooms featuring training complexes, and for practical training, there is a driving range with varied routes, which allows for the effective development of driving skills on vehicles with multi-axle wheeled chassis.
The RS-24 Yars is a mobile or stationary missile system equipped with a solid-propellant intercontinental ballistic missile featuring a multiple re-entry vehicle. Deployment of the Yars began in December 2009, when the system was put on test combat duty with the Strategic Missile Forces. It is a modification of the Topol-M missile.

A German conservative mayor backed the AfD. Now Merz is on the spot.
Unknown

2026-08-21

Friedrich Merz stands next to a flag showing the German federal eagle as he attends the dismissal and confirmation ceremony of government cabinet members. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
A conservative German mayor’s €10,000 donation to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is making things awkward for his party’s leaders.
Bernd Prange, a Christian Democrat who serves as mayor of Altmärkische Höhe in Saxony-Anhalt, wrote in an open letter on Wednesday that he would be voting for the AfD in the state’s upcoming election on Sept. 6. “I want the AfD to become so strong in the Saxony-Anhalt election that it can govern alone,” wrote Prange.
The goal, he said, was for his own party to “finally wake up,” tear down Germany’s political firewall and abandon what he called its shift to the left.
Advertisement
The letter prompted swift criticism from within his own party: “I don’t like it. I can say that very clearly,” Saxony-Anhalt CDU Premier Sven Schulze told POLITICO’s Berlin Playbook Podcast on Thursday. “I think his approach is wrong. Definitely,” adding that he did not share Prange’s views “in any way.”
As for whether the mayor will remain a Christian Democrat, Schulze was in no rush to make a call: “We’ll deal with the issue after the election,” he said. “Right now, it’s campaign time.”
In an interview published earlier on Wednesday, Schulze had dismissed speculation about possible defections after the election: “No, someone switching from the CDU to the AfD will not happen,” he said. And while Prange hasn’t formally changed political allegiance, he said he wants Chancellor Friedrich Merz “removed” as CDU leader and accused him of running a party that is “giving up the conservative core of the Union.”
The episode hits the CDU at a perilous moment, as Merz struggles to maintain the country’s “firewall” against cooperation with the far right while support for the AfD surges across eastern Germany.
The AfD is polling between 41 and 43 percent in Saxony-Anhalt — almost twice the CDU’s 22 to 24 percent — putting the far right within striking distance of governing alone. Merz continues to rule out cooperation with the AfD, but September’s elections will put that under sustained pressure: Saxony-Anhalt votes on Sept. 6, followed by Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sept. 20.
