Russia conducts missile tests on disputed islands as Japan protests drills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
10:29:59 UTC
19:29:59 KST

The Pacific Fleet conducted a Bastion missile test just days after Putin's visit to the islands prompted Tokyo to summon Russia's ambassador to Japan and drew a US statement of support for Japanese sovereignty.
Moscow's decision to conduct missile tests off disputed islands visited by President Vladimir Putin earlier this month sparked another wave of protests from Japan, as tensions between the two countries continue to escalate.
Japanese news agency Kyodo quoted Russia's Pacific Fleet as saying that it had conducted the missile test, although it was unclear when it took place.
Kyodo reported that a unit equipped with the Bastion surface-to-ship missile system conducted the test from the chain's largest island, Etorofu.
Flagship of Russia's Pacific Fleet, the guided missile cruiser Varyag, also took part in the test, along with the Omsk nuclear-powered submarine, the news agency said.
The exercise simulated an attack on enemy vessels and hit all intended targets at a range of at least 300 kilometres, the fleet added, according to Kyodo.
"We believe Russia's military buildup in the Northern Territories including these missile drills runs counter to Japan's position regarding the Northern Territories, and is unacceptable," Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi told reporters Thursday during a trip to Oman.
"We cannot tolerate moves (by Russia) to strengthen military power on the four northern islands because they go against our country's stance (on the territories)," Motegi added.
He also said Tokyo will respond in a timely manner by comprehensively considering what serves Japan's national interests, according to Japanese public broadcaster HNK.
Relations continue to worsen
The Japanese government maintains that the four islands and groups of islets that make up the Northern Territories — Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and Habomai — are part of its territory that the Soviets illegally occupied and Russia has continued to occupy since the breakup of the Soviet Union in 1991.
Putin made his first official visit to the islands on 13 August, prompting Japan to summon Russia's ambassador.
Putin went there after visiting the nearby island of Sakhalin — where Russia's navy has been conducting drills — and the Varyag flagship.
After Putin's stop, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the islands "are an inherent part of Japan's territory, both historically and under international law".
Putin's visit "offends the sentiments of the Japanese people and is absolutely unacceptable," she added.
Ties between Japan and Russia have worsened since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, when Tokyo joined other G7 countries in sanctioning Moscow and aiding Kyiv.
Analysts said Putin's visit to the Kurils could have been aimed at warning Japan against deepening its support for Ukraine — potentially including the direct supply of Patriot missiles — and against closer cooperation with NATO.
Japan currently provides only non-lethal defence aid to Ukraine.
While Japan has eased restrictions on defence exports in recent years, it is still barred from supplying lethal military equipment directly to a country at war.
Kremlin's sabre-rattling
Moscow has reinforced its military presence on the islands as recently as December 2021, when it deployed Bastion coastal defence missile systems on an uninhabited volcanic island in the middle of the chain.
The island hosted a Japanese army base prior to the Soviet occupation. A Soviet base there was shut down amid funding shortages in the wake of the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Moscow previously deployed Bal and Bastion missile systems on two of the four southernmost islands in 2016.
In the following years, Russia further beefed up its arsenal on the islands by sending top-of-the-line air defence missile systems, setting up an air base on Etorofu Island, and deploying fighter jets.
The sparsely inhabited islands are strategically significant to the Kremlin as they sit at the entrance to the Sea of Okhotsk and give Russia's Pacific Fleet access to the open Pacific without passing through Japanese-controlled waters.
Putin's visit was the first trip to the islands by a Russian president since Dmitry Medvedev in 2010.

Ukrainian soldiers use training in Germany to desert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
10:29:09 UTC
19:29:09 KST

Around 80 Ukrainian soldiers have deserted while undergoing military training in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt since 2022, with cases across Germany estimated in the hundreds, Die Zeit reported on Aug. 20.
The soldiers had been sent to Germany for training to fight Russia, but they left the training grounds unauthorized to avoid returning to Ukraine.
The report comes as Ukraine struggles with a worsening manpower shortage after more than four years of full-scale war, increasingly relying on mobilized recruits as the pool of volunteers shrinks.
More than 25,000 Ukrainian soldiers had undergone military training in Germany by early 2026, according to the Bundeswehr.
Germany provides training as part of the EU Military Assistance Mission for Ukraine (EUMAM UA), launched in 2022. By early 2026, 22 participating European countries had trained around 87,000 Ukrainian soldiers. The training includes instruction in operating military equipment, weapons handling, camouflage, and first aid.
Die Zeit reported that most soldiers who deserted had been mobilized for military service rather than volunteered. Some reportedly used their deployment to the Altengrabow military training area in Saxony-Anhalt as an opportunity to leave their units and remain in Germany.
Under Ukrainian law, leaving a military unit with the intention of avoiding service can be prosecuted as desertion. During martial law, desertion can carry a prison sentence of up to 12 years.
The soldiers also face an uncertain legal status in Germany.
Having been sent to Germany officially by the Ukrainian government, they are not considered displaced people and therefore not eligible for temporary protection under Section 24 of Germany's Residence Act, according to Die Zeit.
The EU formally agreed in July to renew temporary protection for 4.4 million Ukrainian refugees for another year, while Germany and other EU countries have also moved to tighten rules for newly arriving Ukrainian men of military age, aged 23 to 60.
Berlin and Kyiv are also discussing ways to encourage, and potentially pressure, Ukrainian men living in Germany to return to Ukraine, Ukraine's ambassador to Germany Oleksii Makeiev said on July 3.

This year's El Nino set to be strongest in more than a century, UK forecasters say
Britain's Met Office has predicted sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific will reach an "unheard-of" level of potentially more than three degrees above average, triggering severe droughts across South America and the West Pacific. Such an event would have serious knock-on effects for global food security.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
This year's El Nino weather pattern will be the biggest in over a century, warming sea surface temperatures to an "unheard-of" level, Britain's national weather agency predicted Friday.
The El Nino weather pattern is declared when sea temperatures in the tropical eastern Pacific rise 0.5C above the baseline average, triggering worldwide changes in winds, atmospheric pressure and rainfall patterns, and causing warmer global temperatures overall.
Adam Scaife, head of long-range forecasting at the Met Office, told the BBC that: "We are expecting the biggest El Nino for over a century, peaking at something over three degrees – that is unheard-of in modern climate records."
He called it "an unprecedented event", adding that "I have never seen an El Nino signal this intense in our forecasts."
Watch moreExtreme heat: 'We're really starting now to understand how global climate is impacting our health'
The anomalous warmth, which is "up to nearly two degrees already", will have particularly strong effects throughout the Tropics, Scaife said, "where we expect really severe droughts in places like South America, and the West Pacific".
'Long-term, persistent conditions'
Temperatures in the region are currently running about 2.6C above a rolling 30-year average, according to the Climate Brink dashboard.
Read moreStrong 6.7-magnitude earthquake strikes southern Peru, damaging homes and schools
"These are not short-term weather forecasts. We're talking about really long-term, persistent conditions here. There are well-known impacts on other systems including food, food security," said Scaife, a physicist who specialises in climate modelling.
The weather pattern is also expected to cause "increased rainfall and storminess in the autumn here in the UK around November time", Scaife said.

Israel receives second of six ordered KC-46 refueling aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
10:25:24 UTC
19:25:24 KST

- A second Boeing KC-46 "Gideon" tanker landed at Nevatim Airbase and joined the Israeli Air Force's 46 Squadron.
- It is the second of six KC-46 aircraft Israel has purchased, following the first delivery on May 27, 2026.
A second Boeing KC-46 “Gideon” aerial refueling aircraft landed at Nevatim Airbase and joined the Israeli Air Force’s 46 Squadron, the service said Friday.
The aircraft is the second of six KC-46 tankers Israel’s Ministry of Defense has purchased through the Pentagon’s Foreign Military Sales process. It joins the “Gideon” Squadron, formally Squadron 46, which was activated earlier this year to receive the type. The Israeli Air Force said the addition strengthens its capabilities for what it described as multi-front warfare and operations at long range.
The KC-46 is a militarized derivative of the Boeing 767 airframe. It refuels other aircraft in flight and extends their range and time aloft, while also serving as a cargo and troop transport. The Israeli Air Force said the tanker adds both refueling capacity and what it called advanced, multi-role transport capability.
Israel received its first Gideon on May 27, 2026, at Nevatim, less than a month after the aircraft’s first U.S. test flight on May 4. That delivery followed a 2020 Foreign Military Sale authorization valued at $2.4 billion for up to eight KC-46s and a 2022 Boeing contract worth $930 million covering the first four aircraft. Israel’s Ministry of Defense approved the KC-46 purchase in 2021.
Squadron 46 was stood up days before the first aircraft’s arrival to receive the new fleet. The Israeli Air Force has said it will continue flying its older refueling aircraft alongside the KC-46s during the transition. Those aircraft, known in Israeli service as the “Re’em,” are converted Boeing 707s that entered service in 1973. Squadron 120, the “Desert Giants,” operates the Re’em fleet from the same base.
The tanker fleet has drawn attention in Israel over its age. Cirium, an aviation data firm, has put the average age of Israel’s KC-707 fleet at roughly 50 years. Israel also operates seven Lockheed Martin KC-130H tankers with a similar average age, according to the same data.
Israel’s tanker capacity became a point of discussion following the February and March 2026 air campaign against Iran, when Israeli fighters flew missions roughly 2,000 km (1,200 miles) from Israeli territory, distances beyond the normal operating range of Israeli fighter aircraft without aerial refueling. During that period, Israel relied in part on U.S. Air Force tankers to extend the range of its strike aircraft.
The KC-46 can carry about 90.7 tons of fuel, roughly 15 percent more than Israel’s existing refueling aircraft, according to figures the Israeli Air Force has released. The aircraft is built with Israeli-specific systems installed after delivery, a standard practice for major platforms Israel buys from U.S. suppliers, including the F-35I fighter.
Boeing has faced production and quality-control setbacks on the KC-46 program dating back several years, issues that have drawn scrutiny from the U.S. Air Force, the type’s primary operator with 98 aircraft in service. Japan is the only other export customer to have received the KC-46 to date; Italy previously planned to acquire the type to replace its KC-767 fleet but has since paused that procurement.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke says he's been advised by domestic spy agency ASIO that one of its former agents can give evidence to the Bondi royal commission in public.
The former agent, known as Marcus, has been seeking a visa to return to Australia, arguing his evidence about the Bondi gunmen must be heard on Australian soil due to its sensitivity.
What's next?
Mr Burke says his evidence is declassified and could be heard over the phone, but advocates for the former agent say the safest option remains for him to give evidence in Australia.
A former ASIO agent who wants to give evidence to the Bondi royal commission can do so in open hearings, the Home Affairs minister says, meaning he does not need a visa to travel to Australia.
It is the first time Tony Burke has publicly addressed the man's intent to testify after previously denying his Australian visa request.
The former agent, known as Marcus, wants to give evidence about what he knew of the Bondi gunmen in the years before last December's terror attack.
He spent years infiltrating Islamic extremist groups in western Sydney, working as a paid source for domestic spy agency ASIO before his cover was blown.
Marcus has repeatedly made a case to give evidence from within Australia, due both to the sensitivity of his evidence and the legal protections he gains from being on Australian soil.
The royal commission has previously held classified hearings to ensure it can take evidence on sensitive intelligence information.
Mr Burke told reporters this morning he had been advised any evidence Marcus gives can be heard in public and heard remotely.
"Mike Burgess, the director-general of ASIO, has advised and made clear to the royal commission that any evidence that would come from this particular individual is declassified," he said.
"He's happy for it to be given in a complete public forum. It could be given over the phone on (Microsoft) Teams. It could be given in any way that the individual wants."
The royal commission has previously reached out to Marcus, it stated it is "eager" to hear his evidence and work out the best means for that to take place.
He is currently living abroad and cannot reach an Australian embassy.
Separately, NSW Police has also reached out to the former agent seeking assistance with its own investigations into last December's shooting.
Marcus has expressed fears for his personal safety while living overseas. He has sought protection and resettlement in Australia in the past.
His first visa application was rejected on the grounds that immigration authorities did not believe he had a genuine intention to leave the country, and his second application remains pending.
Mr Burke said the applications have followed all the normal channels.
"The department has its normal processes in working out whether or not someone qualifies for a visa under the Migration Act, and there hasn't been interference with that process," he said.
"The department looks at the Migration Act, looks at the application, and makes their own decision."
Advocates maintain call for visa
Whistleblower advocates have continued to back Marcus' cause, arguing the safest place for the former agent to give evidence is on Australian soil.
Marcus has previously told the ABC's Four Corners about his interactions with the Bondi gunmen, Sajid and Naveed Akram.
He claims he warned ASIO about the Akrams years before the attack.
ASIO has described the former agent as disgruntled and unreliable, but Marcus has rejected the characterisations.
Gabriel Shipton, from the whistleblower advocacy group the Information Rights Project, said he is in danger abroad.
"The protections offered by the royal commission do not extend outside Australia," he said.
"Marcus continues to risk his safety and the safety of his family. He is willing to give evidence and again the government is not acknowledging the threats he is under from the associates of the Akrams."
The group has provided support to the former agent as he lives overseas.
Mr Shipton said he should be allowed to give his evidence within Australia.
"The government has left it up to Information Rights to keep one of its ex-employees safe after years of undercover service, and again the minister has shown they are not serious about hearing evidence that contradicts the facts given by the institution in his own ministry."

Palestine Action group will not be sentenced as terrorists – judge
An attack on a Barclays Bank by five people from the Palestine Action group will not be treated as terrorism when they are sentenced, a judge has ruled.
Palestine Action was not proscribed as a terror group at the time of the attack when the group targeted the Barclays branch on St James’s Street in Burnley, Lancashire, on 5 August 2024.
The defendants, dubbed the “Barclays five”, claimed the 2am attack was designed to pressure Barclays into withdrawing financial support for weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems, a firm based in Israel. The defendants said that they did not realise that their cases would be considered as terrorism until after they were found guilty, Guardian journalist Raphael Boyd has reported.
The jury that found them guilty of criminal charges were also unaware that such a consideration was a possibility.
Pro-Palestinian group Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in July 2025 and has been behind a string of direct action protests targeting Elbit due to the firm’s links to the Israeli military.
But Judge Robert Altham, the Recorder of Preston, ruled section 69 of the Sentencing Act, establishing a terror link to the criminal damage offence, did not apply – so the defendants will face lesser sentences when they are dealt with.
Judge Altham said while the damage was substantial, it was not of the size of other attacks or on a sensitive property, such as an arms firm, as has happened during previous Palestine Action action. He said:
“Whilst the damage is undoubtedly significant, I’m not satisfied it amounts to serious damage for the purposes of the Terrorism Act.
“Section 69 does not apply in this case.”
The judge’s decision means all five defendants will still be sentenced next month at Preston Crown Court for criminal damage in the attack costing £200,000.
About 100 supporters, many waving the red, white, black and green flag of Palestine, cheered and banged drums on the steps outside as the defendants left court.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the issue of settlers in the West Bank is coming to the fore ahead of elections in Israel, with “small extremist parties dictating policy”.
Speaking to the BBC, Badenoch said:
Israel has a political issue with the elections coming up, and this is what happens in systems with proportional representation.
You have small extremist parties dictating policy, the tail effectively wagging the dog, and that’s why I’m very much against creating a proportional representation system in our country.

Footage shows French police clashing with people on beach
Footage has captured the moment French police officers clashed with people on a beach in northern France as the authorities attempted to intercept a dinghy attempting to reach the UK.
Men wearing lifejackets appear to throw objects at the police to try to keep them away from their dinghy. The officers then use Pava spray before slashing the inflatable boat with a knife.
The footage has emerged as the French government said it has prevented 185 “small boat crossing events” in the three months since a new £660m UK-France deal.
A small boat event is defined as stopping launches, seizing equipment including boats, engines and lifejackets, and arresting smugglers.
Since the signing of the deal in April, extra police units have been active on French beaches, including a 50-person riot squad.
Police action has included interceptions on beaches and at sea, the UK Home Office said.
Since March, 12 “taxi boats” have been stopped from moving further up the coast and loading more migrants.
More resources have also been dedicated to seizing boats and engines before they can be used in the Channel.
The UK government ran a larger than expected £1.8bn deficit in July, underlining the challenges facing the chancellor, John Healey, as he draws up his first budget.
City economists had expected a shortfall of zero for July, a month when Treasury receipts tend to be swollen by self-assessment income tax payments.
At £17.1bn, the self-assessment tax paid in July was £1.7bn higher than the same month last year. However, the Office for National Statistics said the government still ran a £1.8bn deficit, as “spending growth outpaced receipts”.
In the first four months of this financial year the cumulative deficit was £56.7bn – lower than last year but still running £2.3bn ahead of the Office for Budget Responsibility forecast.
Healey will announce his budget on 28 October. The public finances are expected to be gloomier than forecast at Rachel Reeves’s spring statement in March, when the Iran war had only just begun.

Police shooting in Sittard wounds Nijmegen man
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Police in Sittard in Limburg shot a man outside the city’s police station on Stationsplein overnight Friday due to what they called a “suspicious situation”.
The suspect, a 34-year-old man from Nijmegen, was injured in the leg and received first aid on the scene. He was then arrested and transferred to hospital.
Police shootings are rare in the Netherlands. Last year, officers shot at people 15 times.
Still, the national police are investigating the incident, as all cases involving an officer shooting that results in injury or death must be looked into.
Police are also looking into the cause and background of the incident.

Iran start 2026 AVC Women Asian Continental Championship in style

The 2026 AVC Women's Volleyball Continental Championship is the 23rd staging of the AVC Women's Volleyball Continental Championship, a biennial international volleyball tournament by the Asian Volleyball Confederation (AVC) with China Volleyball Association (CVA).

Mondo can sing, too: Duplantis releases ‘Gold’ as anthem for Ultimate Championship

Mondo can sing, too: Duplantis releases ‘Gold’ as anthem for Ultimate Championship
BUDAPEST, Hungary (AP) — Swedish pole vaulter Armand “Mondo” Duplantis is singing about his favorite color in a promotion for the first Ultimate Championship.
The two-time Olympic champion released “Gold” with World Athletics on Friday as the anthem of the upcoming meet that boasts a total prize fund of $10 million.
Ultimate Championship will be staged in Budapest from Sept. 11-13 showcasing Olympic, world and Diamond League champions over three evening sessions. Gold medalists in individual events will win $150,000.
The 26-year-old Duplantis has dabbled in music for several years and released his first single, “Bop,” in 2025.
Duplantis, the world-record holder, says he dreams of winning a Grammy.
“Gold” was written by Duplantis with Carl Silvergran and Oscar Chase, and was produced by Chase, the World Athletics announcement said.
“I wrote the song around representing something that’s a lot bigger than yourself,” Duplantis said in the announcement. “I think that’s what we all do when we’re on the track. We represent our family, our team, our coaches, and I love that concept. Music and sports are the two things that bring people together in the best way, and ‘Gold’ is an expression of that.”
The accompanying music video was filmed in the Hungarian capital and includes archival footage of Duplantis as a young athlete.
The Louisiana-born Duplantis told the Olympics channel last year he uses his music “as a way of therapy. I really love to have something else to be able to do, and to kind of take myself away from sports a little bit.”
At the Ultimate Championship, his new song “will be woven into the broadcast and live-event experience, connecting fans in-stadium with audiences around the world,” World Athletics said.
Duplantis is scheduled to perform “Gold” live in-stadium to close out the event.
“The Ultimate is purposefully designed to showcase the talents and passions of our sport’s biggest stars, on and off the track,” World Athletics President Sebastian Coe said. “Mondo is one of our most recognizable and accomplished athletes, and we could not be more excited that he is the one who created the Ultimate Anthem.”
The championship will be a biennial event.

Fall books: Fiction takes the spotlight in bookstores during the midterm season

Fall books: Fiction takes the spotlight in bookstores during the midterm season
NEW YORK (AP) — Midterm election news will fill the headlines this fall, but, among book buyers, fiction will likely have top billing.
Former President Joe Biden’s “Promise Me, America” stands out not just as a White House memoir — presidential memoirs are events unto themselves — but as a rare high-profile political book over the next few months. Nonfiction sales have slumped in recent years and political books haven’t approached the peaks of President Donald Trump’s first term.
“The energy in political books seems to be subdued. I think folks are just ranted out,” says Kristen McLean, an analyst and vice president for client insights at Circana, which tracks retail book sales.
“I think the (news) cycle is moving a bit too quickly for a lot of the very specific political books to catch on,” says Shannon DeVito, Barnes & Noble’s senior director of books.
Michael Lewis’ “Blockers,” a probe into Trump’s second term through the eyes of government workers, may be the only new release to rival the impact of Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan’s summer bestseller, “Regime Change.” This fall’s notable political offerings otherwise revisit the Biden years, from “Promise Me, America,” to former Middle East envoy Brett McGurk’s “Brink: Inside the Race to Free the Oct. 7 Hostages” to Akbar Shahid Ahmed’s study of Biden’s Gaza war policies, “Crossing the Red Line.”
Even Bob Woodward, who for decades released timely exposés of sitting presidents, is passing on current politics. In “Secrets: A Reporter’s Memoir,” he reflects on presidents and White House sources dating back to the Nixon administration and the Watergate scandal that made him famous..
“Because he’s going more into his own life, I expect he’ll have a different and broader audience than for his other books,” DeVito says.
A feast of fiction
Novelists Barbara Kingsolver and Hernan Diaz, co-winners three years ago of the Pulitzer Prize, will share honors again as two of the featured authors in a busy season. Kingsolver’s “Partita,” about a onetime musical prodigy drawn again to her past, is the first since “Demon Copperhead,” her Pulitzer-winning retelling of Charles Dickens’ “David Copperfield.” Meanwhile, Diaz has followed his Pulitzer-winning “Trust” with the dystopian, Dickensian “Ply,” about a young thief in a chaotic future society.
Diaz says he met Kingsolver at the Pulitzer ceremony, where the two drank bourbon and bonded over literature and other common interests.
“I don’t think literature is a race or a tennis tournament,” Diaz says. “I think the more good books that are out there, the richer the conversation becomes and the more readers are engaged.”
Fiction sales have been solid in 2026 and will likely remain high if only because the two most prominent romantasy authors, Rebecca Yarros and Sarah J. Maas, have new books coming. Maas is releasing “A Court of Splintered Harmony,” the sixth volume of “A Court of Thorns and Roses,” with the seventh installment scheduled for early next year. Yarros’ “Threshing Day” compiles 13 stories featuring characters from her Empyrean series, and her stand-alone “Peculiar Stars” finds protagonist Callista Moran stranded on an island after a sailing accident and discovering unexpected sides to herself.
The new fiction list also features Nobel laureate Jon Fosse’s latest, “Vaim Hotel,” and three contenders for the Booker Prize — Marlon James’ “The Disappearers,” Emma Cline’s “Switzy” and Rebecca Perry’s “May We Feed the King.” The book most primed for gossip is Rachel Cusk’s “Life of M,” a meta-novel about a movie star who may or may not be based on Natalie Portman. The season’s longest-awaited novel is likely Chad Harbach’s “The Brightness”: The parallel and intertwining lives of two close friends in their 20s is his first novel since his acclaimed 2011 debut, “The Art of Fielding.”
Min Jin Lee’s “American Hagwon” is her first novel since 2017 and her celebrated “Pachinko.” Emily St. John Mandel’s “Exit Party” is a story of futuristic breakdown from the author of the futuristic classic “Station Eleven.” Yiyun Li, Edwidge Danticat, Kate Atkinson, Deesha Philyaw, Diane Williams, Laleh Khadivi, R.F. Kuang and Norah Labiner also have fiction coming out.
Fans of Stephen King (and the late Peter Straub) can look forward to “Other Worlds Than These,” the final “Talisman” novel. Alice Hoffman launches a new series with “The Witches of Cambridge” and Brandon Sanderson has begun “Blightfall,” written with Janci Patterson. “The French Illusion” is John Grisham’s latest thriller. S.A. Cosby’s “Truth to Power” is a Marvel Crime novel featuring superhero/sleuth Luke Cage.
Celebrities share their stories
A trio of Oscar-winning superstars will tell their stories this fall: Sylvester Stallone’s “The Steps,” its title a reference to the actor’s iconic upward run in “Rocky”; Michael Douglas’ “One Helluva Ride,” which the actor and producer has called a corrective to the blurry legends of fame; and Dustin Hoffman’s “Look at Me,” promoted by publisher Simon Six as “an intimate memoir about art, ambition, family, friendship, love, aging, and the mysteries of a creative life.”
Gloria Steinem looks back on her early years in “An Unexpected Life” and former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick reflects on his activism in “The Perilous Fight.” Chuck Lorre’s “Sitcom” is a memoir from the creator behind “Two and a Half Men” and “The Big Bang Theory.” Eric Dane’s “My Book of Days” comes out just months after the “Grey’s Anatomy” star died from ALS.
Poetry for all times
Ancient poetry seems new again thanks to Christopher Nolan’s adaptation of “The Odyssey,” which has placed editions by Emily Wilson and the late Robert Fagles high on bestseller lists. Wilson has a new book out this fall, “Crossing the Wine-Dark Sea,” essays that cover everything from Greek tragedy to “slut-shaming” Helen of Troy to the “sly laughter” of Cardi B and Megan Thee Stallion’s “WAP.”
In “Cloud Runner,” former U.S. poet laureate Joy Harjo tries to express what she acknowledges may be inexpressible, the death three years ago of her daughter, Rainy Ortiz: “I have lost my girl./Some things do not belong in words,” Harjo writes. Jennifer Franklin channels the mind of James Joyce’s gifted, ill-fated daughter Lucia in the collection “A Fire in Her Brain.”
New work is also expected from Layli Long Soldier, Tina Chang, Patricia Lockwood, Dalia Taha, Avis Blackbird and Hieu Minh Nguyen. The anthology “Other Legacies” features tributes from Rae Armantrout, Edward Hirsch and other prizewinners to such lesser-known poets as Rachel Loden, Julia de Burgos and Stephen Jonas.
Making history
Another writer enriched by a Nolan movie — Kai Bird, co-author of “American Prometheus,” the biography adapted into “Oppenheimer” — has co-written “American Scoundrel,” the story of lawyer/political fixer/Trump mentor Roy Cohn. In “The Rush,” award winner Nathaniel Philbrick revisits the 19th century quest for gold. The acclaimed science writer James Gleick examines the evolution of communication in “The Telephone: A New History.”
Two books, Timothy W. Ryback’s “53 Days” and Victor Sebestyen’s “Weimar Germany,” examine the fall of democracy in 1930s Germany, while other releases warning of contemporary threats include Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor’s “End Times Fascism” and Pulitzer winner Jill Lepore’s “The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State.”
Public radio host Celeste Headlee’s “Freedom’s Daughters” is one of many works this fall that center on race and racism. Grandmaster Flash has collaborated with Robert “Scoop” Jackson on a history of rap and hip-hop, “Birth of a Culture,” and Stephanie Phillips’ music history “We Were Here” highlights artists from Sister Rosetta Tharpe to Living Colour.
Pulitzer winner Alan Taylor’s “Tower Hill” offers a fresh look at the 1831 rebellion led by the enslaved Nat Turner. In “Renaissance Men,” Harriet A. Washington honors three groundbreaking and overlooked Black physicians in a narrative spanning the mid-19th century to the mid-20th century, and resonating today.

5 books to read this fall, from Marlon James to Joe Biden

5 books to read this fall, from Marlon James to Joe Biden
NEW YORK (AP) — Book lovers this fall can look forward to a wealth of fiction, biographies, memoirs, poetry collections and topical nonfiction. Here are five upcoming works you’ll likely be hearing about.
“The Disappearers,” Marlon James
Marlon James’ fantasy series “Dark Star” was a showcase for his extraordinary and boundless imagination. In “The Disappearers,” he returns to his native Jamaica and to the murderous reality of his Booker Prize-winning “A Brief History of Seven Killings.” The new novel, longlisted for the Booker, is framed around the horrifying beating in 1988 of eight gay men who had been rehearsing for a play. James weaves together humor, popular culture, compassion and some very hard experience. “I refuse to believe there is any lesson to be learned from suffering an atrocity,” James writes, “other than always be on guard for the ways people turn on you.” (Sept. 1)
“American Scoundrel,” Kai Bird and Susan Goldmark
Kai Bird is best known as the co-author with Martin J. Sherwin of “American Prometheus,” the biography of nuclear scientist J. Robert Oppenheimer that became the basis for Christopher Nolan’s Oscar winner “Oppenheimer.” In “American Scoundrel,” he and Susan Goldmark (his wife) trace the influence of the late political operator Roy Cohn, from his early years as the top aide to Sen. Joseph McCarthy to his mentorship of a young Donald Trump. “American Scoundrel” draws upon government documents, archival material and dozens of interviews, including, to the authors’ surprise, Trump, who “answered our cold calls on his personal cell on several occasions,” Bird writes in the acknowledgments section. Trump was “gracious, if not exactly forthcoming about his memories” and declined to meet in person, because, he told them, “I’m the president. I’m very busy. I have China calling. I have Russia calling. I cannot do it.” (Sept. 1)
“Switzy,” Emma Cline
Emma Cline has well established her mastery of inhabiting the alienated mind, of dramatizing youthful transience, aspiration and deception, most famously in her celebrated debut, “The Girls.” In “Switzy,” longlisted for the Booker Prize, Cline gives us a retired businessman with failing mental capacity, en route to an assisted dying facility in Zurich. Cline breaks up the story into brief, affectless passages as a once-“Valuable Person” reckons with his memories and concludes that “He had always stayed on the surface. His whole life.” (Sept. 8)
“Music Against the Night,” Yiyun Li
“Music Against the Night” is Yiyun Li’s sixth novel, and first book since last year’s Pulitzer Prize-winning “Things in Nature Merely Grow,” her unsparing memoir about the suicides of her two sons. Li this time appears to have written a very different narrative — about a late 18th-century piano prodigy whose fame barely outlasted his lifetime and the orphaned wanderer-musician who makes the ill-fated decision to marry him. The novel is a story of music, but also a meditation on “the night,” death — parents, friends, children, everybody. “It is despair that one must not submit to,” Li writes late in the book, adding a dark, Shakespearean warning: “A child’s death can never feel neutral to a parent; a child’s death is a negation of time, which no longer has now and then, now and again, now and later, only now and now and now and now and now.” (Oct. 13)
“Promise Me, America,” former President Joe Biden
Memoirs are often presidents’ best chance to define their legacy, although readers and critics may have different priorities, whether Richard Nixon and Watergate or Bill Clinton and Monica Lewinsky. Joe Biden will understandably want to focus on his defeat of Donald Trump in 2020, the passage of landmark legislation on green energy and the appointment of the first Black woman to the Supreme Court, Ketanji Brown Jackson, among other achievements. But the public will likely be seeking answers to more unwanted questions, notably the state of Biden’s health while he was in the White House, the backstory to his disastrous debate against Trump and his decision soon after to call off his reelection campaign. (Nov. 17)

Remains found of American mountain climber who died in an avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak
ISLAMABAD (AP) — Search teams on Friday found the remains of American climber Mallory Geis, the last missing member of a 10-member international mountaineering team that was killed in an avalanche on Broad Peak weeks ago, a mountaineering official and local authorities said.
Geis’ remains were found by a team made up of local volunteers, according to Irfan Arshad Khan, president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan. The expedition was Geis’ first attempt to climb an 8,000-meter (26,247-foot) peak in Pakistan.
Geis, 39, lived in San Antonio, Texas. She announced on social media earlier this year that she was closing her Pilates studio to take “a giant leap of faith into the unknown to see where life goes. I have a sneaking suspicion there will be lots of helmets, harnesses, and crampons involved.”
Her family remembered her in a statement earlier this month as “a bright light who was loved deeply by her family and friends.”
The recovery ended a search that began on July 31 after the expedition, led by renowned climber Nirmal Purja, was swept away by an avalanche on Broad Peak.
Purja, a Nepal-born former British Army soldier widely known as Nims Dai, climbed the world’s 14 highest peaks in a record 189 days in 2019, an achievement featured in the Netflix documentary “14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible.” His record was broken in 2023.
Accidents are common on climbing expeditions in northern Pakistan because of avalanches, falling ice and rock, high altitude and rapidly changing weather.

Bitcoin is heading for its biggest weekly gain in three years

Bitcoin is heading for its biggest weekly gain in three years
Kyiv • UNN
Bitcoin has risen 25% over the week and is trading near $78,500. The increase was supported by ETF inflows and short-position liquidations.
Bitcoin continued its rise on Friday, heading for its best weekly gain in three years, Bloomberg reports, writes UNN.
Details
As of 9:53 a.m. in London, the price of the original cryptocurrency had risen more than 8%, trading at around $78,500. It has risen approximately 25% this week, and if the gain holds, it will be the biggest weekly increase since March 2023.
Enthusiasm returned to the market when U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced on Wednesday that the department would at least double the volume of its long-term bond buybacks, triggering a rally that forced traders to liquidate billions of dollars in short positions. That same day, U.S. President Donald Trump met with cryptocurrency industry leaders, further boosting optimism.
"The real driver was the U.S. Treasury doubling its long-term bond buybacks, which lowered long-term bond yields and generally increased risk appetite," said Rachel Lucas, an analyst at BTC Markets. "Nothing has changed Bitcoin's long-term outlook, but nothing has changed its volatility either," she pointed out.
Short positions on Bitcoin remain the main factor driving Bitcoin price gains, says Adam Morgan McCarthy, lead researcher at LO:TECH, a London-based digital-asset liquidity and market-data firm. According to Coinglass data, more than $2 billion in bearish Bitcoin bets have been liquidated in the perpetual futures market since August 19.
"Gold is the real macro signal this week: it rose cleanly after the Treasury (U.S.) doubled its bond-buying operations, without any forced buying to inflate Bitcoin's price," McCarthy said. "If you are looking for where investors are actually hedging against currency and inflation risks this week, gold shows it, while Bitcoin does not," he noted.
Trump's meeting, attended by executives from companies such as Coinbase Global Inc. and Payward Inc., was seen as a positive signal regarding the administration's commitment to cryptocurrency. Trump urged the Senate to pass the Clarity Act, a bill establishing the structure of the cryptocurrency market that has stalled over disagreements regarding ethics provisions. The bill was not brought to a vote before the Senate's August recess.
Institutional buyers returned to the market this week, while U.S.-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds are on track for their largest weekly inflow since January. The 13 ETFs added more than $1 billion this week.
"Trump's crypto meeting, momentum behind the Clarity Act, and positive ETF inflows added to sentiment, but that is not the whole story," Lucas said.
Another sign of life is that large token holders, known as Bitcoin Whales, recently added approximately $2.75 billion worth of the token over 60 days, according to CryptoQuant.
Bitcoin remains well below its peak of more than $126,000, reached last October, which occurred immediately before a sharp sell-off that drove its price down to $58,642 at the end of June.

Hungary sent commandos to seize Ukraine’s $82 million bank convoy. Its investigators now say they have found no crime
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
10:22:49 UTC
19:22:49 KST

Hungary has closed the Oschadbank case after finding no crime connected to an $82 million shipment of cash and gold belonging to Ukraine’s state-owned savings bank, The Insider reported on 20 August 2026, citing the bank’s lawyer Lóránt Horváth.
Closing the money-laundering case removes the allegation used to justify seizing Oschadbank’s assets. A separate criminal investigation is examining the couriers’ detention, while Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s government has opened an internal review of the agencies involved. Together with the return of the assets, these steps reverse how this case was handled under former PM Viktor Orbán and may help improve relations with Ukraine.
Hungary’s National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV), the country’s tax and customs authority, traced the assets to a documented deal between Austria’s Raiffeisen Bank International and Oschadbank. Raiffeisen provided records establishing the assets’ origin and Oschadbank’s payment, according to Horváth’s account of NAV’s decision.
Meanwhile, a separate investigation into the couriers’ alleged unlawful detention remains open. János Hajdu, the former head of Hungary’s Counter-Terrorism Center (TEK), is a suspect. TEK is the country’s armed counterterrorism police.
A leaked prosecution document named former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and three other former officials, including Hajdu, among those involved in deciding on the operation. Orbán has not been named as a suspect, Euronews reported on 30 June.
Orbán denies wrongdoing and says the raid was lawful.
How the Oschadbank case began
TEK stopped two armored cash-in-transit vans near Budapest on 5 March 2026. They carried $40 million, €35 million, and nine kilograms of gold from Vienna to Kyiv under a routine banking contract, Euromaidan Press reported. Officers detained the seven Oschadbank employees as witnesses, kept them handcuffed for 28 hours, and denied them lawyers and Ukrainian consular access, Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry said.
Hungary deported the couriers and imposed three-year Schengen bans, which barred them from most of Europe, although none had been charged with a crime. The orders and bans were later annulled.
Orbán’s government nevertheless portrayed the shipment as possible money laundering. Fidesz politicians also alleged, without evidence, that it was intended to finance Magyar’s then-opposition party, Tisza.
Hungary returned the vans, cash, and gold by 6 May. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the handover a break with Orbán-era “lawlessness” and a sign that relations could advance through “mutual respect and healthy pragmatism,” Reuters reported.

The Netherlands said Friday it will send back to Italy migrants who arrived after June 12 , the date of the entry into force of the European Union's new Migration and Asylum Pact, following similar moves by Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Finland and Sweden. The Netherlands will proceed with the transfers of migrants to Italy in compliance with the rules of the Migration Pact, which came into force on June 12. Those who entered before that date, however, will not be covered by the measure, Dutch media reported, citing a spokeswoman for Asylum Minister Bart van den Brink. "We are starting from scratch," the minister stated, according to the AD newspaper. Van den Brink met with Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi this week.

A general in a civilian post: the workaround that will enable Khmara to succeed Fedorov at the Defence Ministry
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:20:00 EEST
19:20:00 KST

A general in a civilian post: the workaround that will enable Khmara to succeed Fedorov at the Defence Ministry
Editor's note: This article was originally published before the vote on Yevhenii Khmara's appointment. The vote took place on 19 August, and Khmara was appointed Ukraine's defence minister.
On 18 August, the Verkhovna Rada (Ukrainian parliament) returned from its summer recess, opening the new political season. Everyone had hoped that the main personnel issue of recent weeks would finally be resolved that day – the issue that has sparked street protests in many cities across the country.
It concerns the position of defence minister, from which President Zelenskyy recently removed Mykhailo Fedorov, despite resistance and outrage from the public and a significant part of the military.
The main outstanding issue to be decided now appears to have been resolved. Ukrainska Pravda's political sources claim that the new head of the Defence Ministry will be its current acting minister, Yevhenii Khmara.
The day before, on Monday 17 August, coordination meetings were held throughout the day in the office of the Verkhovna Rada speaker. In the afternoon, parliamentary faction leaders joined them, including Batkivshchyna party leader Yuliia Tymoshenko – as focused and composed as her tightly wound signature hairstyle – as well as other representatives of the parliamentary majority.
According to Ukrainska Pravda's sources in the parliamentary leadership, the coordination meeting was long and difficult, but the discussion never reached the point of addressing the appointment issues, only touching on the fact that they needed to be resolved.
Despite this, on Tuesday 18 August, Zelenskyy submitted Khmara and Andrii Sybiha's candidacies to the Verkhovna Rada for the positions of defence and foreign ministers respectively.
Fedorov himself had called the 18th – the day the Verkhovna Rada returned to work – the point after which he would be able to decide on his next steps.
Will Khmara have enough votes in the Rada to be appointed? Will Fedorov's team remain at the Defence Ministry? And what plans does the former minister have? Ukrainska Pravda explores these questions below.
The day the vote could take place
A source in the top ranks of Zelenskyy's Servant of the People faction explained to Ukrainska Pravda that the personnel issue could be put on the agenda at any moment, meaning events could move very quickly.
"We calculated that even if there is a desire to push this whole thing through as quickly as possible, it would still take about an hour and a half to two hours just for the signed documents from Bankova Street [home to the Office of the President] to reach Hrushevskoho Street [the location of the parliament building] and be submitted to the committee," said the source.
"Because, as a statesman of the highest calibre, the parliament's speaker Stefanchuk is categorically opposed to such issues being considered without a committee decision and in violation of procedures. So, on the one hand, this issue could appear at any time. But on the other, it still won't be an instant process. It will take some time and everyone will be able to prepare for the decision-making process."
Most likely, the vote on the candidates for defence and foreign ministers will take place on Wednesday 19 August.
This will give MPs some time, albeit very limited, to discuss and communicate the decision.
In theory, the vote could also be postponed until Thursday. However, recently there has been an effort not to leave personnel issues until the end of the parliamentary week: on Thursdays, MPs are traditionally less disciplined, and quite a few previous votes have failed to take place on that day. The leadership of Servant of the People also insists that the decisions have not yet been finalised.
Will there be enough votes for Khmara?
Ukrainska Pravda's sources in the Rada said that there would be enough votes to appoint Khmara, "with some to spare". MPs had previously prepared an appeal to the president asking him to reinstate Mykhailo Fedorov as defence minister – but only three MPs signed it. This clearly demonstrates that there is no appetite in parliament to fight for Fedorov.
"Even those MPs who previously said they would not vote for anyone have already changed their tune and are now saying they will take part in the vote," an Ukrainska Pravda source said.
Khmara himself has already attended several meetings of the Verkhovna Rada's National Security Committee in his capacity as acting minister. According to Ukrainska Pravda's sources, he is viewed very positively there and considered worthy of becoming defence minister. Some committee members add that, in Khmara's nearly month-long tenure, the Defence Ministry has become more open in its communications and cooperation with them.
Roman Kostenko, secretary of the Verkhovna Rada's National Security Committee, told Ukrainska Pravda that he is ready to support the potential ministerial candidate. He had previously backed the appointments of both Fedorov and Denys Shmyhal.
"First and foremost, I believe that during wartime, the country certainly cannot remain without a defence minister for so long. So we need to appoint one and move forward. I haven't counted the votes, but I think there will definitely be enough. Khmara is a combat officer; he has shown himself to be a patriot and a worthy person. I don't think anyone will oppose his appointment as defence minister. I believe it is a good decision," Kostenko said.
One potential problem with the appointment
There is an important nuance to this story – the issue is now less about who is going to become defence minister and more about finding a formal mechanism that will allow Yevhenii Khmara to be appointed to the role.
Under Ukrainian legislation, the defence minister can only be a civilian – this is designed to ensure democratic control over the army and effective management of finances and decision-making.
Khmara is a serving general in the military, which means he cannot legally become defence minister. There are three ways this appointment could therefore take place:
- either the law is changed to accommodate the new minister
- or Khmara leaves military service
- or he becomes defence minister in violation of the law.
"Davyd [Arakhamiia, leader of the Servant of the People faction in parliament] was running around with this amendment last week – they wanted to change the law so that a serviceman could be defence minister," a source told Ukrainska Pravda. "They tried to find a way to squeeze it in somewhere, but then it all suddenly went quiet, and now no one's talking about any amendment.
"So they have probably found some other solution. Because to suggest that Khmara, who looks like Rambo, would be discharged through a military medical commission would be even more ridiculous than in the case of Zaluzhnyi.
"So, if they are not changing the law and he is not being discharged through a military medical commission, then they will probably simply appoint a general as defence minister under martial law. Why not? Although this still needs to be clarified, because no one has communicated anything to the MPs formally."
Our sources say that Khmara has agreed to leave military service. It is highly likely that he will go to the vote no longer holding the status of a serviceman. Notably, the acting minister had previously been unwilling on principle to be "struck off" military service. However, it now appears that the President's Office has found a way to persuade him after all.
The new minister may receive a "personnel surprise"
Khmara attended one of the sittings of the national security committee, where he presented his plan for the further conduct of the war. There are few details, as the meeting was held behind closed doors. However, sources of Ukrainska Pravda say that there was considerable discussion with his deputies – Mstyslav Banik and Oleksii Vyskub – about procurement matters.
At the sitting, the acting minister introduced all his deputies and explained their respective areas of responsibility. For now, there are no changes in the team – it has remained the same as it was under Fedorov.
"All the deputies joined [the committee meeting], plus there was one deputy, Mykola Shvydkyi, who was appointed already after Khmara took his post [at the Ministry of Defence]," explained Kostenko. "As for whether he's planning to replace any deputies, there has been no mention of that so far. Currently everyone is working in the same way, and in due course he [Khmara] will assess their work and make decisions."
However, Fedorov's team appears to be planning something rather different. UP's sources say that at the Ministry of Defence the majority are in fact in a state of waiting to see what happens after 18 August. As soon as a new defence minister is appointed, part of the team will leave to join Fedorov for whatever he does next.
"So the further question here is how Khmara will move, given he will not have a team and has no one to put in the top positions," a source from Fedorov's team told UP. "I don't think he even has any candidates for the director-level roles. All the deputies, the key managers – that was the best thing Mykhailo could have left for Khmara."
Fedorov met with Khmara immediately after his dismissal in order to hand over his team's strategy. In terms of Khmara's plans, for now he is trying to understand what needs to be improved. The secretary of the national security committee asserted that Khmara will continue to hold the course on areas he considers to be working well.
"Everything that is positive will continue to move forward," said Kostenko. "It would be unfair to take away the good things and say that the previous minister did everything wrong. Of course, Khmara has plenty of his own ideas for development. In some areas they don't align with Fedorov's vision, in others they do, but he sees things differently. So that's the direction we'll take. I think he has enough of his own ideas and experience to bring something new to the Ministry of Defence."
And what about Fedorov?
The sources in the Servant of the People faction surveyed by UP are unified in saying that Mykhailo Fedorov's return to the post of defence minister is impossible for now.
Another source from the presidential faction gave his view of the situation:
"Well, Misha [Fedorov] has now become the leader of the youth and the protests, while we have a team of older people. So I do not think his return to the Ministry of Defence is possible. But at the same time we can't say that all bridges have been burned. It is similar to the situation with Kubrakov. If he does not climb onto the barricades and try to break through walls with his head, then it is entirely possible that some place in the team will be found for him after all. Mykhailo worked with us for a long time. The history of the relationship is long, so it will always be possible to reach an understanding. But this is definitely no longer about the Ministry of Defence."
Oleksandr Kubrakov, referred to by the source above, had been the deputy prime minister for Reconstruction. Following his dismissal and after some time had passed, he was given the post of freelance presidential adviser on infrastructure and engagement with hromadas (administrative units designating a village, several villages, or a town, and their adjacent territories). It is highly doubtful that Fedorov will have any prospect of being appointed to a formal post as an adviser with unclear responsibilities and powers. Moreover, the former defence minister himself does not appear likely to accept such an offer.
Fedorov's team told UP that dialogue with the president has not been active of late. They have also not met in person in recent days. After Fedorov turned down the offer of becoming deputy prime minister, there have been no further offers. Fedorov had previously stated that he would not agree to any other post other than returning as defence minister. He has not changed his position, and the subject of returning to the post has not come up in the dialogue with the president.
The former minister and his team are awaiting the Verkhovna Rada's decision. Should Khmara be appointed, Fedorov's "plan B" will come into effect – he will launch a series of projects, one after another, connected to the war and Ukraine's defence, sources said. In what status and in what sector this will take place is not being disclosed for now.
***
And while the country waits to see what the future holds for the Ministry of Defence, it appears there is no suspense here at all – the ending of the story is obvious. The only question is when the vote will take place and which mechanism will be chosen for Khmara's appointment, given his general's rank in the military.
At the conciliation board it was announced that on 18 August the candidates will meet with the factions, and on 19 August the vote on the ministers will be held, MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak reported. This also concerns the submission of Andrii Sybiha's candidacy for the post of foreign minister.
On this matter, according to UP's sources, there are no disputes whatsoever. This appointment is expected to go through very quickly and easily.
Roman Romaniuk, Tetiana Kryvishyn, Natalia Bodnar, UP

U.S. Navy adds $41.5M for Tomahawk warhead production in Alabama
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
10:19:42 UTC
19:19:42 KST

- General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems will build 559 WDU-36/B warhead cases and 559 fuzewells for Tactical Tomahawk missiles under a $41.57 million Navy contract modification.
- Work runs through April 2028 and is centered in Anniston, Alabama, as Tomahawk prime contractor Raytheon separately ramps missile production toward more than 1,000 units a year.
General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems Defense Research Institute Inc., of Anniston, Alabama, has been awarded a $41.57 million contract modification to build 559 warhead cases and 559 fuzewells for the U.S. Navy’s Tactical Tomahawk missile.
The modification, designated P00016, adds the work to a previously awarded firm-fixed-price contract, N6893619C0039. It covers production and delivery of the parts for the U/RGM-109E Tactical Tomahawk, the surface- and submarine-launched land-attack version of the missile family. The Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division at China Lake, California, is the contracting activity.
Work on the order will be performed primarily in Anniston, Alabama, which accounts for 99 percent of the effort, with the remaining 1 percent completed in Houston, Texas. The Navy expects the work to be finished by April 2028. Fiscal 2026 weapons procurement funds covering the full $41,571,985 will be obligated when the award takes effect. The contract was not competed.
The parts being ordered support the WDU-36/B, the blast-fragmentation warhead fitted to the Tactical Tomahawk. The warhead has a titanium case and weighs about 310 kg (690 pounds), carrying roughly 120 kg (265 pounds) of PBXN-107 high explosive. It replaced the heavier WDU-25/B warhead used on earlier Tomahawk variants starting in 1993, a change that also freed up space in the missile body for additional fuel. A fuzewell is the internal housing that holds the warhead’s fuze assembly, which triggers detonation.
The order arrives as Tomahawk’s prime contractor, RTX unit Raytheon, ramps up production of the missile under a separate arrangement. Raytheon announced on Aug. 17 that it had won a $22.9 billion, seven-year Navy contract to accelerate Tomahawk output, awarded under the Department of War’s Arsenal of Freedom initiative. That award followed framework agreements Raytheon signed with the department in February, which set a target of ramping annual Tomahawk output to more than 1,000 missiles. RTX has said Tomahawk production stood at roughly 60 missiles per year for U.S. forces before those February agreements, putting the planned ramp at more than 15 times that rate.
RTX also said it delivered three times more Tomahawks in the first half of 2026 than in the first half of 2025, and that it will work with hundreds of small and mid-sized suppliers nationwide to scale output under the new contract. GD-OTS functions as one of those suppliers, producing warhead hardware that feeds into Raytheon’s final missile assembly. The Anniston work is separate from the Raytheon contract and funded through a different procurement line, but it points to the same production increase across the Tomahawk supply base.
RTX did not disclose current annual production figures or a timeline for reaching the 1,000-missile target when it announced the new contract. It also did not say which Navy platforms or allied programs the additional missiles would support. The company has said the Tomahawk has been flight tested more than 550 times and used operationally more than 2,300 times since it entered service.
Tomahawk missiles launch from Navy surface ships and submarines and strike targets at ranges of roughly 1,600 km (1,000 miles). The U/RGM-109E variant covered by the new GD-OTS order is the Tactical Tomahawk configuration, which added a two-way satellite datalink allowing the missile to be redirected or given a new target while in flight, along with the ability to loiter over a target area.

Who was Fathi Khazem, killed by the Israeli army in Jenin?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
10:16:50 UTC
19:16:50 KST

Breadcrumb
Who was Fathi Khazem, the Palestinian killed by the Israeli army in Jenin?
On Friday, the Israeli army killed Palestinian Fathi Zeidan Khazem, known as "Abu Ra'ad," during a raid on his Jenin home in the northern West Bank.
Separately speaking with The New Arab, local sources said that an Israeli special forces unit stormed Khazem's home in the early morning, amid a heavy military presence and intense gunfire. Israeli reinforcements later arrived in the area.
The sources said soldiers entered the house with gunfire heard from inside. Bloodstains were visible throughout, including the stairs, and Khazem was shot inside his home.
Israeli forces took his body as they withdrew.
Palestinian ambulances tried to reach the house but were blocked during the operation, according to local sources.
But the Israeli army claimed that its forces were conducting an operation in Jenin when "an armed assailant attempted to stab one of its soldiers", prompting soldiers to open fire and "neutralise" him.
The army claimed none of its soldiers was injured and did not identify the man by name.
Israeli Channel 12 also claimed that a Palestinian man had been killed after allegedly attempting a stabbing attack in the Jenin area.
The circumstances of the shooting inside Khazem's home remain disputed, with Palestinian witnesses describing a raid on his house and the Israeli army characterising the incident as an attempted stabbing.
Security officer to wanted man
Khazem was born on 9 September 1966 in Jenin refugee camp to a Palestinian family displaced from the Shafa'amr area in 1948 Palestinian territories.
He left school at an early age and worked in construction to support his family before being arrested by Israel during the First Intifada and spending years in Israeli prisons.
Following the establishment of the Palestinian Authority, he joined the Palestinian National Security Forces and eventually rose to the rank of colonel. He served as deputy commander of the Nablus district, becoming part of the Palestinian security establishment.
But his life changed dramatically after the death of his eldest son, Ra'ad.
In April 2022, Ra'ad Khazem carried out a shooting attack on Dizengoff Street in central Tel Aviv that killed three Israelis and wounded others, and then killed by Israeli forces.
Fathi Khazem refused to surrender to Israeli authorities and became wanted by Israel. His family home was subsequently raided during the search for him, turning the household into a repeated target of Israeli operations.
Months later, Khazem suffered another devastating loss. His second son, Abdul Rahman, who was affiliated with armed groups in Jenin, was killed in a clash with Israeli forces in September 2022.
Within months, the former Palestinian security officer had lost both of his sons.
The deaths transformed Khazem from a relatively unknown former officer into one of the most recognisable faces associated with Jenin.
Videos of his speeches at his sons’ funerals circulated widely, particularly his calls for Palestinian unity and his denunciations of the Israeli occupation.
Rather than withdrawing from public life, Khazem continued appearing at funerals, community gatherings and political events. Among Palestinians in Jenin, he became known as "the father of martyrs".
"Fathi Khazem wasn't just the father of Ra'ad and Abdul Rahman for us; he was one of the faces that encapsulated Jenin's story over the past years," Youssef Faraj, a resident of Jenin refugee camp, told TNA.
"People saw in him a father who lost two sons, yet he remained steadfast and present among them, speaking about Jenin, about unity and about rejecting the occupation," he said.
"That's why he became a symbol. His story was no longer just the story of one family, but became part of the story of the city itself and what it has endured in terms of raids, killings and destruction," he added.
Israel targets Palestinian symbols
Khazem's killing comes amid continued Israeli military operations across the northern occupied West Bank, particularly in Jenin and its refugee camp, areas that have witnessed repeated raids, arrests, armed clashes and targeted killings.
Israel claims its operations are intended to pursue armed Palestinians and prevent attacks against Israelis.
Palestinians, however, argue that the raids and killings extend beyond armed groups, affecting communities and targeting people who have acquired social or symbolic influence.
Khazem's case highlights the increasingly blurred line between Israel's stated security objectives and the broader Palestinian perception that influential figures are also being targeted.
For many Palestinians, the significance of Khazem lay not in a formal political position or military command.
It was rooted in his personal story: a former Palestinian security officer who became wanted by Israel, lost two sons and subsequently emerged as a public voice associated with Jenin’s resistance and suffering.
In that sense, his killing is likely to be interpreted by Palestinians as extending beyond the death of an individual.
Israel, meanwhile, has repeatedly argued that individuals who influence public opinion or provide social support for armed groups can contribute to mobilisation and encourage further attacks.
Yet assassinations can produce an outcome opposite to their intended effect. A person who is killed may become more powerful as a symbol, particularly when their life is already tied to stories of loss, resistance and displacement.
That symbolism extends across Palestine.
In Gaza, where the war has turned the deaths of parents, children and entire families into a defining feature of daily life, Khazem's story resonated with Palestinians who saw in him another image of a father whose family was destroyed through years of confrontation with Israel.
"We in Gaza know Fathi Khazem even though we are far from Jenin, because his story reached every Palestinian home, especially after the killing of his two sons, Ra'ad and Abdul Rahman," Rizq Shomer, from Gaza, told TNA.
"For us, he was not just the father of two martyrs. He became a symbol of a Palestinian family that paid a heavy price during the years of conflict," he said.
"His killing is therefore not seen here as an incident specific to Jenin alone, but as part of an ongoing targeting of Palestinian figures who have become symbols in the eyes of the people."
Shomer said Palestinians had watched influential figures, including political leaders, activists, journalists and community figures, become targets during years of conflict.
"Israel claims it is targeting people it considers a security threat, but for us, when a person who has become part of people’s conscience is killed, the issue goes beyond the person himself," he said.
"We see targeting symbols as also an attempt to break morale and send a message that no one is protected, not even figures who have become part of the national memory," he added.
For Palestinians in Jenin and beyond, Khazem's death may therefore add another chapter to a story that began with the loss of his sons. In death, as in life, his significance is unlikely to remain confined to his family or his hometown.

- Japan and international bodies condemned the US action, stressing support for the ICC, which prosecutes serious crimes globally as a last resort.
AI generated
TOKYO - International Criminal Court President Tomoko Akane of Japan warned on Aug 21 against “the demise of international rule of law” after the United States targeted her with sanctions.
Washington sanctioned Akane and trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal on Aug 18 as part of the Trump administration’s campaign against what it calls a “corrupt and fatally politicised” body.
“The sanction against me this time was something I had anticipated to an extent, so I’m not surprised,” Akane said in a statement released on X by her publisher Bungei Shunju.
“The important thing is not to let this be the beginning of the demise of international rule of law.”
The measures bar Akane and Seye from entering the United States and from carrying out transactions in the US financial system.
Akane’s statement – her first public comments since the sanctions – comes after the ICC on Aug 19 called the US measures a “flagrant attack” on the court’s independence.
The United Nations rights chief Volker Turk and top EU officials threw their support behind Akane and her institution.
Washington’s latest move follows sanctions it imposed on several ICC officials, seen as largely in response to the court’s investigations involving Israel, a US ally.
Japan has also objected to the sanctions on Akane, with the foreign ministry saying it “consistently supported the ICC... in its efforts to prosecute and punish the most serious crimes of concern to the international community and to uphold the rule of law”.
Japan is the biggest funder of the ICC and a close US ally.
Established in 2002, the ICC prosecutes individuals accused of the gravest atrocities and acts as a last resort when countries do not have adequate legal systems to ensure accountability.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier said in a statement, without providing examples, that the sanctioned “individuals have directly engaged in efforts by the ICC to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction”.
The United States signed the Rome Statute establishing the ICC but never ratified the treaty. Israel, Russia and China are not ICC members either.
In 2023, the ICC issued an arrest warrant for Russian President Vladimir Putin over the war in Ukraine, prompting Moscow to issue its own arrest warrants for senior court officials.
These included Akane, 70, an ICC judge since 2018 who was elected as the court’s president in March 2024.
“Even if one judge were to die, we are easily replaceable, so there is really no value in targeting us,” she said after the Russian announcement. AFP

Germany is seeking to extradite a suspect from Romania over the discovery of an underground stash of weapons in a forest near Berlin that German media reports have linked to Russian intelligence.
Two weeks after German authorities found a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport, the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, confirmed federal prosecutors had opened an investigation related to the secret cache of guns “on suspicion of preparing a serious act of violence that threatens national security”.
“This case demonstrates that we are operating under a high threat level,” he told reporters. As with the Leipzig incident, Dobrindt said he could not rule out the involvement of “foreign powers”.
Earlier, local media had reported that German authorities had unearthed two handguns and ammunition about a year ago in a wooded area outside the German capital after agents of the domestic intelligence service received a tip.
The find has been the focus of covert investigations by state security and counterespionage services on suspicion Russian intelligence was plotting assassinations on German soil, according to separate reports by Der Spiegel magazine and an investigative team led by Süddeutsche Zeitung.
Rather than removing the arms, German authorities left them on site after rendering them unusable in the hope they would lead to clues during a months-long electronic surveillance operation, Dobrindt said.
No one was observed trying to collect the weapons, leading investigators to believe the agent or agents had learned of the cache’s discovery and it was now “dead”.
Dobrindt described the suspect in Romania, whose nationality was not disclosed, as a “low-level agent” and noted several other such operatives had been detained so far this year.
Although the investigation into the Berlin stash has been long-running, the revelations apparently led Dobrindt to hastily call the news conference on Friday.
Sinan Selen, the head of the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, has warned for months of more aggressive tactics by Russian secret services, including plans for targeted attacks on German soil.
Moscow’s potential hit list is believed to include weapons contractor executives, opposition figures in exile and other prominent Ukraine supporters, according to the report by Süddeutsche and the public broadcasters NDR and WDR.
The federal prosecutor’s office and the Russian embassy declined to comment. A BfV spokesperson said: “As a matter of principle, we don’t comment on matters relating to any specific intelligence activities.”
Spiegel said German authorities were looking into possible links between the arms cache – a familiar Soviet tactic during the cold war – and a sabotage campaign against Ukrainian logistics routes blamed on Russia.
Last year Polish security officials arrested several people allegedly planning to mail parcels containing incendiary devices or detonators, some of them reportedly posted from Romania.
Investigators believe the packages could have been remotely ignited or set off using timers during transit to do serious damage to vehicles, cargo planes or logistics centres and spread fear in the EU.
In 2024, a firebomb in a parcel posted via DHL exploded in a freight container on the tarmac at Leipzig airport. Only a delayed flight kept it from going off in the air.
Ukraine has been using the facility in Leipzig as an alternate location for the transport of military goods since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to official records.
This month the German newspaper Die Zeit reported that Russian secret services were plotting an attack against Stefan Thumann, the head of German drone manufacturer Donaustahl.
The report said German investigators were tipped off by a foreign intelligence service at the end of last year and arrested a Ukrainian man and a Romanian woman this spring.
Thumann is said to be under police protection. The case recalled reports in 2024 that US intelligence services had foiled a Russian plot to assassinate the chief executive of Germany’s leading arms manufacturer, in an apparent attempt to retaliate over the company’s role in providing armaments for Ukraine.
The plan to murder Armin Papperger, the chief executive of Rheinmetall, was reportedly one of several Russian government schemes to kill defence industry executives in several countries in Europe that have been supporting Ukraine’s war effort. The plot against Papperger was believed to be the most advanced.
Russia has repeatedly denied any involvement in sabotage, disruption or intimidation against EU member states.

"It's obvious that Kosovo's 'police' will under no circumstances protect Serbs and will unleash their entire arsenal of repressive means against them at the first opportunity," Zakharova stated.
She also drew attention to the actions of the European Union.
"Brussels has openly sabotaged the implementation of the 2013-2015 agreements it itself guaranteed to establish the Community of Serb Municipalities of Kosovo, but at the same time demands that Belgrade implement the unsigned 2023 'agreements' with Pristina and recognize the 'state sovereignty' of its own southern province," Zakharova noted. "Given the ongoing extreme instability in the province, KFOR's withdrawal from key deployment locations is unacceptable. The multinational contingent deployed under UN Security Council Resolution 1244 must continue to fully carry out its assigned duties without the involvement of the obviously unreliable Kosovo Albanian security forces," she concluded.
