Global markets trade mixed amid bond market uncertainty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
09:06:47 UTC
18:06:47 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu and Emir Yildirim
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
Global markets traded on a mixed trend on Thursday due to the inflationary environment and high government spending, while the US Treasury’s plan to lower borrowing costs came to the fore as a temporary solution as high energy prices continued fueling inflation fears.
Investors are skeptical about the impact of the US Treasury’s intervention in the bond market, as the decision to expand long-term bond buyback operations may not reduce risks.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the buyback operations for long-term bonds could exceed $4 billion, while the department is ready to impose the harshest sanctions against Tehran, in line with US President Donald Trump’s statements about some sort of economic operation against Iran, fueling concerns over geopolitical tensions.
Additionally, San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said she has seen little evidence that there is a need for a preemptive rate hike, while St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said gradual rate hikes are preferable.
Meanwhile, US initial jobless claims fell 6,000 to 206,000 in the week ending Aug. 15, below market estimates.
The US 10-year Treasury yield rose above 4.7%, and the 30-year bond yield climbed from 5.2% to 5.26%. The US Dollar Index is trading down 0.1% at 98.8 due to high public debt and bond market concerns.
Investor demand for the dollar declined as the US economic administration adopted a more interventionist stance toward markets.
The falling dollar supported gold, driving up the precious metal by 0.4% to $4,535 per ounce.
At the same time, US retail giant Walmart’s shares fell 9.2% after its sales forecasts did not meet expectations.
The New York Stock Exchange closed lower on Thursday, as the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 0.15%, the S&P 500 dropped 0.45%, and the Nasdaq was down 0.45%. American indexes started Friday on a positive note.
Meanwhile, European stocks traded mixed on Thursday amid geopolitical uncertainties and the worsening energy crisis.
Europe’s Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) data to be released on Friday will show the impact of the rise in oil and natural gas prices since August.
Germany’s five-year bond yield hit 3.008%, its highest since 2008, while public debt in the country is expected to reach new records due to expectations of increased defense spending.

Mainland Affair Council says most Taiwanese reject China unification

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Mainland Affairs Council said Thursday that nearly seven in 10 people in Taiwan support maintaining the cross-strait status quo while rejecting unification with China.
CNA reported that the council's survey found 68.9% supported maintaining the status quo without moving toward unification. Another 81.2% opposed China's proposed "one country, two systems" principle.
The poll also found that 83.6% supported the government's approach to maintaining the cross-strait status quo. In addition, 83.9% said Taiwan's future should be decided by its 23 million people.
On recent cross-strait developments, 70.5% said Chinese coast guard patrols in waters east of Taiwan showed "malicious intent." The survey also found that 76.4% supported tougher penalties for foreign nationals who commit violent crimes in Taiwan.
The latter question followed a recent case in which a Chinese national surnamed Liao (廖) attacked commentator Akio Yaita in Taiwan. The council cited the case as an example of concerns over pressure and intimidation extending across borders.
The Mainland Affairs Council said the results showed that most people in Taiwan continue to oppose "one country, two systems" and unification with China. It said Beijing has continued using gray-zone pressure and transnational repression to create instability in Taiwan.
The council said the government will continue measures aimed at strengthening Taiwan's defense and social resilience. It also called on Beijing to recognize that Taiwan and China are not subordinate to each other and to hold talks with Taiwan's elected government without preconditions.
The council commissioned National Chengchi University's Election Study Center to conduct the telephone survey from Aug. 13-17. It surveyed 1,086 Taiwan residents aged 20 and older and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.97 percentage points at a 95% confidence level, per FTV News.

Kinmen villagers hold rites for war dead of Battle of Guningtou
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
09:05:04 UTC
18:05:04 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Residents of Jinning Township in Kinmen County held rites Thursday for those killed in the Battle of Guningtou, a pivotal 1949 battle that halted the continued advance of Communist forces.
Communist troops launched an amphibious assault on Kinmen on Oct. 25, 1949, landing along the coast of Guningtou Village and surrounding areas, per CNA. Nationalist forces emerged victorious after days of intense fighting.
Former Guningtou Village Chief Li Chao-chin (李朝金) said the battle caused heavy casualties on both sides. He said local residents decided to hold rites for the dead at the direction of the local guardian deity, Lord Guan, adding that roadside rites helped bring peace to the village.
After the Battle of Guningtou, villagers began holding rites inside the village and near the mouths of nearby rivers every July 8 on the lunar calendar. In addition to roadside rites, general temples scattered across northwestern Kinmen are also dedicated to fallen soldiers.
National Quemoy University scholar Wang Hong-nan (王宏男) said the general temple near the Beishan Broadcasting Wall was likely funded and built by local farmers who helped collect the remains of war dead. He said Kinmen has experienced numerous battles, resulting in many temples dedicated to wandering spirits who did not receive proper burials.
Wang explained that temples dedicated to you-ying spirits are generally associated with wandering souls, while Kinmen's general temples are specifically dedicated to soldiers. Temples dedicated to wandering spirits date back to the Qing dynasty (1644-1912), when the high mortality rate among Han settlers and hurried burials sometimes left remains exposed to the elements.
One notable example is a temple in Taichung's Dongshih District, where about 20,000 remains from the Lin Shuang-wen (林爽文) Rebellion surfaced after a local temple collapsed in an earthquake, per CNA. Lin's forces were driven into Indigenous territory by Qing forces, local militias, and Indigenous groups allied with the Qing, and were ultimately defeated in Dongshih District.

Ebola outbreak: five big questions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
09:02:22 UTC
18:02:22 KST

On 23 August, it will be 100 days since the Bundibugyo strain was first reported. How did it became the DRC’s most deadly outbreak and what must be done to stop it becoming the world’s largest?
There have now been almost 5,000 cases and more than 2,000 deaths since 15 May, making this Ebola outbreak the biggest and most deadly in the DRC’s history.
It is on course to be “the largest one in the world”, according to Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), speaking at a press briefing in mid August.
Why are case and death figures still increasing?
The outbreak was declared on 15 May, but is thought to have been spreading unreported for months before that date. That means “the outbreak had a big head start, it is still way ahead of us and we are playing catch-up,” Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director general of the World Health Organization (WHO), said last week.
The Bundibugyo virus causing the latest outbreak is a rarer type of the Ebola disease, and has no licensed vaccine or medicine. That means health workers trying to bring the outbreak under control must rely on painstaking efforts to identify cases, isolate them for treatment, and then also identify their contacts for monitoring.
But in Ituri and North Kivu, the DRC provinces with the highest numbers of cases, and where armed conflict has displaced tens of thousands of people, officials have been unable to identify enough contacts to get on top of transmission. Africa CDC estimates the response is tracing about 12% of contacts – the target is 95%.
Authorities are now switching to a new approach that will see them going door to door to seek people with symptoms, and appointing people in every village to be part of the response effort.
Where are the 850 people who tested positive but are unaccounted for?
As of 15 August, there had been 4,945 confirmed cases, with 730 people in treatment centres, 1,040 people recorded as surviving the virus, and 2,325 deaths.
That leaves 850 people who have tested positive, but are unaccounted for in the number of patients, survivors and victims. People who have the virus, but whose whereabouts are unknown, represent a high risk of onward Ebola transmission.
In the hardest-hit areas, many locals have extremely little trust in the authorities. They ask why the government is suddenly present, when communities had been struggling alone before – including with other diseases such as cholera and malaria.
People searching for gold this month at a mine in Ituri, one of the DRC provinces with the highest numbers of cases. Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/AP
Mistrust translates into infected people coming forward for treatment late, if at all – and sometimes, fleeing Ebola treatment centres because they do not trust that they will get the necessary care there.
Some families prefer to care for their loved ones at home – and, if they die, to follow their usual burial practices that involve touching the bodies. Ebola is spread through body fluids, and carers without the proper protective equipment face a high risk of infection.
Is money that has been promised reaching the frontline?
The availability of banknotes has been a real issue for paying workers involved in the response. The airport in Bunia, the provincial capital of Ituri, has been closed to commercial flights for months, making it harder to bring cash in.
In remote areas, there are no banks and mobile money systems are unavailable, says Prof Yap Boum, of Africa CDC. “The frontline responders, the community healthcare workers, the people working in treatment centres […] you need to pay them with cash.
“If you don’t have the cash in the city, and therefore in those villages, it’s difficult to run some operations,” he says.
Some staff, including nurses and the teams in charge of safe burials, have gone on strike over the lack of pay. In the face of attacks from the community, many of whom do not believe the Ebola outbreak is even real, they say they “see no point in risking our lives” without compensation.
Health workers protest over unpaid wages outside the provincial governor’s office in Ituri in early August. Photograph: Constant Same Bagalwa/AP
The new, village-based approach that goes from door to door will need more workers and probably be more expensive than the approach up to now.
However, officials have insisted that payment problems are being ironed out.
Africa CDC says $518m (£382m) is needed for the direct health response to Ebola, and another $882m to tackle surrounding humanitarian issues.
Donors including the US, EU, African Union member states, the World Bank and its Pandemic Fund have pledged more than enough to cover that amount – but not all the funding has been released. Tedros said last week that only $264m of the $518m had been disbursed. Getting ahead of the outbreak, he warned, “depends on financing”.
Do we have any treatments or vaccines available?
In the wake of Covid-19, the world launched an ambitious initiative to make diagnostics, therapeutics and vaccines available within 100 days of any future pandemic. And while Ebola is not a pandemic, the International Pandemic Preparedness Secretariat has been tracking progress on that basis. The world is not going to meet the 100-day deadline – but there has been progress.
Testing is now available in labs in Ituri, rather than requiring samples to be sent to Kinshasa for confirmation.
A health worker holds a blood sample as part of the Ebola response in Mongbwalu, Ituri province. Photograph: Michel Lunanga/Getty Images
Safety trials have begun of two vaccines designed specifically to protect against the Bundibugyo strain. And new evidence suggests that an existing Ebola vaccine called Ervebo, designed to fight the Zaire strain of the virus, may offer enough cross-protection against Bundibugyo to cut death rates, even if it does not prevent infection – officials are planning to roll it out on that basis.
Trials have begun on some drugs both as treatment and as prophylaxis when given to someone exposed to a Bundibugyo patient.
In the coming months, the cost and access to any drugs or vaccines that prove successful in trials are likely to be a test of international solidarity.
What will things look like in another 100 days?
The outbreak will not be over by the start of December. But WHO officials hope a renewed focus, and shifting their approach to actively seeking cases on a village-by-village basis will reverse the spread of the disease in the DRC within three months.
One early indicator of progress would be a fall in the case-fatality rate – the proportion of people testing positive who die, which has risen in recent weeks. As of 15 August, it stood at 47%.
Patients at an Ebola treatment centre in Rwampara, Ituri, in June. Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/EPA
A high death rate is likely to reflect people coming forward late, when it is harder for doctors to treat them, and cases not being reported. A fall would suggest improvements in tracing efforts, as well as potentially better treatment.
Another key thing to watch for is any further spread to neighbouring countries – South Sudan, which neighbours Ituri, has its own ongoing humanitarian crisis that would make a response to Ebola harder. Authorities in the country have been stepping up surveillance, including by training health workers in border towns to spot signs and symptoms of the disease.
Potential vaccines and treatments, and an intensified response, are reasons to be hopeful. But if current efforts fail to bear fruit, the outbreak is on course to surpass the biggest on record, which killed more than 11,000 people in west Africa between 2014 and 2016.

EXPLAINER - From floods to famine: What past El Nino disasters reveal about 2026-2
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
09:01:10 UTC
18:01:10 KST

The strongest El Nino events in modern history have shown how changes in Pacific Ocean temperatures can develop into a worldwide humanitarian and economic crisis.
The 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16 episodes brought destructive flooding to parts of the Americas and East Africa, while contributing to drought, wildfires and failed harvests across Australia, Southeast Asia and southern Africa.
Their consequences included tens of thousands of deaths, the displacement of millions of people and severe disruption to food production, public health, transport and national economies.
Those events are now attracting renewed attention as another potentially exceptional El Nino develops.
The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) said on Aug. 13 that the 2026-27 El Nino is strengthening and has a greater than 90% chance of becoming very strong during the Northern Hemisphere autumn and winter.
NOAA also placed the probability that it will exceed the strength of every El Nino recorded since 1950 at 69% during the October-December period.
However, the agency stressed that the strength of an El Nino does not automatically determine the severity of its effects.
The 1982-83 El Nino was one of the strongest and most destructive climate events of the 20th century.
In Ecuador and northern Peru, as much as 100 inches of rain fell over six months. Flooding transformed normally dry coastal areas into lakes and grassland, while damaging roads, homes, crops and other infrastructure.
On the opposite side of the Pacific, shifts in rainfall contributed to severe drought and destructive forest fires in Indonesia and Australia, according to a NOAA historical assessment.
The World Health Organization has linked El Nino to the wider global food crisis, including the famines that affected the Horn of Africa and the Sahel during that period.
Close to 450,000 drought-related deaths were reported in Ethiopia and Sudan in 1983, according to the World Meteorological Organization.
That figure**, however,** represents the wider drought and famine emergency and cannot be attributed directly to El Nino.
Because disaster reporting was less comprehensive at the time, the exact impact of the event is difficult to gauge.
NOAA estimated direct global economic losses at more than $8 billion.
A later peer-reviewed study published in Science calculated a far larger economic impact, attributing $4.1 trillion in cumulative global income losses to the event over the following five years.
The figure does not represent destroyed buildings or crops. Instead, it reflects modeled losses from slower economic growth that persisted after the immediate disasters had ended.
The 1997-98 El Nino became a modern benchmark for a global climate emergency.
The UN attributed more than 20,000 deaths to the event, while NASA estimated about $36 billion in infrastructure damage.
Floods and landslides struck parts of Peru and Ecuador, while heavy rainfall caused emergencies across East Africa.
The UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) estimated that about 10 million people in East Africa required emergency assistance.
In Somalia alone, flooding killed an estimated 2,000 people, displaced 250,000 and destroyed as much as 80% of crops in some of the worst-affected southern agricultural areas, it said.
The unusually wet conditions also contributed to one of East Africa's largest recorded outbreaks of Rift Valley fever.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimated that as many as 89,000 people may have been infected in northeastern Kenya and southern Somalia.
In Indonesia, the opposite rainfall pattern produced severe drought. Fires deliberately started to clear forests and peatlands burned out of control, blanketing parts of Southeast Asia in toxic haze and damaging agriculture, transport and public health.
The environmental damage extended into the oceans. Around 16% of the world's coral reefs were effectively lost during a global bleaching event in 1998 as El Nino added to unusually warm marine conditions, according to the International Coral Initiative.
The economic effects continued long after the weather pattern faded.
The Science study estimated that the 1997-98 El Nino caused $5.7 trillion in cumulative global income losses over five years, with poorer tropical countries bearing a disproportionate share.
The 2015-16 El Nino was one of the strongest events ever recorded.
A World Food Program assessment estimated that it affected the food security of between 60 million and 100 million people.
The humanitarian effects were particularly severe in Africa. More than 40 million people in East and southern Africa were projected to be food insecure, according to a UN assessment.
In Ethiopia, repeated crop failures and livestock losses left 10.2 million people food insecure, according to UN figures.
Southern Africa experienced its worst drought in more than three decades, with widespread maize failures, water shortages, livestock deaths and sharp increases in food prices.
Indonesia again experienced extensive forest and peatland fires. Many of the fires were started by people clearing land, but severe El Nino-related drought allowed them to spread and burn for months.
Around 2.6 million hectares were burned. The resulting air pollution affected 43 million people**, and** more than 500,000 received treatment for respiratory illnesses.
The World Bank estimated that the fires cost Indonesia $16.1 billion, equivalent to 1.9% of its gross domestic product.
Official reports recorded several dozen immediate deaths, while later scientific modeling suggested that prolonged smoke exposure may have contributed to as many as 100,000 premature deaths across the wider region.
Flooding also affected South America. More than 150,000 people were displaced in Uruguay, Paraguay and Argentina in early 2016.
Unlike the 1982-83 and 1997-98 events, there is no single widely accepted estimate of total global economic losses from the 2015-16 El Nino.
Country-level figures, humanitarian costs and losses in agriculture, fisheries and health nevertheless amounted to tens of billions of dollars.
The history of the three strongest events shows that the greatest danger is not one isolated flood or drought. It is the possibility of simultaneous shocks across several continents.
Failed harvests in major producing regions can raise food prices elsewhere. Drought can reduce hydropower production and river transport. Floods can destroy roads and health facilities, while standing water can create conditions for disease outbreaks. Wildfire smoke can cross national borders and disrupt schools, airports and businesses.
The events also demonstrate that extreme outcomes are not inevitable. Forecasting, early warnings, food reserves, drought-resistant seeds, livestock protection, disease surveillance and the preparation of flood defenses can substantially reduce casualties and economic losses.
The UN estimates that every $1 invested in anticipatory programs can save between $3 and $7 in avoided losses and emergency response costs.
The central lesson from 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16 is therefore not that the same disasters will repeat in exactly the same places. It is that a powerful El Nino can expose and deepen existing vulnerabilities across the world, with consequences that continue for years after Pacific Ocean temperatures return to normal.

Nolan's "Odyssey" overtaken "Deadpool & Wolverine" to become highest-grossing R-rated film
Kyiv • UNN
The film grossed $1.352 billion worldwide, surpassing «Deadpool & Wolverine». The movie also topped Nolan's box office and the IMAX rankings.
Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster "The Odyssey" (The Odyssey) has officially become the highest-grossing R-rated film of all time, grossing $1.352 billion worldwide and surpassing the record set by the 2024 film "Deadpool & Wolverine" (Deadpool & Wolverine), which grossed $1.338 billion, UNN reports, citing Variety.
Details
"The Odyssey" was released in theaters on July 17, bringing in an impressive $123 million in its domestic U.S. debut, and remains a big-screen sensation. Since then, the big-budget adaptation of Homer’s epic poem has grossed $516 million in the domestic U.S. market and $835 million internationally—a huge figure for any film, but especially for an R-rated nearly three-hour "sword-and-sandals adventure," the publication notes.
It is the fifth release this year and the third R-rated film (after "Joker" (Joker)) to surpass $1 billion in revenue.
Among its many other box-office achievements, "The Odyssey" ranks first among Nolan’s films in all-time box-office earnings, surpassing 2012’s "The Dark Knight Rises" ( $1.08 billion, not adjusted for inflation), as well as becoming the highest-grossing film of all time in the Imax format, overtaking 2009’s "Avatar" (Avatar) ($271 million, not adjusted for inflation).
"The Odyssey" stars Matt Damon as Odysseus, King of Ithaca, and tells the story of his seemingly endless, perilous journey home after the Trojan War. Damon leads an all-star ensemble that includes Tom Holland, Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson, Lupita Nyong’o, Zendaya, Charlize Theron, Elliot Page, Jon Bernthal, and John Leguizamo.

Riyaz ul Khaliq
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
China Friday pushed back against the US framing of the detention of American national, Min Zin, as “wrongful,” stressing the judicial authorities were handling the case according to the law.
Stressing that China “upholds rule of law,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian said: “there is no so-called wrongful detention.”
“The relevant people from the United States are suspected of engaging in activities that endanger China’s national security and breached China’s laws,” said Lin.
He was responding to a statement from the US State Department which said Thursday that Secretary Marco Rubio declared US national Min Zin "wrongfully detained" in China and called for his release.
Min, a scholar, was detained on June 3 in China's southern Yunnan province, where he traveled at the invitation of the Chinese government to attend an academic conference, according to the US State Department.
A graduate student at UC Berkeley and founder of a Myanmar-based research group, Min disappeared in Kunming, the capital of Yunnan province, which borders Myanmar. On June 12, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs publicly confirmed that he had been arrested and formally detained on suspicion of espionage
“China’s judicial authorities are handling the case in accordance with the law,” said Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin.

Russia Deploys North Korean Ballistic Missiles Within Reach of 7 Ukrainian Regions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
08:57:27 UTC
17:57:27 KST

Russia is preparing to expand its use of North Korean ballistic missiles, with six launchers deployed in Voronezh Oblast that could put seven Ukrainian regions within range, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) reported on Friday, Aug. 21.
The Ukrainian military’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) confirmed on Aug. 20 that North Korea had transferred around 50 KN-23, KN-24 and KN-30 ballistic missiles to Russia as of July 2026, according to ISW.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Russian launchers in Voronezh could reportedly strike targets in Sumy, Kharkiv, Chernihiv, Poltava, Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts, ISW said.
The KN-30, also known as the Hwasong-11C, is an upgraded version of the KN-23 ballistic missile and can reportedly carry a warhead weighing up to 2,500 kilograms (2.75 tons).
ISW said it has not observed evidence that Russian forces have used the KN-30 against Ukraine.
Russia expands North Korean missile capability
According to Ukraine’s military intelligence, Russia has begun deploying six launchers for North Korean missiles in Voronezh Oblast. The launchers could collectively fire up to 120 missiles, ISW reported.
The deployment would give Russia another ballistic missile capability for striking Ukrainian targets from Russian territory.
Ukrainian military expert Anatoly Khrapchinsky cautioned that Russia does not necessarily use every available launcher as part of a strike package during a single mission.
How Energy-Exporting Russia Is Turning Into a Fuel Importer – Thanks to Ukraine
Russia has around 160 Iskander launchers capable of carrying two missiles each, but Russian forces launch an average of 16 to 26 missiles per strike package, Khrapchinsky said.
North Korean missiles also differ from Russia’s Iskander-M missiles in accuracy and warhead size.
Khrapchinsky said Iskander-M missiles can strike within approximately 5 to 20 meters of their intended target, while North Korean KN-23 missiles have reportedly missed their targets by hundreds of meters or even kilometers.
However, the North Korean missiles can carry substantially heavier warheads.
KN-23-series missiles can reportedly carry warheads weighing up to 1ton (970 kilograms), compared with the standard 480-kilogram warhead on Russia’s Iskander-M, resulting in larger craters and stronger shock waves.
The reported deployment indicates that Russia continues to develop ways to incorporate North Korean missiles into its assaults against Ukraine.

Law enforcement authorities have referred to court an indictment against a 33-year-old Kyiv resident accused of committing sexual violence against five young children. This was reported by UNN, citing the Office of the Prosecutor General.
Details
The investigation established that the suspect lived in the same apartment with his mother, sister, and nieces and nephews.
Between December and May 2025, he repeatedly committed sexual acts against his sister’s young children. In order to satisfy his own sexual urges, the man touched the genitals of his nieces and nephews—three boys aged 8, 6, and 2, as well as girls aged 5 and 4
The investigation also found that the family was registered with social services, and in December 2025, the woman and her five children were placed in a Center for Social and Psychological Rehabilitation after an inspection of their living conditions and neighbors’ complaints that the children were left at home without adult supervision.
The oldest boy, followed by the other children, told a psychologist about the suspicious actions of their mother’s brother.
The detainee was notified of suspicion of committing violent sexual acts against his underage nieces and nephews, as well as repeatedly committing such acts (Part 4 of Article 153 and Part 6 of Article 153 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine). The sanctions under these articles provide for imprisonment for up to 15 years or life imprisonment.
The suspect is currently being held in custody without the right to bail.
Recall

Ambassador Bencini Delivers His Final Address at the Conference on Disarmament
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
10:56:06 CEST
17:56:06 KST

Ambassador Leonardo Bencini, Italy’s Permanent Representative to the Conference on Disarmament (CD), delivered his final address to the plenary today, marking the end of his four-year term in Geneva. 
In his remarks, Ambassador Bencini noted that, while 2025 had seen a “remarkable achievement” with the timely establishment of subsidiary bodies under the Italian presidency—the first time since 1996 that this had occurred at the start of the session—in 2026 “a step backward was taken,” returning to a less structured format, according to a press release from the Embassy. 
He emphasized that the CD’s difficulties do not stem from inherent shortcomings of the body itself, but from “deeply rooted and politically sensitive divisions that have persisted for decades” and from the current state of tension in international relations. “When mutual trust is at an all-time low and dialogue is faltering,” Bencini observed, “how can we expect a breakthrough on the sensitive security issues we address in this body?”
Ambassador Bencini—the press release notes—expressed concern over a growing trend of criticism toward the CD, “not counterbalanced by constructive proposals or alternative approaches,” while recalling the concrete proposals put forward by Italy. He reaffirmed the enduring value of the CD as a forum for discussion—including on emerging issues related to new technologies—and welcomed high-level political participation, such as the visit by U.S. Under Secretary of State DiNanno last February.
                                    
                                       
				 Concluding on a hopeful note, he praised the “competent and committed diplomats” who make up the disarmament community, calling them “human capital that we will greatly need one day—hopefully soon—when we negotiate treaties again.”

Did CM Vijay 'dilute' Tamil Nadu's delimitation stand? TVK, DMK clash in assembly

TVK-DMK verbal clash in Tamil Nadu assembly
NEW DELHI: The Tamil Nadu assembly witnessed a sharp political face-off between the ruling TVK and opposition DMK on Friday, with the two parties clashing over the state's official stance on the upcoming delimitation exercise.The exchange came after chief minister C Joseph Vijay, according to the DMK, omitted the term "freeze" while referring to the number of Lok Sabha seats (543) during Thursday's Zonal Council meeting chaired by Union home minister Amit Shah and attended by chief ministers of southern states."The TVK government passed a resolution in this House to freeze the total number of Lok Sabha seats at 543, but chief minister Vijay did not use the word 'freeze' at the Southern Zonal Council meeting," Udhayanidhi said, suggesting that the TVK-led government had "diluted" Tamil Nadu's demand.Defending the government, TVK MLA CTR Nirmal Kumar replied that the agenda of the 31st Southern Zonal Council meeting was specifically designed to address broader issues concerning all southern states.Intervening in the debate, Tamil Nadu minister Adhav Arjuna asserted that the government's position remained "unwavering.""Our government has no change in stand with regard to delimitation," he maintained.
The exchange intensified as both sides traded charges of "compromising" Tamil Nadu's interests. Udhayanidhi reiterated that the DMK remained committed to a total freeze on the redrawing of constituencies or, at the very least, ensuring that Tamil Nadu's current 7.18% representation was not reduced.Arjuna, however, hit back at the LoP, alleging that the DMK had "shifted" its position in the past. "If they ask only for fair delimitation, it would be a betrayal to Tamil Nadu," he remarked, claiming that the DMK had previously not insisted on the 543-seat cap.He also challenged MPs of the MK Stalin-led party not to walk out of the Palrliament if the BJP-led Centre introduces the Delimitation Bill."When the Bill comes up in Parliament, the DMK should not stage a walkout... All 39 MPs of the DMK should stay inside the House and register their opposition. If you boycott, that too will turn out to be favourable for the ruling party," he added.
'We accept Delimitation did not become law because DMK opposed': TVK
However, Arjuna acknowledged that the DMK had also played a significant role in ensuring that the Delimitation Bill did not become law, prompting AIADMK leader and former chief minister Edappadi K Palaniswami to seek clarification."We have not forgotten that the DMK stood firm for state rights. We accept that the Delimitation Bill did not become law because the DMK opposed it. Just as we united for states' rights in the past, let us unite now as well," Arjuna said.Palaniswami then asked, "Delimitation is a law. Does TVK need its number of constituencies to be increased or decreased? Clarify that."Arjuna responded: "After the census, Vajpayee brought a special law to freeze the LS numbers. To bring that again, let your MPs, including yours, raise their voice; that is our request."

These are the world’s most beautiful summer cities, according to eye-tracking technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
08:55:23 UTC
17:55:23 KST

European destinations dominate the top 30 most beautiful city rankings, with 19 gorgeous spots making the list.
As the end of August brings (marginally) cooler weather to the northern hemisphere, travellers who have sensibly shunned hot urban centres might be looking to get back to city breaks.
For a little inspiration, hotel chain Premier Inn decided to try to classify the most beautiful cities to visit in summer using a bit of science.
The company collected images of over 60 major cities across the globe in summertime and, using eye-tracking technology, studied which pictures people were drawn to quickest and where their gazes lingered the longest.
These are the world’s most beautiful summer cities
The study revealed that Banff in Canada is the most beautiful summer city, achieving a score of 96.0/100.
Participants spent an average of 3.2 seconds gazing at the image of this Canadian city of rustic timbered houses cradled by majestic mountains – the longest time for any image in the study.
In second place is Mykonos in Greece, with an overall score of 87.3/100. Mykonos, with its iconic white-washed dwellings and electric blue sea, was the top city to get people’s attention – taking only 1.5 seconds for those in the study to notice it.
Following closely behind Mykonos is Sydney, Australia, a city whose vibrant urban beaches and laid-back vibe encapsulate summer, with a score of 85.6/100.
Bruges in Belgium – a labyrinth of canals and gabled townhouses – ranks in fourth place (84.1/100), with Bristol, a historic port city in the United Kingdom, rounding out the top five (83.7/100).
A total of five UK cities appeared in the top 30 rankings – Bristol, Liverpool (15th place), Bath (25th place), Glasgow (27th place) and Brighton (29th place).
Germany also has four cities in the top 30 rankings, including Munich (14th place), Freiburg (16th place), Hamburg (22nd place) and Dresden (23rd place).
Overall, European destinations dominate the top 30 most beautiful city rankings, with 19 gorgeous spots making the list.
Here’s the full top 10:
- Banff, Canada
- Mykonos, Greece
- Sydney, Australia
- Bruges, Belgium
- Bristol, United Kingdom
- Palma de Mallorca, Spain
- Kyoto, Japan
- Kotor, Montenegro
- Auckland, New Zealand
- Los Angeles, United States

Germany news: Berlin losing its appeal for many Germans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
08:51:00 UTC
17:51:00 KST

Germany news: Berlin losing its appeal for many Germans
Published August 21, 2026last updated August 21, 2026
What you need to know
- More Germans think Berlin 'lacks charisma' than those who find it 'fascinating,' according to a survey
- Panda twins Leni and Lotti celebrate their second birthday at Berlin Zoo
- The German government is reportedly considering sanctioning a Russian cultural center in the capital over the recent drone incident at Leipzig airport
- Nearly a quarter of German companies are facing a shortage of skilled workers
- A leading economic institute says states in eastern Germany need immigrants to avoid running out of workers
This blog has been paused. Read below for a roundup of the stories making headlines in Germany on Friday, August 21 2026:
Watch: Can low-water ships help with low Rhine levels?
When the Rhine River runs dry, supply chains come under pressure. Low-water ships are intended to help transport goods even when water levels are extremely low.
But how do they work, and why are there still so few of them?
Berlin Briefing: Germany is overheating: Why isn't politics responding?
This week, DW's Berlin Briefing looks at how German politicians are — or are not — addressing climate change.
Eastern Germany needs immigrants to avoid running out of workers: IW institute
Eastern German states are facing a severe decline in their working-age populations without immigration, a leading economic research institute said Friday.
The German Economic Institute (IW) said that by 2045, more than a fifth of eastern German states' workforces would be lost without immigration.
The IW said around 7.7 million people between the ages of 15 and 66 currently live in eastern Germany. That number would fall to around 6 million without immigrants.
"As a result, the economic situation — particularly with regard to the provision of services — is unlikely to be sustained," write IW economists Philipp Deschermeier and Wido Geis-Thöne.
"If a region is massively short of workers, the economy can no longer provide for the population," the IW researchers explained.
The shortage would be most felt in sectors such as care workers, hairdressers, craftspeople and doctors, they said.
Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Saxony-Anhalt would be especially affected, the IW said.
The institute's findings come as both states prepare to hold crucial elections, in which the anti-immigrant, far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is set to make record gains.
In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD could win an absolute majority and enter a state government for the first time.
The AfD has called for much stricter immigration policies and for more repatriations and deportations of migrants.
Germany probes arms cache found in woods near Berlin
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has confirmed media reports on Friday that a weapons cache was found in a forest near Berlin last year and that a suspect had been detained in Romania.
But Dobrindt did not address reports that the weapons stash, which included handguns and ammunition, was meant to be used as part of an assassination on behalf of Russian intelligence services.
For more on this story, head over to our report.
At least 8 injured after car crashes into storefront in Hesse
At least eight people sustained minor injuries after a car appeared to lose control and hit people in a pedestrian-only section in Hofgeismar in the central German state of Hesse.
Police cited witnesses as saying that the driver of the car appeared to have been experiencing medical difficulties right before the incident unfolded.
Locals noticed the man behind the wheel at a crosswalk and approached him to help, but he sped into the pedestrian zone and hit several people.
His car ultimately came to a stop after he crashed into a storefront.
Other passersby immediately offered help to the driver, who has now been taken to hospital, where his condition is reportedly critical, according to police.
The accident site remains cordoned off.
Berlin weighing sanctions against Russian cultural center over Leipzig drone incident
Amid mounting evidence that Russia was behind the planned drone attack on Leipzig Airport this month, the German government is reportedly considering imposing sanctions on the controversial Russian House cultural center in Berlin.
German government officials have avoided publicly blaming Moscow for the incident, in which an explosive-laden drone was found at the airport in Leipzig.
But according to Der Spiegel, Berlin is weighing possible sanctions against Russia, including targeting the Russian House on Friedrichstrasse.
Moscow says it is a cultural center, but security officials in Germany suspect it is also used for espionage activities.
Despite the frosty ties between Berlin and Moscow in recent years, Germany has resisted closing the center for fear that Russia would retaliate by closing Goethe Institutes in Moscow and St. Petersburg — the last remaining representations of German civil society in Russia.
Almost 1/4 of German companies face shortage of skilled workers
Nearly one in four companies in Germany are facing a lack of skilled workers, the Munich-based ifo institute said Friday.
The survey found that 23.2% of German firms had reported a shortage of skilled staff in July, a 2-point increase since April.
The long-term average of German companies reporting skilled labor shortages remains much higher, at 31.7%.
A "weak economy" is currently limiting demand for skilled workers, ifo researcher Daria Schaller said.
But she warned that as Germany's economy recovers, "the shortage of skilled workers is likely to increase considerably again."
Demand rose most sharply in the telecommunications sector, where 31.1% of firms were lacking skilled workers, compared to 16.3% in April.
Nearly 65% of companies in the consultancy and auditing sectors were facing skilled labor shortages, up from 52.4%.
Germany's gas stores at 'historic low' for time of year
Gas storage facilities in Germany are less full for the time of year than at any point since 2011, when records began.
"The current gas storage level is by far the lowest ever recorded for this time of year in Germany," Sebastian Heinermann, INES managing director told German news agency dpa. "It is therefore a historic low."
Find out why Germany's gas storage levels are so low in this in-depth report by DW's Nik Martin.
Panda twins celebrate second birthday at Berlin Zoo
Berlin Zoo held a birthday party for two of its most popular residents: twin pandas Leni and Lotti, who are turning two years old this weekend.
The panda cubs were treated to a special ice cake made of beetroot and carrot juice, which was waiting for them on the climbing frame in their outdoor enclosure, Berlin Zoo said in a statement.
"The two panda twins devoured the icy birthday surprise with obvious enthusiasm," the zoo said.
Born on August 22, 2024, the sisters have grown from tiny cubs weighing less than 170 grams (under 6 ounces) each into giant pandas. Leni weighs more than 70 kilograms (154 pounds), while Lotti weighs around 61 kilograms.
"Two years ago, Leni and Lotti could still fit in our hands; today, together they weigh more than 130 kilograms. Watching them develop is very special for our entire team. As true Berliners, they have long since found many fans in the city," said Zoo and Animal Park Director Dr. Andreas Knieriem.
The pandas' names have a special connection to Berlin: Leni is named after iconic German actress and Berlin native Marlene Dietrich, while Lotti is named after Charlottenburg, which neighbors the zoo.
Their mother Meng Meng arrived in Germany in 2017 as part of an agreement with China, which has gifted pandas to friendly nations as part of its "panda diplomacy" policy.
China maintains ownership of the animals and any cubs that are produced, and virtually all cubs born outside China are eventually returned.
Knieriem said Leni and Lotti are "ambassadors for a species whose protection can only succeed through international cooperation. Because we mustn't forget that fewer than 2,000 giant pandas live in their natural habitat."
The giant panda is listed as "vulnerable" to extinction by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).
Berlin not as appealing to Germans today compared to 20 years ago — survey
A new survey has found that Berlin is losing its appeal to many Germans.
An Allensbach Institute poll published by the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ) on Friday found that 31% of respondents consider their capital city to be a "fascinating metropolis."
The same survey found that 36% of the 1,039 people polled think Berlin lacks charisma.
The figures represent a sharp decline in Berlin's appeal among Germans. A previous Allensbach survey from 2007 showed that 66% thought the capital was "fascinating," with only 14% saying it lacked appeal.
Famously described by former mayor Klaus Wowereit as "poor but sexy," Berlin has seen tens of thousands of workers move to the city, causing rents to soar.
This has in turn placed increasing strain on world-famous Berlin's nightclubs, many of which are being priced out by property developers.
Hamburg (48%) and Munich (47%) lead the way for Germans who were asked which cities are particularly appealing.
Asked which cities they would not want to live in, Berlin scored 46%, making it the least popular city alongside financial capital Frankfurt am Main.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Morgen! from Bonn, where the long-overdue rain from the past two days has eased ahead of the weekend.
We begin our coverage of Germany today with the news that Berlin, widely considered one of the world's coolest cities for its vibrant cultural and nightlife scenes, is losing its appeal to many Germans.
Boosting the German capital's appeal — at least for today — is the second birthday celebration of panda twins Leni and Lotti at Berlin Zoo.
In other news from Berlin, the federal government is considering sanctioning a long-standing Russian cultural center in the capital over the recent explosive-laden drone that was found at Leipzig Airport this month.
Bleibt dran as we bring you more on these headlines and plenty more besides.

Iran executes 'foreign national' over alleged involvement in January protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
08:50:54 UTC
17:50:54 KST

Iran executed another protester on Thursday over the deadly 2026 Isfahan unrest, as rights groups warn of forced confessions and death sentences used to stifle dissent.
Iran executed a foreign national accused of taking part in anti-government protests in the city of Isfahan in January, the judiciary’s Mizan news agency reported on Thursday.
The judiciary identified the man as Qaim Hosseini, but did not disclose his nationality. Mizan said Hosseini, who was also known by the alias “Arian,” had confessed to taking part in protests held on 8 January in Ali Khani Square in Isfahan.
The judiciary had previously said that four security personnel were killed during protests in the square. Authorities arrested 59 people after the incident on charges of taking part in the demonstrations.
Four other detainees in the case — Abolfazl Sepahi, Amirhossein Safari, Erfan Esfandiari and Golmohammad Mohammadi — had previously been executed.
Hosseini was carrying a “cold weapon” during the protests, Mizan reported. According to the news agency, based on evidence in the case and “explicit confessions” by other defendants, Hosseini had been actively present at the scene where security forces were killed and had kicked the bodies of the dead officers.
Mizan also reported that Hosseini had been accused of taking items from a charity organisation and setting them on fire.
Iran’s judiciary said Hosseini’s trial was held in the presence of a lawyer and that the death sentence was reviewed and upheld by the Supreme Court following his appeal.
Human rights organisations have repeatedly raised concerns over reports of forced confessions by detainees in Iran, as well as restrictions on effective access to legal counsel, fair trial guarantees and defendants’ rights during detention, investigation and trial.
Rights activists and organisations have also accused Tehran of using the death penalty in protest-related cases as a tool to spread fear and suppress dissent.
A report released earlier this week by the Washington-based Abdorrahman Boroumand Center for Human Rights in Iran stated that Tehran has executed at least 901 people since the beginning of 2026, including 28 executions carried out in August alone.
In a report to the United Nations General Assembly, Secretary-General António Guterres said at least 975 people were reportedly executed in Iran in 2024, a 17% increase from the previous year and the highest annual figure recorded since 2015.
The report also documented a further sharp rise in the first half of 2025, with at least 612 executions recorded between January and June, or 119% more compared with the same period in 2024.
The UN has repeatedly raised concerns over the use of the death penalty in Iran, particularly in cases involving drug offences, national security charges and ethnic minorities, as well as over fair-trial guarantees and the use of torture-tainted confessions.

Bulgarian Eclipse Hunters return from Spain with magical footage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
08:50:51 UTC
17:50:51 KST

Friday 21 August 2026 10:01
Friday, 21 August 2026, 10:01
PHOTO Eclipse Hunters
Font size
Being an eclipse hunter is a calling that requires not only serious knowledge of astronomy and great technical literacy, but also a strong love for the astronomical phenomenon itself. "We literally chased it! We drove over 250 kilometers to find clear sky!", says Gancho Ganchev, a professional astronomer and leader of the Bulgarian expedition that filmed the latest celestial spectacle, about the eclipse hunt. His team, which this year consists of only three Bulgarians, includes Hristo Iliev, who works in the banking sector, but has been involved in astronomy since childhood, and since 1999 to this day, he has been travelling around the world to capture every solar eclipse, as well as 29-year-old Tsvetoslav Nikolov, a software engineer, for whom solar eclipses are "the only thing that provokes to experience the full palette of emotions" that a person is capable of:
Gancho Ganchev and Hristo Iliev
PHOTO Radio Bulgaria
"Suddenly it becomes completely dark and you feel a sense of uncertainty. You don't know where you are and whether what you are observing is real. This explains why ancient people perceived them as a sign from the gods and an omen of an upcoming event. It is understandable, because this phenomenon is extremely rare, and when a person lives in one place, they can usually be lucky enough to observe it only once in a lifetime." To film the total solar eclipse on August 12, the three Bulgarians went to Spain. "We were looking for a location in the central part of the country," says Gancho Ganchev and adds:
PHOTO Eclipse Hunters
"We had chosen about 5 or 6 backup locations, but the place we were shooting from was a medieval castle from the 13th century, located on a peak, from where you could see perfectly 360 degrees. And, of course, we weren't the only ones! Most photographers had come with a tripod and a camera and the rest were amateurs enjoying the moment."
PHOTO Eclipse Hunters
Unlike most photographers, the "Eclipse Hunters" use high-end professional cameras, lenses, telescopes and computers, but Gancho Ganchev is still skeptical about artificial intelligence. He says that "as an assistant for the planning of the process itself, artificial intelligence is good." He draws a parallel with the shots used in cinema - they look beautiful, but are far from reality, while this is a very important component for them. This is also the reason why the astrophotographs of the "Eclipse Hunters" are like those published in scientific journals and on official NASA platforms. Ganchev adds that each shot is unique because:
The hill and the final phase of the eclipse at sunset
PHOTO Eclipse Hunters
"This eclipse was low above the horizon and other times it can be early in the morning or high up in the sky. The sun's corona itself changes depending on its cycle and its activity. The eruptions are not the same and change every minute. Each total eclipse is radically different."
Tsvetoslav Nikolov
PHOTO Eclipse Hunters
For the Bulgarian "Eclipse Hunters", however, one of the reasons they film each subsequent solar eclipse is the experience itself. The youngest member of the group, Tsvetoslav Nikolov, says: "During the event, I honestly switch off and don't think about what happens to the photographs, because the phenomenon is so unique that even when it's over you start thinking about the next one and can't wait to experience it again."
Hristo Iliev told us more about the natural anomalies that accompany it and the reasons for their occurrence:
PHOTO Eclipse Hunters
"Animal reactions are very similar to every solar eclipse. They behave quite strangely because eclipses occur in the same place on average every 200 years and this phenomenon is not programmed into their DNA. They don't know how to behave - they see that it is getting dark and go to sleep, but after 2 minutes the sun rises again and they fall into a kind of panic. In one of the videos of the current eclipse, huge flocks of birds can be seen passing over people's heads. In addition, the temperature drops sharply, the air density also changes sharply and this is the reason for the wind that appears every time. Its name is «eclipse wind». However, when there is broken cloud cover, this very wind blows the clouds away, so we can at least see the full phase of the eclipse. The colours around us also change a lot - the grass is not its usual colour, as the light is muted, but not as red as at sunset, which changes the colours of everything around. And when the total phase occurs, suddenly it's as if someone has pulled the curtain - it becomes night, the stars rise, the planets begin to be visible and the constellation in which the eclipse occurs is different each time. And at 360 degrees you can see an orange sunset, as if the sun had set everywhere at the same time!"
PHOTO Eclipse Hunters
And since the next total solar eclipse that will be visible from the territory of Bulgaria will be on September 3, 2081, what remains for those of us who do not plan our excursions according to this astronomical phenomenon is to enjoy the astrophotography of the specialists who literally chase the solar eclipse to capture it in a photo.

Details
In line with the government’s transparency and open data initiative, the Military Court Service is to publish the court listings for the military court centres.
Each court listing covers the next one or two week assize period. This will be published on the internet by the last working day in advance of the assize period.

Please be aware that the court listings are subject to change after publication, if you wish to find out more please contact the relevant military court centre. Details can be found at the bottom of each court listing.

2026-08-21
08:50:00 UTC
17:50:00 KST

Lithuania's government will not cut value-added tax on fuel even if oil prices continue to rise, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said on Friday.
This distances Vilnius from a move by neighbouring Poland, which this week temporarily reduced VAT on some fuels from 23% to 8%, a cut estimated to lower pump prices by up to €0.23 per litre depending on fuel type. The measure is expected to cost the Polish state budget around €115 million.
"We are not discussing VAT," Sinkevičius said. "It would likely be difficult for us, as a country, to compare ourselves with the Polish economy. Poland's economy is nearly 11 times larger, giving their government slightly more room for manoeuvre than smaller Lithuania."
Instead, Lithuania has prepared a contingency plan centred on excise duty reductions. The prime minister has previously indicated that such measures would be considered if diesel prices exceeded €2.20 per litre.
In mid-April, following an escalation of conflict in the Middle East, the government cut the diesel excise duty by six cents per litre for a two-month period.
Sinkevičius said a similar excise-based response remained on the table if the situation in the Middle East were to worsen and push oil or petroleum product prices sharply higher.

Iran turns to Iraq, vows to withstand ‘toughest’ US sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
08:48:00 UTC
17:48:00 KST

Iran vowed Friday to strengthen its economy and withstand what it called “unjust sanctions,” a day after U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatened the toughest-ever financial measures against Tehran.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammed Baqer Qalibaf, one of the country’s most influential political figures and a senior negotiator in talks with the United States, said economic resilience and national security were closely connected.
Speaking to Iranian and Iraqi business representatives in Baghdad, Qalibaf accused the United States and Israel of waging economic and “cognitive” warfare after failing to defeat Iran through direct military confrontation.
“If you look at the resources and raw materials of Muslim countries, you will realize that our enemies come to plunder them,” Qalibaf said, according to a statement posted on his Telegram channel. “Therefore, we must make plans to deal with the unjust sanctions so that we can overcome them.”
Qalibaf also called for closer economic cooperation between Iran and Iraq, including greater use of their national currencies in bilateral trade to reduce dependence on the U.S. dollar.
His comments came as Washington prepared a new round of economic pressure against Tehran following months of conflict that have killed thousands of people, disrupted energy markets and threatened one of the world's most important oil shipping routes.
Bessent said Thursday that the United States would unveil details of what he called “the toughest sanctions in history” on Iran at a news conference Monday.
He suggested the campaign could reduce the likelihood of another major military escalation.
“I’m not sure why oil has popped up on this,” Bessent told CNBC. “If we are doing the maximum economic pressure, then that means that likely there will not be a large-scale kinetic restart,” he said, using a term for military action.
The announcement followed President Donald Trump’s warning Wednesday that Washington would pursue “Economic Warfare” and impose severe consequences on any country that helps Iran.
Trump said any country allowing its financial institutions, businesses, airports or government entities to provide “any type of lifeline” to Iran would face what he described as “TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences.”
The threats have added further uncertainty to global energy markets. Oil prices climbed to more than a three-week high Thursday as traders assessed the potential impact of tighter sanctions on Iranian exports and the wider Middle East.
The conflict has already disrupted the movement of oil through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway that previously carried roughly one-fifth of global oil trade. Iran has demonstrated its ability to restrict shipping through the strait, raising fears that any renewed military confrontation could trigger another major energy shock.
The United States and Iran have announced ceasefire agreements twice, in April and June, in efforts to restore shipping through the waterway and move toward an end to the conflict. Both agreements, however, quickly unraveled.
Iran has lived under extensive U.S. sanctions for nearly five decades, dating to the 1979 Islamic Revolution. Tehran has repeatedly accused Washington of using economic pressure to undermine the country’s sovereignty and political system.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry condemned the latest U.S. measures before Bessent’s announcement, describing American economic and trade sanctions as “economic terrorism.”
The ministry said the measures would not weaken Iran’s determination to defend its independence, dignity and national sovereignty.
Bessent said the new sanctions would form part of a broader strategy aimed at putting maximum pressure on Tehran.
“It is a one-two punch. We have the blockade on Iran, and we are going to have the toughest sanctions in history,” he said, referring to a U.S. naval blockade imposed in April and paused for a month in mid-June.
“It is going to work in Iran and we are going to collapse this regime,” Bessent added, calling on U.S. allies and other countries to decide whether they would support Washington’s campaign.
One of the biggest questions is how far the United States will go in targeting countries that continue doing business with Iran, particularly China.
China buys more than 80% of Iran’s seaborne oil exports, according to 2025 data from analytics firm Kpler. But any attempt to impose secondary sanctions on Chinese entities could carry significant consequences for Washington because China is also a major supplier of goods and critical minerals to the United States.
Asked whether Washington could target China over its trade with Iran, Bessent said some discussions would be better handled privately.
“Keep in mind that the Chinese get 50% of their energy from the Gulf,” he said, arguing that Beijing would benefit from cooperating with Washington.
China has rejected the use of sanctions and pressure as a solution to the crisis.
“Sanctions and pressure do not help resolve the problem,” a Chinese Embassy spokesperson in Washington said, calling on the parties involved to pursue political and diplomatic solutions.
Trump’s economic threats have also intensified domestic pressure on his administration to bring the conflict to an end.
Higher fuel prices have added to concerns over the economic impact of the war and could become a political liability ahead of the November midterm elections, when Republicans will defend their control of Congress.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi accused Trump of using the confrontation with Tehran to divert attention from economic problems at home, including record U.S. debt and rising interest rates.
Araqchi said Washington’s continued reliance on policies Iran considers failed would only produce further setbacks and deepen Iranian resistance.

Trump’s threat to Oman signals more than the end of US diplomacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
08:47:06 UTC
17:47:06 KST

Breadcrumb
Trump’s threat to Oman signals more than the end of US diplomacy
Trump has threatened to “bomb the s**” out of Oman for the second time this year. A shocking repeat threat against a country that has served as a friend and mediator for the US for years.
What’s new about US power in the Middle East under Trump is not its destructive capacity, its blatant disregard for the lives of ordinary people, or its desire to keep oil and petrodollars flowing its way. No, all of this is simply how America operates. Trump is no aberration.
What is new is the absence of any diplomatic speak that paints over its violence and gags its belligerent confidence. Trump’s particularly fickle form of verbal vomit sees him adulate dictators in the same week he threatens his partners. The volatility of American discourse under his leadership compounds the anxiety and instability resulting from his behaviour.
Threats and more threats
Fox News reporter Trey Yingst said he had asked the president about parallel talks taking place between Iran and Oman about the control of the Strait of Hormuz, to which Trump replied: “If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the s*** out of them.” In May, also speaking about opening the Strait, Trump made a similar threat: “Oman will behave like everybody else, or we’ll have to blow them up.”
The day after the latest threat, the White House shared Donald Trump’s Truth Social post on their official X account, with an image identifying the Strait of Hormuz as “New U.S. Territory,” echoing the president’s comment that “pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States.”
Encompassed within the identifying circle in the image of the Strait are not only Iranian territory but also Omani and Emirati territory. Crossing this key waterway requires ships to pass through the territorial waters of Iran and Oman, making Iran’s ability to close it and threaten international shipment a key thorn in the side of the president’s flesh.
Trump’s threats sound alarming in the world of diplomacy, even if no one expects him to actually bomb the Sultanate.
Why target a longstanding ally?
Today, Oman is appreciated as a country that has carefully cultivated its neutrality, allowing it to serve as a trusted mediator. It is credited with playing a key role behind the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), and Muscat has served as a vital backchannel between Washington and Tehran for years.
The Gulf country has also played an important role in the release of various American hostages in Iran and Yemen over the years.
This relationship emerges from a long history of friendship between the countries, with ties sitting among the longest of any Arab nation. These extend from the 1833 treaty of friendship and commerce between the two nations to the signing of the US-Oman Free Trade Agreement in 2006 (in effect since 2009) – one of the US’s only 20 bilateral FTAs worldwide.
This rich diplomatic history includes Oman being credited with dispatching the first Arab emissary to the United States in 1840 when Ahmad bin Na̔aman, special envoy of Sayyid Sa̔id bin Sultan (the Sultan of Oman and Zanzibar), visited New York. Not only this, but the first Arab head of state to make an official visit to Washington was Omani Sultan Sa̔id bin Taimur who met with US President Franklin Roosevelt in 1938.
Within this context, Trump’s threats to Oman appear puzzling. Both instances emerge as reactions to Oman’s role negotiating with Iran over access and navigation through the Strait. It’s not only Oman’s record of diplomacy and its proven status as a mediator with Iran, but also the geographic position that makes it both logical and necessary for the Gulf country to be involved.
Even more peculiarly, the June 17th 14-point Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding Between the United States of America and the Islamic Republic of Iran specified in point 5 that: “Iran will conduct dialogue with the Sultanate of Oman to define the future administration and maritime services in the Strait of Hormuz”. Observers had hoped the current dialogue would be a precursor to a renewal as the 60-day MOU was about to expire.
The agreement had already frayed by the beginning of July as Iran launched strikes on a number of ships and the US renewed its strikes on Iran for nearly two weeks. It was after this that Iran blatantly refused direct talks with the US, accusing it of first violating the terms of the MOU, and began talks with Oman.
Mediators Pakistan and Qatar were reportedly exchanging messages, but Iran has denied any negotiations. In the end, the deal expired.
Undermining peace
Oman’s independent policy toward Iran means it does not always align with US foreign policy, but this characteristic is what enables the country to facilitate dialogue and negotiations. Oman was in fact hosting nuclear talks between the US and Iran just before Trump and Netanyahu launched the war in February. Oman’s foreign minister Badr Al Busaidi tried to pre-empt this by publicly declaring that “a peace deal is within our reach” just the night before bombs started falling.
He later expressed his dismay that “active and serious negotiations [had] yet again been undermined,” referring to the launch of the 12-day war the previous year, which Israel started just two days before the sixth round of US-Iran nuclear talks were set to begin in Oman.
Trump is indeed upending the niceties of American diplomacy and rupturing long-standing relationships. He has recently given a cold shoulder to South Korea as he rekindles his love affair with Kim Jong-Un, has sided with Russia in UN resolutions on Ukraine, and has repeatedly made obnoxious, expansionist threats to make Canada the fifty-first state and seize control of Greenland. In that vein, Trump has already unilaterally renamed the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America and violated international law by abducting Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro.
It’s muzzle off, open bullying.
No force of good
We might consider it a collapse of American diplomacy and its cover of democracy promotion around the world.
But let’s not kid ourselves. People who mourn the US’ role in the world are mourning an illusion. Authors have challenged this virtuous self-delusion for decades, trying to explain to Americans just why people hate America.
Indeed, the US in the Middle East was no force for good. Ask the Palestinians bearing the brunt of American support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza under Biden, Yemeni wedding attendees murdered by Obama’s drones, or the hundreds of thousands of children who died of starvation under Clinton-supported sanctions (infamously deemed “worth it” by then US ambassador to the UN, Madeleine Albright). The list can go on at length and extend well beyond the confines of the Middle East.
The US’ ongoing support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza and its war on Iran are only the latest episodes in what Marc Lynch has dubbed America’s “ruination of a region.”
Trump’s only stable regional pursuit may be expanding the number of Gulf signatories to the Abraham Accords, a desire that Kayhan Valadbaygi calls “low-cost US hegemony,” which positions Israel as its central military-security node.
The Accords are consistent with around four decades of USFP in the region, built on several goals. One includes fostering or forcing Middle East allies into relations with Israel – exemplified by the 1996 Qualifying Industrial Zones initiative, which gives goods produced in Jordan and Egypt duty-free access to US markets on the condition that they include Israeli inputs. The other goal is containing (previously Iraq and) Iran and its proxies. The war has exposed the failure of the latter.
Iran has not been contained, and this policy has had deleterious effects on people, communities, and regional security.
Oman’s foreign minister recently wrote that containment is a “myth” and “an error of nearly half a century” and has called for replacing containment with a new security logic to govern the region - one based on inclusion. This will require, in his assessment, “Gulf conversations for Gulf states” to reassess their ties with powerful allies like the US – “not to discard these…but perhaps to reset them” to match the realities revealed during the war. This avoidable war has forced an “essential” question for Oman and its GCC partners: which partnerships genuinely delivery security, and which "bring unwanted vulnerabilities.”
The unsettling difference in current US foreign policy is Trump’s unpredictability. Sandwiched between the US and Iran, Oman remains the only adult in the room – a stable mediator not retaliating in words but sufficiently confident to condemn poor behaviour and violations of international law.
Indeed, the region, middle powers worldwide, and the wider international community would benefit from considering Oman’s words. In fact, the region is overdue for a new security arrangement that takes into account the lives and aspirations of its people.
Crystal A. Ennis is a scholar of global political economy and international relations based at Leiden University, the Netherlands. She is author of Millennial Dreams in Oil Economies (Cambridge University Press, 2025).

No kettle needed: Japan’s cold-water cup noodles fly off the shelves
Nissin’s new product sold out in a week as social media buzz and severe summer heatwaves drive demand across the region
Nissin Foods, the company that invented instant noodles, appears to have created an entirely new category with a hit product: cup noodles made with cold water.
Initial supplies of the handy meal – available in Spicy Kimchi and Chicken Salt Lemon flavours – sold out a week after hitting store shelves on July 20, according to Nissin. While the Tokyo-based company did not disclose sales figures, it had anticipated supplies to last one to two months.
“Nissin is accelerating the launch of innovative products and flavours tailored to increasingly diverse food cultures and focusing on balanced distribution across multiple channels,” Macquarie Equity Research analysts Linda Huang and others wrote in a report.
Ever since Nissin founder Momofuku Ando invented instant noodles in 1958, the basic formula has always relied on hot water, even for some varieties meant to be chilled before eating. The new product, which sells for 307 yen (US$1.93) apiece and was developed over five years, can be consumed after just five minutes, responding to growing demand for cool foods during hot weather.
Nissin, which has a market capitalisation of 869 billion yen, said its new product used a new patented process that resulted in smooth yet firm noodles.

Mexico: Aura battles turn a viral meme into live contests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
08:45:22 UTC
17:45:22 KST

Participants face off in informal “aura battles”, using dance moves, poses, facial expressions and playful gestures to show who can command the crowd’s attention. There are no physical fights: spectators usually choose the winner based on confidence, charisma and creativity.
The trend takes its name from the online slang “aura”, used to describe someone with a strong, charismatic presence. The phrase “farmear aura”, or “farming aura”, began as a joke about collecting imaginary “aura points” online before becoming a real-world competition.
At one recent event, 16-year-old Kaled Rosales Salazar won 2,000 Mexican pesos, around €100 at the time, after beating his rival, 14-year-old Carlos Irving Quintana, known as “Thanos”. The runner-up received 1,000 pesos.
Organisers say the battles are designed to be fast-paced, echoing the short, high-impact videos that helped the trend spread on TikTok. Competitors take turns performing for just a few seconds, using viral dances, meme references, exaggerated expressions and improvised moves.
What began as an online meme is now becoming a street spectacle in Mexico and beyond. Events have been held in Veracruz and announced in Xalapa and Mexico City, while similar competitions have appeared in Brazil, Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay and Peru.
