‘Tuscany may be beautiful, but do they sell sticks of rock?’: readers’ favourite UK holidays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
06:00:27 UTC
15:00:27 KST

Dorset’s take on the Mediterranean
Mudeford feels like one of England’s best-kept secrets, the sort of place visitors from abroad might never imagine exists here. Golden sand and sparkling water give it an almost Mediterranean feel, while Hengistbury Head adds beautiful coastal walks and wide-open views. Our perfect day is simple: arrive early, wander along the headland, let the children play on the beach, then stop at one of the relaxed cafes for lunch or an ice-cream. My tip is to take the little ferry across the harbour – it turns an already lovely day out into a proper seaside adventure.
Priti Singer
Lancashire’s Forest of Bowland
The Forest of Bowland covers a staggering 312 square miles of moorland, forests and valleys, dotted with the occasional village. It may be one of the best places for peace and quiet in England, and is also a Dark Skies area. It’s perfect for walkers and cyclists. I visited Gisburn forest (where I only met two other people during a five-hour hike); Barley village, which attracts lots of walkers who climb Pendle Hill; and, for spectacular scenery, a trip through the Trough of Bowland is a must. For town life, I’d recommend Skipton, a 35-minute drive away, which has it all with a castle, canal and plentiful shops and restaurants. It’s also the southern gateway to the Yorkshire Dales.
Cat
Crabbing and clean beaches in Suffolk
Walberswick is popular with walkers and birders, and young families who come here to relax and go swimming on the clean beach or crabbing in the creek. A brilliant way to arrive at the town is on the rowing-boat ferry (March to November) across the River Blyth from Southwold. It’s been in the same family for five generations. We had great seafood at heritage pubs like the Anchor and the Bell. Across the water, there’s a lot of wonderful fish shops and the famous Harbour Inn. 
David Innes-Wilkin
In search of the Lundy Bunny, Devon
Lundy, off the north Devon coast, offers a hidden adventure for all ages by following the treasure trail of 27 Lundy letterboxes spread over the island. Some are wooden boxes, some metal, but they are all hidden. There’s a set of clues to follow, and stamps collected including the elusive Lundy Bunny. My two preteen boys and I loved our exploration of this remote granite island, binoculars and compass in hand, identifying letterboxes, birds and wildlife during our magical trip there. 
Carol Godsmark
A spectacular rail trip in County Antrim
No trip I’ve made as an adult has matched the buzz of my annual childhood day trip from Derry to Portrush. The Troubles were at their peak but Portrush was still largely unscathed and had a totally different atmosphere to Derry. The journey was completed by train from Coleraine, and what a train journey it is. The train hogs the coast the whole way and we would be beside ourselves when the big dipper of Barry’s Amusements came into view. We would spend the morning on the beach, fish and chips for lunch and a few hours in Barry’s before heading home. Tuscany may be beautiful but do they sell sticks of rock?
Eve Kearney
An arty town in Shropshire
Foxholes campsite sits on a hill above the arty west Shropshire town of Bishop’s Castle. The views across the Shropshire hills are splendid, and a 10-minute walk through fields leads you past a stone Buddha into the town stretched along a medieval high street. Visit the House on Crutches museum to get a feel for Shropshire rural life history, and be sure to check out its two brilliant pubs: the Three Tuns is probably Britain’s oldest licensed brewery, having started in 1642, while the Six Bells provides an unpretentious family-friendly welcome. For us, though, the highlight was the Chai Shop and its charismatic owner Tahira. She serves delicious Indian snacks like bhajis and dal as well as traditional Indian sweets.
Matt Lunt
Camping in south Wales
We’re by no means an experienced camping family, but we pitched up on Rhydywernen Farm near Brecon after the last August bank holiday and were able to feed goats that were as happy and hoppy as it gets. Before falling asleep to the whisper of a nearby stream and mini-waterfalls, we spent time stargazing as there was no light pollution – it felt we were somehow closer to the stars. A cool stream helped soothe us after a day of hiking on Pen y Fan, the tallest peak in Britain south of Cadair Idris in Eryri (Snowdonia). We had only just bought a tent that summer and then we fell in love with Wales, so we keep coming back for more. 
Izabela
Northumberland’s atmospheric border town
Berwick-upon-Tweed is one of those places that feels more dramatic than its size suggests. I have visited twice, and I loved simply walking around, camera in hand. Its slightly strange sense of being a border town seems to permeate everything. Stand beside the River Tweed and you can see three bridges together: the old Berwick Bridge, the elegant Royal Tweed Bridge and the great Victorian railway viaduct of the Royal Border Bridge. Add the Elizabethan walls, the North Sea and castle ruins, and Berwick feels perpetually poised between countries, centuries and land and sea. It makes a wonderfully atmospheric short break. 
Susanna Callaghan
The natural wonders of the Wirral
The Wirral and its country park, south-west of Liverpool, is a brilliant under-the-radar place for a UK summer holiday, full of walks and beaches. Birkenhead Park is 57 hectares (140 acres) of meadows, fields, gardens, woodland, lakes and structures – we had picnics and family treasure hunts last summer. Opened in 1847, it inspired the 19th-century US landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted in his design of New York’s Central Park, so close your eyes and imagine you are in the Big Apple! Since 1995, it has been listed as a Grade I landscape by English Heritage. With its paths, fossil-hunting areas, bike trails and dramatic sunsets, Wirral country park helped us entertain our teenagers. Thurstaston beach and Port Sunlight village are great options too.
Nicoletta
Winning tip: Caribbean vibes on the Isle of Mull, Inner Hebrides
David Balfour’s Bay is a remote and breathtaking sandy bay with clear turquoise waters and pristine white sands in a stunning setting – the tidal island of Erraid, just off south-west Mull. The play of bright sunshine on crystal clear water and waves is dazzling – it’s a literally brilliant place to visit. Throw in a few palm trees and, on a clear day, you could imagine you were in Barbados – and the sea temperature can reach a pleasant 18C in August and September. To reach the bay, walk from lovely Knockvologan beach at low tide. This scenic walk can be extended to explore the north side of Erraid, where there are magnificent views of the Sound of Iona. Just be careful of tides so you don’t get caught there – a swim back is invigorating – as I found out after an overlong afternoon snooze when some lapping waves woke me up. 
Peter

Israeli settler attacks shift to heart of territory earmarked for Palestinian state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
06:00:26 UTC
15:00:26 KST

Violent Israeli settler attacks in the two areas of the occupied West Bank under direct Palestinian rule have almost doubled since 2025, as settlers pursue a self-proclaimed “great settlement revolution” in the very heart of the territory earmarked for a Palestinian state.
According to a report by the Israeli human rights organisation Yesh Din, shared with the Guardian, data shows that almost two-thirds of incidents of settler violence so far in 2026 have taken place in the so-called Areas A and B – placed under Palestinian Authority governance in the 1995 Oslo accords.
The report, The Next Frontier, Violence by Israeli Civilians in Areas A and B, describes the “rapid shift” in “violence and pressure exerted by the government, military and settlers on Palestinians … from Area C into Areas B and even A”.
While all three designated administrative areas on the West Bank were intended under the Oslo peace deal to encompass the shape of a future Palestinian state, successive Israeli governments, driven by the settler movement, have pursued a long-term policy of undermining Palestinian claims.
In Area C, accounting for 60% of the West Bank, Israel was initially given what was supposed to be temporary responsibility for all civil and security affairs pending a final status agreement for a Palestinian state. This arrangement was exploited for settlement. All government-approved Israeli settlements (regarded as illegal under international law) are located in Area C, as are the main roads and traffic arteries of the West Bank.
In Area A, which makes up about 18% of the West Bank and includes the major Palestinian cities, the Palestinian Authority became responsible for civil affairs and internal security. In Area B (22%), which includes the built-up areas in Palestinian rural spaces, the PA became responsible for civil affairs and public order.
Since 2024, Israel’s settlement movement has explicitly and violently expanded its efforts by establishing new farming “outposts” in areas A and B. Settler leaders have said openly that these are designed to “gain a foothold” in “very strategic” Palestinian locations. As the report says: “Most Palestinian daily life occurs in these areas.”
According to the report’s analysis, the percentage of violent West Bank incidents taking place in Area B stands at 55% so far this year, compared with 25% last year, while attacks in Area C declined in the same period from 67% to 37% of the overall figure, indicating a deliberate change in strategy.
“As settler and state violence against Palestinian communities in Area C has intensified in recent years, Palestinians have been forcibly pushed into Areas A and B, making these areas increasingly critical for maintaining safety and a semblance of normal everyday life,” said Yesh Din, which has been documenting settler violence for more than two decades.
A map posted earlier this summer in the WhatsApp group of the Hilltop Foundation, an organisation that supplies equipment, support and funding for the establishment of Israeli outposts in the West Bank, showed 16 outposts between the major Palestinian cities of Ramallah and Nablus alone. The map was accompanied by text boasting of “the great settlement revolution under way in the Oslo areas” and pledging the foundation’s continuing support for the establishment of outposts in Area B.
The Yesh Din report said that “the successful establishment of so many outposts in obvious violation of Israeli law, demonstrates that Israel is deliberately choosing not to effectively address the issue and that the settlers’ openly declared goals align with government policy”.
“Senior ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich [who have both called for the cancelling of the Oslo accords] openly speak of their ambition to gain control of Area B and abolish the division created under the Oslo accords.”
There is increasing international concern over the escalating pace of settler violence on the West Bank. Sanctions have been placed in the US and Europe on settlers and pro-settler figures, including Ben-Gvir, Israel’s national security minister.
Announcing France’s sanctions against Ben-Gvir on Wednesday, the French foreign, minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, said what was happening on the West Bank was “ utterly disgraceful and should fill us all with revulsion”.
According to the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, as of 20 July, 18 Palestinians had died during attacks involving settlers, of whom 12 were killed by settlers and three by Israeli forces. Responsibility for the remaining three deaths was disputed, OCHA said.
According to the UN agency, there were about 190 attacks a month in the first four months of 2026, putting the West Bank on a trajectory to reach more than 2,000 attacks by the end of this year.
Yesh Din concludes: “This Israeli strategy, implemented in part through the expansion of outposts and the settler violence launched from them into new areas, pushes Palestinian residents into the centres of towns and villages and empties surrounding areas of Palestinian presence.
“In doing so, it advances Israel toward the realisation of a policy, already reflected in ministers’ public statements, that seeks to annex as much West Bank territory as possible with as few Palestinians as possible living there.
“The path to this goal is paved with systematic, organised criminality, backed and supported by state institutions, revealing a clear intent: to make the area Palestinian free, in other words, to carry out ethnic cleansing.”
The Israeli military has been approached for comment.

Parchment lives on in its birthplace thanks to apprentices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
06:00:22 UTC
15:00:22 KST

Parchment, made by processing goat hides as an alternative to papyrus in the second century BC, has deep roots in Bergama.
Apprentices trained by the late Ismail Araç, one of the last traditional “karatabak” masters in Bergama, are keeping the ancient art of parchment-making alive in Türkiye and abroad using methods passed down by their master.
Parchment, made by processing goat hides as an alternative to papyrus in the second century B.C., has deep roots in Bergama. Araç, who died at the age of 93 on May 28, devoted his life to preserving the craft and training a new generation of artisans.
Araç was included in Türkiye’s National Inventory of Living Human Treasures in 2021 and received the “Living Human Treasures: Representatives of Heritage Transmitted to the Future” award in 2022.
Known as one of the last “karatabak” masters, Araç produced parchment for decades using natural materials and traditional techniques without chemicals. His apprentices are now continuing the craft in workshops in Türkiye and abroad.
Meltem Demirel, 36, one of Araç’s apprentices who turns parchment into a medium for writing and artwork at her workshop in Bergama, said they were committed to preserving their master’s legacy.
She described parchment-making as a difficult and labor-intensive process.
“We soak goat hides in lime and leave them there. After they have been soaked, we remove the hair and leave the hides to dry. Then the parchment emerges. We use it to create artworks and fulfill orders based on photographs. Parchment is actually an immortal paper, a living paper. It breathes. It is a beautiful memory that lives with you throughout your life,” Demirel said.
She added that they also welcome tourists from different countries and demonstrate the parchment-making process to visitors.
A campaign has been launched to transform a recently restored tannery building in Bergama into a Parchment Museum and name it after Araç. Demirel said the digital petition had collected 6,500 signatures.
“We, the Bergama parchment family, support this campaign. We would very much like to see our master’s name preserved in such a place,” she said.
Demirel recalled Araç’s words that his greatest legacy was not the parchment he had produced but the apprentices he had trained.
Keeping parchment alive in Britain
Demet Tokbay, a parchment maker and designer living in Britain, is also continuing the craft there.
Tokbay said her aim was to demonstrate that parchment is a value originating from Bergama and that the tradition continues to survive in the modern world.
“Fortunately, after our master Ismail, we are here as the apprentices he trained. We are all trying to do our part to ensure that this craft is not forgotten,” she said.
Tokbay said Bergama and parchment had not yet received the recognition they deserved and that the planned museum could help raise awareness of the tradition.
Hazel Aymaz, 41, another of Araç’s apprentices, said she was deeply impressed by the atmosphere of his workshop and his approach to working with leather.
She said Araç took a keen interest in his apprentices and was delighted to see them carry on the craft.
Aymaz added that Araç had later signed an “icazetname,” a traditional certificate of authorization, for her. She said she is now recognized by the Culture and Tourism Ministry as a bearer of intangible cultural heritage and considers the certificate from her master equally valuable.

Recently dug turtle figurines expose ancient ritual heritage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
06:00:09 UTC
15:00:09 KST

The team has uncovered around 25 turtle figures made of limestone. (AA photo)
Archaeologists at the Gedikkaya Hill and İn Cave excavation site in the northwestern province of Bilecik’s İnhisar district have discovered 25 turtle figurines dating from 14,500 to 11,200 B.C., pulling back the curtain on the area’s ancient ritual significance.
The figurines, discovered during excavations conducted by Bilecik Şeyh Edebali University, were identified as belonging to the Epipaleolithic Period, which spans roughly 20,000 to 10,000 B.C.
The excavation was carried out between May 18 and July 18 by a 14-member team led by Professor Deniz Sarı of Bilecik Şeyh Edebali University’s Department of Archaeology.
The team uncovered around 25 turtle figures made of limestone, some coated with clay. The largest measures approximately 30 centimeters in length and 20 centimeters in width.
Carbon-14 dating indicated that the figurines were made between 14,500 and 11,200 B.C. Researchers believe they were created for ritual purposes and deliberately placed inside the cave.
Sarı said the archaeological material at the cave was first identified during surface surveys in 2017, followed by rescue excavations conducted by the Bilecik Museum between 2019 and 2023.
“The turtle figurines we found this year have taken the ritual context of the cave to a different level,” Sarı said.
Sarı noted that most of the figurines had been shaped in a relatively amateurish manner, which researchers believe supports the theory that they were made for ritual purposes.
“During Hıdırellez, people make offerings, write their wishes on pieces of paper and then bury them somewhere. Here, too, there is an architectural arrangement forming circular rings. Around these, we found turtle figurines, mostly half-shaped or quickly fashioned from limestone, inserted into the ground,” she said.
Sarı said people living in the Epipaleolithic Period may have perceived Gedikkaya Hill as resembling a turtle, possibly leading to the development of what researchers interpret as a “mountain cult.”
“It may be too early to speak of such a cult for this period, but we know that most of the small figurines recovered appear to have been deliberately designed in the form of Gedikkaya Hill,” she said.
Sarı added that turtle symbolism was widespread in the Natufian culture of the Near East as well as in much earlier Upper Paleolithic cultures.
She said turtles have represented longevity and endurance in many cultures and suggested that the figurines may also have been created to symbolize these qualities.

The Single English County Saying No to Palantir
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

The UK government has six months to decide whether to terminate a deal worth more than $400 million between the country’s National Health Service and American software company Palantir. If one part of the NHS is already doing without Palantir, politicians are asking, why can’t the rest of the country?
In 2023, the UK commissioned Palantir to develop a “federated data platform” (FDP) that could ingest and organize the tangle of health data produced across the country. According to Palantir and the NHS, the new system is already cutting wait times and the length of hospital stays, and maximizing the use of operating theatres.
But lately, as Palantir technology is deployed in theaters of war and the US administration’s immigration crackdown, its deal with the NHS has become a flashpoint in the UK, drawing protests, petitions, parliamentary inquiries, and a reported rebellion among NHS workers. Other European nations, increasingly at loggerheads with the Trump administration, are also reevaluating their relationships with Palantir in a bid to minimize their dependence on US-made technology.
The health care board for one part of England, Greater Manchester, has repeatedly declined to adopt Palantir’s FDP, choosing to stick with a home-spun platform developed over the best part of a decade. The board claims it doesn’t need Palantir, that its own platform is functionally superior and more trusted by the public. “[Even] a technically strong platform will struggle to realize value if clinicians, data controllers, patients or the public do not trust it,” Matt Hennessey, chief data and analytics officer at NHS Greater Manchester, tells WIRED. “If we were to fully adopt the FDP … it would be a retrograde step.”
That claim—disputed by Palantir and other FDP advocates—has fed into a national debate over whether the government should seize an opportunity next February to terminate the NHS contract early, instead of allowing it to run until 2031.
For decades, NHS workers have used a combination of digital systems, spreadsheets, paper, and whiteboards to keep track of patients. Sometimes, when a patient moves from one care setting to another, their treatment records are left behind with occasionally deadly consequences. Without a way for different types of care providers to share information effectively, NHS administrators have had to base funding and resource allocation decisions on an incomplete patchwork of data. Palantir’s FDP is meant to change all that.
The NHS began to roll out the FDP in early 2024. The platform consists of a national pool of health data meant to help identify care deficiencies, and a bunch of local databases that individual regions can use to perform analyses and develop tools specific to their needs—say, waitlist management or discharge planning. The various components all share the same underlying technology scaffolding, in theory making it possible for tools developed in one corner of the country to be readily adopted in another.
“You can lift and shift. That’s the real power of the FDP,” says Tom Bartlett, an independent IT consultant who previously oversaw the national-level FDP rollout as deputy director of data engineering at NHS England. “The other advantage is that you’ve got a surface for artificial intelligence to work across.”
Within the sprawling NHS, two types of organizations can access the FDP: trusts that run hospitals and local care, and integrated care boards (ICBs), responsible for planning and commissioning health care services at a regional level. Both use data for different purposes, but share the ultimate goal of improving patient care.
NHS figures show 139 of roughly 200 trusts currently “live” with Palantir’s technology, while 35 of England’s 36 ICBs are actively using the system. “It is clear that thousands more patients are benefitting from the FDP every month,” a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Social Care tells WIRED.
But trusts in different pockets of England have resisted the FDP, including in Greater Manchester, where sources claim they are using it for limited purposes only. “They’re not going all in,” claims Andy Haywood, chief digital and data officer at research institute Health Innovation Manchester. “On the spreadsheet they go down as using it, but not in the sense of putting all their data in it.” (Palantir claims that trusts in Greater Manchester are using the FDP extensively.) Greater Manchester—the birthplace of the NHS in the industrial north of England—is also the sole region whose care board has repeatedly and categorically refused to adopt Palantir’s platform.
Instead, Greater Manchester ICB, which covers a population of around 3 million, has stuck with its homegrown Analytics and Data Science Platform (ADSP). At a meeting in May 2025, despite pressure from the national unit of the NHS to adopt Palantir’s technology, the board concluded that its “local capability exceeds anything the FDP currently offers” and some of its functionalities are “two–three years” ahead. The board’s resolve has only hardened since.
The ADSP is fed with primary care data that is not available on Palantir’s platform, and because the system was developed in-house, it can supposedly be reconfigured more easily. “Because the ADSP is a collection of technologies, if we found that our data visualization software had become less than best in class, we could swap it out,” Hennessey tells WIRED.
The ADSP also benefits from a deep public trust in the platform fostered over multiple years, Hennessey claims, meaning people are more likely to volunteer the sensitive health data required for this kind of platform to function.
Palantir says there is scant independent evidence to suggest the ADSP has contributed directly to improving patient care or saving costs—and that its own platform is widely trusted. “Thousands of doctors, nurses, and other NHS staff use the [FDP], with many on the record as to its benefits,” Stephen Childs, head of health care partnerships at Palantir UK, tells WIRED. But the claim that Greater Manchester has developed a superior system in-house has nonetheless colored an ongoing debate over whether the UK government should break off Palantir’s contract next February.
In June, a bipartisan group of UK politicians published a report warning that the country’s reliance on Palantir represents an “unacceptable point of weakness,” handing a single foreign vendor overwhelming leverage. The report argued for the government to activate the break clause and seek out domestic alternatives. The following month, a separate parliamentary committee made similar arguments, drawing from testimony provided by Hennessey on the situation in Greater Manchester. “[Palantir] is evidently not the only show in town,” wrote MP Layla Moran, chair of the committee.
But proponents of the FDP argue that, in reality, there is no viable alternative to Palantir, able to thread together data from across the country and the many sub-components of the NHS—from trusts to ICBs to national bodies. They argue MPs’ calls to break the Palantir contract are based on a narrow assessment of the value the FDP can provide to care boards, compared to Greater Manchester’s platform, and ignore its potential benefits in hospitals and other settings where treatment is administered.
“The claim that the ADSP achieves superior results really doesn’t make sense … [The FDP] does completely different things,” says Bartlett. “To frame the use case as analytics is a complete misrepresentation of the whole goal of the product.” (Hennessey says that Greater Manchester ICB has only ever said its technology is superior to Palantir’s in a care board setting, not across the NHS.)
Bartlett argues that the level of scrutiny directed at the Palantir deal compared to other expensive NHS projects signals political objections are interfering with attempts to assess the FDP’s true performance and value. “There’s an anti-Palantir campaign,” he claims.
Palantir has long insisted it is not a political organization. “Our values are that technology can help transform public services and save lives,” says Childs. But in 2023, Palantir cofounder Peter Thiel said the UK should “rip the whole [NHS] from the ground and start over.” More recently, Palantir published a fiery bullet-point manifesto, based on a recent book by CEO Alex Karp, which one British MP described as “the ramblings of a supervillain.”
“The NHS is a values-based organization,” claims Jessica Morley, a health data researcher at Yale University’s Digital Ethics Center. “Palantir is essentially antithetical to all of those values.”
The MPs who recommended in June that the government terminate Palantir’s contract with the NHS insist they are not “ideologically-motivated.” But they also voiced concern over a “clear mismatch with UK values.”
The public debate around Palantir has also fed into Greater Manchester ICB’s continued refusal to use the FDP. The care board acknowledged in April that it had not begun a scheduled review of its decision on the FDP “because it’s clear that the public concerns have heightened rather than diminished.”
Those who believe politics has infected the discourse around the FDP, distracting from its importance to the NHS, warn that breaking the contract risks squandering several years of progress, with potential consequences for patient care. “If the break clause got triggered, we’d go backwards, because there is no alternative,” claims Bartlett. “The trusts that were previously using paper would go back to paper.”
But even if the FDP were superior to existing NHS technologies, Hennessey argues, any value assessment must take into account the political heat surrounding Palantir because its success hinges on the public’s willingness to feed it their data and doctors’ willingness to use it. “You can have the most amazing thing,” he says, “but if people don’t trust it, then you have something that’s operationally redundant.”

Brattlandsdalen is a dramatic, narrow, and deep gorge along Norway's National Road number 13, shaped by steep mountainsides and the constant force of water. The gorge holds rare geological formations, including glacial potholes, and represents an important chapter in the history of Norwegian roadmaking. The historical pathway, defined by stone posts, steel railing, and the historic Kvelven Tunnel, once served both local travelers and early tourists.

Karahantepe, Sayburç reveal major turning point in human history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
05:59:35 UTC
14:59:35 KST

The progress of excavations has created the potential to transform Sayburç into an open-air museum featuring its public buildings and houses.
Türkiye is set to expand its archaeological footprint and museum network across the southeastern province of Şanlıurfa, according to Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy.
Driven by recent findings at the Karahantepe and Sayburç sites, the ongoing initiatives aim to uncover the architectural and social foundations of humanity’s earliest settled communities.
Ersoy met with Culture and Tourism Ministry General Director of Cultural Heritage and Museums Birol İnceciköz, Deputy General Director Bülent Gönültaş and Professor Necmi Karul, coordinator of the Taş Tepeler Project.
During the meeting, Karul presented the latest findings from archaeological excavations at Karahantepe and Sayburç, as well as plans for future work under the Legacy for the Future and Stone Hills projects.
Ersoy later said on social media that they were “preparing for a new era in Şanlıurfa, where some of the greatest transformations in human history took place.”
According to Ersoy, the region provides important evidence about the emergence of settled life and large Neolithic settlements following the Ice Age.
The area has also revealed evidence of sophisticated hunting and water-management practices dating to the period when early communities were establishing permanent settlements.
Karahantepe is particularly significant for findings that shed light on the origins of myths, while also containing some of the earliest known examples of architectural features such as stairs and windows.
Findings from the site are providing new insights into the early stages of architectural history and the way of life of Neolithic communities.
Nearly 70 structures uncovered at Sayburç
Dating to the mid-9th millennium B.C., Sayburç is a multilayered settlement that bears traces from the Neolithic period through the Roman era and into modern village life.
During the sixth season of excavations, archaeologists uncovered nearly 70 well-preserved houses and special-purpose structures across an area of 2,700 square meters.
The site has yielded reliefs, human sculptures, monumental T-shaped pillars and human-faced bases that are contributing to a better understanding of Neolithic art.
The excavated structures also provide evidence of the transition from circular to rectangular architecture and offer important clues about the emergence of the concepts of the house and household.
The progress of excavations has created the potential to transform Sayburç into an open-air museum featuring its public buildings, houses and works reflecting the artistic traditions of the period.
Its proximity to Şanlıurfa city center, location on the Gaziantep road and position among archaeological sites west of the city are expected to make Sayburç an important stop on the Taş Tepeler route.
Traditional village buildings in the expropriated area are also planned to be restored and turned into a pioneering village museum integrated with the open-air archaeological site.
“Following the discovery of nearly 70 structures across 2,700 square meters at Sayburç, we plan to transform the settlement into an open-air museum and the traditional village buildings into a pioneering village museum,” Ersoy said.
He added that the ministry would continue efforts under the Legacy for the Future and Taş Tepeler projects to uncover, preserve and pass on Şanlıurfa’s unique cultural heritage through scientific research.

Türkiye declares Nemrut Caldera protected national park
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
05:58:52 UTC
14:58:52 KST

Türkiye has designated the Nemrut Caldera in the eastern province of Bitlis as a national park, marking a decisive move that drove a 64 percent surge in the nation’s protected areas over just four days.
According to a presidential decree published in the Official Gazette on Aug. 19, the vast caldera spanning Bitlis’s Tatvan, Ahlat and Güroymak districts near Van Lake has been officially designated to safeguard its biodiversity and encourage sustainable tourism. The decision follows the declarations of the Fethiye-Kaş and North Aegean marine national parks, pushing the total number of protected zones to 1,791 across 62,403 square kilometers.
Erdoğan Özel, the founding head of the Vangölü Activists Association, thanked the president and Bitlis Governor Ahmet Karakaya, saying the new status will end the previously uncontrolled use of the remote area.
“The caldera is not only for Bitlis but an essential center for all humanity, housing the world’s second-largest and our country’s largest crater lake,” he said.
Özel noted that his association has organized festivals and treks over the years to raise public awareness about the high-altitude site, emphasizing that they will keep working to protect it.
Kenan Akın, spokesman for the Bitlis Nemrut Geopark Sports Club, said the step will drive tourism in the rugged region. Visitor Vedat Gültepe said he traveled to the province with his family after hearing the news to see the site’s natural beauty firsthand.
The Nemrut Caldera formed following the eruption and collapse of Mount Nemrut, a dormant volcano in the mountainous terrain of eastern Anatolia. Located at an elevation of nearly 3,000 meters, it features deep freshwater lakes that serve as a critical habitat for regional flora and fauna.

Belarus will close its embassy in Finland, Helsingin Sanomat reported on Friday morning.

Belarusian citizens in Finland or those requiring consular services have been advised to contact either the country's embassy in Stockholm or the Daugavpils consulate in Latvia.

Belarus established its embassy in Finland in 2011. Finland does not have an embassy in Belarus, but instead operates a liaison office of the Finnish Ministry for Foreign Affairs in Minsk, the Belarusian capital.

In Latvia, two people were convicted of carrying out a sabotage operation against PILOT Automotive Labs Europe—a company that develops unmaned vehicles—at the behest of a Russian security service, LSM reports.

Drone attack damages homes and infrastructure in Sumy
Russian drones attacked Sumy early on Friday, Aug. 21, causing fires in residential areas and injuring six people, according to Serhii Kryvosheyenko, head of the Sumy City Military Administration (MVA).
The massive UAV attack targeted civilian infrastructure and the residential sector in the city’s Kovpakiv district, Kryvosheyenko said.

The Air Force said 27 attack UAVs reached 16 locations, while debris from downed drones fell at three additional sites.

Türkiye has brought annual inflation down from its 2024 peak of more than 75 percent to 31.75 percent, Trade Minister Ömer Bolat has said, while outlining expanded financing and export support for businesses.
Speaking at a meeting with business and civil society representatives in the northwestern province of Bilecik, Bolat said the decline had continued despite regional conflicts and difficult global economic conditions.
Official data showed that annual consumer inflation eased from 32.11 percent in June to 31.75 percent in July. Consumer prices rose 1.78 percent on a monthly basis.
Bolat also said Türkiye’s annualized goods and services exports reached $401.1 billion at the end of July.
Goods exports stood at a record $278.6 billion, while annual services exports were estimated at $122.6 billion, according to the minister.
Bolat said the government had raised the volume of Central Bank-backed investment loans from 500 billion Turkish Liras ($12.1 billion) to 750 billion liras and allocated an additional 250 billion liras in working-capital financing for industrial companies.
Exporters also have access to Central Bank rediscount loans, financing from Türk Eximbank and 45 billion liras in government support for goods and services exports this year, he added.
Bolat announced that an additional 100 million liras would be made available to tradespeople in Bilecik through the Union of Credit and Guarantee Cooperatives for Tradesmen and Craftsmen, known as TESKOMB.
Businesses in the province used 471 million liras in loans carrying a 50 percent interest subsidy in 2025 and a further 278 million liras in the first seven months of this year, he said.

Angel Reese has stunning perfect shooting night in the Dream’s 124-88 romp over the Sparks
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Angel Reese had a stunning perfect shooting night after struggling recently to make even the shortest of shots, and the Atlanta Dream set a franchise record for points in a game in a 124-88 victory over the Los Angels Sparks on Thursday night.
Reese was 9-for-9 from the field, hitting two 3-pointers, for 20 points and had 10 rebounds and eight assists for her WNBA-leading 25th double-double of the season. She had 18 points in the first half.
Reese set a Dream record for field goals without a miss and became the third player in WNBA history with a 20-point double-double on 100% shooting. She’s four shy of Alyssa Thomas’ WNBA double-double record of 28 set in 2023.
In addition, she had three offensive rebounds in the first half to break her own WNBA season record of 172 set in 2024.
Rhyne Howard added 26 points and five 3-pointers for Atlanta (23-13), which has won eight straight in the series with Los Angeles. Naz Hillmon had 14 points and Allisha Gray 13.
Cameron Brink scored 14 points off the bench for Los Angeles (12-24), which was eliminated from playoff contention. Rae Burrell added 12 and Nneka Ogwumike had 11.
The Dream led by 42 points and reached the 100-point mark with 8:10 left.
Play was briefly interrupted with 2:59 left in the third quarter after a sex toy was thrown on the court near where Jihyun Park was about to attempt a free throw for Los Angeles.

Misra rejects reports of rift with Champat Rai
NEW DELHI: Nripendra Misra, chairman of the Ram Mandir Construction Committee, on Friday dismissed media reports of an internal rift over the construction of the Ram temple in Ayodhya, calling the claims "completely baseless".Speaking to reporters on the final day of a three-day review meeting, Misra denied reports that former trust general secretary Champat Rai had written a nine-page letter accusing him of taking arbitrary decisions.
"I have not seen any such letter. Until I see the letter, I will only tell you that this is a concocted story of yours (media). There is no such letter, nor is there any such criticism, even if it were 9 pages long; he has not made any such criticism. This is merely a made-up story by you (media) people."Rai had resigned as general secretary of the trust about a month ago amid allegations of misappropriation of donations linked to the Ram Janmabhoomi temple project. His resignation had raised questions about the functioning of the trust.
Most temple construction work completed
Misra also gave an update on the progress of the Ram temple and said most of the construction work has been completed."A review of the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi temple construction has been conducted.
In total, there are approximately 70 construction projects, out of which 60 have been completed. They have already been handed over and transferred to the Trust and the Nyas. The Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Trust will now oversee its maintenance. Most importantly, we will conduct an internal audit of the construction work that has been handed over to the Trust," he said.He also addressed reports of waterlogging on the temple premises during the monsoon and said work was under way to resolve the issue."Yesterday, discussions were held with both the Commissioner and the Municipal Commissioner regarding development. Due to the current rainy season, water was accumulating in the temple premises; discussions were held on how to connect it to the municipal drains. This work will be completed within two months," he informed.
Auditorium, museum and office work in final phase
Misra said the focus has now shifted to completing the remaining facilities, including the auditorium, trust office and museum."There are about four months of work remaining for the auditorium and the Trust office. Yesterday, we held a meeting with the Managing Director of the Rajkiya Nirman Nigam. Today, we are visiting the museum. The main discussion is to be held on the script prepared for each gallery; the promoter company wants to show a 3D presentation according to that script and obtain approval for it. We will look into that and make a decision today," Misra added.
He also highlighted that the temple project was funded entirely through donations collected by the trust and did not use government funds."The matter of greatest pride is that no government money--neither from the Central nor the State government--has been used in this. The temple was built solely from the funds collected by the Nyas."

Without naming Cofnas, the University of Ghent said in a statement it had launched a "preliminary disciplinary investigation" against a postdoctoral researcher embroiled in the furore, suspending him "as a precautionary measure."
Arday, who became Cambridge's youngest-ever black professor when he was appointed in 2023, was found dead Friday aged 41.
He was facing mounting accusations he had plagiarised parts of his doctoral thesis and exaggerated some of his personal life achievements.
Diagnosed with autism and other developmental difficulties as a child, Arday had disputed the allegations against him.
But he quit on 5 August, writing in his resignation letter that he had "reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure."
Plagiarism concerns surrounding Arday first surfaced several years ago but went nowhere at the time, with one reporter backing down from investigating further after the professor threatened legal action.
Last month, however, Cofnas came forward to say he had found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work and the case snowballed, receiving widespread media coverage in Britain and the United States.
British media and right-wing commentators seized on the row, claiming Arday had unfairly benefited from diversity, equality and inclusion (DEI) policies.
Ghent University said it was now "assessing" whether there were sufficient grounds to launch full disciplinary proceedings in the case.
In a previous statement on Wednesday, the university said it was "shocked" by Arday's death and took "very seriously" public statements made by its researcher regarding the former professor.
"Ghent University stands for respect for human dignity and opposes discrimination, hatred and racism," said the statement by the university's rector Petra De Sutter and vice-rector Herwig Reynaert.
"We attach great importance to academic freedom and to open academic debate, even when views are controversial," it added.
"However, that freedom is not unlimited. It goes hand in hand with responsibility and may be restricted in order to protect the rights of others."

Israeli aircraft struck the runways and hangars of the Abu al-Duhur airbase in northwestern Syria on Aug. 18.
The facility lies about 70 kilometers from the Turkish border. No casualties were reported.
Israel said the attack was intended to prevent Turkish troops from deploying at the base, alleging that Syria was close to breaching an agreed security status quo. Both Ankara and Damascus rejected the claim.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said the airbase was being rehabilitated for use by the Syrian Air Force and that no Turkish base or permanent deployment was planned.

It also said Ankara would continue supporting Syria’s efforts to rebuild its infrastructure and military capacity under the principle of “one state, one army.”
Türkiye and Syria signed a memorandum on joint military training and consultancy on Aug. 13, 2025.
Turkish officials have said its implementation covers training, consultancy, technical assistance and reciprocal visits aimed at strengthening Syria’s defense capacity.
Ankara appointed a defense attaché to its embassy in Damascus earlier that year and has supported efforts to bring armed factions under a single national command.
Türkiye says its assistance is provided at the request of the Syrian government and is intended to reinforce the country’s unity, territorial integrity and ability to combat terrorism.
Israel has repeatedly opposed the establishment of Turkish bases or air-defense systems in Syria, arguing that they could threaten its security and restrict its freedom of military action.
In the spring of 2025, Israel struck facilities at the T4, Palmyra and Hama airbases after reports that Turkish teams had assessed some of the sites.
The attacks prompted Turkish and Israeli officials to hold technical talks in Azerbaijan on establishing a channel to prevent unintended clashes.
Israel has carried out hundreds of attacks on Syrian military sites since the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s government in December 2024.
The Israeli military said its initial campaign included more than 350 airstrikes on airfields, air-defense systems, weapons facilities and other military assets.
Following the latest strike, U.S. envoy Tom Barrack said Washington was working to establish a deconfliction mechanism involving Türkiye, Syria and Israel to prevent further miscommunication.

The Ministry of Justice is working to modernize the courts, digitalize processes, strengthen professional capacity, and reduce case-processing times. Latvia’s goal is a faster and more predictable justice system that also strengthens the business environment and investor confidence.
In early September, the Ministry of Justice, together with representatives of the justice sector and the business community, will assess current practical challenges related to investment protection and civil litigation. The goal is to identify practical solutions so that Latvia is a place where both local businesses and foreign investors can rely on prompt, high-quality, and predictable legal protection.
The Minister emphasized that one of the Ministry of Justice’s responsibilities is to support the secure and lawful conduct of elections this autumn by protecting the electoral process from unwanted foreign interference, cyber threats, and disinformation.

Long‑range air defense decision expected in September budget talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
05:43:00 UTC
14:43:00 KST

Long‑range air defense decision expected in September budget talks
Estonian government plans to make a fundamental decision during September's state budget talks on the scope and supplier of long‑range air defense systems, Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur said.
The government intends to procure long‑range air defense systems in addition to the medium‑range IRIS‑T system already delivered to Estonia. These systems would protect strategic targets such as airports, ports, or defense force command centers, whose destruction could significantly weaken Estonia's and its allies' defense capabilities.
Pevkur said the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) has completed an extensive market study. Based on that, the Cabinet will begin discussing in about a month which company to buy the system from and in what volume. This means it is still unclear whether ballistic missile defense will be purchased for less than or more than €1 billion.
"The Center for Defense Investments is still clarifying a few details with the companies. At the same time, we are putting together a Cabinet memo. The goal is to make a fundamental decision within one or two months, and then the Center for Defense Investments can begin contract negotiations if needed," Pevkur said.
ERR reported earlier this year that Estonia is considering the U.S. Patriot system, Israel's David's Sling, and the French‑Italian SAMP/T. In total, offers have been requested from four or five companies. Pevkur said some companies could deliver a system in two to three years, while others would need eight to nine years.
"The market situation varies widely. What companies offer also differs — some offer products not yet in production but in the final stages of development. The offers are not directly comparable, so we need to combine our own analysis with the market study to determine which system is suitable for concrete price and contract negotiations," he said.
The minister said companies' ability to offer long‑range air defense systems to Estonia has also been affected by events such as the U.S.–Iran war.
"The most complicated situation is with U.S. products, because they are actively used in Ukraine, and we see that ammunition supply is the most difficult there. This is the work we must now do with the companies — to understand whether what was offered to us is actually feasible or not," Pevkur said.

The Last Breath of Rayong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
05:42:00 UTC
14:42:00 KST

Fisherfolk in Thailand’s Rayong province are currently facing multiple impacts from industrial expansion in the region – in particular, the construction of a MapTaPhut Phase 3 port and the development of large-scale investment projects including liquefied natural gas (LNG) projects, including LNG terminal and regasification facilities. The expansion of LNG projects in the eastern provinces, part of Thailand’s plan to position itself as a regional LNG hub, has disturbed and now threatens to destroy the coastal fisheries resources that communities have long relied on.
“We used to fish regularly, and we are at ease earning money from fishing,” one fisherman in the Klonglawon community of Rayong province told researchers in 2025.
“Now the seas are changing tremendously due to industrialization and its expansion, with seas filling and other so-called ‘development’ projects. Fish are reducing, and our livelihoods are at the front lines. It will never be the same without rehabilitation.”
Fisherfolk in Rayong are now demanding compensation for the loss of fisheries and livelihoods. The injustice associated with LNG development is not limited to environmental impacts but is fundamentally tied to unequal power structures in which affected communities have little influence over decisions that shape their future.
Thailand is heavily reliant on fossil fuels, and particularly natural gas, to drive the country’s economic growth and industrialization. According to data from Thailand’s Energy Regulatory Commission, natural gas accounts for 58 percent of Thailand’s power generation mix, followed by electricity imports from Laos (14 percent), coal (13 percent), and renewables (12 percent). Natural gas remains the backbone of power generation, sourced from both the Gulf of Thailand and LNG imported from abroad.
Last year, reliance on costly LNG imports was the primary driver of rising electricity bills, and the government has been forced to increase its reliance on LNG imports to ensure energy security. However, we ask who bears the cost of this increase in LNG development and how injustice plays out from the perspective of a just energy transition.
The Thai government has set ambitious targets to reduce its reliance on gas from the Gulf of Thailand to 28 percent by 2037 and to cut gas imports from Myanmar to just 4 percent, filling this gap with imports of LNG. However, as long as Thailand’s dependence on LNG persists, it will continue to significantly affect the country’s electricity prices. In 2024, the Thailand Development Research Institute (TDRI) recommended a plan to reduce reliance on imported gas and LNG and to accelerate the use of clean, renewable energy such as solar.
LNG facilities, such as terminals and regasification facilities, harm coastal ecosystems in many ways. Dredging, deepening navigation channels, and construction of terminals and regasification facilities, all contribute to ecological damage to the ocean and coastal ecosystems. These processes destroy marine ecosystems, fish habitats, marine resources, and wetlands, all of which are important to fisheries. Rehabilitating this loss cannot happen overnight because marine ecosystems are complex and interconnected.
Once operational, LNG terminal projects have been criticized for methane emissions, destruction of coastal and marine environments, and the collapse of coastal communities’ livelihoods. Other environmental damage includes the use of water to cool industrial processes and the release of that water back into the ocean, which harms marine resources. One example is the Freeport LNG project in Texas, United States, which conservation groups criticized for destroying coastal areas and fisheries and for posing health risks to the population.
LNG should not only be seen as just an energy issue; it also has impacts on community rights, the right to nature, and issues of ecological justice. The community’s rights to marine resources are violated because they can no longer fish and earn income from their profession.
In September 2025, Rayong fisherfolk submitted a complaint to the Chairperson of the United Nations Working Group on Business and Human Rights during her visit to Thailand, ahead of the U.N. Responsible Business and Human Rights Forum in Bangkok. The submission highlighted the issue of LNG expansion in Thailand, including in Rayong province. Due to the concerns about the expansion of the LNG projects and how it harms the environment and marine resources, the complaint highlighted the campaign across Thailand against the expansion of the LNG projects and investments.
Concerns raised include ecological and livelihood impacts and, more importantly, human rights violations, as the community and fisherfolk were excluded from the Environmental and Health Impact Assessment (EHIA) process and from decision-making on the LNG projects.
Based on a legal analysis of the EHIA report conducted in late 2024, the EHIA for the first LNG project in Rayong contained limited information about the environmental, health, and economic impacts on Rayong fisherfolk, as well as the potential collapse of Rayong fisheries.
The affected fishermen worry about the project’s impacts (at both the construction and operation stages) on fisheries. They must spend more time fishing and travel farther from their original fishing areas. The EHIA report lacks information on compensation or remedies, as well as on inclusive participation by fisherfolk in any compensation-related discussions. The community’s rights to public participation have been violated.
LNG is widely seen as a “transitional fuel” for the energy transition. This narrative has boosted investment in LNG across the region and in Thailand. This shift to transitional fuels such as LNG ignores the ecological and health impacts that have already been experienced by communities in Rayong. However, the principles of the “just transition” to renewable energy demand that we ask who benefits from this transition and who bears the cost.
The environmental burdens from LNG projects are largely concentrated in marginalized or heavily industrialized regions, while economic and energy gains are felt elsewhere. These disparities underscore essential concerns about whether impacted communities participate meaningfully in the project’s decision-making processes, who bears the environmental and health burdens, and who receives the benefits, and whether the community’s rights and the livelihood of local fisherfolk have been asserted and respected.
These concerns are particularly relevant in coastal industrial zones such as Map Ta Phut, where cumulative impacts from petrochemical industries, ports, and LNG infrastructure intersect with community health and fisheries. Communities share with us that the rapid development of the coast has led to what could be the “last breath of Rayong sea.”
Kanikar Raksawong, a fisherman from Ban Kon Peuk, said, “We urge the authorities to stop the expansion of the industries in Rayong, which is impacting the community’s livelihoods, way of life, and coastal fisheries and natural resources. It is time to stop, as Rayong is heavily polluted. Enough is enough.”
I would like to dedicate all the efforts of working with the communities to document their struggle and stories to Uncle Noi, our legendary activist, for his tireless efforts and bravery. Rest in Peace. His legacy remains in our hearts, and we will continue to follow in his footsteps as a role model for the fight against injustice caused by unjust development projects and industrialization.

STTK: Shorter working hours could support employee wellbeing
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
08:39:26 EEST
14:39:26 KST

Finland should test shorter working hours across different sectors to assess their effects on employee wellbeing, ability to work and productivity, according to a report commissioned by the Finnish Confederation of Professionals STTK.
The report, written by researcher Anna Kuokkanen, reviewed international research and interviewed representatives of Finnish workplaces that have introduced shorter working hours.
It found that reducing hours works best when employers also reorganise tasks, involve employees in planning and monitor the results.
“Simply mechanically reducing working hours does not necessarily work. Work also needs to be reconsidered and reorganised,” Kuokkanen said in STTK’s release.
The report found that shorter hours had improved employee wellbeing at the organisations interviewed without reducing productivity. In some cases, productivity increased.
STTK said shorter hours should form one option for employees facing health pressures, demanding periods in their lives or work patterns that place greater strain on recovery.
The organisation identified night work as one area where reduced hours deserve further testing. Shorter shifts would give workers more time to recover and could help them remain in employment for longer, STTK social impact director Taina Vallander said.
The report comes as mental health has become a major cause of absence from work and loss of working ability in Finland. Mental health disorders became the most common basis for sickness allowance in 2020 and are also the leading reason for moving onto disability pension, according to STTK’s release.
The study examined Finnish companies using different models for shorter working hours.
Oulu-based game developer Fingersoft allows employees to work 80 per cent of standard full-time hours. About 25 to 30 per cent of its workforce uses the arrangement. Employees working four days a week receive 80 per cent of their usual salary, while those working six-hour days receive 90 per cent.
Most employees at Tampere restaurant Kajo work four days a week without a reduction in pay. Vehicle electronics company Sercap in Keminmaa also operates a four-day week on full pay.
Helsinki consultancy Third Rock gives employees Friday afternoons off without cutting salaries.
Kuokkanen said such arrangements depend on how workplaces organise the remaining working time.
Successful trials could remove unnecessary tasks and expose problems in working practices that organisations have previously left unresolved, she said.
STTK is calling for trials in different sectors rather than a single model covering all workers. Vallander said working hours should respond to differences between jobs and changes in employees’ circumstances during their careers.
Trade union Pro also called for the debate to focus on research rather than fixed positions between employers and employees.
Pro chair Niko Simola said changes driven by technology, digitalisation and artificial intelligence raised questions about how productivity gains should affect working conditions.
Pro is seeking a national pilot programme for shorter working hours as part of its parliamentary election objectives. It also wants employees to have greater access to part-time work during different stages of life.
Kuokkanen said workplaces could begin with trials lasting six months or a year and decide whether to continue based on the results.
She said shorter working hours require planning, management, employee participation and systematic monitoring of their effects.

An estimated 1.98 million people in Gaza, or 94 percent of the population, need shelter and basic household assistance, the United Nations has said.

====================================================================================================

Diamonds or duds: Are these the most overrated albums of all time?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
05:38:33 UTC
14:38:33 KST

Time to kill some sacred cows... Euronews Culture throws caution to the wind and reappraises the albums which are too often and perhaps wrongly elevated to 'masterpiece' status.
There are certain albums which no one dares to disgrace or reappraise.
You know the ones: records that are revered by practically everyone and which every self-respecting music fan is expected to cherish. But are these albums truly untouchable, or are we blindly regurgitating accepted wisdom?
The Euronews Culture team bares all and takes a hard listen at 12 so-called ‘masterpieces’ and asks: ‘Isn’t it about time we admitted that these aren’t the sacrosanct triumphs they’re made out to be?’
Different strokes for different folks, of course - we wouldn't want to break any levees. Speaking of which, we start with...
Led Zeppelin – IV (1971)
It’s the album that gave us 'Stairway to Heaven', perhaps the greatest rock song ever made. It’s widely considered Led Zeppelin’s pinnacle of achievement. It’s essential listening, a rock'n'roll classic. And yet… Look, Led Zeppelin’s fourth album opens like a firehose on a scorching summer day. 'Black Dog' and 'Rock and Roll' knock you off your feet. It’s incredible. Later, you get the transcendent 'Stairway to Heaven' and smooth 'Going to California'. But is it as complete an experience as we’re supposed to believe it is? I’m not so sure.The highs do the heavy lifting, and it’s fair to wonder if they distort our view of the work in its entirety – if the band’s greater mythology hasn’t generated some revisionism. The problem is that once an album is declared the masterpiece, everything else gets measured against it. But Zeppelin made more adventurous records. 'Led Zeppelin III' is restless and eclectic, and 'Physical Graffiti' takes bigger swings across a kaleidoscopic double LP. For all its brilliance, 'IV' shouldn’t have a monopoly on Led Zeppelin’s legacy. CS
Eagles – Hotel California (1976)
Remember that scene in The Big Lebowski when The Dude gets into an altercation with a cab driver when he asks him to change the radio station? "I've had a rough night, and I hate the fucking Eagles, man!" says our favourite stoner. Well, I loudly cheer for The Dude every single time. The Eagles are rubbish, and their most famous album proves it. Not that many would agree, as 'Hotel California' is the sixth-most sold record of all time, with reported global sales of around 44 million copies. To add insult to injury, their greatest hits album remains the best-selling album of all time in the US. Makes you think, don't it? The band's so-called 1976 "rock classic" is chockablock with thoroughly mediocre songs about being good looking in the desert, good looking driving around LA, good looking on the street, and good looking while asking questions like "Should I stay or go? I really want to know / Would I lose or win if I try and love again?" I don't know about the latter part of your inquiry, that's your business and good luck to you. As for the second part, go. Please go away. DM
Fleetwood Mac – Rumours (1977)
I was on a five-hour road trip with two of my best mates, and we decided to spend it doing something that felt vaguely productive: listening, front to back, to albums considered some of the greatest ever made. We started with MJ’s 'Thriller' - brilliant, pretty much faultless, bar perhaps that eye-rollingly saccharine McCartney duet. Then 'The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill': beautiful, soulful, genuinely sublime. So when we arrived at Fleetwood Mac’s 'Rumours' we were expecting our lives to be changed. They sadly weren’t. That isn’t to say 'Rumours' is bad. It’s often excellent. 'Dreams' is arguably one of the greatest songs ever recorded; 'Go Your Own Way' remains an absolute bop; and the iconic bassline and euphoric release of 'The Chain' is top notch. But taken as a whole, the album left all three of us strangely unmoved. Remove all the relationship drama and mythology attached to it and what remains is often remarkably safe, polished, and occasionally beige. 'Second Hand News' is a strangely forgettable opener; 'Don’t Stop' is irritatingly chirpy; and 'Oh Daddy' is frankly a bit of a snooze. In the days after I listened to 'Tusk' and 'Tango in the Night', two of the band's later albums, and both struck me as more adventurous and interesting. _'_Rumours'has a handful of perfect songs, but it’s by no means a perfect album. TF
Pink Floyd - The Wall (1979)
God help me, I love a concept album and Pink Floyd rarely disappointed in this regard. However, their 1979 rock opera – while a towering achievement narratively speaking – is a listening experience that never resonated with me. Put bluntly: it bored me to death whilst depressing me at the same time. Granted, the double-album is meant to be punishing, mirroring the themes of abandonment and isolation wished for by chief architect and gloom meister general Roger Waters. However, 'The Wall' always felt bloated, replete with heavy-handed metaphors and more filler than any other album they'd released until then. 'Another Brick in the Wall, Part 2', 'Hey You' and 'Comfortably Numb' are gems, there's no doubt about that - but that's three standouts in a comfortably plump 26-song slog of a tracklist. And when you look back at the band's discography, every concept album that preceded 'The Wall' continues to surpass it. Give me 'The Dark Side of the Moon' (the original, not that trash version Waters put out three years ago), 'Wish You Were Here' and 'Animals' any day of the week over this one. DM
AC/DC - Back In Black (1980)
Here's the thing with AC/DC... Every tedious riff in their repetive song collection sticks to the same ear-bleedingly naff blue-collar rock formula - so much so that each "hit" sounds completely indistinguishable from the one that preceded it. You could play me tracks from 'Back In Black', 'Highway To Hell' or any of their other 16 albums (yes, I counted), and I'd stare at you blankly like a deflated basset hound yearning for the sweet release of variety. Or tinnitus. Either will do. The defense rests. Your witness. DM
Prince – Purple Rain (1984)
An Oscar. Two Grammys. A No. 1 album that spent 24 weeks atop the Billboard 200. More than 25 million copies sold worldwide. 'Purple Rain' has been canonised as one of the defining albums of the 1980s. And I understand why. Prince was an absurdly talented musician - guitarist, pianist, producer, songwriter, vocalist - and the sheer amount of creativity and craft on display is difficult to deny. But perhaps that’s the problem: 'Purple Rain' sometimes feels like Prince desperately trying to prove he can do everything at once. Guitar solos, key changes, falsetto runs - every song seems determined to throw the entire Prince toolbox at you. The result can be exhilarating like the ending of 'The Beautiful Ones', but it can also feel wildly overcooked, overly-theatrical and exhausting. And lyrically, the album can be surprisingly… thin. For all the hype surrounding Prince as a genius songwriter, some of his stuff like on 'Take Me With U’ is pretty disposable. And as for the title track, yes, it's a classic, no argument there. But does it really need to run for 8 minutes and 41 seconds? I've got places to be, Prince. Things to do! TF
The Smiths – The Queen Is Dead (1986)
I’ll preface this by saying that, unlike Zooey Deschanel in (500) Days of Summer, I personally do not “love The Smiths.” In fact, I think the “For Britain” badge-wearing Morrissey is a whiny, pitchless, pompous moron, so don't expect neutrality here. 'The Queen Is Dead' is one of those albums that seems contractually obliged to appear on every “Greatest Albums of All Time” list, and is regularly hailed as The Smiths’ masterpiece. And I get some of the hype. Johnny Marr’s guitar work is immaculate, the band sounds sharp throughout, the opening track is electric and 'There Is a Light That Never Goes Out' is, dare I say, charmingly catchy. But there are also some absolute stinkers on this thing. 'Frankly, Mr. Shankly' is a twee, irritating novelty song that I cannot understand anyone willingly putting on twice, while 'Vicar in a Tutu' is an even more baffling detour. Even 'Some Girls Are Bigger Than Others' feels like an oddly limp way to close what is supposedly a classic. Maybe I'm missing something. Or maybe Morrissey's voice and ego have just worn me down. Either way - masterpiece? Not convinced. TF
Oasis – Definitely Maybe (1994)
While I wouldn't brazenly affirm that Oasis as a whole is overrated, I will die on the following hill: their debut album is held to unreasonably high regard. Yes, 'Definitely Maybe' was the soundtrack to a new grunge-ending / Britpop striggering era, but the hype around it ever since its release has been exhausting. The singles are catchy, and no one is denying Noel Gallagher's knack for a singalong chorus; but the rest is filler, with lyrics which are either uninspired or the work of someone operating on a full nappy. As for Liam's efforts, there's a reason why his delivery of lines "Toniiiiiiiight I'm a rock 'n' roll staaaar" and "Sun-sheeeee-iiiiiii-ne" have been memed to death. Far from biblical, r'kid. Ultimately, Oasis is a terrific singles band; but when it comes to cohesive albums, the only LP which truly works as a consistent whole was - somewhat ironically - their B-side compilation 'The Masterplan', which remains their best release. As much as I'm aware of my own hang-ups when it comes to the parodical swagger of certain 'Madferit' Oasis fans, you can deify them all you want but two things remain true: 1) As good as they can be, they weren't the saviours of British rock'n'roll; and 2) Their contemporaries Blur, Pulp and Super Furry Animals were significantly more innovative. Fight me. DM
Kanye West – Graduation (2007)
It’s easy to dunk on Ye these days. The man has said some heinous things – so heinous that he was banned from performing in most of Europe. Now, of course, he’s set to take the stage in Russia, which only reinforces his painful spiral into pariah status. Separate the art from the artist, though, and we can appreciate that West’s run of albums is almost unrivalled in contemporary hip-hop. His first six albums were groundbreaking in their own ways. But 'Graduation' isn’t the pop-rap masterpiece it’s hailed to be. Released in 2007, it was engineered for arenas, with huge hooks, gleaming synths and U2-level production. Yes, it helped move mainstream hip-hop toward a more melodic and experimental realm, but 'Graduation' seems shallow and meaningless in comparison to the grander statements Ye made with 'My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy' or 'Yeezus'. It’s more a triumph of commercial instinct than artistic revelation. For an artist who has always been at his best when he’s being unpredictable – even, perhaps unfortunately, now – 'Graduation' is surprisingly conventional. CS
Arcade Fire – The Suburbs (2010)
A decade before frontman Win Butler was outed as a manipulative creep, Arcade Fire reached previously unreached heights for an indie band. In 2011, The Suburbs scored a surprise Grammy win for Album of the Year. Arcade Fire had made it. The album is a 64-minute paean to lost youth and white-bread suburban ennui, full of smooth hooks, mid-tempo guitars and open-road anthems. It’s not a bad listen, if you’re able to divorce Butler’s allegations of sexual misconduct from the experience. In fact, it’s largely enjoyable. But Album of the Year was a stretch then and more of one now. Lyrics like “Rococo, rococo, rococo / Oh, they’re breaking my heart” and “I feel like I’ve been living in / A city with no children in it” are comically overwritten (or underwritten, depending on your perspective). And compared with today’s ambient despair, the schlocky air of suburban angst and coming-of-age theme seem ridiculous in retrospect. CS
Daft Punk - Random Access Memories (2013)
Hailed as a triumphant comeback album after the disappointing 'Human After All' (2005), Daft Punk's fourth and final LP paid tribute to 70s and 80s music – specifically disco and funk. The line-up of collaborators was impressive, with the French electro pioneers recruiting Giorgio Moroder, Pharrell Williams, Nile Rodgers and Julian Casablancas for what was to be their swansong. While it came out to universal acclaim, I'd argue that even if the sonic nostalgia blast was welcome in the moment and their ubiquitous single 'Get Lucky' was inescapably good, 'Random Access Memories' still gets far too much praise. When listening to the Grammy winning LP from start to finish, its pacing isn't as great as you remember, a lot of tracks feel indulgent, and it's... well, clumsy. I suspect the marketing team in charge of the album's rollout is partly responsible for its lingering acclaim, as fans will remember a teaser campaign which worked wonders. But when push comes to shove, 'RAM' may not be le plus faible in the robotic duo's discography, but it is far from their chef-d'oeuvre. Don't get me started on that dire drumless 2023 re-release, which was a complete waste of time. DM
Taylor Swift – Folklore (2020)
When Taylor Swift released 'folklore', I was editing a plucky city magazine in Bangkok and not having a great time of it. About five songs into the swirling 16-track album, I remember telling myself: “This is why the editing profession exists.” Look, Swift doesn’t need my praise for her prowess as a songwriter. She has 14 Grammys and about a billion US dollars to prove her merits. Her canon is largely great. But 'folklore' was the first sign that the ego was perhaps outgrowing the artist. The pivot to piano-driven sweater-weather music was a welcome change and hardly a surprise, considering Swift worked with The National’s Aaron Dessner. But was Dessner the editor she needed? Could anyone edit her? When the album is good ('this is me trying'), it’s very good. When it’s not ('betty', 'illicit affairs'), you wish someone had stepped in to propose some surgical cuts. Looking back on it, 'folklore' marked a turning point for Swift. Since then, her once sharp lyricism has become head-scratching (see: 'Fortnight' and 'epiphany'), and her albums have become increasingly self-indulgent and bloated. CS
There we have it. Heroic takedowns or utter blasphemy? Feel free to get in touch. Just don't bother if you're defending the Eagles. Life's too short.

The British government has separately said it plans to introduce a broader package of measures in the coming weeks, including sanctions against individuals involved in what it described as illegal settlement expansion.

Experts urge calm after 170 microearthquakes off Istanbul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
05:35:29 UTC
14:35:29 KST

More than 170 microearthquakes have been detected around the Princes’ Islands fault in the Marmara Sea since Aug. 18, but experts said the cluster alone was not evidence of an imminent major earthquake.
The strongest tremor, with a magnitude of 3.2, struck south of the islands on Aug. 19.
Most of the activity was concentrated near a limited section of the fault, according to Türkiye’s Disaster and Emergency Management Presidency (AFAD).
Bahadır Aktuğ, a member of AFAD’s Earthquake Science Board and a geophysics professor at Ankara University, said the activity covered only about seven kilometers of the 44-kilometer fault.
The tremors showed no migration in depth or along the fault that would indicate progressive triggering, he said, adding that the data did not reveal a pattern pointing to a larger earthquake.
Board member Şükrü Ersoy said faults can periodically produce clusters of small tremors and warned that predicting an immediate large earthquake from such activity was speculative.
“The public has no reason to panic,” Ersoy said.
“What we should be discussing is not when faults will rupture, but how prepared our building stock is for a possible earthquake.”
In its own catalogue, Kandilli Observatory and Earthquake Research Institute said it located 117 earthquakes with magnitudes ranging from 0.7 to 3.1 within a 20-kilometer radius south of the islands between 6 a.m. on Aug. 18 and 1 p.m. on Aug. 20.
Kandilli described the activity as a microearthquake sequence clustered in time and space, noting that such sequences occasionally occur in active tectonic regions. It said the area was being monitored around the clock.
